en: The Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras.
Oṃ.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. First Chapter:
One who knows the meaning effects the manifestation of that meaning through speech and stainless words.
Out of compassion for suffering beings, being absorbed in that [compassion] in order to cross over suffering,
he demonstrates to those beings who are traveling upon it the unsurpassed, fivefold, and coherent progression of the meaning of the Dharma— the method taught through the Supreme Vehicle. (Msa 1.1)
"One who knows the meaning performs the manifestation of the meaning... [and so forth]. Starting from the section on the Treasury (*koṣa*), who is it that adorns?
One who knows the meaning.
What does he adorn? He adorns the ornament; he performs the manifestation of the meaning.
"By what? By means of pure speech and words.
"Pure speech" refers to [speech that is] clear and so forth; "by pure words" means by those that are appropriate and coherent—this is the detailed explanation.
For indeed, without speech, words, and phonemes, it is impossible to manifest the meaning.

For what purpose? For the sake of crossing over suffering. Because he is compassionate toward suffering beings, he is "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*). That is to say, because of his compassion (*kāruṇya*) for suffering beings, he is "consisting of compassion" (*kāruṇyamaya*), being permeated by it. Whose ornament does he create?
Of the Dharma, in which the method of teaching the Supreme Vehicle is set forth— that is, of that Dharma in which the method of the Supreme Vehicle is taught—
in what does it adorn?
"Among beings who are headed for that"—this is a locative of purpose (*nimitta-saptamī*); the meaning is "for the sake of those beings who are headed for the Mahāyāna.
How many kinds of ornament does it create?
It is fivefold;
demonstrating the fivefold attainment of meaning that is both coherent and unsurpassed: "coherent" means logically consistent.
"Having reached the unsurpassed state" means having reached the vehicle of unsurpassed gnosis.
He now demonstrates this fivefold realization of the meaning with the second verse:
"Like gold that has been fashioned, or like a lotus in full bloom..."
Like well-prepared, excellent food being enjoyed by those afflicted by hunger;
like a well-known fine manuscript, or like a casket of jewels containing pearls.
That Dharma, when revealed here, bestows the highest joy.

By this verse, through five similes, that Dharma is taught with reference to five kinds of objects: that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), that which is to be explained (*vyutpādya*), that which is conceivable (*cintya*), that which is inconceivable (*acintya*), and that which is perfected (*pariniṣpanna*)— the latter being the nature of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*), to be personally realized for the sake of direct realization (*pratyātmavedanīya*).
Thus, when elucidated by this *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, it inspires supreme joy, like gold that has been fashioned into a vessel and so forth.
The third verse is intended to resolve the objection: "Since that Dharma is already endowed with qualities by its very nature, how can it be further adorned?"
Just as a reflection endowed with the qualities of ornaments and natural beauty, when appearing in a mirror, produces exceptional joy in people by virtue of being seen;
so too does the Dharma, though it is always endowed with the qualities of well-spoken nature.
But the meaning that has been analyzed produces a distinguished satisfaction for the virtuous here in this world.
What does this demonstrate? Just as a reflection, which is inherently virtuous due to its adornment, produces a particularly intense joy when seen in a mirror,
so too this Dharma, though already endowed with qualities by its very nature through well-spoken words, generates a distinguished satisfaction when its meaning is constantly analyzed.
Because it produces a particular satisfaction for the wise, it becomes as if adorned.
Beyond this, he shows three kinds of benefits regarding that Dharma through three verses, in order to generate respect:
"Just like a medicine that is pungent when smelled but sweet in taste, so too is it."
The Dharma is established as twofold; it should be understood according to the letter and according to the meaning.
This Dharma is like a king, difficult to propitiate, being vast, profound, and deep;
yet, when propitiated, it likewise becomes the bestower of the wealth of excellent qualities.
Just as a noble gem of priceless value does not satisfy those who lack the power of discernment,
so too this Dharma satisfies the ignorant through its very opposite.
The benefit is threefold:
its being the cause for the abandonment of obscurations, by way of being like medicine;
The "establishment of the two" refers to the establishment of the letter and the meaning.

Its being the cause of mastery is due to its bestowing sovereignty through extraordinary qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), by virtue of which it is like a king. And its being the cause for the enjoyment of the noble ones (*ārya*) is due to its being like a precious, priceless jewel of noble birth.
One should understand that the discerning person is the noble person (*āryajana*).

Regarding the misconception that "this Mahāyāna is certainly not the word of the Buddha; how then could it possess such benefits?", there is a verse concerning the analysis of the reasons intended to establish its status as the word of the Buddha.
Because it was not prophesied at the beginning, because it arose simultaneously, because it is beyond the sphere [of worldly perception], because it is established,
because it does not exist in the presence or absence [of conditions], because it is the antidote, and because it is other than the literal word.

Because it was not prophesied at the beginning: if this [Mahāyāna] were produced later by someone as an obstacle to the True Dharma, why did the Blessed One not prophesy it at the outset, as he did regarding future dangers?

Because of its simultaneous occurrence: the activity of the Mahāyāna is observed to have occurred at the same time as the Śrāvakayāna, not afterwards; how, then, can it be known that this is not the word of the Buddha?
Because this Dharma is so vast and profound, it is not within the domain of logicians;
since no such [teachings] are found in the treatises of the non-Buddhist outsiders,
it is not logical that this was spoken by others.
Even when it is being recited, because there is no conviction in it, [the opponent's position] is not established; or,
if it was spoken after another had awakened to it through direct realization,
then its status as the word of the Buddha is established.
He alone is a Buddha who, having attained full awakening, speaks thus:

"If the Mahāyāna exists as something [distinct] in terms of the existence or non-existence of entities, then its existence is established as the word of the Buddha, because there is no other Mahāyāna apart from this.
Alternatively, if it does not exist, then in its absence, the Śrāvakayāna would also not exist."

It is not tenable to claim that the Śrāvakayāna is the word of the Buddha while the Mahāyāna is not; for without the Buddhayāna, Buddhas would not arise. Furthermore, because it serves as an antidote, the Mahāyāna—when cultivated—becomes the antidote to the afflictions by virtue of being the basis for all non-conceptual gnosis; therefore, it is the word of the Buddha.

Because the literal expression is different, its meaning is not according to the literal expression; therefore, this should not be understood as a non-Buddha-word by following the literal meaning. Regarding what was said previously—that there was no prophecy because of lack of application—someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy this for the future due to a lack of effort; hence, there is a verse concerning the impossibility of such indifference: [Verse: If he were indifferent, he would be like a fool; if he had no knowledge, he would be like a common person. If he had no power, he would be like a weakling; thus, his indifference is not tenable. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were indifferent toward the future, he would be like a fool. If he lacked knowledge of it, he would be like an ordinary person. If he lacked the power to prophesy it, he would be like one who is weak. Therefore, his indifference is not logically consistent. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was weary of answering questions. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were weary of answering questions, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were weary of answering questions, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with other matters. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with other matters, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with other matters, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with teaching the Dharma. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with teaching the Dharma, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with teaching the Dharma, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with meditative concentration. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with meditative concentration, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with meditative concentration, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with the work of maturing sentient beings. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with maturing beings, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with maturing sentient beings, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with the work of purifying the buddha-field. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with purifying the field, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with purifying the buddha-field, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with the work of gathering a retinue. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with gathering a retinue, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with gathering a retinue, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with the work of ripening the roots of merit of sentient beings. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with ripening merits, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with ripening the roots of merit of sentient beings, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with the work of establishing sentient beings in the three vehicles. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with establishing beings in the vehicles, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with establishing sentient beings in the three vehicles, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with the work of subduing Māra. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with subduing Māra, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with subduing Māra, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with the work of manifesting parinirvāṇa. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with manifesting nirvāṇa, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with manifesting parinirvāṇa, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there was no prophecy because of the absence of a question," someone might think that the Blessed One did not prophesy the future because he was occupied with the work of turning the wheel of the Dharma. To refute this, there is another verse: [Verse: If he were occupied with turning the wheel, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like a common person. [Commentary: If the Blessed One were occupied with turning the wheel of the Dharma, he would be like a worldly man. If he were not omniscient, he would be like an ordinary person. Therefore, these two reasons are also untenable. The Buddhas possess direct vision and are the protectors of the teaching;
since their knowledge is unobstructed regarding all things, it is not fitting for them to remain indifferent.
What does this demonstrate?
For three reasons, it is not appropriate for the Buddha to remain indifferent toward a great future affliction of the Teaching:
because the Buddhas' knowledge functions effortlessly; because they possess direct vision; and because they exert effort in the protection of the Teaching.

And because of the power of knowing the future, his knowledge is unimpeded across all times. Regarding what was stated—that [the Śrāvaka vehicle] is absent in both existence and non-existence—it might occur to someone that this very Śrāvaka vehicle is the Mahāyāna, and that by means of it alone one attains great enlightenment (mahābodhi). Therefore, there is a verse concerning the impossibility of the Śrāvaka vehicle being the Mahāyāna:
Because of incompleteness, contradiction, lack of skillful means, and likewise because of the absence of instruction, this which is called the Mahāyāna Dharma is not the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Because the instruction for the benefit of others is incomplete;
for in the Śrāvaka vehicle, no benefit for others is taught, since it teaches only the means for the disciples' own weariness with existence, dispassion, and liberation.
Furthermore, that which is taught for one's own benefit cannot constitute the benefit of others when it is being taught to them.

Because it is contradictory. For when another person is enjoined toward their own goal, they apply themselves solely to that very goal; thus, it is a contradiction to say that one who is engaged for the sake of their own parinirvāṇa will realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, it is not possible for one to become a Buddha by striving for enlightenment through the Śrāvaka vehicle alone over a long period of time.
Because it is not the means.

For the Śrāvaka vehicle is not the means for Buddhahood; and one does not attain the desired goal even by applying oneself for a long time through what is not the means, just as one cannot obtain milk from a horn or from a bellows.
Furthermore, even if there were another way taught here as to how a bodhisattva should practice,
since such an instruction is not found [in this vehicle], the Śrāvakayāna itself cannot be the Mahāyāna;
for no such instruction is to be found within it.
The Śrāvakayāna and the Mahāyāna are indeed mutually contradictory; regarding this mutual contradiction, there is a verse:
"Because of the contradiction in intention, instruction, application, support, and time, that which is inferior is truly inferior. (MSA 1.10)
How is it contradictory? It is contradictory by way of five contradictions:
contradiction of intention, instruction, application, support, and time.

For in the Śrāvakayāna, the intention is solely for one's own parinirvāṇa; the instruction is for that purpose alone; the application is for that purpose alone; and the support consisting of the accumulation of merit and knowledge is limited.
Furthermore, the attainment of that goal occurs in a short time, even in as little as three lifetimes.
In the Mahāyāna, however, everything is the opposite.
Therefore, because they are mutually contradictory, whatever vehicle is inferior is indeed inferior;
it cannot be the Mahāyāna.
This is the characteristic of the Buddha’s word: that which enters into the Sūtras, is seen in the Vinaya, and does not contradict the nature of reality (dharmatā).
The Mahāyāna is not like that, because it teaches the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of all phenomena.
Therefore, someone might think, "It is not the word of the Buddha. To address this, there is a verse concerning the non-contradiction with the [defining] characteristics.
Because it is presented within its own [scriptures], because it is seen in its own Vinaya,
and because of its vastness and profundity, the nature of reality (dharmatā) is indeed not contradictory.
What does this verse demonstrate?
It shows that this [teaching] indeed descends into its own Mahāyāna sūtra, and the discipline for one's own afflictions is seen therein.
That which is called the affliction of bodhisattvas in the Mahāyāna is indeed conceptual construction, for bodhisattvas are characterized by both vastness and profundity.

It does not contradict the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), for such is indeed the nature of reality for the attainment of great enlightenment; therefore, there is no contradiction with the defining characteristics.
Since it was stated that [the Buddha] is beyond the range [of the intellect], there is a verse regarding the impossibility of being within the range of speculative reasoning (*tarka*).
Reasoning is considered to be dependent, uncertain, non-pervasive, conventional, subject to weariness, and based on the intellect of the foolish; therefore, that [ultimate reality] is not its object.
For reasoning (*tarka*), which relies on that which has not yet seen the truth, is dependent upon scripture;
it is uncertain, because one may arrive at a different understanding at another time;
and it is non-pervasive, as its object is not the entirety of all that is knowable.
Furthermore, it has conventional truth as its object and not ultimate truth as its object;
and it is characterized by weariness because its eloquence comes to an end.
The Mahāyāna, however, is non-dependent and so on, up to being free from weariness.

Because of the instructions in numerous sūtras such as the *Śatasāhasrikā*, this is not an object of ratiocination (*tarka*). It has been stated that because it is not a means (*anupāya*), Buddhahood is not attained through the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Now, as for how the Mahāyāna is appropriate as a means (*upāya*), there is this verse regarding its fitness as a means: "Through its vastness and its profundity, there is maturation and non-conceptuality; because both are taught herein, it is the unsurpassed means. (MSA 1.13)
What does this verse demonstrate?
Through the teaching of the magnificence of power, there is the maturation of sentient beings, because they strive through their resolute belief in that power.
Through the teaching of profundity, there is non-conceptualization.

Therefore, the teaching of these two in this Mahāyāna is the means for unsurpassed gnosis; for by means of them, respectively, sentient beings are brought to maturity and one's own Buddha-qualities are brought to maturity.
Furthermore, for those who tremble at this, there is a verse concerning the fault of trembling where there is no basis for it, serving as the reason [for such a warning]:
"That groundless trembling becomes a cause of burning for the worlds for a long time, because it gives rise to a great mass of demerit."
One who lacks the spiritual lineage, lacks good friends, lacks cultivated intellect, and has not previously accumulated mental merit—
such a person, being afraid of this Dharma, falls away from the great benefit here.
Fear where there is no ground for fear is "fear of the groundless";
it results in burning in the miserable states (apāya).
What is the reason?
Because it produces a great mass of demerit;
"for how long a time? means for a long period.
Such is the subsequent disadvantage.
This demonstrates by what cause and for how long [the fear arises]. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "but when the cause exists," he shows the fourfold cause for fear:

his spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is lacking, or he lacks a virtuous friend (*sanmitra*), or his intellect is unrefined regarding the nature of the Mahāyāna Dharma, or he has not previously accumulated merit (*śubha*).
"One falls from a great benefit" means from the benefit that consists of the equipment for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi-saṃbhāra*). By this,
he demonstrates another disadvantage arising from the loss of what has not yet been attained.
The cause of fear has been explained; now the cause of fearlessness must be stated. Regarding this state of fearlessness, there is a verse:
"Because of the absence of anything other than that, because of its supreme profundity, and because of its conformity..."

Because it is told in various ways, because it is connected with constant discourse from many perspectives, because its meaning does not correspond exactly to the literal expression, and because the intention regarding the Blessed One is exceedingly profound,
the wise do not experience fear toward this Dharma when they investigate its source.
"Because of the non-existence of anything other than that" means because there is no Mahāyāna other than that [Śrāvakayāna].
Otherwise, if the Śrāvakayāna itself were the Mahāyāna, there would be no other [vehicle] such as the Śrāvaka or the Pratyekabuddha.
For indeed, all would become Buddhas;
and because of the supreme profundity [of the path],
and because they follow the path of the knowledge of the Omniscient One, it proceeds simultaneously [for all].
Because it is an exposition of the manifold;
for here the manifold path of the assembly is expounded, and not emptiness alone.
Therefore, this must be intentional;

because it is connected with constant discourse, and because emptiness is taught here in many ways and repeatedly through numerous synonyms in those various sūtras, there must be a great purpose in this.
Otherwise, it would have been merely a negation of what was previously honored.
Since the meaning is not according to the literal expression, and its meaning is not as it sounds, fear on this account is also not appropriate.

Furthermore, because the nature of the Blessed One is exceedingly profound, and the nature of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and difficult to comprehend, we should not be afraid due to our lack of understanding of it.
Thus, through such thorough investigation, fear does not arise for the wise.
Regarding the fact that [this reality] is the domain of knowledge that has deeply penetrated, there is this verse:
"In this context, the mental attention which first arises in dependence upon what has been heard..."
From mental attention arises knowledge whose object is the meaning of reality;

from that, the attainment of the Dharma arises, and from that, when the mind is devoted to it, there occurs direct personal realization. How could such certainty exist in the absence of that [attainment]?
Based on what has been heard, there first arises mental attention that is "founded" (yoniśas)—this is the meaning.
From founded mental attention, there arises knowledge whose object is the reality of things, namely supramundane right view;
from that, there is the attainment of the Dharma which is its fruit.
Then, when that [state] has been reached, the cognition of the knowledge of liberation arises.
Thus, when that cognition exists within oneself,
how could there be this determination or certainty that "this is not the word of the Buddha" in its absence?
Regarding the state of being a ground for fearlessness, there is this verse:

"I am not an enlightened one, nor am I a knower of the profound; what is profound in the Buddha’s teaching that is beyond the reach of logic? And why should liberation belong only to those who know the profound meaning? This [objection] is a ground for fear, yet it is not tenable. (MSA 1.17)
If it is argued that "I am not the one who can understand this" is a ground for fear,
that is not tenable.
Furthermore, the notion that even the Buddha is not a knower of the profound meaning of reality, and thus how could he teach what is profound— this is a ground for fear;
however, that is incorrect.
Now, as for the ground for fear that [the Dharma] is profound and therefore inaccessible to ratiocination—
that is not tenable.
Furthermore, as for the ground for fear that liberation belongs only to those who know the profound meaning and not to logicians— [that too is not tenable].
That is not tenable.
Regarding the proof of that very lack of resolute conviction (*anadhimukti*), there is this verse:
"For one who has inferior resolute conviction, whose element is extremely base, and who is surrounded by inferior companions..."
If there is no resolute faith in this Dharma so well taught in its vastness and profundity, [then one's lack of success] is established.
For one whose inclination (*adhimukti*) is inferior or excessive, and from whom a corresponding inferior realm (*dhātu*) has emerged through the cultivation of the *ālayavijñāna*,

who is surrounded by companions of similar inclination and realm— if such a person lacks inclination toward this Mahāyāna Dharma so well-taught in its vastness and profundity, [then how could they have it]?
Therefore, it is established that this Mahāyāna is supreme.
Regarding the impropriety of rejecting sūtras not yet heard, there is this verse:
"For one who, having attained intelligence by following what has been heard, shows contempt for what has not been heard,"
When the sacred teachings are diverse and immeasurable, how can a fool reach certainty regarding what remains?
Granted that there may be no conviction regarding those sūtras not yet heard, yet a blanket rejection of them without distinction is not reasonable.

For it is precisely by following what has been heard that one attains intelligence; how then can that fool, who shows contempt for what he has heard, reach the certainty that "this is not the word of the Buddha" when there remains an abundance of diverse and immeasurable scripture?
For he possesses no power other than what is heard; therefore, it is not reasonable to reject [the teaching] without having heard it.
Furthermore, that which has been heard must be reflected upon properly (*yoniśas*), not improperly; thus, there is a verse regarding the fault of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*):
"When one conceptualizes the meaning according to the literal expression, one's own conviction leads to the loss of wisdom."
He rejects the well-expounded nature [of the Dharma], incurs harm, and becomes as if hostile toward the Dharma—or indeed, he becomes hostile. (MSA 1.20)

"One who relies on their own [judgment]" (*svapratyaya*) refers to one who clings to their own views and does not seek the meaning from others, such as from those possessing higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).

"One's intelligence suffers loss" means that, due to the failure to attain and the abandonment of knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), one rejects the well-expounded nature of the Dharma; and on that account, through the power of demerit (*apuṇya*), one incurs ruin.
Furthermore, hostility toward the Dharma and the obscuration [of it] constitute karma conducive to the destruction of the Dharma; this is the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) in this context.
Since it is not appropriate to feel resentment even toward one who fails to understand the meaning correctly or as it was spoken, there is this verse regarding the impropriety of resentment:

"Hostility of mind is inherently corrupt; it is indeed improper even toward that which is not in accordance with the literal expression, let alone toward one who has fallen into doubt regarding the Dharma. Therefore, equanimity alone is better, for it is free from fault. (MSA 1.21)
"Corrupt by nature" means inherently blameworthy (*prakṛtisāvadya*).
Therefore, equanimity alone is better.
Why?
For that [non-dual nature] is indeed faultless,
whereas resistance is faulty.
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Establishment of the Mahāyāna," in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The second chapter: A summary verse on the excellence of going for refuge.

Indeed, he who has gone for refuge to the Jewels in this vehicle should be known as the supreme refuge among all those who have gone for refuge, distinguished by fourfold aspects of meaning through the distinctions of universality, acceptance, realization, and mastery. (MSA 2.1)
"He alone is the supreme refuge for those who have gone for refuge.
For what reason?
Because of the distinction of the fourfold nature of the object.

The fourfold meaning should be understood through the distinctions of being all-pervasive, acceptance, realization, and mastery: the all-pervasive meaning, the meaning of acceptance, [the meaning of realization, and the meaning of mastery].
The meaning of realization; the meaning of overcoming. These, moreover, will be explained further on.
Nevertheless, because [the path] for those who have gone for refuge here involves many difficult tasks, some do not venture forth. There is a verse:
Because this resolve is difficult at the outset and hard to accomplish even in thousands of aeons;
and because, once accomplished, it has the great purpose of establishing the welfare of sentient beings—therefore, the supreme vehicle is the foremost object of refuge here. (MSA 2.2)
By this, he shows that his resolve to go for refuge is a cause of fame due to its excellence in both aspiration and practice;
it is of great significance because of the excellence of the attainment of its fruit.
There is now a verse concerning the previously mentioned all-pervading meaning.
He who has set out to deliver all sentient beings,
who is endowed with skill in the vehicle and all-pervading wisdom,
and who is of one single flavor regarding both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra— [he is of one single flavor in the peace of cyclic existence].
For this wise one is thus to be known as all-pervading.

By this, the fourfold meaning of being all-pervasive—namely, that which is non-conventional and that which is not acquired through attainment—is explained; thus, the manifestation [of consciousness] has the characteristic of differentiation by way of the distinction between the gross and the subtle.
(MSA_Bagchi 10)
There is a verse concerning the distinction of the practice of going for refuge:

Having gone to this refuge of great purpose, he attains an immeasurable increase in the multitude of his virtues; he vibrates throughout this world with an intention of compassion and spreads the incomparable, great Dharma of the Noble Ones. (MSA 2.4)
In this context, he demonstrates the great significance of taking refuge through the practice of the welfare of oneself and others.
Furthermore, the practice for one’s own welfare is of many kinds, consisting in the increase of immeasurable qualities.
This immeasurability should be understood as being beyond the scope of logic, number, and time.
For that excellence of qualities is not to be measured by logic, nor by number, nor by time, because it is ultimate;
it is the realization of the welfare of others through both intention—the radiance of compassion—and application—the propagation of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
For the Mahāyāna is indeed the Dharma of those with noble vision.
The second chapter, on Taking Refuge, in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra.
The third chapter: A summary verse on the distinctions of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
The supremacy of beings, its intrinsic nature, its characteristic marks, the distinctions of the lineage,
the disadvantages, the benefits, and the two kinds of similes— these are fourfold.

By this, the following divisions are summarized: the existence of the lineage (*gotra*), its preeminence, its intrinsic nature, its signs, its classifications, its defects, its benefits, and its twofold analogy.
Each of these divisions is fourfold.
This is the verse concerning the analysis of the existence of the lineage.

The existence of the spiritual lineage (gotra) is established through the distinctions among elements (dhātu), inclinations (adhimukti), and practices (pratipatti), as well as through the observation of differences in their results.
Because sentient beings possess diverse elements (*nānādhātukatva*), there is an immeasurable differentiation of elements, as stated in the *Akṣarāśisūtra*.
Therefore, such a differentiation of elements should also be understood to exist;
thus, there is a distinction of lineages (*gotrabheda*) within the three vehicles (*yānatraya*).
A difference in the inclinations of sentient beings is also observed;
from the very beginning, a certain person has an inclination toward one specific vehicle or another.
This would not be possible without a difference in their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

Furthermore, even when resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) has been produced through the power of conditions, a difference in practice is observed: some become capable of carrying it through to the end, while others do not; this would not be possible without a distinction in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Moreover, a difference in the results is observed—namely, inferior, middling, and superior enlightenments (*bodhi*);
this too would not exist without a distinction in the spiritual lineage, because the fruit conforms to its seed.
Regarding the analysis of preeminence, there is this verse:
"Because it is the cause of virtue that is intense, universal, of great purpose, and inexhaustible, the preeminence of the lineage (gotra) is established. (MSA 3.3)
Here, he demonstrates the preeminence of the lineage (*gotra*) by way of its fourfold nature as a causal sign (*nimitta*).
For that lineage is the causal sign for the excellence of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), and for their universality.
Regarding its great purpose and its inexhaustibility:
for the roots of virtue of the śrāvakas are not so exalted.
Nor are they all present,
because of the absence of the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and so forth;
nor are they of great significance, because they do not have the welfare of others as their purpose.
And they are not inexhaustible because they terminate in nirvāṇa without remainder.
Regarding the classification of their characteristics, there is this verse:
"By nature, it is both fully developed and the basis as well as that which is based upon it."
It should be understood as both existent and non-existent, in the sense that it carries one across [suffering] by means of its qualities.
By this, he shows the fourfold lineage (*gotra*):

that which exists in its natural state (*prakṛtistha*), that which is acquired (*samudānīta*), the nature of the basis (*āśrayasvabhāva*), and the nature of what is based upon it (*āśritasvabhāva*)— these being respectively as stated.

Furthermore, that [lineage] should be understood as existent by way of being a cause and non-existent by way of being a fruit; it is called a "lineage" (*gotra*) in the sense of "elevating qualities," because qualities emerge and arise from it.
Regarding the analysis of its signs, there is this verse:
"Compassion, resolute conviction, and patience [are the signs] from the initial application."
The noble lineage is also characterized by virtuous conduct.
There are four kinds of signs in the lineage of a bodhisattva:
compassion toward sentient beings from the very beginning of practice;
and resolute conviction in the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Patience is so called in the sense of endurance regarding difficult practices; and right conduct consists of the wholesome qualities comprised of the perfections. This is a verse concerning the analysis of their classifications.
The lineage is determinate or indeterminate, and it is either unshakable or indeed shakable by conditions;
this classification of the lineage is, in brief, fourfold.
In brief, the lineage (*gotra*) is of four kinds: determinate and indeterminate; each of these is, respectively, unshakable by conditions or shakable by them.
Regarding the analysis of its disadvantages, there is this verse:
"Habituation to the afflictions, bad friendship, deprivation, and dependence on others."
The disadvantage of the lineage (gotra) should be known, in brief, as being fourfold.
In brief, there are four kinds of disadvantages within the bodhisattva lineage by which one established in that lineage engages in non-virtues:
an abundance of afflictions and the lack of virtuous friends.
There is the impairment of resources and dependence on others.
Regarding the analysis of its benefits, there is this verse:
Going to the miserable realms after a long time, swift liberation there,
and the experience of slight suffering with a sense of urgency— this is the maturing of sentient beings.
There are four kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva in the spiritual lineage:
they go to the miserable realms only after a long time, and they are quickly liberated from them.
Having been reborn there, he experiences only mild suffering;
with a mind full of spiritual urgency and feeling compassion for the beings born there, he brings them to maturity.
Regarding the analogy of the great gold mine, there is this verse:
It should be known as being like a gold mine, the basis for immeasurable purity,
and the support for the powers of the conjunction with the stainlessness of primordial wisdom.
For the great gold mine is the basis for four kinds of gold: that which is abundant, and so forth.
It is luminous, stainless,
and workable.
By analogy with that, the lineage of the bodhisattva is the basis for immeasurable roots of virtue,
the basis for gnosis,
and the basis for attaining the purity from afflictions.
And it is the basis for the power of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth;
therefore, it should be understood as being like a great gold mine.
There is a verse regarding its resemblance to a great jewel mine:
It should be known as being like a precious jewel-gem because it is the cause of great enlightenment,
and because it is the basis for great wisdom, noble meditative concentration, and the welfare of great beings.
For a great jewel lineage is the basis for four kinds of jewels:
those that are of noble birth, endowed with color, endowed with shape, and endowed with size;
in the same way, the bodhisattva lineage should be understood.
Because it is the cause of great enlightenment, because it is the cause of great gnosis,
and because it is the cause of noble meditative concentration.
For concentration (*samādhi*) is the stabilization of the mind,
and it is so called because it serves as the cause for the maturation of great beings through the ripening of many sentient beings.
There is a verse concerning the classification of those who abide in the absence of lineage (*agotra*):
Some are exclusively devoted to misconduct; some have eradicated their wholesome qualities;
some possess no merit conducive to liberation; and some have inferior wholesome qualities or are even devoid of the causal potential for it.
In this context, one who does not possess the nature of parinirvāṇa is intended as being established in the absence of lineage (*agotra*).
And that, in brief, is of two kinds:
those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa for the time being, and those [who do not attain it] ultimately.
Those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa at that time are of four kinds:
those who are exclusively devoted to misconduct, and those whose roots of merit are severed.
One whose roots of merit do not partake of liberation, and one whose roots of merit are inferior and whose accumulations are incomplete;
whereas one whose nature is absolutely not subject to final nirvana lacks the cause, for him the very lineage of final nirvana does not exist.
Regarding the majesty of the lineage naturally nourished, there is this verse:

Even without understanding it, there arises a vast conviction toward the long-term Dharma— which is profound and sublime in its teaching and proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others— and one becomes capable of its thorough practice.
And that their attainment at the end becomes supreme in both respects should be known as resulting from the Bodhisattva’s nature endowed with qualities and from the fully nourished lineage (gotra).

When, regarding the vast Mahāyāna Dharma— which speaks of profundity and magnificence and is uttered for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others— one possesses extensive faith even without knowing its profound and magnificent meaning, and there is enthusiasm for practice and tirelessness, then at the conclusion there is the attainment of great awakening, which is the supreme among the two types of attainment.

The greatness of the bodhisattva lineage, which is by nature endowed with qualities and fully nourished, should be understood in this way. "Belonging to the two" refers to the two groups: worldly beings and śrāvakas;
"supreme" means distinguished.
Consequently, there is a verse regarding the distinction of the lineage (*gotra*):

Because it has as its fruit the growth of the tree of awakening with its vast qualities, and the attainment of the cessation of intense suffering and the acquisition of intense happiness, this exalted lineage (*samudagra-gotra*) exists for the sake of performing deeds that bring benefit and happiness to oneself and others. (MSA 3.13)
By this, the excellence of the root of the Bodhi-tree—which has as its fruit the welfare of oneself and others—is demonstrated through the lineage of the Bodhisattva.
Thus ends the third chapter, on Lineage, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The Fourth Chapter: A Verse on the Characteristics of the Arising of the Thought of Enlightenment.
The volition of Bodhisattvas— characterized by great enthusiasm, great undertakings, great purpose, and great success, and possessing a twofold aim— is the source of the mind.
It is characterized by great enthusiasm because of the exertion in applying remedies that are profound, difficult to perform, and long-lasting;
it is characterized by a great undertaking through the vigor of application according to the armor [of resolve];
and it is characterized by a great purpose because of its commitment to the welfare of oneself and others.
It is "of great success" because it brings about the attainment of great enlightenment.
Thus, these three kinds of qualities are illuminated:
the quality of human effort by two phrases, and the quality of purposeful activity and the quality of grasping the fruit by [the remaining] two.
It has a twofold purpose because it takes as its object the performance of benefit for great bodhisattvas;
thus, the production of the thought [of awakening] is said to possess three qualities and a twofold object.
There is a verse regarding the classification of the production of the thought [of awakening]:
This production of the thought of enlightenment is considered to be that of resolute belief, another is that of pure high resolve,
then that of maturation on the stages, and likewise that which is free from obstructions.
The production of the thought of enlightenment (cittotpāda) by bodhisattvas is fourfold:
that consisting of resolute belief (ādhimokṣika) on the stage of practice through resolute belief (adhimukticaryābhūmi);
and that consisting of pure high resolve (śuddhādhyāśayika) on the [first] seven stages (bhūmi).
That which is resultant occurs on the eighth stage and those above;
that which is unobstructed occurs on the Buddha-stage.
There are four verses concerning the determination of the production of the thought of enlightenment.

This [great compassion] is held to have compassion as its root; it always possesses the intention for the welfare of sentient beings, as well as resolute confidence in the Dharma and the objective support of seeking knowledge thereof.
This [practice] consists of aspiring for the higher [stages], being established in the restraint of ethical discipline, rousing oneself from the opposing factors, and enduring obstacles. (MSA 4.4)
This is the benefit of the increase of the virtuous; for it consists of merit and wisdom, and it is described as the departure through constant engagement with the perfections.
This determination regarding the production of the thought of enlightenment by Bodhisattvas should be understood as culminating in the [ten] stages, each according to its own specific application.
Thus is this determination:

what is the root of this fourfold production of the thought of enlightenment for bodhisattvas? What is its intention, what its resolve, what its object, what its vehicle, what its basis, what its disadvantage, what its benefit, and what its departure?
"What is its culmination?
He replied: "It has compassion as its root."
Having a constant intention for the welfare of sentient beings,
one has resolute faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma;
this is because, by way of seeking that knowledge, one takes that knowledge as one's object.
One whose vehicle is the aspiration for ever higher stages,
established in the vow of bodhisattva ethical discipline,
[should recognize] the obstacles as faults.
What, then, is its obstacle? It is the arousal or the toleration of the opposing factor, which is the mind directed toward other vehicles.
Its benefit is the increase of wholesome qualities consisting of merit and knowledge;
its departure is the constant practice of the perfections.
And it culminates in the respective stages because of the application to each stage;
for whichever stage one is applied to, its culmination occurs in that stage.
There is a verse regarding the conventional generation of the mind through formal undertaking:

The arising of the thought of enlightenment is said to have an unstable or stable emergence based on the power of a friend, the power of the cause, the power of the root, the power of hearing, the practice of virtue, or through the instruction of another. (MSA 4.7)

For that production of the thought [of awakening] which arises from the instruction of another and through the communication of another is called the conventional production through formal undertaking (*samādāna-sāṃketika*).
Furthermore, it occurs either through the power of a friend, by following a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*),
or through the power of the cause, by the capacity of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

It arises either from the nourishment of the lineage belonging to those who have transcended the roots of virtue; or through the power of hearing, because many generate the thought of awakening when various Dharma discourses are being taught;
or through the practice of the wholesome, by means of constant hearing, grasping, and retaining [the teachings] in this very life as if they were directly perceived.
Furthermore, that [arising of the thought of enlightenment] should be understood as having a weak emergence due to the power of friends,
whereas it has a firm emergence due to the power of the causes and so forth.
There are seven verses concerning the ultimate arising of the thought of enlightenment.
Having well served the Perfectly Awakened One and having fully accumulated the equipment of wisdom and merit,
his supremacy arises from the production of non-conceptual knowledge regarding all phenomena.
Because he has attained a mind of equanimity toward phenomena, sentient beings, their welfare, and supreme Buddhahood, his joy is preeminent.
Nobility of birth, enthusiasm therein, purity of intention, skillfulness in the remainder, and indeed deliverance—these are to be understood [as the characteristics of the lineage]. (MSA 4.10)
Born from the seed of faith in the Dharma and from the supreme mother of the perfections,
he is nurtured in the blissful womb consisting of meditative concentration, with compassion as his nursing mother.
Magnanimity is to be understood from the accomplishment of the twelve great vows;
enthusiasm is to be recognized by its lack of weariness despite hardships, length, and excess. (MSA 4.12)

The purity of intention (āśaya-śuddhi) should be understood as arising from the realization of near-enlightenment and from the attainment of the knowledge of its means; skillfulness (kauśalya), however, pertains to the other stages.
Departure is to be understood through attention according to its established order,
through the knowledge that it is a mental construction, and through the non-conceptualization of that very [construction]. (MSA 4.14)

By the first verse, he demonstrates the ultimate nature of the production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) through its distinctions of instruction, practice, and realization. And that ultimate production of the thought of awakening occurs on the stage called "The Joyous" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);
he shows therein the cause for its preeminence in joy.

In that regard, equanimity toward phenomena arises from the realization of the selflessness of phenomena; equanimity toward sentient beings arises from the attainment of the equality of self and others;
and equanimity toward the tasks of sentient beings arises from the desire for their suffering to be exhausted just as one’s own is.
Equanimity toward Buddhahood arises from the realization that there is no distinction between the dharmadhātu and oneself.
Furthermore, within this very ultimate production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), six points are to be understood:
birth, magnificence, enthusiasm, purity of intention, skill in the remaining [perfections], and departure.
In this context, birth should be understood as resulting from the excellence of the seed, the mother, the womb, and the nurse;
magnanimity results from the accomplishment of the ten great vows; and enthusiasm results from tirelessness in performing difficult practices over a long period of time.
Purity of intention arises from the knowledge that awakening is near and from the attainment of the knowledge of its means.
Skill in the remainder refers to skill in the other stages.
Departure occurs through mental attention directed toward the stages as they have been established.
How is it by way of mental attention?

It is because, through the knowledge that discerns that state of the stages, one realizes "this is mere conceptualization," and because there is no further conceptualization of that very knowledge which discerns conceptualization.
There are six verses regarding the greatness of the similes:
"The arising [of the Buddha-nature] is like the earth; another is similar to fine gold;
it is like the new white moon; and its further development is to be known as resembling fire. (MSA 4.15)
Furthermore, one [type of bodhisattva] is like a great treasure-store, another is like a mine of jewels;
one is to be known as resembling the ocean, while another is like a diamond and similar to the immovable king of mountains.
Another should be known as resembling the King of Medicine and like a great friend;
another should be known as shining like a wish-fulfilling gem and like the sun.
Another is to be known as being like the sweet voice of a gandharva; another is comparable to a king; another resembles a storehouse; and yet another is like a great highway. (MSA 4.18)
It should be understood as being like a vehicle, like a gandharva-city, and like the source of a reed-thicket;
it is similar to the sound of joy and like the current of a great river.
The generation of the mind [of awakening] by the sons of the Victors is indeed said to be like a cloud;
therefore, with joy, one should generate that mind which is so rich in virtues.

The first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*) of the Bodhisattvas is like the earth, because it serves as the foundation for the production of all the qualities of a Buddha and their accumulations. The production of the thought accompanied by intention (*āśaya*) is similar to fine gold, because the higher resolve for benefit and happiness does not undergo transformation.
That which is accompanied by application is like the new moon of the bright fortnight, because of its progression toward the increase of wholesome qualities.

That which is accompanied by resolute intention is similar to fire; just as fire varies according to the specific kind of fuel, so too does this [resolve] vary through the attainment of ever-increasing excellence. For resolute intention (adhyāśaya) is indeed the intention for attaining excellence.

Accompanied by the perfection of generosity, it is like a great treasury, because it satisfies immeasurable sentient beings through the enjoyment of material goods and because it is inexhaustible. Accompanied by the perfection of ethical discipline, it is like a mine of jewels, because all the jewels of virtuous qualities are produced from it. Accompanied by the perfection of patience, it is like the ocean, because it is unshakeable by any falls of undesirable circumstances.
Accompanied by the perfection of vigor, it is like a diamond because of its firmness and indestructibility;
accompanied by the perfection of meditation, it is like the king of mountains because of its immovability and lack of distraction;
accompanied by the perfection of wisdom, it is like the king of medicines because it pacifies the diseases of all afflictions and cognitive obstructions.
Accompanied by the immeasurables, it is like a great friend because it does not neglect sentient beings in any situation;
accompanied by the superknowledges, it is like a wish-fulfilling gem because its fruits flourish according to one's resolve;
accompanied by the means of attraction, it is like the sun because it ripens the crops of those to be trained.
It is accompanied by the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), resembling the sweet voice of a *gandharva*, because it teaches the Dharma that attracts those to be trained.
It is accompanied by the reliances (*pratiśaraṇa*), resembling a great king, because it is the cause for non-destruction.
It is accompanied by the accumulations of merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñānasaṃbhāra*), resembling a storehouse, because it is the locus for the treasury of the vast accumulations of merit and wisdom.

Accompanied by the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), it is like a great royal highway, because all noble persons (*āryapudgala*) have traveled along it and continue to travel upon it. Accompanied by calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), it is like a vehicle, because it carries one with ease.

Accompanied by retention (*dhāraṇā*) and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), it is like a celestial musician (*gandharva*), because—through its similarity to the retention and inexhaustible flow of water—it possesses the retention and inexhaustible flow of the meaning of the Dharma, both heard and unheard.
It is like the sound of joy accompanied by the summaries of the Dharma (*dharmoddāna*), because it is pleasant to hear for those disciples who desire liberation.
It is equal to the current of a river, being accompanied by the path of the single way (*ekāyanamārga*), because it flows by its own natural force.

Upon the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*), there is "the state of the single way" because the Bodhisattvas who have reached that stage perform their activities without differentiation.

Accompanied by skill in means, it is like a cloud, because the performance of the welfare of all sentient beings depends upon it, through the manifestation of dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven and so forth—
just as all the prosperities of the receptacle world arise from a cloud.
Furthermore, these twenty-two similes for the production of the thought [of awakening] are to be understood according to the sequence of the *Akṣayamati-sūtra*.
Regarding the censure of the non-arising of the thought [of awakening], there is this verse:

Because they have the thought for the sake of others, because they obtain the means thereto, and because they see the reality of the meaning of the great intentional terminology, those people who lack the arising of the most precious thought will go toward mere quiescence, abandoning that bliss. (MSA 4.21)

Deprived of that production of the thought of enlightenment, sentient beings do not obtain the fourfold happiness: the happiness that bodhisattvas derive from contemplating the welfare of others; the happiness derived from attaining the means for the welfare of others;
and the happiness derived from perceiving the meaning of the great intentional terminology—that is, from awakening to the intended meaning of the profound Mahāyāna sūtras themselves.
And there is the happiness that arises from the vision of the supreme reality, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Regarding the praise of the generation of the thought of enlightenment, there is this verse based on the absence of fear concerning the exhaustion of miserable rebirths:
"Simultaneously with the arising of the excellent mind of the wise one, the mind is well-restrained from infinite misdeeds."
The virtuous one, increasing both [wholesome roots], always rejoices in both happiness and suffering, being compassionate.

Simultaneously with the arising of that supreme mind, the bodhisattva’s mind becomes perfectly restrained from committing evil deeds on account of its commitment to infinite sentient beings; therefore, he has no fear of the miserable realms.
Increasing both the twofold—wholesome action and compassion—he is always virtuous and compassionate, and because of his virtue, he rejoices constantly even through [ordinary] happiness.
Because he is compassionate, even suffering that has the purpose of acting for the benefit of others does not cause him distress;
therefore, he has no fear even of the exhaustion resulting from having much to do.
Regarding the attainment of the restraint of non-action, there is this verse:
When one, regardless of their own body or life, undergoes supreme exertion for the sake of others,
how could such a person ever engage in an evil deed through the harming of others?

The summary of this [verse] is as follows: For one for whom another alone is more dear than oneself, because of being indifferent toward his own body and life for the sake of others, how could he engage in an evil deed by harming another for his own sake? There are two verses regarding the non-turning back of the mind: [Verse 1] How could that person, who has no longing for his own body or life for the sake of others, ever engage in an evil deed by harming another for his own sake? [Verse 2] How could that person, who does not desire even his own happiness for his own sake, ever engage in an evil deed by harming another for his own sake? Regarding the non-turning back of the mind, there are these two verses: [Verse 3] How could that person, who has no longing for his own body or life for the sake of others, ever engage in an evil deed by harming another for his own sake? [Verse 4] How could that person, who does not desire even his own happiness for his own sake, ever engage in an evil deed by harming another for his own sake?
Having perceived all phenomena as being like an illusion and rebirths as being like a pleasure-trip to a park,
he fears neither afflictions nor suffering, whether in times of prosperity or in times of adversity.

For those whose nature is constant compassion, their own virtues, the joy arising from the welfare of sentient beings, intentional rebirth, and the miraculous display of supernatural powers are their ornaments, their food, their supreme ground, and their delight in play. (MSA 4.25)
Because he perceives all phenomena as being like an illusion, that bodhisattva does not fear the afflictions during times of prosperity;
because he perceives rebirth as being like a journey to a pleasure garden, he does not fear suffering during times of adversity.
From what, then, could his mind of awakening turn back?
Moreover, for Bodhisattvas, their own virtues are their ornament;
joy in the welfare of others is their food;
and intentional rebirth is their pleasure garden.
The playful delight in the miraculous transformations of supernatural power belongs only to Bodhisattvas,
not to those who are not Bodhisattvas.
How, then, could their minds turn back?
There is a verse regarding the refutation of the fear of suffering:

"For one whose nature is compassion and who exerts effort for the sake of others, even Avīci becomes a place of delight; how much less, then, would such a person fear existence (bhava), which arises from the sufferings dependent on others? (Msa 4.26)

Furthermore, for one who is devoted to the welfare of others, even the Avīci hell is delightful because of his compassionate nature; how then could he experience fear again regarding existence due to the arising of sufferings caused by the welfare of others?
For it is from such suffering that fear arises, which leads to the turning back of the mind [from the path].
There is a verse regarding the prohibition of indifference toward sentient beings:

For one whose self is constantly cultivated by the teacher of great compassion, whose mind is tormented by the sufferings of others, there is extreme embarrassment when others must once again be urged to action when a task for another has arisen. (MSA 4.27)

For one whose self is constantly dwelt upon by the Teacher of Great Compassion and whose mind is pained by the sufferings of others, it would be a matter of extreme shame if, when a task for the sake of others has arisen, he must be exhorted by other spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). There is a verse regarding the censure of laziness:
A supreme being who has placed the heavy burden of sentient beings upon his head does not look graceful if his pace is slack;
being bound by the various fetters of self and others, he ought to exert himself a hundredfold.
Having placed the great burden of sentient beings upon his head, it does not become fitting for a Bodhisattva to exert himself with slackened effort;

for he ought to apply a vigor a hundred times greater than that of a Śrāvaka. This is because he is exceedingly bound by various bonds of self and others, consisting of the nature of afflictions, karma, and birth.
The Fourth Chapter: The Generation of the Thought of Enlightenment, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The fifth chapter: A verse on the characteristics of practice.
The practice of the sons of the Conquerors is held to consist in a great basis, a great undertaking, and the arising of great fruit;
it always performs the functions of great giving, great endurance, and the accomplishment of the great goal.
In this context, it has a great basis because it is based on the production of the thought of enlightenment;
it has a great undertaking because it undertakes the welfare of both oneself and others;
and it has the arising of a great fruit because its fruit is great enlightenment.
For this very reason, they are, respectively: "great givers" because they take up all sentient beings;
"great endurants" because they endure all suffering;
and "performers of the task of accomplishing the great purpose" because they accomplish the vast welfare of sentient beings.
Regarding the lack of distinction between one's own welfare and that of others, there is this verse:

"When one has attained a mind toward others that regards them as equal to oneself, or even a mind that holds them dearer than oneself—likewise, for one who perceives the welfare of others as superior to their own, what could be one's own interest, and what indeed could be the interest of others? (MSA 5.2)

Having attained a mind that regards others as equal to oneself— either through resolute conviction upon attaining the conventional generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), or through direct knowledge upon attaining the ultimate generation of the mind of awakening— or alternatively, having attained a state where others are even more beloved than oneself, for that very reason the Bodhisattva perceives the welfare of others as superior to his own; for such a one, what is self-interest and what is the interest of others?
The meaning is that both of these are indeed indistinguishable for him.
There is a verse regarding the qualification of "for the sake of others":
In the world, one does not act with such extreme ruthlessness toward an enemy by means of inflicting suffering as one does toward another.
Just as one whose nature is compassion applies himself to his own person when it is subjected to intense suffering for the sake of others.
He accomplishes the welfare of others in such a way that it excels his own welfare, because he subjects himself to extreme torment for the sake of others.

There are two verses regarding the classification of the practice for the welfare of others: For those established in inferior, middling, and superior natures, there is excellent teaching, winning over, and causing entry;
Discipline in regard to wealth, ripening in regard to the wholesome, as well as instruction, stability, intelligence, and liberation.
The attainment through distinguished qualities, the arising of the lineage, the prophecy and consecration,
the supreme state of the Tathāgata’s wisdom— this is the welfare of others, consisting of thirteen [stages].
Among the three types of classes of sentient beings— those situated in the inferior, middling, and superior lineages— the bodhisattva’s benefit for others is thirteenfold,
consisting of excellent teaching through instruction and admonition, and through the miracle of mental reading.
*Āvarjanā* (attraction) is by means of the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
*Avatāraṇā* (introduction) is from the acceptance of the teaching.
*Vinītiḥ* (guidance) is the cutting off of doubt for those who have been introduced to the meaning.
Maturation in the wholesome;
instruction; stability of mind; liberation through wisdom;
and the full realization of distinguished qualities such as the superknowledges.
Birth in the family of the Tathāgatas,
receiving the prophecy on the eighth stage, and the consecration on the tenth stage—
along with the wisdom of a Tathāgata— constitute the thirteenfold benefit for others of the bodhisattva, as applicable to those established in the three lineages.
Regarding the perfection of the practice for the sake of others, there is this verse:
Teaching that is appropriate to people and unerring, free from pride, devoid of "mine-ness," and discerning;
patient, self-controlled, far-reaching, and inexhaustible—such is the supreme practice of the Sons of the Conquerors. (MSA 5.6)
He demonstrates how that practice for the sake of others becomes perfected.
And how does it become perfected?
If the teaching is both appropriate to persons established in their spiritual lineage and non-erroneous.

His attraction is without arrogance; his introduction [to the path] is without possessiveness. He does not pride himself on his supernormal powers, nor does he regard the beings he has introduced [to the path] as his own.
The wise possess the practice of discernment regarding the meaning; the patient possess the practice of ripening others in what is wholesome;
and the self-controlled possess the practice of providing instruction and so forth.
For one who is not self-disciplined is not capable of providing instruction and so forth to others;
moreover, the practice for the elevation of a family and other such goals requires great distance to traverse.
Indeed, by means of a practice that has not traversed a long way, it is impossible to effect the elevation of a family and other such benefits for others.

Furthermore, this entire practice of the bodhisattvas for the sake of others is inexhaustible because the beings they have undertaken to save are inexhaustible; for this reason as well, it should be understood as perfected.
There are two verses regarding the specific qualities of this practice.
In great fear, those who crave sensual pleasures engage in worldly activity; those who love existence engage in unstable, perverted pleasure;
those who love tranquility engage in the pacification of their own individual afflictions; but one whose nature is compassion always engages in the pacification of all suffering.
The deluded person, ever striving for their own happiness, fails to attain it and instead falls into suffering;
the wise person, however, ever striving for the sake of others, accomplishes the welfare of both and attains final peace.
In this context, sensual desires constitute a great danger because they are the cause for much physical and mental suffering and for rebirth in the miserable destinies.

The happiness of those who delight in the realms of form and formlessness is unstable and perverted, because it is impermanent and, by virtue of being the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), is ultimately suffering.
Mental afflictions (*ādhi*) should be understood as "afflictions" (*kleśa*) because they inflict suffering.
Deluded people, always engaged in pursuit of their own happiness, do not obtain happiness but obtain only suffering;
the bodhisattva, however, engaged in pursuit of the welfare of others, accomplishes the welfare of both self and others and attains the bliss of nirvāṇa— this is another distinction of his practice.
Regarding the transformation of the sphere of activity, there is this verse:

"In whatever way the Son of the Victor, engaged in his course, proceeds within the various spheres of the senses, in that very way he applies himself to the welfare of sentient beings through words of appropriate and equal character. (MSA 5.9)

In whatever manner a bodhisattva engages within the diverse range of the sense faculties, such as the eye, while remaining active in the conduct of his postures and movements, he performs all of that for the benefit of sentient beings through expressions connected with and similar to those very modes. This has been explained in detail in the *Gocarapariśuddhi-sūtra*.
There is a verse regarding the prohibition of impatience toward sentient beings:

A wise person does not harbor resentment toward people whose mental faculties are always rendered independent by their faults; for he perceives that the transgressions of people occur against their own will, and thus his compassion increases. (MSA 5.10)

A bodhisattva does not harbor resentment toward people whose minds are perpetually rendered independent by the afflictions. Why is this? Because he understands that their transgressions occur against their own will, and thus his compassion increases.
Regarding the greatness of practice, there is this verse: Practice itself, which surpasses all states of existence, follows supreme peace,
increases through various multitudes of virtues, and [grasps] the world.
...always with a disposition of compassion. // Msa_5.11 //
It demonstrates a fourfold greatness:
the greatness of overcoming, because it proceeds having overcome the entirety of the three worlds and the five types of destinies;
as it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
Subhūti, if form were an entity and not a non-entity, this Mahāyāna would not emerge having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras; such is the detailed explanation.
[This is due to] the majesty of cessation, because it conforms to non-abiding nirvāṇa;
the majesty of the increase of qualities; and the majesty of not abandoning sentient beings.
The fifth chapter, on Practice, in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra.
The sixth chapter: A verse on the analysis of the characteristics of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*).

Neither existent nor non-existent, neither thus nor otherwise; it is not born, it does not perish, it does not diminish, it does not increase, nor is it purified, yet it is purified again—this is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
For the ultimate truth is the meaning of non-duality;
he demonstrates that meaning of non-duality through five aspects:
it is not existent by way of the imagined and dependent characteristics.
Nor is it non-existent by way of the perfected nature;
nor is it so [identical] as regards the imagined and dependent natures, because the perfected nature lacks identity with them;
nor is it otherwise than those two, because it lacks difference from them.
It is neither born nor does it perish, because the *dharmadhātu* is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).
It neither decreases nor increases, because it remains as it is despite the cessation and arising of the sides of affliction and purification.
It is not purified, because it is by nature undefiled; yet it is not that it is not purified, because adventitious secondary afflictions are removed.
This fivefold characteristic of non-duality should be understood as the characteristic of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the negation of the inversion of the view of self, there is this verse:
The view of self is not itself characterized by a self, nor is its state of being ill-situated characterized by anything else.
There is nothing other than these two; this [world] is an error arising from them, and thus liberation is simply the total exhaustion of that error.
The view of a self is not itself the characteristic of a self,
nor is it the state of being ill-situated;
for it is of a different nature than the imagined characteristic of a self.
Furthermore, that [self] consists of the five aggregates of clinging, because it is produced by the corruption of the afflictions;
nor is any characteristic of a self established apart from these two.
Therefore, there is no self.

This delusion has arisen which is this view of a self; therefore, liberation, which is the absence of a self, should be understood as merely the cessation of that delusion, and not as anyone being liberated at all.
There are two verses on the refutation of error.
How is it that people, relying on mere delusion, do not realize the continuous nature of suffering?
[The self] is neither a knower nor a sufferer; it is not composed of phenomena, yet it is not other than them.
How is it that people, whose activity is directed toward what is directly perceived, rely on [the view] that things are produced by another when all existence arises dependently?
What kind of darkness is this, such that, failing to see, they perceive both the existent and the non-existent?

How is it that this world, relying on the mere illusion of the view of self, does not perceive the nature of suffering that is constantly attached to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)? It is one who is ignorant through knowledge of that nature of suffering, yet an experiencer through direct experience. (MSA_Bagchi 25)
One is "afflicted by suffering" because this suffering has not been abandoned;
one is "not afflicted" because there is no self endowed with suffering;
and one is "composed of dharmas" because, through the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*), there is only the dharmas.
Nor is it composed of phenomena, because of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
And when the world perceives directly the dependent origination of things— that various things come into being in dependence upon their respective conditions—
how can one rely on this view that seeing and so forth are produced by another and are not dependently originated?
What kind of darkness is this that belongs to the world, such that, failing to perceive dependent origination which actually exists, one perceives a self that does not exist?
For it may indeed be possible for darkness to cause one not to see what exists, but it cannot cause one to see what does not exist.
Regarding the connection between peace and birth when there is no self, there is this verse:
In this world, from the perspective of the ultimate reality, there is no difference whatsoever between these two: tranquility and birth.
Nevertheless, for those who perform virtuous deeds, the attainment of tranquility is established through the cessation of birth.
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no distinction whatsoever between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa due to the equality of selflessness.
