Nevertheless, for those who perform virtuous deeds and cultivate the path to liberation, the attainment of liberation indeed occurs through the exhaustion of birth. Having thus provided a refutation of misconceptions—
There are four verses on entering the ultimate knowledge that is the antidote to that [conventional knowledge]:

Having accumulated the infinite and boundless equipment of wisdom and merit, the bodhisattva, through the thorough certainty of reflection upon phenomena, reaches the understanding of objects as being derived from mental verbalization (*jalpa*). (MSA 6.6)

Having understood that objects are mere verbal designations, he abides in that which appears as those [objects]—namely, mind-only. Then the dharmadhātu becomes directly manifest; therefore, it is free from the characteristic of duality.
Having realized through wisdom that there is nothing other than mind, one arrives at the non-existence of the mind itself;
therefore, having realized the non-existence of both, the wise one abides in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) which is free from those two.
By the power of non-conceptual knowledge, which always and universally accompanies the wise one,
the accumulation of faults that are like a thicket and have that [knowledge] as their basis is cast out, just as poison is removed by a great medicine.

By means of one [verse], he demonstrates the entry into those dharmas through the accumulation of provisions, the thorough ascertainment of the reflection on dharmas, and the realization that the appearance of the meaning of those dharmas arises from mental verbalization based on cultivation supported by meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This [entry] lasts for an immeasurable period of time characterized by innumerable divisions.
"Fulfillment" means reaching the infinite limit (*anantapāra*).

By means of the second [stage], having understood that objects are merely mental chatter, one abides in "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) which appears as those [objects]; this is the Bodhisattva’s stage of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Beyond that, [there is] the direct perception of the *dharmadhātu*.
In its progression, it is free from the two characteristics, namely the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper;
this is the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
By means of the third [verse], he demonstrates how that very *dharmadhātu* comes to be directly perceived.
And how does this dharmadhātu come to be directly perceived?

Having understood through the intellect that there is no object of apprehension other than mind, one then understands the non-existence of even that "mind-only," because in the absence of an object to be grasped, there is an absence of a grasper.
And regarding these two... [of this duality...]

Having realized non-existence, one abides in the *dharmadhātu*; not proceeding toward that [duality], being devoid of the characteristics of grasped and grasper, the *dharmadhātu* thus comes to direct perception.

By means of the fourth [verse], he demonstrates the entry into ultimate knowledge through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Through the power of non-conceptual knowledge which always and everywhere conforms to equality—wherein that conformity to equality resides within the dependent nature (*paratantra*)—[one enters].
Because it eliminates the accumulation of defects characterized by *dauṣṭhulya*, which have deeply penetrated into the very nature of its basis— just as a great medicine removes poison—
there is a verse concerning the majesty of the knowledge of ultimate reality:
Having established oneself well in the excellent Dharma ordained by the Sage, and having fixed one's mind upon the fundamental realm (*dharmadhātu*) together with its root...
Having understood that the path of mindfulness consists of mere conceptual construction, the steadfast one swiftly goes to the further shore of the ocean of qualities.

When the excellent Dharma established by the Buddha is well-ordained, that bodhisattva who has entered into the knowledge of ultimate reality fixes his mind upon the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as the root of the mind that takes all phenomena as its object; he understands that every occurrence of mindfulness which is perceived is merely conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*). Thus, he swiftly reaches the further shore of Buddhahood, the ocean of qualities—this is the majesty of the knowledge of ultimate reality.
The sixth chapter, on Reality, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The seventh chapter: A verse on the analysis of the characteristics of power.

The power belonging to the wise consists of knowledge that is unimpeded regarding all things in their various distinctions— namely, birth, speech, mind, the wholesome and unwholesome, their bases, and the state of being essence-less— even when they are beyond the range of perception.
Knowledge regarding the rebirth of others is the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādābhijñā*).

Knowledge regarding speech is the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotrābhijñā*), by which one understands the speech uttered by those who have gone there and been reborn. Knowledge regarding the mind is the supernormal knowledge of the mental states of others (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*).
The supernormal knowledge of recollecting former abodes is the knowledge regarding the prior depositing of wholesome and unwholesome [karma].
The supernormal knowledge of the sphere of psychic power is the knowledge of going to those places where those to be converted reside.
The supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows is the knowledge regarding liberation.

Just as sentient beings emerge from rebirth— regarding these six meanings throughout all world-systems in their various divisions— the knowledge that is direct and unimpeded regarding those bases is the power of Bodhisattvas, comprised within the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
In the analysis of the characteristics of power, the meaning of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been explained.
A verse concerning the meaning of the cause:

Having attained the perfectly pure fourth dhyāna through the embrace of non-conceptual knowledge, one reaches supreme accomplishment of power by means of mental attention according to the established order. (MSA 7.2)
It demonstrates the origin of that power by means of which basis, which knowledge, and which mental attention it is accomplished.
Regarding the meaning of the fruit, there is this verse:
"By means of which he always dwells in noble, divine, incomparable, and sublime Brahmā-abodes."
Having gone to the various directions, he honors the Buddhas and sentient beings, and brings about their purification.
He demonstrates three kinds of fruit resulting from this power:

for oneself, an incomparable and supreme dwelling in the bliss of the noble ones and so forth; and, having gone to other world-systems, the worship of the Buddhas and the purification of sentient beings.
Regarding the meaning of action, there are four verses beginning with sixfold [action].
Regarding the activity of seeing and the activity of manifesting, there is this verse:

He sees all world-systems as like illusions, together with their sentient beings and their processes of evolution and dissolution; and being masterful, he manifests them just as he desires, even in their various diverse forms. (MSA 7.4)
Because he himself perceives all world-systems, together with their sentient beings and their processes of evolution and dissolution, as being like an illusion;
and because he manifests them to others according to his will.
And by other various modes such as trembling, blazing, and so forth,
due to the attainment of the ten masteries,
as described in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* regarding the eighth stage.
A verse concerning the activity of the rays:
By the emission of rays, he causes those in the miserable states who are intensely suffering to go to heaven;
shaking the splendor of the palaces of the lineage of Māras, he terrifies them along with their Māras.
It demonstrates two kinds of activity for the rays of light:
first, producing faith in those reborn in the miserable states and thereby causing their rebirth in heaven;
and second, shaking and terrifying the palaces of Māra along with Māra himself.
Regarding the activity of playful sport, there is this verse:
He displays immeasurable play in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the midst of the foremost assembly;
and through his deeds, births, and supreme emanations, he remains at all times for the sake of sentient beings. (MSA 7.6)

Because he displays the play of immeasurable samādhis within the midst of the circles of the Buddha’s assemblies, and because he constantly performs the welfare of sentient beings through three kinds of emanations;
the three kinds of emanation are: the emanation of the fields of arts and crafts, and the emanation of birth according to one's will in accordance with those to be trained.
And there is the supreme emanation, beginning with the dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven;
regarding the activity of purifying the field, there is this verse:
Through mastery over gnosis, he attains purity so that the field may be displayed according to his wish.
And by proclaiming the name of the Buddha among those who do not know his name, he casts them into another realm.
Through the purification of the two kinds of evil:
by the purification of the vessel [the world], through the manifestation of Buddha-fields composed of crystal, lapis lazuli, and so forth, according to one's wish by means of mastery over gnosis;

and by the purification of sentient beings, by causing those beings born in world-systems devoid of the name of a Buddha to hear the name of a Buddha, thereby inducing faith in them, and subsequently establishing them in world-systems that are not devoid of the name of a Buddha.
Regarding the meaning of yoga, there is this verse:
And he indeed becomes capable of maturing sentient beings, just like a bird whose wings have grown.
He receives excessive praise from the Buddha and his speech becomes authoritative for all beings.
He demonstrates three kinds of yoga:
the yoga of the power to mature sentient beings, the yoga of praise, and the yoga of having speech that is accepted.
This verse begins with reference to the meaning of the commentary.
The sixfold supernormal knowledges, the threefold sciences, the eight liberations, and likewise the eight bases of mastery;
the ten totalities as well, and immeasurable concentrations—such is the power attained by the steadfast one.
The power of a bodhisattva operates through six divisions:

the divisions of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the sciences (*vidyā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the immeasurable concentrations (*apramāṇasamādhi*).
Having thus shown power by means of these six meanings characterized by their classification, there is a verse for the purpose of manifesting its greatness.
For he, having attained a mind of supreme mastery and having brought the helpless world under his own control,
dwells forever in the realms of existence as one who finds sole delight in acting for the benefit of others— truly steadfast like a lion.
It demonstrates three kinds of greatness:

the greatness of mastery, because by attaining mastery over supreme knowledge oneself, one establishes the world—which is otherwise not under its own control due to the afflictions—under one's own control;
and the greatness of delight, because one always takes exclusive pleasure in acting for the benefit of others.
And the majesty of fearlessness regarding existence.
This concludes the seventh chapter, on Power, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The eighth chapter:
A verse on the summary regarding the maturation of bodhisattvas.
Zeal, clarity, tranquility, compassion, patience, wisdom, and indeed strength,
as well as being thoroughly endowed with the limbs that cannot be shaken— this is the characteristic of maturation in a Son of the Conqueror.
Delight in the Dharma taught in the Mahāyāna, serene confidence in its teacher,
and the pacification of the afflictions.
Compassion for sentient beings, patience in the practice of austerities,
and intelligence in grasping, retaining, and penetrating [the teachings].
It consists of attaining strength,
being unshakable by Māra or other proponents of opposing views,
and being endowed with the factors of exertion.
The word "intensely" (*bhṛśam*) indicates the high degree of [the qualities] such as inclination (*ruci*).
In brief, this ninefold maturation of the self of bodhisattvas should be understood.
Regarding the maturation of inclination, there is a verse:
The triad beginning with friendliness, formidable heroism, and the gathering of the supreme dharma culminating in the welfare of others—
this is considered the characteristic of perfect maturation for the compassionate one in the great undertaking of the true dharma.
The triad beginning with friendliness consists of attending upon virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, and proper mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
Fierce vigor is the undertaking of supreme diligence.
Reaching the ultimate for the sake of others is being free from doubt regarding all inconceivable points.
The "compendium of the supreme Dharma" is the protection of the Mahāyāna Dharma,
because it protects those who have entered upon it from calamities.
With reference to the Bodhisattva’s appropriation of the Mahāyāna Dharma, this should be understood as the characteristic of the maturation of inclination.

By this [verse], that by which it matures— namely, through the triad beginning with "good friendship"— and what its maturation is— namely, its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) consisting of intense vigor and culminating in the supreme goal— and what its function is— namely, the gathering of the sublime Dharma— all of this has been fully elucidated.
Regarding the maturation of serene faith, there is this verse:

"Knowledge of virtues, the swift attainment of meditative concentration, the experience of the fruit, and the non-differentiation of the mind—these are considered the characteristics of the correct maturation for the sake of full realization toward the Teacher, the Son of the Jina. (MSA 8.3)
That maturation is also elucidated by way of its cause, its intrinsic nature, and its function.
"Knowledge of qualities" and so forth— namely, that "the Blessed One is a Tathāgata"— constitute the detailed explanation of the cause.
Its intrinsic nature is an unbreakable state of mind resulting from the attainment of confidence through realization (*avetyaprasāda*).
Its function is the swift attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the personal experience of its fruits, such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
Regarding the maturation of tranquility (*praśama*), there is this verse:

Perfect restraint, the avoidance of afflicted discursive thoughts, freedom from obstacles, and delight in the virtuous—these are considered the characteristics of correct maturation for a Son of the Conqueror in order to dispel the afflictions. (MSA 8.4)
The pacification of a bodhisattva is the removal of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Its maturation is also elucidated by way of its cause, its intrinsic nature, and its function.
The cause is the thorough restraint of the sense faculties through mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Its intrinsic nature is the avoidance of afflicted discursive thoughts.
Its function consists in being free from interruption during the cultivation of the antidotes and in taking delight in what is wholesome.
Regarding the characteristic of the maturation of compassion, there is this verse:

Compassion by nature, the perception of the suffering of others, the complete abandonment of a base mind, the attainment of excellence, and being born as the foremost in the world— these are the characteristics of the maturation of supreme empathy for others.
The cause is that it matures through one's own nature, lineage, the observation of the suffering of others, and the avoidance of the inferior vehicle.
Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the state of progressing toward excellence, because it proceeds toward the increase of maturation.
Its function (*karma*) on the stage of non-retrogression is the possession of a physical body that is the most excellent in all the world.

A verse concerning the characteristics of the maturation of patience (kṣānti): Fortitude by nature, cultivation through analytical reflection, constant endurance of extreme suffering such as cold and so forth, the tendency toward excellence, and delight in the wholesome—these are considered the characteristics of the maturation of patience. (MSA 8.6)

Firmness (*dhṛti*), endurance (*sahana*), and patience (*kṣānti*) are synonyms. Its maturation has as its causes the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Its intrinsic nature is the acceptance of intense sufferings such as cold and the like. Its function is the progression toward excellence for one who is patient and a delight in the wholesome.
(32) Regarding the maturation of intelligence, there is this verse:
Purity of ripening, non-forgetfulness upon hearing and so forth, and likewise penetration into both what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
The fitness for the arising of great wisdom from mindfulness is the characteristic mark of the maturation of excellent intelligence.
In this context, the cause is the purity of maturation that is conducive to intelligence (*medhā*).

The nature of the maturation of mindfulness (*smṛti*) consists in not forgetting what has been heard, reflected upon, cultivated, long ago done, or long ago spoken, as well as a thorough penetration of the meaning of both well-spoken and ill-spoken words.
Its function is the capacity for the arising of supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*).
Regarding the maturation consisting in the attainment of power, there is this verse:
Through the two kinds of merit, there is the nourishment of the two elements; at the arising of the fruit, there is supreme fitness of the basis.
The fulfillment of one's aspirations and the state of being the foremost in the world—these are the characteristics of maturation in the attainment of power. (MSA 8.8)
In this context, the nourishment of the seeds of those two—merit and gnosis—by means of merit and gnosis is the cause for their maturation.
The nature of that maturation is the fitness of the basis for realization.
Its function is the fulfillment of one's aspirations and the state of being the foremost in the world.
Regarding the maturation of being unshakable, there is this verse:

The intention to investigate the correct nature through reasoning, the attainment of excellence, the refutation of opposing positions, and furthermore, the constant absence of obstacles from Māra—these are the characteristics of the maturation of being unshakable. (MSA 8.9)
The cause for its maturation is the intention formed through rational investigation of the true Dharma (*saddharma*).
Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the absence of Māra’s interference, such that Māra is no longer able to create an obstacle.
Its function (*karma*) is the attainment of excellence and the refutation of opposing positions.
Regarding the maturation consisting in the possession of the factors of exertion, there is this verse:

"The accumulation of merit, the fitness of the basis for effort, seclusion, and delighting in sublime virtues—these are considered the characteristics of the correct maturation when the Son of the Conqueror possesses the factors of exertion. (MSA 8.10)
The cause of that maturation is the accumulation of roots of virtue;
its intrinsic nature is the fitness of the basis for the undertaking of vigor.
The function [of this] is the excellence of seclusion and delight in the wholesome.
Regarding the greatness of the ninefold maturation of oneself, there is this verse:
"Thus, one whose self is nourished by the ninefold objects has attained the fitness for maturing others."
With his self constantly increased by the nature of virtuous qualities, he always becomes the foremost kinsman of the world.
That majesty is twofold:
it is the state of being a refuge for the ripening of others,
and the constant increase of the dharma-body.
Therefore, regarding the supreme kinsman of the world,
there are eleven verses on the classification of the ripening of sentient beings:
Just as ripening is desired in the case of a wound and in the case of food, respectively, because of their suitability for draining and for consumption;
Likewise, in this basis, there is the tranquility of the two sides, and the state of being well-purified through the side of enjoyment.
By this, he shows the nature of ripening:
just as the ripening of a wound is its fitness for draining,
and the ripening of food is its fitness for consumption.

Thus, in the case of sentient beings, within the basis that is comparable to a wound and its food, the pacification of opposing factors is comparable to the draining [of pus]; and the enjoyment of the counter-factors is comparable to the enjoyment of food. The maturation of the basis is the fitness for these.
In this context, the two sides should be understood as the adverse factors and their remedies.
The second verse states:
"Maturation has been explained, as well as full maturation; furthermore, there is also secondary maturation and further maturation."
It is considered to be well-maturing, thoroughly maturing, ripening, and producing maturity within embodied beings.
By this, he shows the classification of ripening:
ripening through the removal of afflictions is *vipācanā*;
ripening by means of all three vehicles in every respect is *paripācanā*.

Because it is distinguished by external maturation, it is "superior maturation" (*prapācanā*). Because it is a teaching of the Dharma according to those to be trained, it is "conformable maturation" (*anupācanā*). Maturation performed with reverence is "excellent maturation" (*supācanā*).
Maturation through realization is *adhipācanā*, in the sense of being non-erroneous;
constant maturation is *nipācanā*, in the sense of being non-declining;
and gradual maturation, proceeding higher and higher, is *utpācanā*.
Thus, this is the eightfold classification of the various types of maturation;
[this concludes] the third and fourth verses.
Just as the Son of the Conqueror remains here with a heart intent on the welfare of others, maturing the entire world,
neither mother, nor father, nor kinsmen are so well-established toward their children or relatives.

Likewise, ordinary people are not considered to be as affectionate toward themselves as a compassionate being is toward others who are dear to him; for the latter is regarded as being devoted to their welfare and happiness by means of establishing them therein.
What does he show by these two?
He shows the kind of intention with which a bodhisattva brings sentient beings to maturity—
an intention superior to that of parents and kinsmen, and superior to the worldly self-cherishing, because it joins them with benefit and happiness.
The world, however, being fond of itself, applies itself to its own welfare and happiness.
With the remaining verses, he demonstrates through the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*) the method by which he brings sentient beings to maturity.
The following verse concerns the kind of giving and the manner in which he matures sentient beings.
For a bodhisattva, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be given to others from his own body or possessions;
maturing others through these two kinds of assistance, he is never satiated by the equal virtues of giving.
He brings others to maturity through three kinds of giving:
by the giving of all one's possessions, body, and enjoyments; by impartial giving; and by insatiable giving.
How does he bring them to maturity? By providing benefit in both the present life and future lives.
Because he fulfills their desires without causing them distress,
and because he gathers them through that future [state] and establishes them in the wholesome;
regarding the kind of ethical discipline by which he brings sentient beings to maturity, there is this verse:
Always by nature supremely non-violent, himself delighting in this [virtue] and being heedful, he establishes others in it;
thus performing benefit for others in two ways, he matures them through the qualities of both ripening and natural outflow.
By means of fivefold morality:
by constant morality, natural morality, and perfect morality, because of being exceedingly non-violent.
For one who is perfect and non-violent is "exceedingly non-violent," being fully endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action.
As it was said regarding the second stage:
by means of the morality of realization through self-delight, and by means of uninterrupted and unerring morality through heedfulness.
And how? (MSA_Bagchi 35)
He brings them to maturity by establishing them in ethical discipline through two kinds of beneficial action: in the present life and in future lives.
He brings about benefit for others in future lives through a succession of qualities consisting of maturation (*vipāka*) and natural outflow (*niṣyanda*),
because those two— maturation and natural outflow— are uninterrupted by virtue of their mutual compatibility.
Regarding the kind of patience with which he ripens sentient beings and the manner in which he does so, there is this verse:

Regarding others who cause harm, one who possesses the perception of them as benefactors endures even their severe transgressions; through skillful means and thoughts of enduring injury, they lead those who cause harm toward what is wholesome.
He brings others to maturity through the patience that endures intense harm by regarding a harmful person as a benefactor.
Furthermore, this state of regarding them as benefactors should be understood as a mode of conduct conducive to the fulfillment of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
How does he bring them to maturity?
Because he endures harm through favoring them in this present life,
and because he favors them in future lives— the one who knows the means wins over those who cause him harm by establishing them in virtue through those very acts of enduring harm.
Regarding the kind of vigor with which he brings sentient beings to maturity, there is this verse:
Furthermore, relying upon supreme effort, that son of the Conqueror does not grow weary even in the course of thousands of millions of eons,
as he brings the multitude of sentient beings to maturity for the sake of producing even a single virtuous thought in another.
By means of vigor that is characterized by tirelessness over an extremely long period, there is tirelessness over a long duration because of maturing infinite sentient beings;
for the sake of even a single virtuous thought in another, one does not grow weary even throughout billions of thousands of eons.
It is precisely for this reason that it is said how he brings them to maturity.
Because of the application of the wholesome mind, there is benefit in both the present life and future lives.
Regarding the kind of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) by which he brings sentient beings to maturity, there is this verse:
"Having attained supreme mastery over the mind, he draws others toward this supreme teaching."
Having destroyed all desire for honor, he further increases that [desire] through virtue.
He brings them to maturity through meditation that has attained unsurpassed mastery and is free from worldly desire, having destroyed all longing for contempt;
he brings them to maturity by attracting others to the Buddha’s teaching and, once attracted, by increasing their wholesome qualities.
Regarding the kind of wisdom with which he brings sentient beings to maturity, there is this verse:
He is well-ascertained in the method of the meaning of the nature of reality; he makes sentient beings free from doubt.
Consequently, through their devotion to the teaching of that Victor, they cause themselves and others to flourish with virtuous qualities. (MSA 8.21)
That bodhisattva brings them to maturity through wisdom that is well-settled in both the method of the ultimate meaning and the method of the intentional meaning.
How does he bring them to maturity? By dispelling the doubts of sentient beings, and because of their great respect for the teaching, by means of increasing the qualities of themselves and others.
Regarding the summary verse:

"Thus, out of compassion, that Bodhisattva leads the entire world toward a happy rebirth or toward the three types of virtue by means of mild, supreme, and intermediate methods, through a course of conduct identical to that of the world. (Msa 8.22)
By this, where one disciplines—
whether in proceeding to a happy rebirth or in the three vehicles—
and that which one disciplines;
The entire world;
that by which one disciplines it, namely compassion;
and he who disciplines it, the bodhisattva.
By describing the types of ripening— whether mild, supreme, or middling—
as well as the duration of time, he demonstrates, in brief, the majesty of ripening through that exposition.

In that regard, it should be understood that for a bodhisattva, the "slight" degree [of maturation] occurs on the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*); the "supreme" degree occurs on the eighth stage and those following; and the "middling" degree occurs on the seven stages [from the first to the seventh].
"As long as the world exists" means "ultimately," by way of a course of existence identical to that of the world.
The eighth chapter, the Chapter on Maturation, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The ninth chapter: Two verses on the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The third [verse] is an exposition of those two very same points:

"Through hundreds of immeasurable difficult feats, through immeasurable accumulations of virtue, and over an immeasurable period of time, by means of the destruction of immeasurable obscurations. (MSA 9.1)
The attainment of the knowledge of all aspects, purified of all obscurations,
is declared to be Buddhahood, like an opened casket of jewels.

Having performed a marvelous and difficult task through hundreds of labors, having accumulated all that is auspicious over a vast period of time within the supreme eon, and having uprooted even the subtle obscurations residing in the stages through the exhaustion of all veils— this is Buddhahood.
It is like a casket opened up, containing jewels of great power.
Buddhahood has been elucidated by way of its realization, its intrinsic nature, and its similes.

As for "realization": it is that through which [Buddhahood] is fully realized—by means of how many hundreds of difficult feats, by means of how many accumulations of merit and knowledge, over what duration of time, and through the abandonment of how much of the veil of afflictions and the veil regarding the knowable.
This is realization.
The attainment of omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), purified of all obscurations, is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
An open jewel casket is the simile for it.
Regarding that very Buddhahood, which is characterized by non-duality and possesses majestic power, there are two verses.
All phenomena are Buddhahood, yet there is no phenomenon whatsoever;
it consists of pure qualities, yet it cannot be defined by them.
Because it is the cause for the jewel of the Dharma, it is considered to have attained the likeness of a treasure mine;
because it is the cause for the harvest of virtue, it is considered to have attained the likeness of a cloud.
All phenomena are Buddhahood,
because they are non-different from suchness and are characterized by its purity;
yet, within Buddhahood, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that exists.
Buddhahood consists of pure qualities by way of the imagined nature of phenomena, because the perfections and other wholesome factors have undergone transformation into that state.
Yet it is not designated by them, because the perfections and so forth are not established as having the nature of perfections and so forth; this is the characteristic of non-duality.

Its majesty consists in being like a jewel-mine and a cloud, because the jewels of the Dharma taught therein originate from it, as do the crops of virtue in the fields of the mental continuums of those to be trained.

Buddhahood is both the collection of all phenomena and yet devoid of all phenomena; it is like a vast and great mine of the jewels of Dharma because of the emergence of the extensive and great jewel of Dharma;
and it is like a cloud because it is the cause for the production of the great white harvest of living beings.
From giving, there arises for living beings an inexhaustible, well-arranged, and continuous rain of the water of Dharma.
By this third verse, he explains that very same point:
because it is the cause for the emergence of the vast and extensive jewel of the Dharma, it is like a mine of jewels.
Because it is the cause for the production of great, pure crops among living beings, it has become like a cloud;
because it bestows upon all creatures a great, well-arranged, and inexhaustible rain of the water of Dharma—this should be understood as the analysis of the words here.
There are five verses concerning the unsurpassed nature of that very Buddhahood as a refuge.
For Buddhahood is indeed a constant protection from the entire host of afflictions,
from all misdeeds, and even from birth and death.
By this, he demonstrates the nature of being a refuge in brief, for the purpose of protecting [beings] from the defilements of afflictions, karma, and birth:
"From all calamities, from the miserable states, from improper means, from the view of a self-identity, and from the Lesser Vehicle—for these reasons, it is the supreme refuge. (MSA 9.8)
By this second [verse], [the protection] from calamities and so forth is explained in detail.
In that regard, "protection from all calamities" refers to the fact that through the majestic power (*anubhāva*) of the Buddhas, the blind regain their sight and the deaf regain their hearing.
"Those with distracted minds become possessed of stable minds; those who fear are pacified," and so forth.

Its nature as a protection from the miserable states (*apāya*) consists in the liberation of those who have gone there by means of the Buddha’s radiance, and in establishing them so that they do not go there again.

It provides protection from improper means by causing one to rise above the views of non-Buddhists; it provides protection from the view of a self-existent body by bringing about final nirvana through the two vehicles;
and it provides protection from the inferior vehicle by establishing those of indeterminate lineage on the single path of the Mahāyāna.
That incomparable refuge, the desired state of supreme Buddhahood,
is the protection against birth, death, all afflictions, and evils;
it is the vehicle of universal protection for those who have fallen into various fears.
For those who have entered upon the means leading to the miserable states of rebirth, which abound in manifold and continuous sufferings.
By this third verse, he demonstrates through that same meaning the incomparable excellence and supremacy of that very state of being a refuge:
That which has a body perfectly complete with the qualities of a Buddha; that which knows how to lead sentient beings into the true Dharma;
and that which, out of compassion, has reached the further shore regarding all worlds—that Buddhahood is the supreme refuge here [on earth]. (MSA 9.10)
By this fourth [verse], he demonstrates the reasons why that [Buddha] is such an unsurpassed refuge:

because his nature is perfectly complete with the qualities of a Buddha, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, he has reached the culmination of his own welfare; and because he possesses the knowledge of the means for training sentient beings in the True Dharma and has reached the further shore of compassion, he has reached the culmination of the welfare of others.
Thus, until the end of time, Buddhahood is the great refuge for all sentient beings.
It is held that [this] leads to the turning away from all calamities and misfortunes and to the attainment of prosperity.
By this fifth verse, he demonstrates in brief for how long a time, for how many sentient beings, and for what purpose it serves as a refuge.
"For what purpose" means for the turning away from all calamities and for the attainment of prosperity.
There are six verses on the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
It is that in which the seed of the afflictions and the knowable, which has continuously followed for an exceedingly long time, comes to its cessation through all the vast modes of abandonment.
Buddhahood is the transformation of the basis (āśraya) endowed with the most excellent qualities of pure dharmas;
its attainment comes from the path of knowledge that is utterly pure, non-conceptual, and has the Great Object as its domain.

By this, the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) is elucidated through the separation from the seeds of the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) and the endowment with the perfection of the remedial factors (*pratipakṣa*).
Furthermore, its attainment occurs through the acquisition of two kinds of paths:
the acquisition of the path of perfectly pure supramundane gnosis (*lokottarajñāna*).
And because of the attainment of the path of knowledge whose object is the infinite knowable attained subsequent to that [realization];
"for an exceptionally long time" means for a beginningless time; "by very extensive modes of all-abandonment" refers to the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Established therein, that Tathāgata gazes upon the world as if standing atop a great mountain king;
he takes compassion for those people who delight in tranquility, while what need is there to mention other people who delight in sin and worldly existence?
By this second verse, he demonstrates its distinction from other transformations of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
For one who abides therein, like a great mountain king, perceives the world situated at a vast distance;
and having perceived it, he feels compassion even for the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, let alone others.

The transformation of the Tathāgatas is held to be characterized by engagement and withdrawal, non-engagement, the basis, cessation, and recurrence; it is both dual and non-dual, equal yet distinguished, and all-pervading in nature.
By this third [verse], he shows its tenfold division.
For that transformation of the Tathāgatas is "proceeding" (*pravṛtti*) because it proceeds for the sake of others;
it is "exalted proceeding" (*udvṛtti*) because it is a superior proceeding due to its excellence over all phenomena.
Non-occurrence in the cause of affliction;
"basis" indicates that very basis which is the result of transformation;
and cessation through the turning away from affliction is "cessation."
Because it is ultimate, its activity is extensive; thus, it is "non-returning.
Through the activity of manifesting both perfect awakening and final nirvana, it is a dual activity.
Because it does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, it is a non-dual activity in terms of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Their activity is equal to that of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas by virtue of the commonality of liberation;
it is distinguished [from them] because of its inequality with respect to the Buddha-qualities such as the powers and the grounds of self-confidence;
and it is an all-pervading activity because it extends to the instruction in all vehicles.
Just as space is always all-pervading and undifferentiated, so too is that [Buddhahood] always all-pervading and undifferentiated;
just as space is omnipresent among the multitudes of forms, so too is it omnipresent among the multitudes of sentient beings.
By this fourth verse, he demonstrates the omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) of Buddhahood, which has that as its intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāva*),
through its similarity to space (*ākāśasādharmyeṇa*), by means of the summary and the detailed explanation in the first and second halves [of the verse].
The omnipresence of Buddhahood among the multitudes of sentient beings should be understood as its perfection through the realization that it is the very self of all beings.
Just as the reflection of the moon is not seen when a water vessel is broken,
so too the image of the Buddha is not seen among corrupt sentient beings.

By this fifth [verse], he establishes through an analogy that even though [the Buddha] is omnipresent, the image of the Buddha is not seen among sentient beings who are unfit vessels: "Just as fire blazes in one place and then extinguishes in another, so too should it be understood regarding Buddhas: there is both manifestation and non-manifestation. (MSA 9.17)

By this sixth verse, he establishes—through the analogy of the kindling and extinguishing of a fire—that when those to be trained by a Buddha exist, there is the appearance of a Buddha's arising; and when they have been trained, there is the non-appearance of him due to his final nirvana. There are four verses regarding the effortless and uninterrupted performance of the Buddha’s work.
Just as the production of sound occurs from musical instruments that have not been struck,
so too does the emergence of the teaching arise from the Jina even without his deliberate effort.
Just as a jewel displays its own radiance without effort, so too do the Buddhas display their activity without exertion. (MSA 9.19)
By these two verses, it is shown that he accomplishes the work of a Buddha effortlessly, through a similarity to the power of a gem or the sound of an unstruck musical instrument:
"Just as worldly activities are seen to proceed without interruption in space,
even so the deeds of the Victor proceed without interruption in the untainted realm."
Just as in space there is always the cessation and the arising of activities,
so too in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) there is the arising and the passing away of the Buddha's work.
By these two [qualities], the Buddha’s activity remains unceasing because his buddha-deeds are uninterrupted.
Just as in space, although worldly activities are uninterrupted, there is likewise the arising and passing away of various successive activities.
Regarding the profundity of the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), there are sixteen verses.
Although it is undifferentiated by priority or posteriority, and free from all obscurations,
suchness— being neither pure nor impure— is considered to be Buddhahood.
It is not pure because it is undifferentiated throughout its preceding and succeeding stages;
yet it is not impure because, subsequently, all obscurations have been cleared away through the departure of defilement.
When emptiness is purified through the attainment of the path of selflessness,
the Buddhas, by virtue of attaining the pure self, have reached the state of the Great Self.
And therein, in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), the supreme self of the Buddhas is taught.
For what reason?
Because its nature is the foremost selflessness (*nairātmya*).

Supreme selflessness is pure suchness, and that is the self of the Buddhas in the sense of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). When that is purified, the Buddhas obtain a supreme selflessness as their pure self.

Therefore, because they have obtained a pure self, the Buddhas have attained the greatness of the self; with this underlying intention, the supreme self is established for the Buddhas in the uncontaminated realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
For that reason, Buddhahood is said to be neither an entity nor a non-entity.
Therefore, regarding the question of whether a Buddha exists as such, the method of the undeclared (avyākṛta) is held to be appropriate.
For that very reason, Buddhahood is not said to be an existence,
because Buddhahood has the characteristic of the non-existence of both persons and phenomena, and because it is of the nature of that [non-existence].
Nor is it said to be a non-existence, because it possesses the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*).

Therefore, regarding the question of the existence or non-existence of the Buddha— such as whether the Tathāgata exists after death or does not exist— this is considered the method of the undeclared (avyākṛta).
It is like the subsiding of heat in iron, or the clearing of cataracts from vision.
Likewise, in the Buddha’s knowledge of the minds [of others], existence and non-existence are not praised.
Just as the subsiding of heat in iron and the subsiding of cataracts in vision are neither entities— because heat and cataracts are characterized by non-existence—
nor non-entities— because they exist in the form of subsiding.

Thus, regarding the knowledge of the minds of the Buddhas, the pacification of passion and ignorance—which stand in the place of heat and cataracts—is praised not as a positive entity, because it is characterized by their absence; yet it is not a non-entity, because of the existence of that very characteristic of liberation through the liberation of mind and wisdom. In the stainless realm of the Buddhas, there is neither unity nor plurality.
Because they are bodiless like space, yet in accordance with their previous bodies.
In the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*) of the Buddhas, there is no unity by way of following after previous bodies,
nor is there plurality because of the absence of a body, like space.
Within the Buddha-qualities such as the powers (*bala*), awakening (*bodhi*) is like a mine of jewels.
They are considered to be like great clouds for the crops of virtue in the world.
Because it is completely filled with merit and wisdom, it is considered like the full moon;
and because it produces the light of knowledge, it is considered like the great sun.

These two verses regarding the likeness to a mine of jewels and a cloud, and the likeness to the full moon and the great sun, have their meaning already explained. Just as immeasurable rays of light are intermingled within the orb of the sun, so too are the immeasurable rays of the Buddha’s qualities intermingled within the sphere of his gnosis. Just as those rays are not perceived individually because they are mingled together, so too the immeasurable qualities of the Buddha are not perceived individually because they are mingled together. Just as the sun is the cause for the ripening of crops, so too the Buddha is the cause for the ripening of the roots of virtue in sentient beings. Just as the sun is the cause for the manifestation of forms, so too the Buddha is the cause for the manifestation of the Dharma. Just as the sun is the cause for the removal of darkness, so too the Buddha is the cause for the removal of the darkness of ignorance. Just as the sun is the cause for the production of light, so too the Buddha is the cause for the production of the light of wisdom. Just as the sun is the cause for the destruction of cold, so too the Buddha is the cause for the destruction of the cold of suffering. Just as the sun is the cause for the joy of beings, so too the Buddha is the cause for the joy of beings. Just as the sun is the cause for the opening of lotuses, so too the Buddha is the cause for the opening of the lotuses of the faculties of sentient beings. Just as the sun is the cause for the closing of water-lilies, so too the Buddha is the cause for the closing of the faculties of those who are not fit vessels. Just as the sun is the cause for the growth of medicinal herbs, so too the Buddha is the cause for the growth of the medicinal herbs of the perfections. Just as the sun is the cause for the drying up of moisture, so too the Buddha is the cause for the drying up of the moisture of defilements. Just as the sun is the cause for the maturation of fruits, so too the Buddha is the cause for the maturation of the fruits of the three vehicles. Just as the sun is the cause for the manifestation of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the manifestation of the world of the Dharma. Just as the sun is the cause for the cessation of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the cessation of the world of suffering. Just as the sun is the cause for the arising of day, so too the Buddha is the cause for the arising of the day of the Dharma. Just as the sun is the cause for the setting of night, so too the Buddha is the cause for the setting of the night of ignorance. Just as the sun is the cause for the movement of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the movement of the world toward liberation. Just as the sun is the cause for the stability of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the stability of the world in the Dharma. Just as the sun is the cause for the illumination of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the illumination of the world by wisdom. Just as the sun is the cause for the dispelling of clouds, so too the Buddha is the cause for the dispelling of the clouds of defilements. Just as the sun is the cause for the clearing of the sky, so too the Buddha is the cause for the clearing of the sky of the mind. Just as the sun is the cause for the rising of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the rising of the world of merit. Just as the sun is the cause for the falling of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the falling away of the world from suffering. Just as the sun is the cause for the increase of heat, so too the Buddha is the cause for the increase of the heat of wisdom. Just as the sun is the cause for the decrease of cold, so too the Buddha is the cause for the decrease of the cold of craving. Just as the sun is the cause for the appearance of colors, so too the Buddha is the cause for the appearance of the colors of the Dharma. Just as the sun is the cause for the disappearance of colors, so too the Buddha is the cause for the disappearance of the colors of worldly attachment. Just as the sun is the cause for the manifestation of the world of form, so too the Buddha is the cause for the manifestation of the world of the formless Dharma. Just as the sun is the cause for the obscuring of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the obscuring of the world of evil. Just as the sun is the cause for the revealing of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the revealing of the world of the noble ones. Just as the sun is the cause for the exhaustion of fuel, so too the Buddha is the cause for the exhaustion of the fuel of karma and defilements. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-exhaustion of space, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-exhaustion of the realm of phenomena. Just as the sun is the cause for the continuity of light, so too the Buddha is the cause for the continuity of the light of the Dharma. Just as the sun is the cause for the interruption of darkness, so too the Buddha is the cause for the interruption of the darkness of ignorance. Just as the sun is the cause for the uninterruptedness of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the uninterruptedness of the lineage of the Three Jewels. Just as the sun is the cause for the unceasingness of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the unceasingness of the turning of the wheel of the Dharma. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-differentiation of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-differentiation of the Dharma-realm. Just as the sun is the cause for the equality of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the equality of all sentient beings. Just as the sun is the cause for the impartiality of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the impartiality of his compassion. Just as the sun is the cause for the inexhaustibility of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the inexhaustibility of his enlightened activity. Just as the sun is the cause for the immutability of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the immutability of the nature of reality. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-deterioration of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-deterioration of the Dharma-body. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-increase of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-increase of the Dharma-realm. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-decrease of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-decrease of the assembly of bodhisattvas. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-arising of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-arising of the view of a self. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-cessation of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-cessation of the stream of dependent origination. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-birth of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-birth of the afflictions. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-death of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-death of the Tathāgata-nature. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-old-age of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-old-age of the Dharma-body. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-sickness of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-sickness of the path to liberation. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-pain of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-pain of the suffering of saṃsāra. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-fear of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-fear of the four fears. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-grief of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-grief of the loss of loved ones. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-delusion of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-delusion regarding the three times. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-confusion of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-confusion regarding the distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-obscuration of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-obscuration of the light of wisdom. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-hindrance of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-hindrance of the unimpeded knowledge. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-limitation of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-limitation of the scope of his activity. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-boundariness of the world, so too the Buddha is the cause for the non-boundariness of the realm of his gnosis. Just as the sun is the cause for the non-measurability of the world, so too the Buddha
They always act with a single purpose and illuminate the world.
In the same way, within the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu), the Buddhas are immeasurable;
they perform their activities with a unified purpose and are considered to be the bringers of the light of wisdom.
By the first [verse], he demonstrates their commonality of activity through the analogy of rays of light having a single mixed function;
the fact that the rays have a single function is to be understood as their having the common functions of ripening and drying.
By the second [verse], he shows their mixed and single function within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) in activities such as emanation (*nirmāṇa*).
Just as from the emission of a single ray all rays are emitted from the sun,
so too should the emission of the wisdom of the Buddhas be understood.
By the simultaneous emission of all rays,
he demonstrates the simultaneous activity of the wisdom of the Buddhas;
just as in the operation of the sun’s rays, there is no sense of "mine."
In the same way, there is no sense of "mine" regarding the functioning of the Buddha-knowledges.
Just as the world is illuminated all at once by the rays of light emitted from the single sun,
so too is the entirety of the knowable illuminated simultaneously by the primordial wisdoms of a Buddha.
The two verses concerning the absence of the sense of "mine" (*mamatva*) and the illumination of the world as an object of knowledge have their meaning already explained in sequence.
"Just as the obscuration of the sun’s rays is considered to be clouds and the like, so too the obscuration of the Buddhas’ gnosis is the corruption of sentient beings. (MSA 9.34)
Just as clouds and other obstructions prevent the rays [of the sun] from shining,
so too do the obscurations of the Buddhas' gnosis arise from sentient beings' lack of being suitable vessels and their corruption due to the extreme prevalence of the five degenerations.
Just as the presence or absence of variegated colors on a cloth depends upon the dust [upon it].
Likewise, through the power of that penetration, there arises the diversity or lack of diversity in the knowledge of those liberated.
Just as the variegation of colors on a cloth occurs through a particular kind of dye, while in some cases there is no such variegation,
so too, due to the specific power of the application of their previous vows and conduct, there is a variety of knowledge in the liberation of the Buddhas,
whereas in the liberation of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas there is no such variety.
The profundity of the Buddhas regarding the stainless realm, its characteristics, its abiding, and its activity, has been described as being like painting the sky with colors. (MSA 9.36)
Thus, the threefold profundity of the Buddhas in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) has been explained.
Profundity of characteristics is shown by four verses;
profundity of state (*sthāna-gāmbhīrya*) is shown by the fifth verse, because [the Buddha] does not abide in either unity or multiplicity.
The profundity of activity is [explained] by means of ten [points].

Furthermore, that profundity of characteristics is taught with reference to the characteristic of purity, the characteristic of the supreme self, the characteristic of the indeterminate, and the characteristic of liberation.

The profundity of activity consists of the activity of being the locus for the jewels of the factors of enlightenment and so forth, the activity of maturing sentient beings, and the activity of reaching the ultimate consummation.

This has been taught with reference to the activity of teaching the Dharma, the activity of performing deeds such as emanations, the activity of the engagement of gnosis, the activity of non-conceptuality, the activity of gnosis in its various forms, the activity of the non-engagement of gnosis, and the activity of the distinction of gnosis that is common to liberation.

This exposition of the distinctions of profundity within the untainted realm— which, because it is free from conceptual proliferation, is like space— should be understood as being like painting pictures in the sky with colors.
Although suchness is undifferentiated for all, when it has attained purity, it is the state of a Tathāgata; therefore, all embodied beings possess that as their embryo (tadgarbha).

Suchness is undifferentiated in all things, and the Tathāgata has that very purity as his intrinsic nature; therefore, it is said that "all sentient beings possess the embryo of the Tathāgata" (*tathāgatagarbha*). There are eleven verses in the section on the analysis of mastery (*vibhutva*).
By the mastery of the Śrāvakas, that of worldly beings is surpassed;
by the mind belonging to the level of the Pratyekabuddhas, that of the Śrāvaka is surpassed.
The sovereign power of a bodhisattva does not approach even a fraction of that;
the sovereign power of a Tathāgata does not approach even a fraction of that.
By means of these two verses, he demonstrates the sovereignty (*vibhutva*) of the Buddhas through the excellence of their preeminent power:
"The sovereignty of a Buddha is held to be immeasurable and inconceivable;
it proceeds in whatever [place], toward whatever [object], in whatever manner, to whatever extent, and at whatever time. (MSA 9.40)
By this third [verse], through the distinctions of its modes and its profundity, he explains how it is immeasurable or how it is inconceivable:
for which person it proceeds, in which world-system, in what manner, by such modes as these, to whatever extent—whether little or much—and at what time.
With the remaining verses, he demonstrates the distinction of mastery (*vibhutva*) through the distinction of the transformation of the mind (*manas*).
Upon the transformation of the five faculties, supreme mastery is attained,
whereby all [faculties] function toward all objects and there arises the manifestation of twelve hundred qualities.
Upon the transformation of the five faculties, two kinds of supreme mastery are obtained:
[mastery] over the functioning of all five faculties with respect to all five types of objects.
In that regard, when one hundred and twelve qualities arise for each [of the sense faculties],
and when the mind also undergoes transformation, supreme mastery is attained in the non-conceptual, perfectly pure gnosis that accompanies that mastery. (MSA 9.42)
Upon the revolution of the mind, supreme mastery is attained in the non-conceptual, perfectly pure gnosis that accompanies mastery;
accompanied by this, all gnosis of mastery proceeds.
Upon the revolution of the grasping of objects and subjects, supreme mastery is attained.
Indeed, for the sake of purifying the field, it is for the purpose of manifesting enjoyments according to one's desire.

Upon the transformation of the object and the transformation of the grasping, the supreme mastery over the purification of the field is attained, by which one manifests enjoyments according to one's desire.
Upon the transformation of conceptual construction, the supreme mastery is attained, such that all cognitions and activities are at all times unimpeded. (MSA 9.44)
Upon the revolution of conceptual construction, supreme mastery is attained at all times in the non-obstruction of all cognitions and actions.
Upon the revolution of the basis, supreme mastery is attained:
the non-abiding nirvāṇa of the Buddhas in the immovable and stainless state.
Upon the revolution of the basis, supreme mastery is attained: non-abiding nirvana within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*) of the Buddhas;
and upon the revolution of sexual union, supreme mastery is attained.
Furthermore, [this occurs] when dwelling in the bliss of the Buddhas, and when seeing that there is no affliction regarding a wife.

Upon the transformation of sexual intercourse, in the two states of the Buddha’s blissful abiding and the vision of the wife without defilement, upon the reversal of the perception of space, supreme mastery is attained, as well as in the fulfillment of intended aims and in the manifestation of movement and form. (MSA 9.47)
When the perception of space is overturned, there is the fulfillment of the two intended purposes by which one becomes a "Womb of Space" (*gaganagarbha*);
and through the differentiation of movement and form, because of traveling at will and because of bringing [all things] under mastery,
such immeasurable transformation is considered immeasurable sovereignty.
In the stainless basis of the Buddhas, there is the performance of inconceivable activities.
By this means, the transformation is immeasurable.
Furthermore, within that untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of the Buddhas, immeasurable mastery and the performance of inconceivable activities should be understood.
There are seven verses concerning the fact that this very Buddha acts for the sake of maturing sentient beings:
"The world, having increased in virtue, proceeds toward supreme purity;
and by not desisting from virtue, it proceeds toward the supremacy of the increase of virtue."
Thus the world proceeds in every direction through the well-spoken teachings of the Victors; whether unripened or ripened, it does not, moreover, certainly reach total exhaustion here.
By this, he shows what kind of maturation serves as the cause:
for those who have accumulated roots of merit, it leads to the supreme state of liberation; and for those who have not accumulated roots of merit, it leads to the accumulation of roots of merit.

One who is unripe, by attaining the supreme state through the increase of virtue, proceeds toward ripening; one who is ripe, by attaining the supreme state through complete purification, proceeds toward [the ultimate goal].

And thus he proceeds eternally, yet never reaches an end because of the infinity of the world. Having practiced such a course of conduct— which is difficult to attain, endowed with supreme qualities, and marvelous—
he attains great enlightenment, which is eternal, stable, and a refuge for those who are without refuge.
That which the wise always obtain in every direction and at all times—that is a marvel in the world; yet, because they practice their conduct so well, it is not a wonder.
By this second [verse], the quality of being neither marvelous nor non-marvelous regarding the maturation of fully matured bodhisattvas is characterized.
"Always at all times" means constantly and uninterruptedly; practicing the path that consists of experiencing that [maturation] is the practice of the excellent method.
In some cases, he displays the wheel of Dharma through hundreds of diverse gateways.
In some places the disappearance of birth, in others the various activities of beings; in some places complete enlightenment, and in others nirvana repeatedly—
yet he does not waver from that state, and yet he performs all these deeds.

By this third [verse], he demonstrates the state of being a causal sign (*nimittatva*) in the application of the means for maturing many [beings] through various gates simultaneously; namely, how, remaining in whatever place, he disciplines sentient beings through various modes of conduct (*janacarī*) distinguished by the *jātaka* tales.
And he does not move from his station, that is, from the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
It does not occur to the Buddhas: "This person has been ripened by me," nor "This embodied being is yet to be ripened," nor even "He is being ripened right now."
Yet, even without such cultivation, the multitude of beings constantly reaches full maturity through virtuous qualities in every direction, everywhere, and in all three ways.
By this fourth [verse], he shows that the cause for the application of that maturation is through non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
"The three gates" refers to the three vehicles (*yāna-traya*).
Just as the sun, by its widespread and pure rays of light, brings about the ripening of crops everywhere in every direction without effort,
so too does the Sun of Dharma, by means of the swift rays of the teachings on the method of pacification.
It brings about the ripening of the crops in every direction, on all sides.
By this fifth [verse], he demonstrates the simile of ripening without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*):
just as from a single lamp there arises a vast collection of lamps, immeasurable and incalculable, yet that [original lamp] does not undergo exhaustion thereby.
In the same way, from a single Buddha, there arises a vast accumulation of maturation—immeasurable and incalculable—and yet it does not undergo exhaustion. (MSA 9.54)
By this sixth [verse], maturation through a continuous succession is shown:
just as the great ocean does not reach satiety nor undergo increase, even as vast and pure waters enter it.
Likewise, the Buddha-element never reaches satiety or increase through the constant and continuous influxes of purity; this is a supreme wonder here.

By this seventh [verse], through the illustration of the ocean regarding the entry into liberation for those who are fully matured, it is shown that the *dharmadhātu* is neither satiated because it provides space for all things, nor does it increase because there is no addition to its meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
There are four verses concerning the purification of the *dharmadhātu*:
"It has the characteristic of the purity of suchness, which is free from the two obscurations regarding all phenomena."
It is characterized by the inexhaustibility of mastery over the knowledge of things and its objective support.
This is one verse concerning the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It has the characteristic of the purification of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena from the two obscurations— those of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the knowable (*jñeya*)—
and it has the characteristic of the inexhaustible mastery over both the object and the knowledge that takes it as its objective support.
The realization consists in the cultivation of the knowledge of suchness in every respect;
its fruit is the inexhaustibility in every way of the two benefits bestowed upon all sentient beings.
This second verse is undertaken with reference to the meaning of the cause and the meaning of the fruit.
The cultivation of the knowledge of suchness in every respect is the cause for the purification of the *dharmadhātu*.
"In every respect" means by way of all the various approaches to the teachings (*dharma-paryāya-mukha*).
The fruit is the inexhaustibility of bestowing both benefit and happiness upon all sentient beings in every way;
its activity consists of the application of means through the emanations of body, speech, and mind.
Endowed with the two immeasurables: the gate of meditative concentration and the gate of mnemonic formulas (dhāraṇī).
This third verse is undertaken with reference to the meaning of activity (*karman*) and the meaning of yoga (*yoga*).

The threefold emanation of body and so forth is activity; possession of the two—namely, the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*)—as well as the immeasurable accumulations of merit (*puṇya*) and gnosis (*jñāna*), is yoga.
It functions through distinct modes by way of the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), and the emanation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
This purity of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is proclaimed as belonging to the Buddhas.
This is the fourth verse, undertaken for the sake of explaining the functional activity (*vṛtti*).
It possesses distinct modes of activity through the natural (*svābhāvika*), enjoyment (*sāṃbhogika*), and emanation (*nairmāṇika*) bodies.
There are seven verses in the section on the classification of the Buddha-bodies.

The bodies of the Buddhas are indeed divided into three: the essential body (svābhāvika-kāya), the enjoyment body (sāṃbhogya-kāya), and another, the transformation body (nairmāṇika-kāya); yet the first is the basis for the other two.
The bodies of the Buddhas are threefold:

the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), which is the *dharma*-body characterized by the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); and the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*), by means of which one enjoys the Dharma within the circles of assemblies (*parṣanmaṇḍala*).
The emanation body (nairmāṇika) is that by which one performs the welfare of sentient beings through emanations.
The enjoyment body (sāṃbhogya) in all realms is differentiated by its assemblies, fields, names, bodies, and activities for the enjoyment of the Dharma. (MSA 9.61)
In that regard, the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*) is differentiated in all world-systems by its circles of assembly, Buddha-fields, names, bodies, enjoyments of the Dharma, and activities.

The essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) is considered equal and subtle, being the remainder of that [enjoyment body]. It is the cause for the mastery of enjoyment, in that it displays enjoyments according to one's wish. (MSA 9.62)
The essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) of all Buddhas is equal because it is without distinction;
it is subtle because it is difficult to know.
It is connected with the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogikakāya*) and is the cause for the mastery of enjoyment, so that enjoyment may be displayed according to one's wish.
The immeasurable emanation of the Buddha is considered the nirmāṇakāya;
in it, the accomplishment of the two purposes for both [self and others] is established in all its aspects.

The emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*) of the Buddhas consists of immeasurable varieties of Buddha-emanations. The enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika*) is characterized by the perfection of one's own welfare, while the emanation body is characterized by the perfection of the welfare of others.
Thus, the perfection of these two aims is established respectively in the two bodies: the enjoyment body and the emanation body.
Through the display of craftsmanship, birth, great enlightenment, and constant nirvāṇa, this emanation body of the Buddha is a great illusion [a great skillful means] for liberation. (MSA 9.64)

Furthermore, that emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) should be understood as characterized by the fulfillment of the welfare of others, because it serves as a great means for liberation by constantly displaying craftsmanship— such as playing the lute— for the sake of those to be trained, as well as by displaying birth, perfect enlightenment, and parinirvāṇa. The summary of the bodies of the Buddhas should be known through these three bodies.
The welfare of oneself and others, together with their basis, is that which is demonstrated by means of the three bodies.
It should be understood that the entirety of the bodies of the Buddhas is subsumed within these three bodies.
By means of these three bodies, the welfare of oneself and others, together with their basis, is demonstrated;
for two [of these bodies] are characterized by the welfare of oneself and others, while the other two are based upon them, as previously stated.
They are considered equal in terms of their basis, their intention, and their action;
their permanence is found in their nature, their non-interruption, and their continuity.

And these three bodies of all Buddhas are, respectively, without distinction in three respects: by way of their basis, because the *dharmadhātu* is indivisible; and by way of their intention, because there is no separate intention among the Buddhas.

And because they share a commonality of karma, one should understand that within those three bodies there is a threefold permanence, respectively, by which the Tathāgatas are said to possess permanent bodies: the permanence of nature, because the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) is permanent by its very essence; [the permanence of continuity, because the enjoyment body (*sambhogika-kāya*) is uninterrupted]; and [the permanence of transformation, because the emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*) manifests in various forms].
Through non-laxity, because there is no interruption in the enjoyment of the Dharma by the *sāmbhogika* [body];
and through continuity, because the *nairmāṇika* [body], despite its internal disappearance, repeatedly manifests emanations.
There are ten verses on the classification of the Buddha-knowledge.
Mirror-like wisdom is immovable; the other three wisdoms are based upon it:
namely, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of discernment, and the wisdom of accomplishing activities.

The wisdom of the Buddhas is fourfold: the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna), the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna), the wisdom of discernment (pratyavekṣājñāna), and the wisdom of accomplishing activities (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna).
The mirror-like wisdom is immovable, while the other three wisdoms are mobile and dependent upon it.
The mirror-like wisdom is undivided by objects and is ever-present.
It is not deluded regarding any objects of knowledge, yet it is never directed toward them.
The mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) is undivided spatially and ever-present temporally;
it is unconfused regarding all objects of knowledge due to the perpetual absence of obscurations,
yet it does not face toward them because it is formless.
Because it is the cause of all knowledge, the state of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogabuddhatā*) is like a great mine of wisdom; and because the reflections of wisdom arise therein, it is so compared.
Because it is the cause of all types of those knowledges, such as the knowledge of equality and so forth, it is like a mine for all knowledges;
and because the reflection of that knowledge arises from the state of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-buddhatva*), it is called the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
The knowledge of equality toward sentient beings is considered stainless due to the purity of cultivation;
this knowledge of equality is held to be entered into a non-abiding tranquility.

The knowledge of equality that a bodhisattva has acquired at the times of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding sentient beings is intended as the "knowledge of equality" once he has attained awakening; through the purification of its cultivation, it is established in non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).

Furthermore, it is considered to be accompanied by great loving-kindness and compassion at all times, manifesting the image of the Buddha to sentient beings according to their respective inclinations.
It is accompanied by great loving-kindness and compassion at all times, and manifests the form of a Buddha to sentient beings according to their inclinations;
for some sentient beings see the Tathāgata as blue in color, while others see him as yellow, and so forth. The wisdom of discernment is always unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge.
And it is indeed like a treasure-store of dhāraṇīs and samādhis.
It displays all sovereign powers within the circle of the assembly,
cuts through all doubts, and rains down the great Dharma.
Discriminative wisdom is as described in the verse.
Wisdom in the performance of duties acts for the benefit of all sentient beings through emanations that are manifold, immeasurable, and inconceivable throughout all realms.

The knowledge of performing what is to be done consists in accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings through immeasurable and inconceivable emanations of various kinds in all world-systems. That inconceivable Buddha-emanation is to be understood in every respect as being constant, distinguished by the completion of tasks, and differentiated by number and fields. (MSA 9.75)
Furthermore, that emanation of the Buddha should be understood as always and in every way inconceivable,
by way of its variety of activities, its number, and its fields; because it sustains [beings], because of its evenness of mind, and because of its correct proclamation of the Dharma.
And from the performance of duties, there arises the emergence of the four types of knowledge.
In this context, "retention" refers to the retention of the teachings (dharmas) that have been heard.
"Equanimity of mind" toward all sentient beings arises from the equality of self and others.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.

(50) There is a verse concerning the non-multiplicity and non-distinctness of the Buddhas: Because of the distinction of lineages, because of non-futility, because of completeness, and also because of beginninglessness;
Because there is no distinction, there is neither the state of a single Buddha nor multiplicity within the stainless basis.
It is not accepted that there is only one Buddha.
For what reason?
Because of the diversity of lineages (*gotra*).
For sentient beings belonging to the Buddha-lineage are indeed infinite.
