In that case, how could it be that only one has attained perfect awakening and others will not attain perfect awakening?
Furthermore, there would be the futility of the accumulations of merit and wisdom for other bodhisattvas if they were not to attain perfect awakening; yet such futility is not tenable.

Therefore, for the sake of avoiding futility as well, there cannot be only one Buddha, nor would there be the complete fulfillment of the welfare of sentient beings. Furthermore, it is not logical that a Buddha, in his state of Buddhahood, would not establish anyone else in Buddhahood; nor is there any such thing as a "primordial Buddha," because Buddhahood is impossible without the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*), and those accumulations are impossible without another Buddha. Thus, due to its beginninglessness (*anāditva*), it is also illogical for there to be only one Buddha.
Even plurality is not admitted for the Buddhas in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), because the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is undifferentiated.
There are four verses on entering the means to Buddhahood:
that which is non-existence is itself the supreme existence.
And the non-perception of all things is considered the supreme perception.
That which is non-existence by way of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is itself the supreme existence by way of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

And that which is the absolute non-perception of the imagined nature is itself the supreme perception of the perfected nature. Cultivation is considered supreme for those who do not perceive cultivation.
The attainment of others is desired for those who do not perceive [their own] attainment.
That very non-apprehension of cultivation is the supreme cultivation;
that very non-apprehension of attainment is the supreme attainment.
For those who perceive it, there is the weightiness of that [cultivation], its long duration, its causal sign, and their own vigor.
For conceited bodhisattvas, awakening is said to be far away.
And those who perceive Buddhahood as something weighty, endowed with marvelous qualities;
who perceive it as requiring a long period of time for its full realization; and who perceive the causal signs that serve as the objective support for the mind.

And thinking, "By our own vigor, having initiated diligence, we shall attain Buddhahood," for those conceited Bodhisattvas who are characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*), awakening is said to be far off. Behold: all this that has been described is merely conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*).
For Bodhisattvas who are beyond conceptual construction, awakening is described as being attained.

However, for those who perceive that all this is merely a wholesome conceptualization (*kalpanāmātra*), because they do not conceptualize even that mere conceptualization, it is said that for non-conceptualizing Bodhisattvas— at the stage when they have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)— enlightenment is effectively attained in reality.

There are four verses concerning the fact that the Buddhas have a single common purpose for one another: Rivers that have not entered the subterranean realm (pātāla) have distinct bases, distinct waters, small amounts of water, and perform separate functions; they provide only limited enjoyment for the living beings dwelling in their waters. (MSA 9.82)
And once they have entered the ocean, they all become a single support and one great body of water;
unified in their activity, they are always a source of great enjoyment for the multitude of beings that depend upon the waters.

Those steadfast ones who have not yet entered into Buddhahood have diverse bases and diverse views; their awakening is slight, their personal activities are separate, and they are always available for the benefit of limited beings. MSA 9.84.
And having entered into Buddhahood, they all become based on a single foundation and possess a single great awakening;
they perform their activities in common and are always a source of great enjoyment for the multitude of Great Beings.
In that regard, the rivers have distinct bases because their respective vessels (beds) are different;
they perform distinct functions because they carry out their activities separately;
and they are "enjoyed by the thin" because they are enjoyed by few.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
There is a verse regarding the encouragement toward Buddhahood:
"Thus, because of the possession of incomparable pure qualities and because the stage of Buddhahood is the cause of benefit and happiness..."
Because it produces auspiciousness, supreme happiness, and inexhaustibility, one of virtuous mind deserves to attain the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Because it is endowed with incomparable pure qualities, because it is the perfection of one's own welfare,
and because it is the cause of benefit and happiness for others, Buddhahood is the perfection of the welfare of others;
and because it is a source of faultless, supreme, and inexhaustible bliss, it is specifically a dwelling in happiness.
The wise person, in order to take up the bodhicitta that is free from pride, should do so by embracing the vow for it.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on Enlightenment, in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra.
The tenth chapter: Summary Verse.
The beginning, accomplishment, refuge, lineage, and likewise the production of the thought [of awakening];
the welfare of self and others, the meaning of reality, spiritual power, maturation, and awakening. (MSA 10.1)
And this section on awakening (bodhy-adhikāra) is to be followed from the beginning up to the chapter on awakening (bodhi-paṭala).
There are two verses concerning the classification of the characteristics of the different types of resolute belief (adhimukti-prabheda-lakṣaṇa-vibhāga):

It is that which has arisen, that which has not yet arisen, that which is the grasper, that which has become the grasped, that which is received from a friend, that which is [grasped] by oneself, and that which is erroneous.
One is unerring and another is manifest; one proceeds from sound, while others are seeking and examining.
That which has arisen is past and present;
that which has not yet arisen is future.
That which is grasping is internal, by means of which one resolves upon an object.
That which has become an object of apprehension is external; it is resolved upon as an objective support (*ālambana*). That which is received from a friend is coarse;
that which [is derived] from oneself is subtle.
That which is erroneous is inferior because of its mistaken resolve; that which is non-erroneous is sublime. That which is manifest is proximate because its conditions are fully assembled.
That which is not manifest is distant because it is the opposite;
that which functions through sound consists of hearing;
that which seeks consists of reflection.
Resolute belief (*adhimukti*) consists of that which is based on vision and that which consists of cultivation; it is characterized by discernment.

It is removable or unremovable, interspersed with or not interspersed with opposing factors (*vipakṣa*), inferior or sublime, obscured or unobscured, appropriate or inappropriate, accumulated or unaccumulated, deeply entered, and far-reaching. (MSA 10.3)
That which is susceptible to being carried away is weak; that which is interspersed with opposing factors is middling;
that which is not interspersed with opposing factors is superior.
It is inferior in the other vehicle,
sublime in the Great Vehicle,
and obscured and obstructed regarding the attainment of excellence.
"Unobstructed" means being free from hindrances;
"properly applied" means through constant and respectful practice; "improperly applied" means being devoid of those qualities.
That which is "accumulated" is suitable for realization; that which is "unaccumulated" is the opposite. That which is "firmly entered" has entered the [spiritual] stages (*bhūmi*).
[They] go far in the remaining stages. Regarding the obstacles to resolute belief (*adhimukti*), there are three verses:
"Excessive lack of mental attention (*amanasikāra*), laziness (*kauśīdya*), and error in yoga (*yogavibhrama*)."
A bad friend, weakness of virtue, and improper mental attention.
For that which has arisen, an abundance of non-attention is the obstacle;
for that which has not yet arisen, laziness is the obstacle;
and for that which consists of the grasped and the grasper, the error of yoga is the obstacle.
It is likewise due to attachment; for that which is received from a friend becomes [a cause of harm] through a bad friend,
because of grasping it erroneously.
The weakness of the roots of virtue arises from lack of conviction in one's own self.
For that which is non-erroneous, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is the obstacle, because it is antagonistic to it.
(MSA_Bagchi 53)
Heedlessness, limited learning, contentment with little hearing and reflection, pride in mere tranquility, and likewise a lack of mastery are considered [the obstacles].
Negligence pertains to that which is manifest,
because it is produced by non-negligence;
lack of learning pertains to that which follows the sound [of instruction].
Due to not hearing sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*),
there is for the seeker (*eṣikā*) contentment with mere hearing and contentment with limited reflection;
and for the investigator (*īkṣikā*), contentment with mere reflection and the conceit of having attained mere tranquility (*śamatha*).
Lack of mastery over what is to be taken away and what is interspersed is an obstacle;
likewise, lack of agitation, agitation, turning back,
lack of application, and lack of accumulation should be known as obstacles to resolute belief.
Lack of revulsion toward the inferior [vehicle] regarding cyclic existence;
revulsion toward the sublime [vehicle]; obscuration regarding the unobscured;
and lack of application regarding that which is properly applied.
The obstacle to that which has been accumulated is non-accumulation.
There are five verses regarding the benefits of resolute belief:
there is great merit, freedom from remorse, joy, and great happiness.
Non-perishing, stability, and likewise the non-attainment of distinction.
The clear realization of the Dharma, the attainment of the supreme welfare of oneself and others,
and the possession of swift super-knowledge— these indeed are the benefits arising from resolute belief.
When it has arisen and is present, there is great merit;
when it is past, there is freedom from remorse because of the absence of regret.
When it is in the state of grasping and that which is grasped, there is great mental well-being due to the application of meditative concentration.
Non-loss when [insight] is produced by a spiritual friend;
stability in one's own resolute conviction; and, within the non-erroneous, the manifest, and the stages beginning with that consisting of hearing, progress toward excellence up to the middling stage.
In the superior [level], there is the clear realization of the Dharma;
in the inferior, the attainment of one's own welfare;
and in the sublime, the supreme attainment of the welfare of others.
The benefit of swift super-knowledge (*abhijñā*) is found in those belonging to the white side who are unobstructed, disciplined, and have accumulated merit.
Among those with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), that [concentration] of those possessing desire is like a dog; it is like a tortoise for those seeking their own welfare;
it is like a servant for those seeking their own benefit; and it is like a king for those seeking the welfare of others. (MSA 10.9)
Just as a dog afflicted by suffering is constantly unsatisfied and hungry; just as that tortoise is huddled within its hole in the water;
just as a servant wanders about with a body perpetually cowering;
and just as a king exercises his power over the domain of his commands.
Thus he dwells;

likewise, the distinction should be understood as being constant through various forms of resolute belief (*adhimukti*) regarding those who abide in sensual desire, those who abide in the truth, and those who act for the sake of others.
Having understood that this [faith] is supreme in the Mahāyāna according to the prescribed rule,
the steadfast one should here always choose those very two [faiths] within it with great intensity.

Furthermore, the resolve of those who possess desire is like a dog; that of those who have attained worldly meditative concentration is like a tortoise; that of those who act for their own benefit is like a servant; and that of those who act for the benefit of others is like a king.
Having established this very point through further reasoning, he encourages others toward faith in the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the refutation of the deficiency of faith, there are these verses:
"Those who have become human beings attain awakening at every moment."
Since sentient beings are immeasurable, one should therefore not tolerate despondency.
For three reasons, dissolution is not logical:
because those who have become human beings attain awakening,
and they attain it eternally.
And they attain immeasurable [merit]. There are two verses regarding the distinction of the merit of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-puṇya-viśeṣaṇa*):
"Just as one generates merit by giving food to others..."
But he who eats himself does not experience such a great arising of merit.
That which is declared in the Sūtras is obtained from the Dharma taught for the sake of others;
it is not, however, obtained from the Dharma taught for one's own sake.
Just as merit arises for one who gives food because it is directed toward the welfare of others,
but not for one who eats it himself because it is directed toward his own welfare;
likewise, from the Mahāyāna Dharma taught based on the welfare of others, a great arising of merit as described in those various Mahāyāna sūtras is obtained.
But it is not [taught] from the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle, which is taught based on one’s own self-interest.
There is a verse regarding the acquisition of the fruit of resolute belief:
"Having produced [or caused others to produce] [resolute belief] toward the Dharma that is a great flood in its vast course..."
The wise one always attains great resolute faith,
the vast and constant increase of merit, and through incomparable qualities, the state of a Great Being.
In whatever way and by means of whichever kind of resolute belief one grasps a particular result:
within the extensive Mahāyāna Dharma, by means of that noble resolute belief which brings about non-retrogression and full realization, the wise person grasps a threefold result.

The vast increase of merit, the increase of that very same resolute belief (*adhimukti*), and the state of being a Great Being with incomparable qualities—namely, Buddhahood—resulting from those causes.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, "Resolute Belief," in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The eleventh chapter: On the Search for the Dharma. Within the section on the search for the Dharma, there are four verses concerning the search for the objective support (*ālambana*).
The three baskets, or alternatively two,
are accepted as being comprised by nine reasons;
they bring about liberation through the processes of perfuming, awakening, pacifying, and penetrating.
The three baskets (*piṭakatraya*) are the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;
these same three become two by way of the distinction between the Hīnayāna and the Mahāyāna.
The Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Furthermore, for what reason are these three, or these two, called "piṭaka"? He says:
It should be understood as a summary because it summarizes all objects of knowledge.
For what reason are there three?
By way of nine reasons.
The Sūtra is the antidote to doubt, because it is taught for the purpose of providing certainty to one who is uncertain regarding a particular meaning.

The Vinaya is the antidote to the pursuit of the two extremes: by prohibiting the enjoyment of what is blameworthy, it serves as the antidote to the extreme of devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires; and by [prescribing] the use of what is permissible, it serves as the antidote to the extreme of self-mortification.
The Abhidharma exists as an antidote to the extreme of devotion to self-mortification, by authorizing blameless enjoyment;
it is the Abhidharma because it illuminates the characteristics of phenomena without error.

Furthermore, the Sūtra teaches the three trainings, while the Vinaya effects the accomplishment of higher ethics and higher mind, since one who possesses ethical discipline is free from remorse, and through the sequence beginning with freedom from remorse, one attains meditative concentration.
The Abhidharma is for the accomplishment of higher wisdom, because it discerns the meaning of things without error.
Furthermore, the teaching of the Dharma and its meaning is through the Sūtra;
and the realization of the Dharma and its meaning is through the Vinaya, because one who is engaged in the subduing of the afflictions penetrates both of them.
Skill in the definitive determination of discussions concerning the Dharma and its meaning is achieved through the Abhidharma.
For these nine reasons, the three baskets (piṭaka) are intended;
and they are for the purpose of liberation from saṃsāra.
How, then, does it liberate that?
It liberates it through perfuming, awakening, pacifying, and penetrating;
by means of hearing, there is perfuming of the mind.
Through reflection, by means of awakening;
through cultivation, by means of calming (*śamatha*) through pacification;
and through insight (*vipaśyanā*), by means of penetration.
In brief, the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya are considered to have four types of meaning;
through knowledge of them, the wise person attains omniscience in all its aspects.

Furthermore, these—the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—each have fourfold meanings in brief; by knowing them, a bodhisattva attains omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), whereas a śrāvaka, by understanding the meaning of even a single verse, attains the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
It is called *sūtra* because it indicates [the truth] by way of its basis, its characteristics, its phenomena, and its meaning.
Furthermore, it is called Abhidharma because it is directed toward [the truth], because of its frequency, and because it overcomes [the afflictions].
How does each [term] have a fourfold meaning?
It is called *sūtra* because it indicates the basis (*āśraya*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the phenomena (*dharma*), and the meaning (*artha*).
In this context, the basis (*āśraya*) refers to the place where it was taught, by whom it was taught, and for whom it was taught.
The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) consists of the characteristic of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtti-satya*) and the characteristic of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The phenomena (*dharma*) include the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), nutriments (*āhāra*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth.
The meaning is the underlying intention (*anusaṃdhi*).
Abhidharma is to be understood as such because it is directed toward [the goal], because it is frequent, because it overcomes, and because it approaches;
that is, the Dharma directed toward Nirvana is Abhidharma, consisting of the truths, the factors conducive to awakening, and the liberations.

Because it teaches [the nature of] phenomena (*dharma*); because it is the *Abhidharma* as it frequently provides extensive explanations of each phenomenon through various distinctions such as being material or immaterial, visible or invisible;
and because it is the *Abhidharma* as it "overcomes" (*abhibhavati*), since it overcomes the doctrines of others through means such as formal debate and legal adjudication.
Abhidharma is so called because by means of it the meaning of the Sūtras is approached.
It is Vinaya because of [its treatment of] offenses, their origination, emergence from them, and deliverance from them;
and also because of [its treatment of] persons, their designation, their classification, and their determination. (MSA 11.4)
It should be understood in terms of the offense, its origination, its emergence, and its removal.
In this context, the offense consists of the five classes of offenses.
The origination of offenses occurs through ignorance, negligence, abundance of afflictions, and lack of respect.
Emergence is by way of intention, not by way of punitive action.
There are seven kinds of deliverance:
confession, and so forth.
The formal undertaking [of the training] by those who have been granted the training (śikṣādattaka) and others; the infliction of disciplinary measures (daṇḍakarma);
and the communal assembly (samavadyota).

Relaxation [of the training] occurs because, after a training rule has been prescribed, it is subsequently permitted again; relaxation by the entire Saṃgha occurs through the rescinding of a training rule.

Transformation of the basis occurs when there is a change of sexual characteristics from female to male or male to female among monks and nuns, whereby an offense that was specific [to one gender] ceases to apply.
The examination of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) consists of the remainder of the examination by means of the categories of the summaries of the Dharma (*dharmoddāna*).

Furthermore, there is the attainment of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatāpratilambha*) through the vision of the truths, because of the attainment of the true nature of phenomena when there is no occurrence of minor or very minor offenses.
Moreover, the Vinaya should be understood through four kinds of meanings.
In terms of the person: that based upon which the training is prescribed;
in terms of the prescription: when, upon the report of a person's transgression, the Teacher assembles the Saṃgha and prescribes the training.
From the perspective of classification, it is the detailed analysis of the summary of the prescribed training rules;
and from the perspective of determination, it is the definitive resolution regarding how an offense occurs therein, or how there is no offense.
Regarding the search for the attainment of the objective, there are three verses.
The object of focus is considered to be the dharmas, both internal and external;
the attainment of the two is through the meaning of the two, and by means of the non-apprehension of the two.
The objective support of phenomena (*dharmālambana*) is that which has been taught as internal, such as the body and so forth, external, and both internal and external.

Among these, the internal—consisting of the body and so forth—is the nature of the grasper (*grāhaka*), while the external is the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*). The suchness (*tathatā*) of those two is the non-duality.
Therein, the attainment of the two objects—the internal and the external—is achieved through the meaning of non-duality, respectively.
If one perceives the object of apprehension as non-different from the subject of apprehension, and the subject of apprehension as non-different from the object of apprehension,
then the attainment of the suchness (*tathatā*) of the totality of both— the internal and external objects of focus— should be understood to arise from the non-apprehension of those very two.

Through mental discursive thoughts, through the sustained application of one who has faith in the meaning as it has been explained, through the appearance of the object from discursive thought, and through the mind's abiding in the name.
The attainment of the objective support of the Dharma occurs through the three types of knowledge, such as that derived from hearing;
and the previously mentioned threefold attainment of objective supports is based upon that.
Furthermore, the attainment of the objective support of the Dharma occurs through three types of knowledge consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

Among these, for one who has faith in the meaning as it was explained through mental verbalizations with a concentrated mind, there is the attainment [of that objective support] by means of fixing upon it;
thus, its attainment is through knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*).
"By mental chatter" means by conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*).
"Of one who is serene" means of one who is resolved and certain. "By sustained application" means by thorough investigation (*pravicaya*).

Through the sustained attention (*pradhāraṇā*) on the manifestation of objects from verbal discourse (*jalpa*), that [attainment] is acquired by means of knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*).

If one perceives that this object manifests solely from mental discourse (*manojalpa*) and nothing other than mental discourse— as was stated regarding the attainment of the twofold objective support—

then it should be understood that its acquisition is by means of knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), due to the mind’s abiding in the name, because of the non-perception of duality, as was stated regarding the attainment of the twofold objective support.
Therefore, that previously mentioned threefold attainment of the object of focus should be understood as being dependent upon the attainment of the dharma as an object.
There are five verses concerning the search for mental attention (*manasikāra*):
"That which belongs to the three realms, that which performs its function, and another which has a basis characterized by confinement."
Furthermore, another [type of person] is one who is established in resolute faith and possesses intense aspiration.
The basis is twofold, being either deficient or complete; it consists of both discursive speech and non-discursiveness, and is associated with gnosis, having the nature of the secret essence of yoga.
This [object] is both unified and differentiated;
it is fivefold and sevenfold, and its thorough knowledge is likewise fivefold.
The thirty-seven aspects pertaining to cultivation constitute the nature of these two paths; they possess a twofold benefit and are receptive.
The preparatory, the sovereign, the limited, and that which is vast in nature—
this attention (manaskāra) of yogins is considered to be of every kind.

Mental attention is of eighteen kinds: that which is determined by the realm (*dhātu*), that which performs its function, that which is distinguished by its basis, that which establishes resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), that which generates desire, that which relies on concentration (*samādhi*),

that which is associated with knowledge (*jñāna*), that which has a combined object, that which has a distinct object, that which is determined by thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), and that which has entered into the modes of cultivation (*bhāvanākāra*).

The nature of the path of calm abiding and special insight consists of: the mental engagement of benefit, the receptive mental engagement, the preparatory mental engagement, the mental engagement of mastery, the limited mental engagement, and the extensive mental engagement.
Among these, that which is "determined by realm" is that which is determined by the lineage (gotra) of the śrāvakas and so forth.
That which performs the function is that which possesses the accumulated requisites.
That which is distinguished by its basis is that which has as its basis the household life with its constraints and the life of renunciation free from constraints.
That which establishes resolute conviction is that which is accompanied by the recollection of the Buddha.

That which generates desire is that which is accompanied by conviction in it; that which is based on meditative concentration is that which is accompanied by the preparatory and fundamental concentrations, whether with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*),
without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-savicāra*), or without both applied and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*).
And it is accompanied by measure, applied thought, and sustained thought;

it is associated with knowledge, being the secret essence of yoga and accompanied by yoga; furthermore, it consists respectively of that which is produced by hearing, that which is produced by reflection, and that which is produced by cultivation.

The mixed object (*saṃbhinnālambana*) is fivefold: having as its object the discourses (*sūtra*), the summaries (*uddāna*), the verses (*gāthā*), the prose passages (*nipāta*), and that which has been memorized and taught.

The distinct object (*vibhinnālambana*) is sevenfold: having as its object names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), phonemes (*vyañjana*), the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), material phenomena (*rūpi-dharma*), and immaterial phenomena (*arūpi-dharma*). Among these, that which has material phenomena as its object is that which has the body (*kāya*) as its object.
That which has formless phenomena as its object is that which has feeling, mind, and mental factors as its objects.

That which is determined by full comprehension pertains to the thing to be fully comprehended, the meaning to be fully comprehended, the full comprehension itself, the fruit of full comprehension, and the realization thereof.
In this context, the thing to be fully comprehended is suffering; the meaning to be fully comprehended is the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness of that very [suffering].
Full comprehension is the path;
the fruit of full comprehension is liberation;
and the realization of that is the knowledge and vision of liberation.
One who has entered into the mode of cultivation practices four modes and thirty-seven modes.

Among these, the practice of the four modes consists of the practice of the mode of the selflessness of persons, the practice of the mode of the selflessness of phenomena, the practice of the mode of vision, and the practice of the mode of knowledge.
Among these, the practice of the thirty-seven modes is as follows:

In the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), there is the cultivation of the aspect of the unattractive, the cultivation of the aspect of suffering, the cultivation of the aspect of impermanence, and the cultivation of the aspect of non-self.

In the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), there is the cultivation of the aspect of acquisition, the cultivation of the aspect of cultivation, the cultivation of the aspect of expulsion [or removal], and the cultivation of the aspect of the antidote.
There is the cultivation of the mental attention that serves as the antidote to contentment when one generates desire.

When one exerts effort and initiates vigor, it is the cultivation of mental attention as an antidote to distraction and doubt, respectively; when one applies or uplifts the mind, it is the cultivation of the aspect of concentration as an antidote to restlessness;
and when one applies or uplifts the mind, it is the cultivation of the aspect of concentration as an antidote to lethargy.

These are to be understood respectively in relation to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). For one whose mind is stabilized, there is the cultivation of the aspect of conviction regarding supramundane accomplishment; and just as there is the cultivation of the aspect of conviction, so too are there the cultivation of the aspect of exertion, the cultivation of the aspect of non-forgetfulness of the dharmas, the cultivation of the aspect of mental stability, and the cultivation of the aspect of discernment among the faculties.

These same five [mental applications] constitute the mental applications for the powers (*bala*) once their opposites have been eliminated. In that same context, there are the mental applications consisting of the cultivation of the aspects of the manifestation of enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*), as well as the cultivation of the aspects of investigation, enthusiasm, joy, adaptability, and stability of mind; these constitute the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptasaṃbodhyaṅga*). Furthermore, there are the mental applications consisting of the aspect of certainty regarding attainment, the aspect of protecting the ground of preparation, and the aspect of the attainment of others.

Regarding the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), there is cultivation in the form of entering into the morality beloved by the noble ones; cultivation in the form of practicing a refined mode of livelihood; cultivation in the form of practicing the path previously cultivated and attained; cultivation in the form of not forgetting the signs of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitinimitta*); and cultivation in the form of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) through abiding in the signless (*animitta*).
There is no further explanation regarding the intrinsic nature of the path as consisting of the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The mental engagement of benefit is twofold: that which removes coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and that which removes the signs of views (*dṛṣṭi-nimitta*).
The receptive mental engagement is that which receives instruction from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas within the stream of the Dharma.
The preparatory mental engagement regarding the domain of meditative concentration (*samādhi-gocara*) is fivefold.
The application of observing enumeration is that by which one observes the enumeration of names, phrases, and phonemes in the sūtras and other texts.

The application of observing occurrence is that by which one observes two kinds of occurrence: the occurrence of limited measure regarding phonemes, and the occurrence of unlimited measure regarding names and phrases.
The application of observing conceptual construction is that by which, based on duality, one observes the conceptual construction of duality.
Based on the conceptualization of names, there is the conceptualization of objects; based on the conceptualization of objects, there is the conceptualization of names. The syllable is non-conceptual.
There is the application consisting of sequential observation, by which one observes that the engagement in grasping objects is preceded by the grasping of names;
and there is the application of penetration.
Furthermore, it should be understood as being of eleven kinds:
through the penetration of adventitiousness,
and through the penetration of the signs of manifestation.
Through the penetration of the non-apprehension of objects, through the penetration of the non-apprehension of apprehension,
through the penetration of the dharmadhātu, and through the penetration of the selflessness of persons.
Through the penetration of the selflessness of phenomena,
through the penetration of inferior dispositions,
through the penetration of noble and magnanimous dispositions, and through the penetration of the establishment of the Dharma according to realization.
And through the penetration of the established dharma,
the mental application of mastery is threefold:
that which is thoroughly purified of the obscuration of afflictions, and that which is thoroughly purified of both the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.
And it is perfectly pure through the accomplishment of qualities.
Regarding the search for the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), there are two verses:
Reality is that which is constantly devoid of duality.
It is the basis of error,
and it is utterly impossible to describe that which is non-conceptual in nature;
it is considered the object of knowledge, that which is to be abandoned, and that which is to be purified, being by its very nature stainless.
The purification from afflictions is considered by him to be like that of space, gold, and water.
Reality is constantly devoid of duality; the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is so because it is absolutely non-existent in the form of the grasped and the grasper.
The dependent nature (*paratantra*) is the basis of delusion, for it is by means of that [dependent nature] that the [imagined] is constructed.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is inexpressible and non-conceptual in essence.
Among these, the first reality is to be fully known, the second is to be abandoned, and the third is to be purified; it is pure by its very nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha*) from adventitious defilements.
For that which is pure by nature, its purification from afflictions is like that of space, gold, or water.
For space and the other [elements] are not impure by nature, nor is it denied that their purification occurs through the removal of adventitious defilements.
Indeed, there exists nothing else in the world apart from that;
yet the entire world has its intellect utterly deluded regarding it.
How has this kind of worldly delusion arisen, which clings to what is non-existent while completely abandoning what is real? (MSA 11.14)
Indeed, nothing else whatsoever exists in the world apart from this dharmadhātu characterized in such a way, because the dharma-nature (dharmatā) and the phenomenon (dharma) are non-different.
The remainder has been explained.
There are fifteen verses concerning the investigation of reality as being like an illusion.
Just as an illusion is described, so is unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) described;
just as that which is produced by illusion, so is the delusion of duality described.

Just as a magical illusion (*māyā*)—consisting of wood, clods of earth, or the like, which serves as the cause of delusion and is sustained by mechanical devices (*yantra*) and mantras (*mantra*)—is to be understood as the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); so too is the form of that dependent nature to be understood.
Just as the forms of elephants, horses, gold, and so forth, produced by magic within that illusion, appear as having the nature of those very things; [so does the dependent nature appear].

Thus, in that unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa), the error of duality— which appears as the grasped and the grasper— is to be understood as having the form of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Just as its non-existence therein is accepted as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
so too its perception is accepted as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Just as the absence of the state of being an elephant and so forth exists in that which is produced by illusion, so too the absence of the imagined dual characteristic is held to exist within that dependent nature in the ultimate sense.
Just as there is the perception of that illusory creation as having the form of an elephant and so forth, so too there is the perception of the unreal imagination as conventional truth.
Just as manifestation of the cause of that [image] is obtained when it is absent,
so too, upon the revolution of the basis, the manifestation of that which is like a non-existent is obtained.

Just as when an illusory creation ceases to exist, the reality of its cause— the wood or other material— is perceived, so too, upon the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because the error of duality has ceased, the true reality of the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is perceived.
Just as the world, being free from delusion regarding that cause, would act according to its desire.
Upon transformation, he is no longer subject to error; likewise, he is a master who acts according to his will.

Just as the world, being undeluded regarding the cause—such as wood and so forth—acts according to its desire and independently, so too the noble one, being free from error upon the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), acts according to his will and independently.
Its appearance exists there, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of illusions and the like.
This verse has its meaning already explained:
"Therein, existence is not non-existence, nor is non-existence simply existence;
and the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in relation to illusions and the like."
Therein, existence is not non-existence; that which is the appearance of its form is not non-existent.
And non-existence is indeed existence; that which is the absence of elephant-ness and so forth is not non-existent.
Furthermore, no distinction is established between those two—existence and non-existence—in illusions and the like.
For that which is the existence of its form there is precisely the non-existence of elephant-ness and so forth;
and that which is the non-existence of elephant-ness and so forth is precisely the existence of its form.
Thus, the appearance of duality exists there, yet its substantial reality is not found.
Therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other [aggregates].
Likewise, here in the unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa), there is the appearance of duality, but the existence of duality does not exist.
Therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other [aggregates], which have the unreal imagination as their intrinsic nature:
"Therein, existence is not non-existence, and non-existence is indeed existence."
And the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established with respect to form and the other [sense objects].
Therein, existence is not non-existence,
nor is non-existence simply existence; this is the state of appearing as duality.

The non-existence of duality and the lack of distinction between existence and non-existence regarding form and the other aggregates are thus established: for that very existence which is the appearance of duality is itself the non-existence of duality.
It is intended for the purpose of negating the extremes of superimposition and denial,
and also for the purpose of negating the departure by means of the Hīnayāna.
But for what purpose is this absolute identity and lack of distinction between existence and non-existence asserted?
[It is] respectively for the sake of avoiding the extremes of superimposition and denial.
It is intended for the purpose of negation,
specifically for the purpose of negating the departure by means of the Hīnayāna;
for, having realized that non-existence is indeed non-existence, one does not engage in superimposition.
Having understood the substantiality of entities, one does not engage in deprecation;
and having understood the lack of distinction between those two, one does not feel aversion toward entities, and therefore does not depart by means of the Hīnayāna.
Delusion and its objective cause are held to be the representation of form.
And if non-manifestation (avijñapti) were formless, it would not exist because of its lack of substantiality, nor would the other [manifest action] exist.
The representation of signs that arises from the error regarding form is accepted as the representation of form, which is designated by the term "form.
However, that error regarding form is itself a non-material (arūpin) representation.
Because the representation of form would not exist, the other non-material representation would also not exist.
Because there is no cause [for it to exist],
the duality is illustrated by the delusion of grasping at the form of an illusory elephant.
Just as that duality does not exist there, yet duality is nevertheless perceived.
The duality is taught due to the error of grasping at the reflection and the frame;
therein, the duality does not exist in the way it appears, yet duality is nevertheless perceived.
Due to the error of perceiving the form of a magical elephant, the duality of the grasped and the grasper is illustrated;
therein, although the duality does not exist, it is nevertheless perceived.
For one who attends to the reflection and the skeleton, the duality [of subject and object] is taught as before, due to the error of grasping them as such.
(MSA_Bagchi 62)
Because they exist in such a way and do not exist in such a way, and because there is no distinction between existence and non-existence,
those phenomena characterized by delusion are both existent and non-existent, like illusory appearances.
Those phenomena which have the characteristic of delusion and possess the nature of the adverse side are both existent and non-existent, and are like an illusion.
Why?
Because they exist as such by virtue of being unreal mental constructions (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
They are non-existent because they do not exist in that way as the grasped and the grasper;
and since existence and non-existence are indistinguishable in those two, they are both existent and non-existent, and even illusion has such a characteristic;
therefore, they are like an illusion.
Because they exist as such, because they exist as such, and because they exist as such,
those remedial factors which have been taught as being like an illusion are without defining characteristics.
Even those counteractive dharmas taught by the Buddha, such as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, are taught to be without characteristics and like illusions.
For what reason?
Because they do not exist in the way they are grasped by the foolish.
They exist as they have been taught;
they exist as they have been demonstrated by the Buddha—namely, the descent into the womb, birth, renunciation, the attainment of perfect enlightenment, and so forth.
Thus, though they lack defining characteristics and do not truly exist, they appear; therefore, they are like an illusion.
Like a king of illusion defeated by another king of illusion,
those sons of the Victor who perceive all phenomena as such are free from pride.
Those factors that are counteractive are like a phantom king, because they exercise sovereignty over purification in the abandonment of affliction;
those factors that are afflictive are also like kings, because they exercise sovereignty in the production of affliction.
Therefore, by means of those counteractive factors, the defeat of affliction is like [the defeat of] a phantom.
The defeat of one king by another king is to be viewed in this same way;
and through that knowledge, Bodhisattvas become free from pride regarding both sides.
There is a verse for the purpose of illustration:

They are like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, and a reflection; they are comparable to an echo and a flash of lightning; they should be known as resembling the moon reflected in water, and furthermore, they are equal to a magical creation.
Six, six, two, and again six, two, and three for each one.
Indeed, the conditioned phenomena have been explained here and there by the Buddhas, the supreme among the fully awakened.
Regarding what was said by the Blessed One— that phenomena are like illusions, up to being like magical emanations— therein,
phenomena that are like illusions are the six internal sense-bases (*āyatana*),
because they appear in such a way despite the non-existence of a self, a living being, and so forth.
The six external sense bases are like dreams, because the enjoyment of them lacks any substantial reality.
The two factors—mind and mental concomitants—are like mirages, because they produce delusion.
Furthermore, the six internal sense bases are like reflections, because they are the reflections of prior karma.

The six external sense-bases alone are like reflections, because they are like shadows of the internal sense-bases, arising through their dominant influence (*ādhipatya*). "Six are considered pairs" means that the six are held to be in pairs.
The dharmas of the teaching are like echoes.
The dharmas based on meditative concentration (samādhi) are like the reflection of the moon in water, because concentration is like water due to its clarity.
They are like magical emanations (nirmāṇa) in their undertaking of intentional rebirth in existence, because they employ all activities without affliction.
Regarding the investigation of the knowable, there is this verse:
Unreal imagination, that which is neither real nor unreal, and that which is simply non-conceptual; that which is neither conceptual nor non-conceptual—all this is defined as the knowable.
Unreal conceptualization (*abhūtakalpa*) is that conceptualization which is not conducive to supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*);

that which is neither real nor unreal and is conducive to it, up to the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); non-conceptualization (*akalpa*) is suchness (*tathatā*) and supramundane knowledge.

It is neither conceptual construction (*kalpa*) nor non-conceptual; it is mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) obtained subsequent to the supramundane (*lokottara-pṛṣṭhalabdha*). All that which is to be known (*jñeya*) is comprised within this much.
There are two verses concerning the investigation of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).

From one's own constituent element (svadhātu), conceptual constructions (vikalpa) arise as manifestations of duality; they are devoid of the substance of duality, yet they proceed with the activity of ignorance and the afflictions (kleśa). MSA 11.32.

"From its own constituent element" means from the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is the seed of its own existence. "Appearing as a duality" means appearing as the grasped object and the grasping subject.
Because their activity occurs together with ignorance and the afflictions, they are called "those whose activity is accompanied by ignorance and afflictions.
They are "devoid of the two substances" in the sense of being devoid of the substance of the grasped object and the substance of the grasper.
In this way, the affliction is to be investigated.
The attainment of the distinction of the object occurs through the application of abiding in one's own realm;
for those very [objects] proceed as non-dual appearances, like a hide or a piece of wood.
"The attainment of a specific object" refers to the attainment of the object that is the Dharma, which was previously mentioned.
"By means of abiding in one's own realm" means that the realm of one's own conceptualizations is suchness (*tathatā*); "abiding" therein means the mind abides in the name.
"By means of yoga" means by means of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).
Through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), those very same conceptual constructions proceed as manifestations of non-duality for one whose basis has been transformed (*parāvṛttāśraya*).
It is like leather and like an arrow:
for just as that very same leather becomes soft through the removal of its stiffness, [so too do the conceptual constructions become non-dual].
Just as that very arrow becomes straight through heating it in fire, so too,

through the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), when liberation of mind and wisdom is attained, for one whose basis has been transformed (*parāvṛtta-āśraya*), those very conceptual constructions no longer proceed with the appearance of duality. In this way, purification is to be sought.

There are two verses on the investigation of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā): The mind is held to manifest as a duality; likewise, it manifests as passion and so forth, and similarly as faith and so forth. There is no other dharma that is either afflicted or wholesome. (MSA 11.34)

Mind-only alone is asserted to manifest as duality— manifesting as the apprehended object and manifesting as the apprehending subject; likewise, it is asserted that this very mind manifests as the afflictions such as attachment and so forth.
Or [it appears as] the manifestation of wholesome factors such as faith;
however, there exists no afflicted factor characterized by passion and so forth, nor any wholesome factor characterized by faith and so forth, that is other than that manifestation.
Just as there is nothing characterized by duality that is other than the appearance of duality.
Thus the mind proceeds with variegated appearances and variegated forms;
such appearance is the existence and non-existence [of the mind], but it is not considered to be the existence and non-existence of dharmas.
In that regard, it is mind alone that, as a real entity, proceeds as various appearances;
alternatively, it appears as passion, or as hatred,
or as the appearance of other such dharmas.

And it has variegated forms simultaneously, such as the forms of faith and so forth. Manifestation (*bhāsa*) refers to the presence or absence [of these] in a mind that is in an afflicted or wholesome state; however, it does not refer to the [afflicted] dharmas themselves.
Or rather, because among wholesome states there is no characteristic apart from their appearance; thus,
there are eight verses on the investigation of characteristics.
The summary is by means of one [verse], and the detailed exposition is by means of the remainder:

"The characterized, the characteristic, and the characterization, according to their divisions, have been fully revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones for the sake of favoring sentient beings. (MSA 11.36)

By this, the summary is given: that mind which is accompanied by views, its state and its lack of transformation therein—this is the object of definition in brief; for it is immeasurable in its detailed divisions. (MSA 11.37)
In that context, mind refers to consciousness and form;
view refers to mental factors;
and therein, state refers to factors dissociated from mind.
The unchanging is the unconditioned, such as space and so forth, because its representation always proceeds in that manner.
Thus, in brief, these are the five kinds of objects of characterization; by way of division, they are immeasurable.
[These consist of: the sign of the perception of an object according to how it is expressed in speech, and the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for that.
Therefore, the manifestation of objects as well is the imagined characteristic.
In brief, the characteristic is threefold: the characteristic of the imagined and so forth.

Among these, the characteristic of the imagined is threefold: the sign (nimitta) of the perception of an object according to verbal expression; the latent predisposition (vāsanā) for that verbal expression; and the object that appears from that predisposition even to those unskilled in conventional usage, despite the absence of the perception of an object according to verbal expression.

In this context, the mental perception of an object according to its verbal expression is the "perception of an object as it is expressed" (*yathājalpārthasaṃjñā*). Its objective support is the "sign" (*nimitta*). Thus, both that which is imagined and the causal latent impression (*vāsanā*) from which it arises—these two are intended here as the "imagined characteristic" (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, there is the manifestation of the object according to the name, and the manifestation of the name according to the object.
For the imagined characteristic is indeed the cause of conceptual construction that is non-existent.

Another formulation is as follows: the name as it is, and the object as it is; the manifestation of the object according to the name and the manifestation of the name according to the object—this is the manifestation of the object according to the name.

If the object manifests according to the name, or the name manifests according to the object, this is the object of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), which is the imagined characteristic (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*). For only this much is imagined: namely, either the name or the object.
"Or rather:
'The unreal imagination, which has a threefold and threefold appearance and is characterized by the grasped and the grasper, is indeed the characteristic of the dependent nature. (MSA 11.40)
It is called "having a threefold-threefold appearance" because its appearance is of three kinds and each [of those] is again threefold.
Among these, the threefold appearance consists of the appearance of words, the appearance of objects, and the appearance of bodies.
Furthermore, the threefold appearance consists of the appearances of mind (*manas*), apprehension (*udgraha*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The mind (*manas*) is that which is always afflicted;
apprehension (*udgraha*) consists of the five bodies of consciousness;
and conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
In that regard, the first threefold appearance has the characteristic of the apprehended (*grāhya*);
the second has the characteristic of the apprehender (*grāhaka*).
Thus, this unreal imagination is the characteristic of the dependent nature.

That which is both non-existence and existence, the equality of existence and non-existence, and that which is neither unpeaceful nor peaceful and is non-conceptual— this is the characteristic of the perfected nature.

Furthermore, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) is suchness (*tathatā*); for it is both the non-existence of all imagined phenomena (*parikalpita-dharma*) and their existence as that very non-existence.
And there is the equality of existence and non-existence because those two— existence and non-existence— are non-different;
it is unpeaceful due to adventitious secondary afflictions,
yet peaceful because of its natural purity.
And it is non-conceptual because it is not within the sphere of conceptualization due to its being free from proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

By this, the threefold characteristic of suchness is fully elucidated: its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), its characteristic as affliction and purification, and its characteristic as non-conceptuality. Thus, the threefold characteristic has been stated.
Based upon the outflow-dharma (*niṣpaṣyanda-dharma*), there is appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
Abiding in the element of the mind and seeing the existence and non-existence of objects.
Furthermore, the stage of yoga characterized by these marks (*lakṣaṇā*) is fivefold:
the basis (*ādhāra*), the placement (*ādhāna*), the mirror (*ādarśa*), the light (*āloka*), and the support (*āśraya*).
Among these, the basis is the dharma that is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*); it is the realization taught by the Buddha, which is the natural outflow of that very realization.
The basis is appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*).
The mirror is the mind’s abiding in the realm (*dhātu*), which is concentration (*samādhi*); this is what was previously called "abiding in the name.
The light is the vision of objects as being either existent or non-existent, which is supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*).
Thus, one sees the real as it truly is, and the unreal as unreal;
this is the basis and the transformation of the basis.
Reaching equality therein is indeed the stainless noble lineage.
It is considered to be equal, distinguished, neither deficient nor excessive; this is the definition [of the teaching].
The attainment of equality occurs within the uncontaminated realm (*anāsravadhātu*), the noble lineage (*āryagotra*), together with other noble ones;
and that stainless noble lineage belongs to the Buddhas.
It is equal in its liberation, being the same as that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
it is distinguished by five distinctions:
by the distinction of purity, through the purification of the afflictions along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanakleśa*).
By the excellence of purity, through the complete purification of the field; by the excellence of the body, through being the Dharma-body;
and by the excellence of enjoyment, through the uninterrupted engagement in the enjoyment of the Dharma within the circles of the assembly.
And through the excellence of karma, by means of emanations such as dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, one carries out activities for the benefit of sentient beings.

There is neither deficiency in that [state] when the side of affliction ceases, nor excess when the side of purification arises; this fivefold stage of yoga is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), for by it both the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic itself are defined.

There are six verses concerning the search for liberation: The transformation of the appearance of objects, words, and the body is the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), resulting from the transformation of the seeds; and it is the omnipresent basis.
"Due to the transformation of the seed" means due to the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The transformation of the consciousnesses that manifest as objects, bodies, and locations is the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), which is liberation.
And that is the universal basis, pertaining to both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
There is a fourfold mastery over the obstruction of the mind, of grasping, and of conceptualization, [respectively] regarding non-conceptuality, the field, knowledge, and activity. (MSA 11.45)
The meaning is: through the revolution of the mind, of apprehension, and of conceptualization.
Mastery becomes fourfold, respectively, in non-conceptuality, in the field, in gnosis, and in action.
Furthermore, that fourfold mastery exists in the three stages beginning with the Immovable (Acalā).
In one [state] there are two kinds, while in the other there is considered to be one kind of mastery for each.
And this fourfold mastery should be understood as existing within the three stages beginning with the Immovable (acalā);
it is twofold in the single stage of the Immovable,
pertaining to non-conceptuality.
And because it is non-conceptual and free from volitional effort;
and regarding the field, because of the purification of the Buddha-field.

On each respective stage other than that, there is one specific mastery: on the stage of Sādhumatī, there is mastery over knowledge due to the attainment of the excellence of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
In the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), because there is no obstruction to the activities of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*),
the wise one, having understood the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*) present here in existence and having known them as equal, enters into reality by way of grasping.
Then, because of that state, even that [object] does not appear to the mind here;
that non-appearance is liberation, the supreme cessation of apprehension.
Another formulation of liberation:

having realized the two kinds of selflessness pertaining to the three realms of existence, and having understood that twofold selflessness equally— namely, the absence of an imagined person and the absence of imagined phenomena— the Bodhisattva [proceeds].
But it does not enter into reality by way of total non-existence;
rather, through the apprehension [of objects], one enters into the reality of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā), thinking, "This is merely an apprehension.
Then, because the mind abides there in the reality of representation-only, even that reality—representation-only itself—no longer appears.
Liberation is the non-perception of that [duality], which is the supreme disappearance of apprehension due to the non-apprehension of both the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*).
For when the basis exists through the accumulation of provisions, one sees it as mere name;
seeing indeed that it is mere name, one no longer perceives even that at all. (MSA 11.48)

Another synonym for "basis" (*ādhāra*) is [found] in the scripture as "from the equipment" (*saṃbhārāt*), meaning that one who has accumulated the equipment [attains it] through the acquisition of prior equipment. "When the basis exists" refers to the appropriate mental attention (*yoniso-manaskāra*). "Seeing only the name" means seeing that which is devoid of referential objects, being merely a verbal expression.

For he sees "only the name," that is, mere representation (*vijñapti-mātra*), since the four formless aggregates are designated as "name. Seeing that, he no longer sees even that; because the object is absent, there is no perception of its representation. This is "non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*).
Liberation:

This mind, which is always accompanied by functional rigidity (dauṣṭhulya) and bound by the fetter of the view of self, continues to evolve; its cessation, however, is considered to result from abiding within [the realization of] the internal. (MSA 11.49)
There is another way [to explain it]: this mind proceeds through births accompanied by *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption).
By stating "it is bound by the view of self," he shows the cause of *dauṣṭhulya*.
Because it is bound by two kinds of views of self, it is therefore "accompanied by *dauṣṭhulya*."
But cessation [occurs] through its abiding within itself; that is, because that mind remains in the mind alone due to the non-apprehension of an object.
There are two verses on the investigation of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*):
"Because it does not exist by itself or through its own self, and because it does not abide in an intrinsic nature..."
And because that [object] does not exist in the manner it is grasped, its lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) is asserted.
The lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of phenomena is due to their non-existence by themselves, because they are dependent upon conditions;
it is also due to their lack of existence through their own self, because once ceased, they do not arise again with that same self-nature.

Because it does not abide in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and because it is momentary, there is the absence of intrinsic nature; thus, this threefold absence of intrinsic nature should be understood as following upon the three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, there is the absence of intrinsic nature because that [object] does not exist in the manner it is grasped.
"Because that does not exist" means because of the non-existence of intrinsic nature itself.

Just as the grasping at intrinsic nature by the foolish—whether as permanent, pleasant, pure, or as a self, or by any other imagined characteristic—does not exist in that way, for that reason also the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of phenomena is asserted. [By way of this lack of intrinsic nature, they are established as being successively dependent; unarisen, unceasing, quiescent from the beginning, and naturally in a state of nirvāṇa. (MSA 11.51)
[Established are] non-arising and so forth by way of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
For that which is without intrinsic nature is unarisen.
That which is unarisen is unceasing;

that which is unceasing is primordially quiescent; and that which is primordially quiescent is by nature in a state of parinirvāṇa. Thus, through these successive dependencies—beginning with the absence of intrinsic nature—the states of non-arising and so forth are established by means of the absence of intrinsic nature.
The verse concerning the pursuit of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattikadharmakṣānti):

Regarding identity and difference at the outset, regarding specific characteristics, regarding self-existence and transformation, and regarding affliction and distinction—the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena is thus described. (Msa 11.52)
The receptivity toward the eight things that do not arise is the "receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
This refers first to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), for there is no such thing as its initial arising.
Regarding identity and difference among preceding and succeeding [moments],
there is indeed no arising in saṃsāra of those very same phenomena that have already arisen previously, because they do not arise again in that same state.
Nor does it belong to other things, because no previously unarisen mode arises;
[this refers to] the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) with respect to the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
For there is never any arising of that [nature],
since the dependent nature does not arise by itself;
nor is there any arising of the alteration of the perfected nature, for there is no arising of its alteration.
When affliction has been abandoned,
those who have attained the knowledge of destruction no longer perceive the arising of affliction;
[this is] with respect to the excellence of the Buddha-dharmas and the bodies.
For there is no arising of distinctions among them;
thus, patience regarding these dharmas that do not arise is called "the dharma of non-arising.
There are seven verses on the search for the single vehicle (*ekayānatā*).
Because of the equality of the selflessness and liberation regarding the Dharma, because of the distinction of lineages,
because of the attainment of two intentions, because of emanations, and because of the ultimate limit, there is a single vehicle (ekayānatā).
There is the single vehicle because of the equality of the dharma, since the dharmadhātu of the śrāvakas and others is undifferentiated, considering that the vehicle is that which is to be traveled;
there is the single vehicle because of the equality of selflessness.
Because the absence of self is common to the Śrāvakas and others, it is considered "the vehicle" (yāna);
because liberation is equal, there is the state of a single vehicle (ekayānatā), considering that which goes as the "vehicle" (yāna).

The single vehicle (ekayānatā) exists due to the distinction of lineages (gotrabheda), because those of the indeterminate śrāvaka lineage attain deliverance by means of the Mahāyāna; it is called a "vehicle" (yāna) in the sense that they go by means of it. Furthermore, the single vehicle exists due to the attainment of two intentions (dvyāśaya).
Because the Buddhas have attained the mental disposition (*āśaya*) toward all sentient beings as being themselves,

and because those Śrāvakas who are fixed in that lineage— having previously practiced the accumulations for enlightenment— have attained the mental disposition of a Buddha within themselves through the acquisition of the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in an undifferentiated continuum;

and because, by the power of the Buddhas, they have obtained a portion of the Tathāgata’s special grace through the attainment of the single-minded disposition, they are one due to that unity of disposition.

The single vehicle (ekayānatā) of the Buddhas and their disciples arises from emanation (nirmāṇa). As it has been said, "I have attained final nirvāṇa through the Śrāvaka vehicle many hundreds of times," because such an emanation is displayed for the sake of those to be trained.
The single vehicle also exists by way of its final limit, because there is nothing further to be traveled beyond it;
thus, Buddhahood is the single vehicle.
In this manner, the single vehicle should be understood according to those various respective intentions in each respective sūtra.
It is not, however, that the three vehicles do not exist.
For what purpose, then, have the Buddhas taught the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) with those various underlying intentions?
The Perfectly Enlightened Ones have taught the single vehicle (ekayāna) for the sake of attracting some and for the sake of retaining others who are not yet fixed [in their destiny]. (MSA 11.54)
For the sake of attracting some— those who belong to the lineage of the śrāvakas but are not fixed— and for the sake of sustaining others—
those who belong to the lineage of the bodhisattvas but are not fixed.

The śrāvaka who is not fixed is twofold, according to whether he has seen or not seen the goal and according to his vehicle; that one who has seen the goal is both free from passion and not free from passion, and he is also weak.
Furthermore, the śrāvaka who is not fixed is to be understood as being of two kinds:

one who has seen the goal of the vehicle and has realized the truths but departs by means of the Mahāyāna, and one who has not seen the goal of the vehicle and departs by means of the Mahāyāna without having realized the truths.
Furthermore, one who has seen the goal (dṛṣṭārtha) is both one who is free from passion regarding sensual desires and one who is not free from passion.
It should be understood that he is of dull faculty and slow progress;
this refers to the two types of those who have seen the goal mentioned previously.
And because they dedicate the noble path they have attained toward [the welfare of] existences,
they are endowed with a birth resulting from inconceivable transformation.

And those two, having seen the goal, should be understood as being endowed with a birth resulting from the inconceivable transformation, because they transform the Noble Path they have attained toward [further] existences.
For that transformation of the Noble Path toward rebirth is indeed inconceivable; therefore, it is called "resulting from inconceivable transformation.
By the power of their vow, one of them enters into rebirth.
Being alone, through the application of non-returning, he proceeds by means of emanations.
Of these two, one who is not free from passion takes rebirth according to his wish by the power of his vow;
the other does so through emanations by the power of his attainment of non-returning (*anāgāmitā*).
Because they delight in [the state of] nirvana, both are considered to have a slow progress.
Again and again, through the application of the mental activity of one's own mind.
Because both of them delight in *nirvāṇa*, they are considered to be of slow progress, attaining perfect awakening only after a very long time;
this is due to the frequent manifestation of their own śrāvaka-mind, which is accompanied by world-weariness (*nirveda*).
Indeed, having failed to accomplish his goal and being born when no Buddha is present, he exerts himself for the sake of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Seeking emanations, by relying upon that, one attains supreme enlightenment.

Furthermore, one who has seen the truth but is not yet free from passion—being a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has not yet accomplished his purpose—is born in a time devoid of a Buddha; intent upon meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), he seeks to produce emanations (*nirmāṇa*).
Relying upon those emanations, he gradually attains supreme enlightenment (*bodhi*).
With reference to one who abides in these three states, the Blessed One stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:

"Having become a śrāvaka, one becomes a pratyekabuddha, and then again a Buddha. And by means of the analogy of fire, it is shown that when one previously abided in the state of having seen the truths, at a time devoid of a Buddha, one personally generates meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), abandons the birth-body (*janmakāya*), and assumes a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
And when he attains supreme enlightenment—
regarding the search for the fields of knowledge, there is this verse:
Without applying himself to the fivefold field of knowledge, the supreme noble one can by no means attain omniscience.
Thus, for the sake of restraining or favoring others, or for the sake of his own realization, he indeed applies himself to yoga therein.
The fields of knowledge are fivefold:
the inner science, the science of logic, the science of grammar, the science of medicine, and the science of arts and crafts.
This shows for what purpose these should be sought by a bodhisattva.
For the sake of attaining omniscience, he seeks all [sciences] without distinction;
however, for the purpose of refuting others who lack faith in them, he specifically seeks the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) and the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*).
Furthermore, for the purpose of benefiting others who desire them, he seeks the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*) and the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*).
One studies the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*) for the sake of personal realization.
There are thirteen verses concerning the search for the nourishment of the elements (*dhātupuṣṭi*).
Those mental orientations associated with the perfections (*pāramitā*), which serve to fulfill the perfections and lead to the nourishment of the elements, are taught by these verses.
Satisfaction in perceiving the causes, mindfulness of that reliance, the desire for a common fruit, and resolute conviction according to one's awakening. (MSA 11.61)
Furthermore, these range from the mental application of satisfaction in finding the causes up to the mental application of ascertaining oneself as being supreme.
Among them, first of all, regarding the mental application of satisfaction in finding the causes:

a bodhisattva established in the lineage (gotrastha), seeing within himself the lineage of the perfections (pāramitā), brings about the nourishment of the element (dhātu) of the perfections through satisfaction in finding the causes.

Immediately after [the stage where] one established in the lineage (gotrastha) generates the mind for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, there follows the mental application of mindfulness toward that basis (niśrayatadanusmṛti-manasikāra).

For that bodhisattva, perceiving within himself the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) as the very foundation of the perfections (pāramitā), reflects thus: "These perfections will certainly reach fulfillment, for we possess this mind of enlightenment."

For one who has generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), there is the mental application of desiring a common fruit when engaging in the practice of the perfections for the benefit of oneself and others; this is because of the volitional formation [of the wish]: "May the fruit of these perfections be shared with others, or otherwise, may it not be otherwise.

Since one who engages in the practice for the benefit of self and others penetrates the reality of things (*tattvārtha*)—the means for non-affliction—there follows immediately after the mental application of being resolved toward awakening as it is.
In this way, the sequence should be understood to apply everywhere;

for one forms the mental construction: "Just as the perfections were fully awakened to by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will be fully awakened to, and are being fully awakened to, so do I resolve with firm conviction.
(MSA_Bagchi 71)
Through the fourfold majestic power, there is delight, lack of weariness, and certainty;
and there is a fourfold practice regarding the adverse factors and their antidotes.
The mental application of delighting in the majestic power consists in delighting in seeing the fourfold majestic power;
the fourfold majestic power is the abandonment of opposing factors and the maturation of the accumulations.
The benefit of oneself and others,

and the granting of the fruit of maturation and the concordant fruit in the future; and the mental attention of firm resolve free from weariness, directed toward the ripening of sentient beings and one's own buddha-qualities.

The mental application regarding the fourfold practice concerns the determination to remain untiring despite all the misconduct of sentient beings and the onset of all sufferings and calamities, for the sake of attaining supreme enlightenment;
as well as the confession of the opposites of generosity and the other perfections, such as stinginess and so forth.
There is rejoicing in the antidotes such as giving and so forth,
requesting the Buddhas for the sake of teaching the Dharma that has those as its predominant theme,
and dedicating these toward enlightenment.
Serene confidence, patient endurance, the desire to give for the sake of others,
armor-like resolve, the vow, and the mental engagement of rejoicing.
