Beginning with the acquisition of the power of resolute belief (*adhimukti*), there is the mental application of serene confidence toward the teachings and meanings that have the perfections (*pāramitā*) as their predominant subject.
Beginning with the search for the Dharma, there is the mental application of receiving [the teaching], by way of grasping that very Dharma through the practice of non-opposition.
Beginning with the teaching, there is the mental application of the desire to give, for the sake of illuminating the Dharma and its meaning for others.

With reference to practice (*pratipatti*), there is the mental application of armor (*saṃnāha-manasikāra*), because of the donning of armor for the sake of fulfilling generosity and the other perfections.
There is the mental application of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-manasikāra*), for the purpose of encountering the conditions for attaining that fulfillment.
There is the mental application of rejoicing (*abhinanda-manasikāra*), because of rejoicing with the thought: "O, may I truly accomplish [the path] through the practice of generosity and the rest."
These three very same forms of mental attention (manasikāra) are to be applied within the instruction and admonition (avavādānuśāsanyā):

first, mental attention toward action conjoined with skillful means (upāya), because of the mental engagement in the practice of giving and so forth in all their various modes through intentional thoughts (saṃkalpa);
and second, constant eagerness once power has been attained, which is the sixfold exertion regarding giving and the other perfections.
In maturation, in worship, and in service, there is compassion.
The mental application of eagerness (*autsukya-manasikāra*) is fourfold:
regarding the attainment of capacity in the sixfold [perfections] beginning with giving— ranging from the giving of giving up to the giving of wisdom—
and likewise in the sixfold [perfections] beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Through the perfections themselves, one brings beings to maturity by means of the application of the articles of attraction;
and in worship, one performs it through giving as the worship of gain and honor,
and through the remaining perfections as the worship of practice.
One should understand that there is the mental application of zeal toward serving spiritual friends for the sake of receiving instruction on the perfections (*pāramitā*) without error;
and there is the mental application of compassion through the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), being friendly toward sentient beings by providing them with generosity and so forth,
and feeling pity for them when they encounter stinginess and other such faults.
Joy arises from being endowed with generosity and the other perfections;

equanimity arises from the resolute conviction that they are free from affliction; and there is shame regarding what was not done or what was poorly done, as well as remorse and delight in the [proper] object.
The perception of [the teaching] as an enemy, weariness, and the notion that it is merely a fabrication or a mere display.
The mental application of shame concerning inferior dharmas is shame regarding [unwholesome acts] not performed,
or shame regarding [virtuous acts] such as giving that have not been performed, or have been performed incompletely or incorrectly.
Feeling shame, one experiences remorse as a secondary consequence for the sake of engaging in what is right and desisting from what is wrong.
Based on steadfastness (*dhṛti*), there is the mental application of delight (*rati-manaskāra*), because it holds the mind without distraction upon the objects of giving and so forth.
There is the mental application of indefatigability (*akheda-manaskāra*), because one regards weariness in the practice of giving and so forth as an enemy.
The mental application of composition (*racanā-manasikāra*) consists in the formative activity of composing treatises connected with the perfections (*pāramitā*).

The mental application of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-manasikāra*), starting from the knowledge of the world (*lokajñatā*), consists in the formative activity of manifesting that very same treatise in the world according to the capacity of the recipients.
Generosity and the other perfections are the refuge for awakening, not Īśvara and the like.
And because of the experience of both faults and virtues. // Msa_11.66 //
The mental application of reliance is for the sake of attaining awakening, relying on generosity and the other perfections rather than on Īśvara and the like;
the mental application of analytical knowledge arises from the realization of the faults and virtues of the discordant factors, such as stinginess, and their remedies, such as generosity;
and there is the joy of recollecting the accumulation [of merit] and the vision of its great purpose.
There is aspiration for yoga, for non-conceptuality, for its maintenance, and for the arrival of favorable conditions. (MSA 11.67)

The mental application of joy through recollection consists in observing the accumulation of the provisions of merit and wisdom during the gathering of generosity and the other perfections. The mental application of observing great significance consists in observing that generosity and the other perfections have the purpose of attaining great enlightenment by way of their cultivation as factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*).
Furthermore, that mental application of aspiration is of four kinds.
The mental application of longing for yoga arises from the longing to cultivate the yoga of calm abiding and insight;
the mental application of longing for non-conceptuality arises from the longing for skillful means in order to fulfill the perfections;
and the mental application of longing for steadfastness arises from the longing to uphold the meaning of the teachings that have the perfections as their dominant influence.
The mental application (*manaskāra*) consisting of the desire to attain the conditions [for enlightenment] arises from the formation of correct vows (*samyak-praṇidhāna*).
There is the vision of the capacity for rising above the seven types of false grasping (*asad-grāha*), as well as the fourfold perception of what is marvelous and what is not marvelous. (MSA 11.68)
The mental application that perceives the power to eliminate the seven types of false grasping;
there are seven kinds of false grasping:
grasping at what is non-existent as existent, [and so forth].
Grasping at what is faulty as being virtuous; grasping at what is virtuous as being faulty;
and the false graspings of permanence and pleasure with respect to all conditioned phenomena.
Regarding all phenomena, there is the false grasping at a self;
and regarding nirvana, there is the false grasping at it as being non-quiescent.
As an antidote to these, the three samādhis beginning with emptiness and the four summaries of the Dharma are taught.
Regarding the marvelous, there is mental attention consisting of four kinds of perceptions:
the perception of the magnificence of the perfections and the perception of their long duration.
The perception of being indifferent toward recompense and the perception of being indifferent toward karmic maturation;
and, regarding that which is not marvelous, the mental application consisting of fourfold perceptions.
The fourfold non-marvelous magnanimity consists in both vastness and extensiveness, because it brings about the fruit of Buddhahood through the perfections;
and because, while these two exist, one establishes a state of mind of equality toward oneself and others,
and [surpasses] those who are distinguished by them.

When receiving honors and the like from Śakra and others, there is no expectation of recompense; even when obtaining a body and enjoyments superior to those of all the worlds, there is no expectation of karmic maturation.
There is equanimity toward all sentient beings, as well as a magnanimous vision, and a constant lack of hope for reward for the virtues of others. (MSA 11.69)
The mental application of equanimity arises from the intentional cultivation of equal engagement through giving and the other perfections toward all sentient beings.

The mental application of the vision of the Great Self arises from the manifestation of the perfections as a means of benefiting all sentient beings. The mental application of not hoping for a return favor arises from the engagement in the virtues of giving and so forth for the sake of others.

The mental application of aspiration consists in aspiring for three states regarding sentient beings: the culmination of the perfections, the culmination of the bodhisattva stages, and the fulfillment of the welfare of sentient beings. The uninterrupted mental application consists in the cultivation of generosity and the other perfections so as not to let time pass fruitlessly, and in the volition that does not stop midway from the practice prescribed by the Buddhas.
Through the decrease or increase of that [merit], there is a lack of joy or the feeling of joy toward sentient beings.
The mental attention of correct application arises from not dwelling on anything inferior due to practicing without error.
The mental attention of non-delight arises toward those who are declining in generosity and other virtues.
The mental attention of delight arises toward sentient beings who are increasing in generosity and other virtues.
There is no lack of interest in cultivation that is merely a semblance or counterfeit;
there is no mental engagement of acquiescence, but rather a longing for that which is predicted and fixed [in liberation].
There is mental attention characterized by lack of interest regarding the cultivation of counterfeit perfections; mental attention characterized by interest regarding the genuine [perfections];
and mental attention characterized by non-acceptance, because it involves the formative activity of subduing opposing factors such as stinginess.

The mental application of aspiration is twofold: the mental application of aspiration for obtaining the prophecy of the fulfillment of the perfections, and the mental application of aspiration for obtaining the state of certainty regarding the stages of the perfections.
[Verse 11.72]: There is the volition of conduct arising from the vision [of the Buddha] in the future, and the contemplation of equality;
and through conduct in the supreme dharmas, there is the determination of oneself as being supreme.

The mental application of conduct based on future vision is so called because, having gone to whatever state of existence (*gati*) a bodhisattva may go, he forms the volitional impulse (*abhisaṃskāra*) that [the perfections] must necessarily be practiced. The mental application of observing the equality of generosity and the other perfections is for the sake of resolving upon the continuous practice of the perfections by oneself together with other bodhisattvas. The mental application of determining one's own superiority is due to seeing one’s own preeminent status through the engagement in the supreme dharmas of the perfections.
These virtuous mental orientations, accompanied by the ten perfections, indeed always serve to nourish the element of the bodhisattvas. (MSA 11.73)
Thus, the concluding verse has its meaning already explained.
Regarding the classification of the search for the Dharma, there are two verses:
"The wise one’s great search is held to be [motivated] by nourishment and by resolute intention."
For them, [the mastery] is both with effort and effortless, as well as sovereign.

For Bodhisattvas, there is the aspiration that is without body, the light body, and the fully perfected body; it is considered to be characterized by great respect, subtle pride, and being free from pride.
The search is of thirteen kinds: by way of nourishment, through the nourishment of faith in what has been heard; and by way of resolute intention, through the stream of the gateways of the Dharma.
Among those who have attained great mastery over the mind,
the first [type of supernormal power] is accompanied by departure;
the second is without departure.
The third is that which pertains to mastery (*vaibhūtikī*).

That which is "without body" (*akāyā*) consists of [wisdom] derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintāmayī*), because it is devoid of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). That which is "with body" (*sakāyā*) consists of [wisdom] derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), belonging to the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
The body is acquired in a minor form on the seven stages; it is fully perfected on the remaining stages;
and it is characterized by great reverence on the stage of practice through resolute belief.
Subtle pride exists in the seven [stages];
emanation exists in the remaining ones.
There is a verse regarding the investigation into the cause of the Dharma:
In the realms of form and formlessness, dharma is the cause of characteristics; likewise, it is the cause of health, sovereignty through the superknowledges, and the inexhaustibility of the wise.
In the realm of form (*rūpa*), it is the dharma that is the cause of the marks;
in the formless (*arūpa*), it is the cause of health because it pacifies the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*);

it is the cause of sovereignty through the superknowledges (*abhijñā*); and it is the cause of its inexhaustibility because it is not interrupted even in the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
Therefore, it is said in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:

"Endowed with four qualities, Bodhisattvas seek the Dharma: with the perception of it as a jewel, in the sense that it is difficult to find; with the perception of it as medicine, in the sense that it pacifies the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*); with the perception of it as wealth, in the sense that it is never lost; and with the perception of it as nirvāṇa, in the sense that it pacifies all suffering."
For the marks are like jewels because they produce beauty; therefore, because they are the cause of that [beauty], they are designated as the "jewel of the Dharma.
Because they are the cause of health, they are designated as "medicine. Because they are the cause of mastery through the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), they are designated as "wealth."
Because it is the cause of that inexhaustibility, it is [the perfection of wisdom] in the sense of being fearless through the exhaustion of the notion of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the investigation of conceptual construction, there is this verse:
"The conceptualizations of non-existence, existence, superimposition, and denial; the conceptualizations of unity, diversity, self-nature, and distinction."
The conceptualizations that adhere to names according to their literal meaning should be completely abandoned by the sons of the Victors.

A bodhisattva must avoid ten kinds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Regarding the conceptual construction of non-existence (*abhāva-vikalpa*), as its antidote, it is said here in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "A bodhisattva, being truly a bodhisattva..."
The conceptualization of existence is that for which he says, as its antidote:
"He does not perceive a bodhisattva," and so forth.
The conceptualization of superimposition is that for which he says, as its antidote: [the following].
"Form, Śāriputra, is empty of intrinsic nature"—
this refers to the conceptualization of negation (*apavāda-vikalpa*), for which he states as an antidote:
"not by means of emptiness."
The conceptualization of oneness is that for which he said, as its antidote:

"That which is the emptiness of form is not that form. The conceptualization of difference is that for which he said, as its antidote: [that which is the emptiness of form is not other than that form].
Nor is form other than emptiness; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form.
This is said as the antidote to the conceptualization of specific characteristics:
"This which is called 'form' is merely a name."
As for the conceptualization of distinctions, it is taught as its antidote:
"For form, there is neither arising nor cessation, neither defilement nor purification.
As for the conceptualization of adherence to objects according to their names, it is taught as its antidote: [as follows].
"Fabricated names," and so forth;
and as for the conceptualization that clings to names according to their literal meaning, it is said as an antidote to this:
"The Bodhisattva does not perceive any of those names; not perceiving them, he does not cling to them as having a literal reality. This is the intended meaning.
Thus, having applied strenuous effort with a virtuous mind and having realized the true reality of the nature of phenomena through the investigation of both [subject and object],
he therefore becomes a constant refuge for all beings, filled with qualities like the ocean.
By this concluding verse, he demonstrates the threefold greatness of the search (*paryeṣṭi*):

the greatness of the means, through its fierce vigor and by way of searching for the reality of the phenomena of both conventional and ultimate truth—where "reality" (*tattva*) means "truth" (*satya*);
and the greatness of the welfare of others, because it serves as a refuge for all beings.
And the greatness of its own purpose is due to its being completely filled with qualities, like the ocean.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the Search for the Dharma, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The Twelfth Chapter: A Verse on the Prohibition of Stinginess Regarding the Teaching of the Dharma. (MSA_Bagchi 76)
The wise, with joyful minds, constantly bestow upon suffering beings their lives and enjoyments— things acquired with great difficulty yet devoid of essence— through various forms of sublime giving;
how much more so, then, the noble Dharma which repeatedly and in every way brings benefit to all creatures!
It is not obtained through hardship; rather, it increases greatly for those who bestow it and is inexhaustible.

Out of compassion for those who suffer, Bodhisattvas— having exhausted even lives and enjoyments that were obtained with great difficulty and are devoid of essence— constantly bestow them with magnificent liberality; how much more so the Dharma, which neither increases nor diminishes for those who give it away, whether with ease or even with great effort.
Regarding the meaninglessness and meaningfulness of the Dharma, there are two verses:
"The Dharma was not taught at all by the Blessed One, since it is to be personally realized;
yet the multitude has been drawn toward their own true nature (dharmatā) by means of Dharmas established through reasoning."
Within the vast, pure, common, and inexhaustible cavity of their own peace,
those whose nature is compassion— resembling pythons— have brought [the world] together as if with a suction-cup.
In that regard, the Buddhas are like pythons; their own tranquility is the cavity of the mouth, which is the Dharma-body—
vast and pure due to the purification of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable along with their latent predispositions.
It is common to all Buddhas and inexhaustible because it is ultimate;
therefore, that cultivation of yogins is by no means fruitless,
and that teaching of the Sugata is by no means fruitless.
If the object were perceived through mere hearing alone, then meditative cultivation would be useless;
if one could enter into meditative cultivation without having heard it, then the teaching would be useless. (MSA 12.3)

Therefore, the cultivation of yogins is not without purpose, because through it one attains the dharma that is to be personally realized. Nor is the teaching without purpose, because by means of dharmas established through reasoning, it draws people toward their own true nature (*svadharmatā*).
Furthermore, he shows how cultivation or teaching may be purposeful with the following half-verse:
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
Regarding the classification of teaching, there is this verse:
"The teaching for the supreme beings is [based] on scripture, on realization, and on mastery."
...the emergence [of the voice] from the mouth, from form, and from all directions of space as well. // Msa_12.4 //
In that regard, [the voice] by way of mastery is that which belongs to those who have entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*);
it issues forth from all directions, even from forms and so forth, and from trees, musical instruments, and the like.
The rest has its meaning already explained.
Regarding the perfection of teaching, there are two verses:
It is clear, it dispels doubt, it is authoritative, and it reveals reality; it is twofold.
This teaching, which is to be understood as the perfection of the Bodhisattvas, is now complete.
This verse is an exposition of four points, as stated in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā*:

"Endowed with four qualities, bodhisattvas bestow the great gift of Dharma: by way of upholding the true Dharma, by way of refining their own wisdom, and by way of performing the deeds of a true person."
And by way of teaching both affliction and purification:
for by the first, the teaching is clear due to great learning (*bāhuśrutya*); by the second, it is so due to great wisdom (*mahāprajñatva*).
It eliminates the doubts of others by cutting through their uncertainty.
By the third [quality], it is authoritative because its actions are blameless.
By the fourth, it reveals reality in two ways: the reality characterized by affliction and the reality characterized by purification, each through two truths.
The teaching of the supreme beings is sweet, free from intoxication, and not weary;
it is clear, variegated, logical, intelligible, disinterested, and all-pervading.

In this second verse, it is "sweet" because it consists of non-harsh speech when one is challenged by another; it is "free from intoxication" because it does not follow upon pride when praise or success is achieved;
and it is "unwearied" because of the absence of laziness.
It is clear because it is free from the "teacher's fist" (i.e., withholding essential instructions) and because it teaches everything in its entirety;
it is diverse because it is non-repetitive;
and it is logical because it is not contradicted by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is "going" because its words and syllables are not obscure;
it is "free from worldly motives" because it seeks no reward beyond the service of those with faith;
and it is "universal" because it pertains to all three vehicles.
Regarding the perfection of speech, there is this verse:
The speech of the Son of the Victor is undepressed, sweet, well-spoken, intelligible, and likewise clear; it is appropriate, non-materialistic, measured, and likewise lucid. (MSA 12.7)
It is undepressed because it fulfills the assembly;
it is sweet and lovely;
it is well-spoken and clear because its syllables are well-articulated.
It is intelligible because it is expressed in terms that are already understood;
it is appropriate because it is worth hearing, being in accordance with those to be trained;
and it is non-material because it is independent of gain, honor, and fame.

It is extensive because it is immeasurable; it is agreeable because it is not limited by weariness; it is clear because it is inexhaustible. Regarding the perfection of the phrasing, there are two verses:
Because of its summary, because of its detailed exposition, likewise because it conforms to the vehicles, because of its elegance, because it is intelligible,
because it is appropriate, because it leads to liberation, and because of its conformity.
It is through the use of appropriate words and syllables by way of enumeration; through the use of coherent [words] by way of detailed explanation, without contradicting the enumeration;
and through being conformable to the vehicles by way of conformity, without contradicting the three vehicles.
Because they are smooth, appropriate, and free from harsh sounds; because they are intelligible, suitable, and lead to the comprehension of the meaning through their clarity of sense.
They are appropriate because they are suitable for those to be trained;
they are conducive to liberation because they have nirvāṇa as their objective;
and they are favorable because, through the equipment of the factors of the adept, they are in accordance with the Noble Eightfold Path of the learner.
This perfection of phonemes should be understood in every respect as belonging to the supreme beings;
it consists of sixty components, is inconceivable, and the voice of the Sugatas is indeed infinite.
That sixty-fold [speech] is inconceivable, which was taught as the sixty aspects of the Buddha’s speech in the *Guhyakādhipatinirdeśa*.
Furthermore, Śāntamati, the speech of the Tathāgata issues forth endowed with sixty aspects: it is smooth, soft, agreeable, delightful, and pure, and so forth.
In that regard, it is "smooth" because it supports the roots of virtue within the realm of sentient beings.
They are gentle because they provide a pleasant touch in this very life;
they are agreeable because their meaning is excellent; they are delightful because their phrasing is beautiful.
It is pure because it is obtained subsequent to the unsurpassed supramundane [wisdom];
it is stainless because it is dissociated from all afflictions, latent tendencies, and habitual propensities;
it is luminous because its words and phrases are clearly understood.
It is "excellent" (*valgu*) because it possesses the power and qualities that destroy the evil views and misconceptions of all non-Buddhist teachers;
it is "worth hearing" (*śravaṇīyā*) because its practice leads to definitive deliverance;
and it is "unfailing" (*anantā* or *anelā*) because it cannot be refuted by any opposing disputants.
It is graceful because it is pleasing;
it is disciplined because it serves as an antidote to passion and the like;
it is not harsh because it provides a pleasant means for the formulation of the training rules.
It is not harsh because it teaches the means of deliverance through the perfection of transcending those transgressions;
it is well-disciplined because it teaches the method of the three vehicles;
and it is pleasant to the ear because it is the antidote to distraction.
It brings refreshment to the body because it induces meditative concentration;
it brings elation to the mind because it results in the joy induced by insight;
and it brings satisfaction to the heart because it cuts through doubt.
It generates joy and bliss because it removes false certainties; it is free from burning anguish because there is no regret in its practice;
and it is to be fully understood because it serves as the basis for perfected knowledge consisting of hearing.
It is to be understood as such because it is the basis for perfected knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmayajñāna*);
it is perfectly clear because it is established through the Dharma without the "teacher's fist" (*anācāryamuṣṭi*);
and it is lovable because it inspires affection in those who have attained their own goal.
They are to be congratulated because they have attained their own goal and are thus objects of admiration;
they are to be obeyed because they correctly reveal inconceivable dharmas;
they are to be understood because they correctly teach conceivable dharmas.
It is "logical" because it is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
it is "conjoined" because it teaches disciples according to what is appropriate for them;
and it is "free from the fault of redundancy" because it is never fruitless.
It has the speed of a lion’s roar because it terrifies all non-Buddhist teachers;
it has the sound of a dragon’s voice because of its magnificence;
it has the resonance of a thundercloud because of its profundity.
They possess the voice of the lord of nāgas because it is authoritative; the sound of the music of kinnaras because it is sweet;
and the cry of the kalaviṅka bird because it is not harsh or fragile.
It possesses the resonance of the voice of Brahmā because it reaches far;
it possesses the resonance of the voice of the jīvañjīvaka bird because it is an auspicious omen that precedes all accomplishments;
and it has the sweet sound of the lord of gods because it is not to be transgressed.
It has the sound of a drum because it precedes victory over all Māras and adversaries;
it is not haughty because it is unafflicted by praise;
it is not dejected because it is unafflicted by blame.
It penetrates all sounds because it enters into all grammatical forms and all characteristics;
it is free from corrupt words because they do not issue forth when mindfulness is lost;
it is unimpaired because it is ever-present for the sake of accomplishing the needs of those to be trained.
It is not dejected because it does not depend on gain or honor;
it is not depressed because it is free from fault;
it is joyful because it is untiring.
It is "extended" because it follows from skill in all branches of knowledge;
it is "unfailing" [or "not narrow"] because it accomplishes every goal for sentient beings.
It is continuous because its flow is uninterrupted;
it is graceful because it manifests in diverse forms;
it fulfills all sounds because it presents the cognition of many words from a single sound.
It satisfies the faculties of all sentient beings because it presents itself as the cognition of both single and manifold objects;
it is irreproachable because it accords with its promise;
and it is unshakable because it is applied at the appropriate time.
It is not agitated because it is produced without haste;
it resounds throughout all assemblies because it is heard equally by those in the assembly whether far or near;
and it is endowed with the excellence of all aspects because it transforms the Dharma through worldly meanings and examples.

There are four verses on the greatness of the teaching: "Indeed, [the teaching] is accompanied by frequent practice, through speech consisting of well-joined words that provide detailed instruction, divisions, and the cutting away of doubts, for those who understand through concise statements and those who understand through elaboration. (MSA 12.10)
He declares it by means of speech;
he makes it known through well-constructed phrases;
he establishes, analyzes, and elucidates it respectively through summary, detailed exposition, and the cutting away of doubts.
He makes manifest; "making manifest" is a teaching followed by repeated practice for the purpose of bestowing the power of certainty.
He teaches to those who understand through concise statements (*uddhaṭitajña*), and he elucidates fully to those who understand through detailed exposition (*vipañcitajña*).
This teaching of the Buddhas is indeed pure by virtue of the three spheres;
furthermore, it should be understood as being free from these eight faults.

"Pure by way of the three spheres" means: that by which one teaches— namely, by means of speech and words— and the manner in which one teaches— namely, through methods such as the brief exposition and so forth.
And regarding those who are "knowers by what is condensed" (*uddhaṭitajña*) and "knowers by elaboration" (*vipañcitajña*),
this very teaching should be understood as being free from eight faults respectively:
namely, laziness, lack of understanding, failure to provide an opportunity [for questioning], and lack of thoroughness.
The non-elimination of doubt and the failure to consolidate its removal.
Furthermore, those eight faults are as follows:

laziness, lack of thorough understanding, failure to provide an opportunity [for instruction], the state of not having reached the definitive meaning, not cutting through doubt, not consolidating the removal of that [doubt], and lack of certainty—this is the meaning.
Moreover, weariness and stinginess; for these are considered the faults in discourse.
Due to the absence of that [defilement], the teaching of the Buddhas becomes unsurpassed.
Exhaustion is that by which one does not teach repeatedly; and stinginess is due to not revealing the teaching in its entirety. Regarding the perfection of the meaning, there are two verses.
This sublime Dharma, being the cause of devotion, satisfaction, and wisdom,
possesses a twofold purpose, is easily grasped, and teaches the holy life endowed with four qualities.
Exclusively shared with others, it brings about the abandonment of the afflictions of the three realms;
it is pure by nature and purified of stains—this is held to be the practice of the fourfold Brahma-vihāra.
The Dharma is the proclaimer of the holy life endowed with four qualities;
it is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, because it serves as the cause for devotion, satisfaction, and wisdom through hearing, reflection, and cultivation respectively.
In this context, devotion (*bhakti*) is resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which is trustful confidence (*saṃpratyaya*); satisfaction (*tuṣṭi*) is joy (*prāmodya*).

Having understood through reasoned reflection that [the goal] is attainable, the intellect of one whose mind is concentrated is the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*). It has a twofold object; therefore, it is "well-meaning" (*svartha*) because of its connection with both the conventional and ultimate truths.
It is easy to grasp; therefore, it is well-phrased because its words and syllables are intelligible.
The holy life possesses four qualities:
it is complete because it is not shared by others, and it is perfect because it fulfills the abandonment of the afflictions of the three realms.
It is pure by virtue of its intrinsic purity because it is free from outflows (*anāsrava*);
it is cleansed by virtue of the purification of stains through the purification of the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) for those whose outflows are exhausted.
There are two verses regarding the analysis of intentional terminology (*abhisaṃdhi*).

The intentional terminology (saṃdhi) of introduction, another intentional terminology based on characteristics, the intentional terminology of the antidote, and also the intentional terminology of transformation.
Regarding the disciples, regarding intrinsic natures, regarding the discipline of faults,
and likewise regarding the profundity of the expression— this is the fourfold intentional meaning (saṃdhi).
Four kinds of intentional terminology (*abhisandhi*) are to be understood regarding the Buddha’s teaching:

the intentionality of introduction (*avatāraṇābhisandhi*), the intentionality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisandhi*), the intentionality of counteracting (*pratipakṣābhisandhi*), and the intentionality of transformation (*pariṇāmanābhisandhi*).
Among these, the intentionality of introduction is to be seen in relation to the Śrāvakas.

The intention regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisandhi*) is to be seen in the three natures—the imagined (*parikalpita*) and so forth—because of the teaching on the existence of form and other phenomena for the purpose of introducing beings to the teaching without causing them fear. The intention regarding remedies (*pratipakṣābhisandhi*) is to be seen in the subduing of faults, as will be stated in the two verses concerning the benefits of the discourse on the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*), which serves as the remedy for the eight obscurations. This is because of the teaching that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unproduced, and so forth.
The intention of transformation (pariṇāmanābhisandhi) is to be seen in the profundity of the expression, as it is said:
"Those who perceive the essential in the inessential, who are well-established in perversion,
and who are thoroughly afflicted by affliction— they attain supreme enlightenment" (Msa 12).
This is the intended meaning here:

"Those who perceive the essential in the unessential" refers to those whose perception of the essential—that is, their perception of what is primary—is directed toward non-distraction; for distraction is the scattering of the mind.

And "well-established in error" means they are well-established, through non-retrogression, in the error of impermanence and so forth, which is the opposite of the grasping at permanence, pleasure, purity, and self.
"And they are afflicted by affliction" means they are excessively distressed by the fatigue of long-term exertion in difficult practices.
Regarding the analysis of the intended meaning, there is this verse:
"It should be understood [as intended] in terms of equality, in terms of another object, and likewise again in terms of another time."
And regarding the disposition of the person, the intention is fourfold.
There are four kinds of intention (*abhiprāya*).

The intention regarding existence (*samatābhiprāya*) is as when he said, "At that time, I myself was the perfectly enlightened one Vipaśyin," because of the non-distinction of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The intention regarding another meaning (*arthāntarābhiprāya*) is as when he says,
"All phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), unarisen," and so forth, because the meaning is not according to the literal expression.
The intention regarding another time (*kālantarābhiprāya*) is as when he says:
The intention is that those who make a vow for Sukhāvatī will be reborn there after some period of time.

This is the intention regarding the dispositions of individuals (*pudgalāśayābhiprāya*): that he praises one particular root of virtue while censuring another, in order to lead those who are satisfied with only a small amount toward the vast [teaching]. Taking up two verses that contain the benefits of the Mahāyāna sūtras, he says:
Contempt for the Buddha and the Dharma, laziness, contentment with a mere trifle,
conduct characterized by passion and pride, remorse, and instability— these are the obstacles.
That which is an obscuration for sentient beings is the discourse on the Supreme Vehicle as its antidote;
through that, the abandonment of all faults that constitute obstacles occurs for them.
The wise one, supreme among beings, who applies himself to memorizing these two verses either by way of the text or the meaning, indeed obtains ten kinds of benefit.
And at the time of death, there is complete nourishment of the elements and supreme joy;
furthermore, one obtains birth according to one's wish and the recollection of past lives in all circumstances.
Encountering the Buddhas, hearing from them the Supreme Vehicle,
possessing faith along with wisdom, the two gateways, and swift awakening.
Regarding "disrespect toward the Buddha and the Dharma," there are five verses.

In that context, "the breach of those who are not fixed" refers to the deviation from the Mahāyāna by those bodhisattvas who are not yet fixed in their destiny. "Discourse on the Supreme Vehicle" refers to the teaching of the Mahāyāna.
The discourse on the remedy for the obscuration of contempt toward the Buddha is:
"At that time, I myself was the perfectly enlightened one, Vipaśyin.
The discourse on the remedy for the obscuration of contempt toward the Dharma is:
"Having attended upon as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, realization in the Mahāyāna arises"—
this is the discourse that serves as the antidote to the hindrance of indolence.
"Those who make a vow for Sukhāvatī will be reborn there."
"By merely grasping the name of the Tathāgata Vimalacandraprabha, one becomes fixed in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
This is a discourse on the remedy for the obscuration of being satisfied with only a little;
it is where the Blessed One in some places disparages giving and so forth, while in other places he has praised them.

The discourse on the remedy for the obscuration of one whose temperament is dominated by passion is that in which the Blessed One describes the splendor of the Buddha-fields. The discourse on the remedy for the obscuration of one whose temperament is dominated by pride is as follows:
In this regard, the Blessed One describes the superior excellence of a certain Buddha;
it is a discourse that serves as an antidote to the hindrance of remorse, stating:
"All those who commit harm against Buddhas and Bodhisattvas shall all go to the heavenly realms."

The discourse on the antidote to the obscuration of indeterminate differentiation consists of the teaching of the prophecy of the great śrāvakas regarding their future Buddhahood and the teaching of the Single Vehicle (ekayāna). The nourishment of the entire element (*dhātu*) refers to the nourishment of the element for the sake of sustaining the entirety of the Mahāyāna; this occurs because, through the removal of that obscuration, one attains resolute faith (*adhimukti*) in the Mahāyāna everywhere.
The two gateways are the gateway of meditative concentration and the gateway of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*).
It should be understood that there are two kinds of benefits in the present life and eight kinds in future lives, due to the gradual attainment of ever-higher distinctions.
The verse on the benefits of teaching:

Thus, the Bodhisattva who possesses a lucid intellect, is untiring, compassionate, renowned, and endowed with knowledge of the proper methods, becomes an excellent teacher; indeed, he illuminates the people through his teachings just as the sun shines. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 12.24.
Being a skilled speaker is due to five causes,
and the benefit is that one shines like the sun,
because of being highly esteemed for winning over the world.

There are five causes of being a good teacher by which one demonstrates without error: [teaching] repeatedly, with a mind free from worldly desire, with acceptable speech, and in accordance with those to be trained.
This concludes the twelfth chapter, on Teaching, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The thirteenth chapter, on the classification of practice, consists of six verses.
Having understood the twofold selflessness of persons and phenomena, the wise one should indeed abandon the threefold [conceptions] of falsity and correctness regarding these two.

Having understood reality as it is and having understood the Dharma, one becomes a practitioner of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, a practitioner of proper conduct, and a follower of the Dharma; this he demonstrates.
In that regard, the knowledge of the selflessness of persons and phenomena is twofold, by virtue of the absence of the grasped and the grasper.
Having abandoned the two—falsity and correctness—there are three [points] to be avoided.
The concentration on emptiness pertains to the non-existence of the imagined nature;
the concentrations on wishlessness and signlessness pertain to the existence of the dependent and perfected natures, respectively.
These three concentrations are mundane, yet they are not false because they bring about supramundane knowledge.
It is not right [to rely on the letter] because it is not supramundane.
One who knows the meaning perceives all phenomena as being like a raft;
one who knows the Dharma is so called for the sake of abandoning satisfaction with mere learning. (MSA 13.2)
Thus, one who knows the meaning understands that all phenomena, such as the sūtras and so forth, are like a raft;
by abandoning contentment with mere learning, he becomes a knower of the Dharma.
Having likewise penetrated duality through mundane knowledge, [he proceeds further].
Upon the perfection of that knowledge, one enters into accordance with the Dharma.

Having realized the two-fold nature of selflessness through these two types of knowledge belonging to ordinary persons— namely, the knowledge of the meaning and the knowledge of phenomena— he practices for the sake of perfecting that knowledge, having realized selflessness in the manner previously described. In this way, he practices in accordance with the Dharma (*anudharma*).
Then he attains supramundane, unsurpassed knowledge;
on the first stage, he becomes equal to all those bodhisattvas who possess that same nature.

Then he attains supramundane, unsurpassed knowledge; for there is no vehicle more distinguished than this. On the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā*), he becomes one who has correctly entered into practice by being equal with all bodhisattvas who share that same nature—that is, by equality with the bodhisattvas belonging to that very stage.
Having brought about the complete destruction of all afflictions to be abandoned through vision,
one applies oneself to cultivation for the sake of abandoning the cognitive obscurations.
The verse has its meaning already explained:
"By means of the knowledge that is accompanied by the conceptualization of the established state..."
In this way, one practices in accordance with the Dharma throughout the remaining stages.
By the remainder, he demonstrates the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*anudharmacāritva*).
"By means of establishment and non-conceptualization" refers to the knowledge of the establishment of the stages (*bhūmi*) and by means of non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*).
"Accompanying" means moving in continuous connection, through mutual uninterruptedness.
By these two verses, practicing in accordance with the Dharma has been shown.
Regarding the practice of heedfulness in application, there are four verses:
"Easy to obtain, well-supported, on good ground, and having good companions..."
A favorable place is one that possesses good qualities, where a wise person takes up residence.
By means of four wheels—beginning with dwelling in a suitable locality—he demonstrates the practice of heedfulness.
Therein, by this verse, he demonstrates dwelling in a suitable locality:
because the requisites for life, such as robes and alms-food, are easily obtained without difficulty.
It is well-established because it is not occupied by wicked people such as thieves and the like;
it is a good location because it is a land free from disease;
and it has good companions because its companions share the same ethical conduct and views.
Good association [is characterized] by having few distractions and conversations during the day, and by having little noise and the like at night.
A Bodhisattva who is learned, has seen the truth, is eloquent, compassionate, and untiring should be known as a great and noble person. (MSA 13.8)
By this second verse, he shows the true person (satpuruṣa),

because of his possession of the qualities of scriptural learning (āgama), realization (adhigama), eloquence (vāk-karaṇa), a mind free from worldly motives (nirāmiṣa-citta), and tirelessness (akilāsitva).
He has taught that which has its own objective support (svālambana), is well-prepared (susambhara/sustabdhā), is truly cultivated (subhāvanā), and is indeed well-expedient (supāya).
And it is the state of being correctly self-exerted, characterized by well-applied practice for deliverance.
By this third [verse], he demonstrates his own state of correct aspiration as comprised by wise attention (*yoniso-manaskāra*):

through having the true Dharma as its object, through having well-accumulated the provisions, through cultivating the signs of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth from time to time, through not being satisfied with a mere trifle, and through constant and respectful application when there is further work to be done.
For the attainment of leisure, for the occurrence of favorable moments, and even for health,
as well as for meditative concentration and analytical discernment, the cause is indeed merit performed in the past.
By this fourth [verse], he demonstrates the state of having previously performed merit through five kinds of causes:
as the cause of delight, because one takes pleasure in dwelling in a suitable location;
and as the cause of birth at a favorable time, because one obtains reliance upon a true person.
And because it serves as the cause for health, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), one’s own correct aspiration (*samyak-praṇidhāna*) is accomplished.
Regarding the very emergence from afflictions through the afflictions themselves, there are three verses:
"Since no phenomenon (*dharma*) exists apart from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)."
Therefore, the Buddhas consider passion and the other afflictions to be the very means of liberation for them.
Regarding what was said by the Blessed One:
"I do not speak of the escape from passion as being anywhere other than through passion itself; likewise for hatred and delusion," he now demonstrates the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) therein.

Because there is no phenomenon (dharma) that is separate from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), since no phenomenon exists apart from its true nature (dharmatā); therefore, even the true nature of passion and so forth receives the designation "passion" and so on, and that is the escape from passion and so forth—it is with this intention that it should be understood. Because no phenomenon is found that is separate from the realm of phenomena.
Therefore, in the exposition of affliction, that [connection] is considered by the wise to be a connection of consciousness (*saṃvid-saṃdhi*).
As for what was said— that ignorance (*avidyā*) and awakening (*bodhi*) are one—
even there, in the explanation of the defiled state (*saṃkleśa*), that very same intention applies:
ignorance would be the true nature of awakening (*bodhidharmatā*) through metaphorical designation.
Because one practices those very [afflictions] such as attachment in a systematic manner (*yoniśas*), one is thereby liberated from them; thus, their emergence is from that [practice].

By correctly applying oneself to those very things—passion and so forth—one is liberated from them; therefore, it is their thorough understanding that constitutes their transcendence. This is the intended meaning here.
Regarding the avoidance of the mental orientations of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, there are two verses:
"Indeed, for the Sons of the Conqueror, even intense suffering is not an obstacle."
For the sake of sentient beings, they may somehow dwell even in the abodes of hell;
however, for the wise, various virtuous conceptualizations in the Lesser Vehicle— though impelled by the perceived qualities of peace and the defects of cyclic existence— are obstacles.
Indeed, dwelling in the hells does not at all constitute an obstacle for the wise toward pure and vast enlightenment at any time; rather,
it is the conceptualization of another vehicle that is extremely cold toward one's own welfare.
It also creates an obstacle even to dwelling in supreme happiness.

Of these two verses, the second is the proof for the first; both have their meaning already explained. There are four verses regarding the refutation of fear concerning the absence of intrinsic nature and natural purity.
The perception of phenomena where there is no existence, and the state of purity despite the absence of affliction,
should be known as being like an illusion and likewise like space. (MSA 13.16)
Just as in a painting properly executed according to rule there is no actual elevation or depression, yet they are seen;
so too, in the construction of the unreal, duality never exists in any way, yet it is seen.
Just as when turbid water has been clarified, that clarity does not arise from elsewhere;
rather, it is merely the removal of impurities therein—such indeed is the method for the purification of one's own mind. (MSA 13.18)
And it is held that the mind is always luminous by nature, yet it is defiled by adventitious faults;
apart from the mind as the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), no other mind is established as being luminous by nature.

The non-existence of phenomena and the perception of phenomena are grounds for fear; likewise, the fact that the *dharmadhātu* is by nature free from affliction and yet subsequently becomes pure are grounds for fear for the foolish.
Establishing these respectively through the analogy of illusions and the like, and through the analogy of space, he negates that fear.
Similarly, he does so respectively through the analogy of the depressions and elevations in a painting, and through the analogy of water that is turbid and then clarified.
By the fourth verse, he demonstrates the analogy of water with respect to the mind.
Just as water is clear by nature but becomes turbid through adventitious impurity, so too the mind is considered luminous by nature but defiled by adventitious faults;
however, natural luminosity is not predicated of any other mind characterized by dependence (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) apart from the mind that is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-citta*).
Therefore, in this context, it should be understood that "mind" refers precisely to the suchness of the mind (*cittatathatā*).
There are four verses concerning the prohibition of offenses arising from passion:
A bodhisattva’s love for sentient beings is profound and great.
Therefore, it is considered always to act for the benefit [of others] as if they were an only son.
Because he acts for the benefit of sentient beings, he incurs no downfall born of attachment;
however, hatred toward any sentient being is entirely contrary to his path.

Just as a female pigeon, exceedingly affectionate toward her own offspring, remains embracing them who are her very nature, so too is resentment contradictory toward such beings; likewise, it is contradictory toward embodied beings who possess compassion for their children.
Since loving-kindness exists, the mind of resentment is its opposite;
since tranquility exists, the mind of affliction is its opposite;
since benefit exists, the mind of deceit is its opposite.
For that from which fear arises is not contradictory to that [which is its opposite].

The love that a bodhisattva has for sentient beings is what is intended here by the term "attachment"; he prohibits any transgression committed against them because it serves as the cause for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
He cites the example of the female pigeon because of her intense passion and her excessive affection for her offspring.
In a compassionate Bodhisattva, resentment toward sentient beings who are givers is contradictory.
For Bodhisattvas, there is loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward sentient beings, which brings peace from calamity, the giving of wealth, and joy;
because it generates delight, resentment is therefore opposed to these qualities, such as loving-kindness.
And preceded by that [lack of faith] are the states of mind such as addiction and so forth.
Regarding the distinctions in practice, there are five verses:
"Just as a sick person applies himself to excellent medicine, so does one apply oneself to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)."
And just as a physician applies himself to those who are ill, so does he act toward sentient beings.
Just as one behaves toward an untrained servant,
and just as a merchant behaves toward his merchandise, so does he behave toward sensual pleasures.
Just as a washerman applies himself to his work on a garment,
so does a father apply himself toward his young child without causing it any harm.
One who seeks fire proceeds with the lower fire-drill for the sake of continuity;
or one who is trustworthy applies himself to the higher mind when it has not yet been accomplished.
Just as a magician proceeds toward his objects of knowledge through wisdom,
so too is the practice of the bodhisattva considered to be in that manner and toward that object.
This illustrates that in which one practices:
"as" refers to those such as the sick with respect to excellent medicines and so forth;
"wherein" refers to cyclic existence and so forth, because one frequents cyclic existence after having applied discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).

Because, through compassion, one does not abandon sentient beings who are afflicted by the defilements; because one makes one's own mind free from self-interest; and because, through the perfections such as generosity, one leads to the increase of enjoyments in their respective order.
Through the purification of actions of body and so forth,
through not being provoked by the harm of sentient beings,
and through uninterrupted application to the cultivation of the wholesome.
Because of not relishing meditative concentration and because of the absence of error regarding the objects of knowledge,
there is a verse concerning the purity of the three spheres in practice.
Thus, constantly endowed with noble vigor and well-engaged in the ripening and purification of the two,
he proceeds step by step toward supreme accomplishment through the purity of ultimate, stainless non-conceptuality.

Thus, by means of non-conceptual knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*), the absence of conceptualization regarding the practitioner, the object to be practiced, and the practice itself should be understood as the purity of the three spheres (*trimandalapariśuddhi*).
"Well-engaged in the ripening and purification of the two" refers to sentient beings and oneself.
The thirteenth chapter, the Chapter on Practice (*pratipattyadhikāra*), in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The fourteenth chapter: In the section on instruction and admonition (*avavādānuśāsanī*), there are fifty-one verses.
Having emerged from incalculable eons while increasing his resolute faith,
he is filled with wholesome qualities just as the ocean is filled with waters.
"By increasing resolute conviction" means by bringing it to the state of intensity (*adhimātra*).
The rest has its meaning already explained.
Thus, having accumulated the provisions, the Son of the Victor is pure from the beginning.
Being wise and having a pliable mind, one applies oneself to meditative cultivation.

He is pure from the beginning through the purification of the bodhisattva vows and by straightening his view in the Mahāyāna through the apprehension of the non-perverted meaning. He is well-knowing because of his great learning; he is pliant of mind because of his freedom from hindrances.
Then, within the stream of the Dharma, he receives from the Buddhas extensive instruction for the sake of attaining the vastness of tranquility and primordial wisdom.
The meaning of this verse is already explained.
Thereafter, regarding the Dharma consisting of the sūtras and so forth, which reveals the non-dual reality, the ascetic should first fix his mind upon the names of the sūtras and so on. (MSA 14.4)
Then, one should proceed sequentially through the various divisions of the words;
one should investigate their meanings both through internal personal reflection and through fundamental reasoning.
Having ascertained those meanings, he should then integrate them with the Dharma;
thereafter, he should form a firm aspiration for the realization of that meaning.

Regarding the Dharma consisting of the discourses (*sūtra*), verses (*geya*), and so forth—such as the names of the *sūtras* and so on, including the *Daśabhūmika*—one should first fix the mind upon them.
By these three verses, six types of mental states are taught:

the root-mind (*mūlacitta*), the following-mind (*anucaracitta*), the investigating-mind (*vicāraṇācitta*), the determining-mind (*avadhāraṇācitta*), the synthesizing-mind (*saṃkalanacitta*), and the aspiring-mind (*āśāsticitta*).
In that context, the fundamental mind is that which takes as its object the names of phenomena such as the sūtras—
whether having heard instruction or having conceptualized it for oneself—
such as "impermanent," "suffering," "empty," "selfless," and so forth, in accordance with proper reflection (*yoniśas*).
The following mind is that by which one pursues the distinctions of the words of the sūtras and so forth once they have been taken as objects by way of their names.
The investigating mind is that by which one investigates both the meaning and the phrasing.
Therein, one investigates the meaning in four ways: by counting, by weighing, by examining, and by scrutinizing.

In this context, "calculation" (*gaṇanā*) refers to subsumption (*saṃgrahaṇa*), such as: form consists of ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one [base]; feeling consists of six groups of feeling (*vedanākāya*), and so forth. "Comparison" (*tulanā*) refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon (*dharma*) that possesses a numerical count.
Grasping is by way of neither superimposition nor denial.
Investigation is the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Contemplation is the observation of an object that has been analyzed, calculated, weighed, and investigated.
One examines the phoneme through two aspects:
by way of its meaningfulness when combined with all [other phonemes], and by way of its meaninglessness when isolated.
The mind of ascertainment is that by which one ascertains the sign of that which has been followed or examined accordingly.
The synthesizing mind (*saṃkalanacitta*) is that which functions by condensing and unifying into a single form the object already investigated within the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*).

The aspiring mind (*āśāsticitta*) is that which functions accompanied by desire for the sake of that goal for which one is engaged— whether it be for the sake of meditative concentration, for the sake of fulfilling [a specific aim], for the sake of the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), for the sake of entering a stage (*bhūmi*), or for the sake of attaining excellence.
For it is mind alone that arises as the appearance of an object; there is no object other than mind. Whether one knows "mind-only" or does not know it, mind alone is the object and nothing else.
Thus, mind is established as the sixfold object. One should seek and investigate these through a continuous stream of mental discursive thoughts.
And one should also investigate with mental attentions that are non-discursive and of a single flavor.
The path of calm abiding (śamatha) for this [yogin] should be known as the condensed names of the dharmas;
the path of insight (vipaśyanā) should be known as the investigation of their meanings.
Furthermore, the path should be understood as the union (yuganaddha), which is the synthesis of those two;
one should seize the mind when it is sluggish and again pacify it when it is agitated.
When equanimity has been attained, one should remain indifferent toward that object;
then, once again, one should apply oneself to it continuously and with reverence in every respect.
By these four verses, eleven modes of mental attention (*manaskāra*) are taught:
that with both applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*),
and that without applied thought but with sustained thought alone (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ*).
Without applied thought and without sustained thought;
the mental application of tranquility;
the mental application of insight.
The mental application of the yoked pair;
the mental application of the sign of exertion; the mental application of the sign of calm abiding; and the mental application of the sign of equanimity.
There is continuous mental attention and respectful mental attention.
Having bound the mind to the object, one should not allow it to be distracted from its forward momentum.
Having quickly recognized distraction, one should withdraw [the mind] back into that [object] once again.
The wise person should repeatedly withdraw the mind within themselves;
thereafter, they should discipline the mind in meditative concentration by perceiving its virtues.
One should pacify aversion toward that [object] by perceiving the fault of distraction;
likewise, one should pacify covetousness, dejection, and other such states when they have arisen.
Then, through that practice, the yogi further attains a state of mind that flows spontaneously,
first with effort and subsequently without effort.
By these four verses, the means for stabilizing [the mind] is taught through the nine modes of mental abiding.
These nine modes are: he places the mind, settles it, fixes it, draws it near, tames it, pacifies it, thoroughly pacifies it, makes it one-pointed, and concentrates the mind.
Then, having obtained a subtle pliancy of body and mind,
he should be known as one possessing mental application (samanaskāra), further increasing those very [qualities].
Through its far-reaching increase, he attains the fundamental state;
purifying that state for the sake of the superknowledges (abhijñā), he reaches supreme adaptability (karmanyatā).

Through the accomplishment of the superknowledges (abhijñā) within meditative concentration, he goes to world-systems for the sake of making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and for the purpose of hearing [the Dharma].
Having attended upon immeasurable Buddhas for immeasurable eons,
he attains supreme flexibility of mind through that service.
Thus, "supreme flexibility in meditation" is how it should be connected.
"By immeasurable eons" means by those that have reached an incalculable number.
The remainder of these verses has its meaning already explained.
Then, through those five purities, he first attains the five benefits;
thereafter, he becomes a vessel for unsurpassed purity.
For his entire body of subtle corruption dissolves moment by moment,
and his body and mind are filled on all sides with pliancy.
He perceives the undifferentiated manifestation of phenomena in every respect; in a state of complete purity, he beholds signs that are non-conceptual.
In this way, the wise one constantly effects the gathering of causes for the complete fulfillment and purification of the Dharma-body in every respect. (MSA 14.22)
Then, prior to purification, one obtains five benefits that precede it;
"of purification" means of the stage of pure intention (*śuddhyāśaya-bhūmi*). And by obtaining these, one attains the state of being a vessel for complete purity.
It is "unsurpassed" because there is no higher vehicle.
Regarding the fulfillment and purification of the *dharmakāya*, fulfillment occurs on the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) and purification occurs on the Buddha stage (*buddhabhūmi*).
Among these five benefits, it should be understood that three belong to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and two belong to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Therefore, as long as there is mundane attainment,
that Bodhisattva, having become thus and being in meditative equipoise,
does not perceive any objects as being separate from mental discourse.
One exerts firm vigor for the sake of increasing the light of the Dharma;
and through the increase of that light of the Dharma, one abides in mind-only.
Then he perceives within the mind the appearance of all objects;
at that time, his distraction regarding the perceived object has been abandoned.
Then, only the distraction of the subject remains for him;
and at that time, he again quickly touches the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
Beyond this are the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

A Bodhisattva who has become thus, with a concentrated mind, does not perceive any phenomena as being distinct from mental discourse; rather, it appears that they are merely mental discourse, designated by their specific and general characteristics.
This is his stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
This is that light concerning which it was said in the *Kṣāranadī*:
"Light" is a designation for the receptivity to the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*).
For the sake of increasing that very light of the Dharma, he exerts firm vigor through sustained application.
This is his stage of the "Summits" (mūrdhan).
And through the increase of the light of the Dharma, he abides in mind-only,
because of the penetration that "this is mind."
Thereupon, he perceives that all objects appear within the mind alone,
and no object exists apart from the mind;
at that time, his distraction regarding the grasped object is abandoned.
Only the distraction of the grasper remains;
this is his stage of patience (kṣānti),
and at that time, he quickly touches the immediate concentration (ānantarya-samādhi).
This is his stage of the supreme mundane dharmas.
For what reason is it called "uninterrupted"? Because immediately thereafter, the distraction of the subject is abandoned.
For these stages, beginning with "Heat" (uṣmagata), are to be known respectively as follows.
These are the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), beginning with "heat" (uṣmagata).
Furthermore, he attains a knowledge that is free from the two types of grasping, supramundane, unsurpassed, non-conceptual, and devoid of stains.
Beyond this is the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

It is "free from the twofold grasping" because it is dissociated from the grasping of the object (*grāhya*) and the grasping of the subject (*grāhaka*). It is "unsurpassed" because of its immediacy (*anantarya*) in relation to the vehicle.
It is non-conceptual because it is dissociated from the conceptualization of grasped object and grasping subject;
it is free from defilement because of the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision and cultivation. By this, it is said to be "dustless" and "free from stain."
This transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) is held to be his first stage;
and through immeasurable eons, it attains complete purification.
The meaning of this verse is clear:
Furthermore, having realized the equality of the dharmadhātu at that time, one attains a state of mind that is always equal toward oneself and all sentient beings. (MSA 14.30)
Regarding selflessness, the nature of suffering, what is to be done, and the absence of requital,
he is even-minded toward sentient beings, just like the other sons of the Conquerors. (MSA 14.31)
And by penetrating the equality of phenomena through the selflessness of phenomena, one always attains a mind of equality toward all sentient beings by means of five kinds of equality: first,
the equality of selflessness, because there is no distinction between self and others regarding selflessness and suffering within their respective continuums.
By the equality of duty, because there is a commonality in the desire to eliminate the suffering of both oneself and others;
and by the equality of non-reciprocity,
because one does not delight in receiving recompense from others as one would from oneself.
And by way of equality with other bodhisattvas, because he realizes [reality] just as they have realized it,
he perceives the conditioned phenomena of the triple world— which are unreal imaginings— as being non-existent in their true sense, through perfectly pure primordial wisdom. (MSA 14.32)
He perceives the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three realms as being merely unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpamātra*),
by means of perfectly pure knowledge because it is supramundane;
that is, in the sense of non-duality, meaning in the sense of the absence of grasped object and grasping subject.

Having attained the existence of that non-existence, which is liberated from those things that cause one to fall into views, one indeed then attains the path of vision; therefore, it is designated by that name.
He perceives the existence of that very absence of the grasped and the grasper as the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), liberated from the afflictions to be abandoned by vision.
Having known the emptiness of non-existence, and likewise the emptiness of existence,
and having known the emptiness of intrinsic nature, he is called a "knower of emptiness."
And that bodhisattva is called "one who knows emptiness" because of his knowledge of the three kinds of emptiness.
Emptiness of non-existence refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it lacks existence by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The emptiness of the state of being "thus" refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), for that is not a state of being "thus" as it is imagined; rather, it is an entity by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because its very essence is emptiness.
The state of signlessness (*animitta-pada*) should be known as the complete exhaustion of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
And unreal imagination is indeed that which is not the object of the wishless.
The signless state (*animittapada*) should be known as the complete exhaustion of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is the state of non-aspiration (*apraṇidhāna*); this is the meaning of its objective support (*ālambana*).
Its acquisition is held to be constant, occurring together with that path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
O Son of the Conqueror, [this applies] to all the various factors conducive to enlightenment.

By means of that path of seeing, it should be understood that the Bodhisattva attains all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Having realized through his intellect that the world consists of nothing but conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and is devoid of self, he perceives it as merely the growth of suffering.
Having abandoned the view of self that consists of what is meaningless, she relies upon the great-souled view which possesses great meaning.
One who possesses the view of self here even without a [false] view of self, and who is deeply pained even without suffering;
who accomplishes all goals yet has no desire for being an agent, having performed what is beneficial for himself as if for his own self. (MSA 14.38)
He whose mind is liberated by supreme liberation, yet remains bound by firm and long-lasting bonds,
applies himself and acts even while not seeing the end of suffering.
In this world, people are unable to bear even their own suffering; how much less could they bear the accumulated suffering of others?
They do not even consider a single lifetime that has passed, being indifferent to it; but the Bodhisattva is the opposite of that.

The love, the affection, the application, and the lack of weariness toward sentient beings that Bodhisattvas possess is a supreme wonder amidst worldly existences; yet it is not so because they regard all beings as equal to themselves.
With these five verses, the majesty of the bodhisattva who has attained the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is elucidated.
The "view of self consisting of what is not beneficial" is the afflicted view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The "great view of self" is the view of self that has great purpose, which consists in attaining a mind of equality toward all sentient beings as oneself.

For she is of great purpose because she is the cause for performing the welfare of all sentient beings. Without the view of self—which consists of what is harmful—the view of self is of great purpose; for even without suffering born of one's own continuum, she is deeply pained by the suffering born of the continua of all sentient beings.
He whose mind is liberated from that which is to be abandoned by vision through supreme liberation and the unsurpassed vehicle.

Bound by a firm and extensive bond that extends through the continuums of all sentient beings, he does not see the end of suffering because the realm of sentient beings is infinite like space; yet he applies himself to bringing about the end of suffering and indeed accomplishes it for immeasurable sentient beings.
But by the opposite, the Bodhisattva is indeed capable of bearing the accumulated suffering of all sentient beings as far as the world extends.

That affection which the Bodhisattva has for sentient beings, that desire for their welfare and happiness, that application toward that end, and that lack of weariness in one so applied— all this is the supreme marvel in the worlds.
And this is not at all surprising, because [the Bodhisattva] regards all sentient beings as equal to himself.
Therefore, on the remaining stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
he applies himself here to the cultivation of the two kinds of knowledge.
That gnosis is non-conceptual and purifies the qualities of a Buddha;
the other [gnosis] is according to conventional designation and brings sentient beings to maturity.
And the departure from cultivation occurs through the completion of two incalculable aeons;
having reached the final cultivation, the Bodhisattva becomes one who is consecrated.
And having attained the diamond-like concentration, which cannot be shattered by conceptual constructions,
one reaches the final transformation of the basis, which is free from the stains of all obscurations.
And he attains omniscience, the unsurpassed state,
abiding in which he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.
By these, the path of cultivation is illuminated as being twofold wisdom:
the non-conceptual [wisdom] by which one purifies one's own Buddha-qualities,
and the mundane [wisdom] obtained subsequent to the supramundane, according to its established arrangement, by which one brings sentient beings to maturity.
Upon the completion of two incalculable eons, having reached the final stage of cultivation at its ultimate conclusion, one who has been consecrated attains the diamond-like samādhi.
It is called "diamond-like" in the sense that it is impenetrable by conceptual constructions and latent tendencies.
Thereafter, one attains the final transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which is free from the stains of all afflictive and cognitive obstructions.

And [the Bodhisattva] abides in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), the unsurpassed state, wherein for as long as saṃsāra lasts, he acts for the benefit of sentient beings by manifesting perfect enlightenment, nirvāṇa, and so forth.

How could there not be great purpose in such a Sage whose sight is so difficult to obtain? For one whose mind is constantly and intensely nourished by the surges of serene faith arising from incomparable hearing, there can never be constant sight [of him]. (MSA 14.47)
Constantly and directly exhorted by the Tathāgatas while established in the gateway of the Dharma, he is—
as if seized by the hair— dragged out from the thicket of faults and forcibly established in enlightenment.
Having completely overcome the entire world through utterly pure visions and non-conceptual awakenings,
he shines with great magnificence upon the world like a great sun, having dispelled the vast darkness.
By these three verses, he demonstrates the greatness of instruction:
for one who receives instruction in the stream of the entrance to the Dharma, there is constant vision of the Buddhas,
and from that, the hearing of the peerless Dharma.
Because his faith is exceedingly great, and because his mind is nourished by the surges of that faith, constant vision of the Buddhas becomes of great benefit to him.
The rest has its meaning already explained.
The Buddhas constantly bestow correct praise upon one who is rightly engaged in their own welfare.

The Victors have duly shown here to the supreme being all kinds of factors conducive to obstacles— those arising from censure and envy, and those intent on remaining in distraction— by avoiding which and cultivating which, one attains vastness in this yoga within the teaching of the Sugata. (MSA 14.50)
By this verse, he demonstrates the fourfold instruction:
first, by way of bestowing praise upon a bodhisattva who is correctly engaged in his own welfare with respect to higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*);
and second, with respect to higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), [by way of pointing out] the obstacles to those who are intent on stability and investigation.
And by teaching all kinds of dharmas conducive to that [attainment],
