as well as those things to be avoided and those to be cultivated— namely, the obstacles and the favorable conditions respectively—
"yoga" refers to the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Thus, having become fully perfected through the constant accumulation of merit and having attained a vast meditative concentration of the mind, that supreme being— having received the constant great instructions of the Sage— becomes one who has reached the further shore of the ocean of virtues.
The concluding verse has its meaning already explained.
This concludes the fourteenth chapter, "Instruction and Admonition," in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The fifteenth chapter:
Summary Verse (uddāna).
Abundance of resolute belief, the seeking and teaching of the Dharma, practice, and likewise correct instruction and admonition. (MSA 15.1)
There are four verses on the classification of action conjoined with skillful means:

Just as the earth is everywhere the foundation for forests, living beings, mountains, and flowing rivers, so too is the threefold action of the wise declared to be the universal basis for all virtues such as generosity. (MSA 15.2)
By this verse, he shows the means of origination;
for every kind of wholesome [action], such as giving and so forth—including the perfections and the factors conducive to enlightenment—is originated by the three types of action.
"Among the wise" refers to the bodhisattvas.
The mention of forests and so forth is for the purpose of illustrating objects that are both stable and unstable to be enjoyed.

For the Sons of the Conquerors who exert themselves with extremely difficult deeds of various forms extending over many eons, there is no exhaustion here of their action consisting of body, speech, and mind. (MSA 15.3)
Just as one who seeks his own welfare would protect his own person from poison, weapons, or great thunderbolts hurled by an enemy,
so too does the Son of the Conqueror protect himself from the threefold karma and from the various lower vehicles.
With these two verses, he shows the means for emerging from [the state of weariness].
"Emerging" refers respectively to emerging from weariness with the Mahāyāna and from falling into other vehicles;
"sinking" (saṃnati) is the meaning of weariness.

There is a similarity to poison and other such things in action associated with the Hīnayāna, because it involves the dedication of the mind toward the Hīnayāna, the total severance of the roots of virtue in the Mahāyāna, the non-arising of unarisen roots of virtue,
and the destruction of arisen roots of virtue.

And because it is an obstacle to the attainment of the perfection of Buddhahood, one who is always free from conceptual construction does not perceive the agent, the action, or the performance of the action in a threefold way. Therefore, through the inclusion of those skillful means, his action becomes infinite and reaches the further shore of purity. (MSA 15.5)
By this fourth verse, he demonstrates the means for the purification of action;
that is, through the complete purity of the mandala, because of the non-apprehension of agent, action, and activity.
"Infinite" means inexhaustible.
The Fifteenth Chapter: Action Accompanied by Skillful Means from the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The sixteenth chapter, on the Compendium of the Classifications of the Perfections, contains this summary verse:
One should know their number, their characteristics, their sequence, their etymological definitions, and the qualities of their practice;
as well as their classification, their synthesis, their opposites, their benefits, and their mutual determination.
There are six verses on the classification of number:
Prosperity consists of the excellence of enjoyments, the excellence of the physical basis, the excellence of attendants, and the excellence of undertakings;
furthermore, it includes being free from the power of the afflictions and always being free from error regarding what is to be done.
Thus ends the first [section].
In that regard, through the four perfections, there is a fourfold prosperity:
through generosity, the perfection of wealth.
Through ethical discipline one attains excellence of the physical body; through patience, one attains excellence of attendants;
for by practicing those [virtues], one becomes very dear to many people in the future.

Through vigor, there is perfection in undertaking because of the perfection of all undertakings; through the fifth [perfection], there is freedom from being under the sway of the afflictions because of the suppression of the afflictions by meditative concentration;
through the sixth, there is non-delusion regarding duties because of the thorough knowledge of all tasks as they truly are.
Thus is spiritual progress (*abhyudaya*). In that regard, the six perfections (*pāramitā*) are established with reference to non-affliction and the undertaking of unerring activity.
Being well-engaged in the welfare of sentient beings, one acts through generosity, non-harming, and forbearance;
and by means of the causes, stability, and liberation, one practices for one's own benefit in every way.
Thus is the second [section].

A bodhisattva correctly engaged in the welfare of sentient beings accomplishes the welfare of others through the three perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience—by means of relinquishment, by non-harming, and by enduring harm respectively.
Through the three [perfections] of meditative concentration, wisdom, and liberation—which possess their respective causes—he practices every aspect of his own welfare.

Relying upon vigor, through the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) respectively, there is the stabilization of the unconcentrated mind and the liberation of the concentrated mind.
Thus, with reference to the welfare of others and one's own welfare, there are the six perfections (*pāramitās*),
characterized by non-harming, non-injury, endurance of injury, and lack of weariness in action.
Through captivating and well-spoken words, he acts for the sake of others; from this, it follows that it is also for his own sake.
Thus ends the third [section].
Through generosity and the other perfections, the bodhisattva’s entire welfare of others is accomplished,
by means of providing for others and not obstructing them, respectively.
By not harming others and by enduring their harm;

by being untiring in providing assistance; by attracting others through the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) and so forth; and by cutting through doubts with well-spoken and eloquent speech—through this benefit for others, the bodhisattva achieves his own self-interest.
Because making the welfare of others one's own task and because of the attainment of great enlightenment,
there are six perfections due to the commitment to the entirety of the welfare of others.
(MSA_Bagchi 98)
Lack of attachment to enjoyments, intense reverence for the two [truths], tirelessness, and non-conceptual yoga— this entire collection constitutes the supreme vehicle.
Thus is the fourth:
through giving, the bodhisattva has no attachment to possessions because of his lack of regard for them;
through the undertaking of ethical discipline, he possesses intense reverence for the bodhisattva trainings.

Through patience and vigor, there is non-exhaustion respectively regarding the two types of suffering—those caused by sentient beings and those not caused by sentient beings—and regarding the application to the wholesome.
Through meditative concentration and wisdom, there is non-conceptual yoga comprised of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This much constitutes the entirety of the Mahāyāna.
Based on the section concerning the summary of the Mahāyāna, there are six perfections:

one is the path of non-attachment toward sense objects; another is the restraint of distraction regarding the attainment thereof; another is the non-abandonment and increase of sentient beings; and another is the purification of obscurations.
Thus ends the fifth [chapter].
In this context, generosity (*dāna*) is the path of non-attachment toward sense objects, because attachment to them is removed through the practice of relinquishment.

Ethical discipline (*śīla*) consists in the restraint of distractions regarding the attainment of those [objects]; for one established in the monastic vows (*bhikṣusaṃvara*), there is no engagement in the distractions of all worldly activities for the sake of obtaining sense objects.
Patience consists in not abandoning sentient beings because one is undisturbed by all harms and sufferings.
Diligence consists in the increase of the wholesome, since for one who has initiated diligence, that leads to the attainment of awakening.
Meditative concentration and wisdom constitute the path for the purification of obscurations, because through them the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable are purified.
The "path" refers to the means.
Thus, because of the focus on the path in all its aspects, there are six perfections;
and with reference to the three trainings, the Victors have fully explained the six perfections.
The first three are twofold by reason of the last two; one [is so] among the three.
Thus ends the sixth [chapter].
Among these, the first three perfections constitute the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), because they include their respective equipment and retinues.
For, through generosity, one takes up ethical discipline without regard for enjoyments; and once taken up, one protects it through patience by not reviling in return when reviled, and so forth.

"Twofold" refers to the training in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*); this [training] is subsumed by the latter two, namely meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), respectively.
It should be understood that the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) is present in all three trainings, because vigor is the companion to them all.

There are six verses on the analysis of the characteristics: Generosity is free from its opposite, is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge, fulfills all desires, and matures sentient beings in three ways. (MSA 16.8)
The generosity of bodhisattvas possesses four characteristics:
it is free from its opposite because of the abandonment of stinginess;
it is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge due to the application of the penetration of the selflessness of phenomena; and it fulfills all desires by giving whatever anyone wishes for.
The ripening of sentient beings is threefold: by means of generosity, one gathers sentient beings and establishes them in the three vehicles according to their respective capacities;
and morality is that which is free from its opposite and is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge.
It fulfills all desires and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Patience is free from its opposite, is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge,
fulfills all desires, and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Vigor is free from its opposite, endowed with non-conceptual knowledge,
fulfills all aspirations, and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Dhyāna is free from opposing factors, accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge,
fulfills all desires, and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Wisdom is free from its opposites and has reached non-conceptual knowledge;
it fulfills all desires and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Just as the characteristic of generosity is fourfold, so too should it be understood for ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the others.
Their respective adversaries (*vipakṣa*), however, are immorality, anger, laziness, distraction, and faulty wisdom.

The fulfillment of all desires through ethical discipline and the other perfections occurs because they fulfill the desires of others by means of restraining all bodily and vocal actions, enduring offenses, providing assistance, and cutting through doubts.
The quality of ripening sentient beings consists in attracting them through ethical discipline and the other perfections, thereby bringing them to maturity within the three vehicles.
Regarding the analysis of their sequence, there is this verse:
they are taught in that order because the latter arises based upon the former.
Also by way of inferior and superior states, and by way of grossness and subtlety.
These three reasons constitute the sequential teaching of giving and the other perfections:
because each subsequent one arises based on the preceding one.

For one who is indifferent to enjoyments undertakes ethical discipline; being endowed with ethical discipline, one becomes patient; being patient, one exerts vigor; having exerted vigor, one generates meditative concentration; and with a concentrated mind, one understands things as they truly are.
Because the former is inferior and the latter is a state of excellence;
for giving is inferior while ethical discipline is superior, and so on up to meditation being inferior while wisdom is superior.
Furthermore, because the former is coarse and the latter is subtle.
For generosity is coarse because it is easy to enter and easy to perform;
wisdom is subtle because it is difficult to enter and difficult to perform.
In this way, it continues up to the point where meditative absorption is coarse and wisdom is subtle.
Regarding the analysis of the etymological definitions, there is this verse:

"Because of the removal of poverty, the attainment of coolness, the destruction of anger, the possession of excellent qualities, the concentration of the mind, and the knowledge of the ultimate truth, it is called [Dharma]. (MSA 16.15)
It is called *dāna* because it removes poverty;
it is called *śīla* because it brings about coolness, for one who possesses it is free from the burning afflictions caused by the signs of sense objects;
it is called *kṣānti* because it is the destruction of anger, since through it anger is destroyed.
It is called *vīrya* because it joins one with the excellent, due to its application to wholesome qualities;
it is called *dhyāna* because it holds the mind within;
and it is called *prajñā* because by means of it one knows the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
In the section on the analysis of cultivation, there is this verse:
"Relying upon the basis of cultivation, as well as mental attention and intention..."
And the skillful means and the mastery of all [perfections] are indeed explained.

The cultivation of the perfections is fivefold. Among these, that which is based on the substratum (*upadhi-saṃniśritā*) has four aspects. Therein, that which is based on the cause (*hetu-saṃniśritā*) is the practice and cultivation of the perfections by means of the power of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
That which is based on maturation is by the power of the excellence of one's physical existence;
that which is based on aspiration is by the power of former aspirations;
and that which is based on analytical discernment is the practice of application toward the perfections by the power of wisdom.
The cultivation of the perfections based on mental attention is fourfold:
(1) through the mental attention of resolute belief, for one who has resolute faith in the sūtras associated with all the perfections;
and (2) through the mental attention of relishing, for one who relishes the perfections already attained by way of perceiving their qualities.

The cultivation of the perfections based on intention is sixfold: through the mental application of rejoicing, one rejoices in the giving and other virtues of all sentient beings in all world-systems; and through the mental application of aspiration, one aspires for the future excellence of the perfections for oneself and for all sentient beings.

[It is] with an insatiable intention, a vast intention, a joyful intention, an intention of benefit, an unstained intention, and a virtuous intention. Among these, the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding giving is that wherein a bodhisattva, in a single moment, might offer to a single sentient being world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, filled with the seven precious jewels,
and likewise as many physical bodies as there are sands in the river Ganges.
And in this way, he would provide for them moment by moment for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā;
and just as he would do for one sentient being, so too would he provide for the entire realm of sentient beings who are to be ripened for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by this same method.
Yet, the bodhisattva’s intention for giving remains entirely unsatiated.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding giving;
and the bodhisattva does not let such a succession of gifts lapse for even a single moment, nor does he interrupt it until he sits at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s expansive intention regarding generosity.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva becomes even more joyful while thus favoring those sentient beings with his gift than those sentient beings themselves are when being favored by that gift.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s joyful intention regarding giving. Furthermore,
that bodhisattva regards those sentient beings whom he thus benefits through giving as being more beneficial to himself than he is to them.
"By virtue of their being a support for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—
such a disposition as this is the bodhisattva’s beneficial intention regarding giving.
Furthermore, even after having performed such vast merit consisting of giving toward sentient beings, the bodhisattva does not seek any recompense nor any karmic maturation.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s stainless intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of generosity:

that the bodhisattva rejoices in the maturation of even such a vast mass of giving for the sake of sentient beings, and not for himself; and having made it common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s virtuous intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of generosity.
In that regard, the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention concerns the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Or, suppose a bodhisattva, throughout bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with a lifespan lasting for as many eons as there are sands in the river Ganges,
were to provide a constant supply of all necessities while performing the four modes of conduct within a great trichiliocosm filled with fire,
and were to cultivate even a single moment of the perfection of ethical discipline up to a single moment of the perfection of wisdom— by this method, [he would generate a vast amount of merit].

To whatever extent there is the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) and to whatever extent there is the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*) by which one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—

one should cultivate the aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of wisdom; for the Bodhisattva’s intention in the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is indeed insatiable.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to and including the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

namely, that the bodhisattva does not slacken and does not interrupt that succession of cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to and including the succession of cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, until sitting at the seat of awakening.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to and including the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva becomes even more joyful while benefiting sentient beings through the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
it is not so for those sentient beings who are being benefited.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s joyful intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva regards those sentient beings as more beneficial to himself than he is to them;
for it is by means of their cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to and including the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, that he benefits them, and not himself—
this being because they serve as the support for his attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s beneficial intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. And having performed such vast merit consisting of the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva does not seek a reward or a karmic maturation.

Such an intention as this—extending from the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom—is the bodhisattva’s unstained intention (*nirlepa-āśaya*).

In this regard, when a bodhisattva rejoices only for the sake of sentient beings in the maturation of the mass of merit consisting of the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, and not for his own sake;
and having made it common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s virtuous intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Cultivation based on skillful means is threefold in form,
by virtue of examining the complete purity of the three spheres through non-conceptual knowledge.
For that means is for the accomplishment of all mental orientations (*manasikāra*).

The cultivation of the perfections (*pāramitā*) based on mastery (*vibhutva*) is threefold: by virtue of mastery over the body; by virtue of mastery over objects; and by virtue of mastery over activity.
Through mastery over conduct and through mastery over teaching.
In that regard, mastery over body should be understood as two bodies in the Tathāgata: the essential (svābhāvika) and the enjoyment (sāṃbhogika).
In this context, mastery over conduct should be understood as the emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*),
by which one displays to all sentient beings every form of conduct in accordance with the Dharma. Mastery over teaching—
There is no obstruction in the teaching of all aspects of the six perfections.
There are twelve verses on the summary of the classifications,
based on the sixfold classification of the meanings of each [perfection], beginning with generosity.
There are six meanings: the meanings of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), cause (*hetu*), fruit (*phala*), activity (*karman*), endowment (*yoga*), and occurrence (*vṛtti*).
Regarding the classification of giving (*dāna*), there are two verses:
"The bestowing of wealth, the volition rooted in certainty," [and so forth].
The perfection of enjoyments and the perfection of the personal existence fulfill the two types of assistance.
Having fully understood that giving is endowed with non-avarice and consists of the gift of the Dharma, material goods, and fearlessness, the wise person should practice it accordingly.
The nature of giving is the communication of wealth to recipients.
Its cause is the volition co-arising with non-attachment and other such qualities.
Its fruit consists of the perfection of enjoyments and the perfection of the personal existence (ātmabhāva) as comprised by longevity and so forth, as described in the *Pañcasthāna-sūtra*.
Its function is the benefit of oneself and others, as well as the fulfillment of the accumulations for great enlightenment.
Its activity consists in its application to those who are free from stinginess,
through the distinctions of bestowing the gift of the Dharma, material goods, and fearlessness in this very life.
There are two verses on the classification of ethical discipline:
It consists of six limbs, culminates in peaceful cultivation, and bestows a happy rebirth and stability;
it is established in tranquility, free from fear, and joined with the accumulation of merit. (MSA 16.19)
Ethical discipline acquired through convention exists among those who abide in the vows;
having thus fully understood ethical discipline, the wise person should cultivate it.

"Six-limbed" refers to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Possessing six limbs" means that one dwells endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth, up to training by undertaking the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). "Ending in the state of tranquility" refers to the cause (*hetu*).
Because it is undertaken with the intention of [attaining] nirvāṇa,
"bestowing a happy rebirth and stability" is the fruit; for by means of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one goes to a happy rebirth.
Furthermore, because one attains stability of mind through the sequence beginning with freedom from regret,
it is said that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is "the foundation, peace, and fearlessness," which refers to its function; for ethical discipline is indeed the foundation of all virtuous qualities.

It is "peaceful" because of the calming of the burning heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is "fearless" because there is no production of fear, blame, or enmity caused by [the commission of] killing and so forth;
and it is "endowed with the equipment of merit" because of the constant engagement in the performance of actions of body, speech, and mind—this is its "yoga."

"It exists among those who abide in restraint" means that it is found in those established in the vows. Regarding this, "obtained through convention" refers to what is comprised within the *prātimokṣa* restraint;

"obtained through the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*) refers to what is comprised within the meditative (*dhyāna*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints. This is its "differentiated activity," because it functions through these three types of differentiation.
"It exists among those who abide in restraint" constitutes its "activity as a basis."

There are two verses regarding the classification of patience (kṣānti): The knowledge of endurance and acceptance arises from compassion and reliance upon the Dharma; it is said to possess five benefits and to accomplish the welfare of both [self and others]. (MSA 16.21)
Among those, that threefold austerity is considered to be conjoined with intensity;
having thus fully understood patience, the wise person should bring it to perfection.
"Knowledge of endurance and acceptance" is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the threefold patience (*kṣānti*); for,
in the case of the patience that endures harm, "endurance" (*marṣa*) is so called because it consists of enduring (*marṣaṇa*).

The causes are, respectively, compassion and reliance upon the Dharma, pertaining to the patience of enduring suffering and the patience of reflecting on the Dharma. Furthermore, reliance upon the Dharma is as follows:
The undertaking of ethical discipline and the mastery of what has been heard are declared to have five benefits; this is the fruit,
as stated in the Sūtra.
There are five benefits in patience:
one does not become full of enmity, nor does one become full of dissension.
He becomes abundant in happiness and mental gladness;
he dies without regret; and after the dissolution of the body, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.

And that which brings about the welfare of both is what is intended here by "endurance" (*marṣa*) and "acceptance" (*adhivāsana*). As it has been said: "He accomplishes the welfare of both himself and another, who, knowing another to be angry, personally remains calm in that situation."
Yoga is that which is conjoined with the power of austerity (tapas),
as it has been said:
"Patience is the supreme austerity."
Regarding these, "that" refers to the functioning [of patience] upon its basis, because it functions within those who possess it.
It is considered to be threefold, which refers to the functioning according to its divisions, namely through the three types of patience as previously explained.
There are two verses concerning the divisions of vigor (*vīrya*).
Right effort is properly established upon faith and aspiration for the wholesome;
it increases qualities such as mindfulness and serves as the antidote to the afflictions.
Endowed with qualities such as non-attachment, it is sevenfold in those [contexts];
having thus fully understood diligence, the wise person should cultivate it.
"Right enthusiasm for what is wholesome" is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Wholesome" is intended to exclude enthusiasm for other activities; "right" is intended to exclude enthusiasm for the liberation of non-Buddhist outsiders (*anyatīrthika*).
"Established upon faith and aspiration" is the cause (*hetu*), for one who has faith and is intensely desirous of the goal initiates vigor (*vīrya*).
"In the increase of qualities such as mindfulness" refers to the fruit;
for one who has initiated vigor, qualities such as mindfulness and meditative concentration arise.
"Being an antidote to affliction" refers to its function.
As it has been said:
"One who has initiated vigor dwells happily, unmixed with evil and unwholesome states.
Thus, "endowed with qualities such as non-attachment" refers to yoga.
"In them"—referring to those who have initiated vigor—is the function of the basis (*ādhāra-vṛtti*).
"Sevenfold" refers to the function of differentiation (*prabheda-vṛtti*).
Furthermore, that [vigor] is the physical and mental vigor applied continuously and with reverence toward the three trainings, beginning with higher ethics (*adhiśīla*).
There are two verses regarding the distinctions of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
The stability of the mind within, established upon mindfulness and vigor, leads to the attainment of happiness, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and mastery over dwelling [in meditation]. (MSA 16.25)
Among all phenomena, meditation is preeminent, and it exists in three forms;
having thus fully understood meditation, the wise person should cultivate it. (MSA 16.26)
The stabilization of the mind within is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Its cause (*hetu*) is being established upon mindfulness and vigor; for when there is no loss of the object of focus, one accomplishes meditative attainment by relying on vigor.
"For the sake of rebirth in happiness" refers to the fruit, because the fruit of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is rebirth in a state free from affliction.
"Mastery over the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and the [divine] abodes" refers to its function (*karman*), because through meditative absorption one exercises mastery over the superknowledges.
And because of mastery over the noble, divine, and Brahma-abodes,
there is a connection with preeminence, as it is said: "the foremost among all phenomena."

"All dharmas have concentration as their foremost" means that this [concentration] exists within those who meditate; thus, this is the function of the substratum (*ādhāravṛtti*). And it is threefold: with applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), without applied thought but with sustained thought alone (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ*), and without both.
It is without applied thought and without sustained thought;
furthermore, it is accompanied by joy,
and it is accompanied by pleasure.
And it is accompanied by equanimity;
this is its classification.
There are two verses regarding the classification of wisdom.
Right discernment should be known as that which is established in concentration;
it is the excellent teaching on wisdom and its livelihood for the sake of complete liberation from affliction.
Among those phenomena, there exists a superior one, and it is threefold;
having thus fully understood wisdom, the wise person should bring it to perfection.
"Correct discernment of the knowable" is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Correctly" means not erroneously; this is for the purpose of excluding the correct discernment of mundane affairs.
"Established in meditative concentration" is its cause (*hetu*).
One whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are;
because it leads to complete liberation from affliction, this is the fruit.
For by means of that, there is complete liberation from affliction.
By means of mundane, supramundane-inferior, and great supramundane discernment;
"living by wisdom and teaching well" means that living by wisdom and teaching well are his activities,
for by them he lives as the unsurpassed among those who live by wisdom.

"He teaches the Dharma correctly" means that he possesses the quality of being superior to all phenomena; as it has been said: [he is] "superior" (uttara) by virtue of his superiority over all phenomena.

"All phenomena have wisdom as their supreme [quality]"; the commentary states that "it exists in them in a threefold way," because it abides within those possessing wisdom and through its threefold differentiation.
There is the mundane, the inferior supramundane, and the great supramundane.
Thus has been explained, for each [type of person]—the base and so forth—the distinction according to the sixfold differentiation of meanings. There is a verse regarding the analysis of the summary:
All pure dharmas should be known as being either dispersed, concentrated, or both;
they are embraced by two, two, and two perfections respectively.
All pure dharmas are dharmas such as giving and so forth.
Among them, those that are distracted are subsumed by the first two perfections, because giving and the undertaking of ethical discipline are non-concentrated;
those that are concentrated are subsumed by the last two, namely meditative absorption and wisdom as it truly is.
Because they are concentrated;
both [groups] possess two, namely patience and vigor,
because those two exist both in a concentrated and an unconcentrated state.

There are six verses concerning the analysis of the opposing factors: The generosity of Bodhisattvas is neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; it is indeed not attached, nor attached, nor attached. (MSA 16.30)
There are seven kinds of attachment that are the opposites of giving:
attachment to enjoyments, attachment to delay, attachment to being satisfied with only that much, attachment to partiality, attachment to seeking a return, and attachment to the ripening of results.
Attachment to the adverse side, however, arises from not having eradicated the latent tendencies (anuśaya) for the acquisition of those very adversaries;
and there is also attachment to distraction.
Furthermore, that distraction is of two kinds.
There is distraction of mental attention due to longing for the Lesser Vehicle,
and distraction of conceptual construction due to conceptualizing the giver, the recipient,
and the gift. Therefore, because it is free from these seven kinds of attachment, the non-attachment of giving is said to be sevenfold.
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; indeed not attached is the morality of the Bodhisattvas—neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. (Msa 16.31)
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; patient acceptance is not characterized by attachment.
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached—such is the state of the bodhisattvas.
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; and yet it is indeed attached—such is the vigor of the bodhisattvas. Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. MSA 16.33.
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; not even attached is the meditation of the Bodhisattvas—neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. (MSA 16.34)
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; non-attachment is not wisdom.
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached—such is the state of the Bodhisattvas. (MSA 16.35)
Just as attachment to generosity has been described, so too should it be understood for ethical discipline up to wisdom.

However, here one should understand that attachment to immorality and so forth replaces attachment to specific enjoyments; attachment to the adverse factors refers to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of those adverse factors, because they have not been eradicated;
and discursive distraction occurs, as appropriate, through the conceptual construction of the three spheres.
In the analysis of the qualities, there are twenty-three verses:
"The sons of the Buddha have always renounced even their own lives upon encountering a supplicant;
out of compassion, they have not sought any recompense from others, nor have they prayed for any desired fruit."
By that very act of giving, all people are established in the three types of enlightenment;
and through the embrace of wisdom, that giving is further established as inexhaustible in the world.
Thus the meaning of the words is easily understood:

the sons of the Buddha have always adopted the threefold ethical discipline consisting of restraint and exertion; heaven is not desired by them, and even having attained it, they do not form an attachment to it.
By that very morality, all people have been established in the three types of enlightenment;
and through the embrace of primordial wisdom, that morality has been made inexhaustible in the world. (MSA 16.37)
Ethical discipline is threefold: the ethical discipline of restraint, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous qualities, and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings.
And there is the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
Among these, one has the nature of restraint (*yama*),
while two have the nature of exertion (*udyama*).

The sons of the Buddha have practiced forbearance, which is exceedingly difficult to perform, even when subjected to every kind of injury by men; yet they do so not for the sake of heaven, nor out of inability, nor from fear, nor with a view toward receiving a benefit in return.
And through this unsurpassed forbearance, they are planted in the three types of enlightenment by means of all the elements of the teachings.
Furthermore, through the embrace of knowledge, patience is established as inexhaustible in the world.
Thus, through the patience of acceptance regarding suffering and the patience of enduring harm from others, respectively,
the sons of the Buddha have exerted incomparable vigor, consisting of the application of armor,
in order to destroy the host of afflictions and to attain supreme enlightenment for themselves and for others.
By that very vigor, all people have been established in the three types of enlightenment;
and through the embrace of primordial wisdom, that vigor has been made inexhaustible in the world.
Thus, there is the vigor of armor and the vigor of application.
The sons of the Buddha have accomplished meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in abundance through their various excellent meditative joys; yet, out of compassion, they resort to inferior rebirths.
By that very meditation, all people have been established in the three types of enlightenment;
furthermore, through the embrace of primordial wisdom, that meditation has been made inexhaustible in the world.
Thus it is said: "Abounding in samādhi" means being encompassed by the infinite samādhis of the bodhisattvas.

The sons of the Buddha have known the reality (*satattva*) and the entirety of all that is to be known in every respect; and since no attachment has been produced toward even *nirvṛti* (cessation) by the Buddhas, how could there be any toward *saṃvṛti* (conventional reality)?
And by that very wisdom, all people have been established in the three types of enlightenment;
furthermore, through the embracing of sentient beings, that wisdom has been made inexhaustible in the world.

Thus: "Reality" (*satattva*) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which comprises the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*). "And that which is to be known in every way" refers to that other object of knowledge (*jñeya*) which is distinguished by infinite differences in characteristics, such as one's own conventions and so forth. The "indestructibility" (*akṣayatva*) of generosity and the other perfections arises from their being embraced by non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because they do not perish even in the *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Furthermore, because wisdom embraces sentient beings through compassion, it does not abandon them.
Moreover, the summarized meaning of these six verses is indicated by the seventh verse.
Magnificence, non-materiality, great purpose, and inexhaustibility—
these four qualities of generosity and the other perfections should be understood in their entirety.

Thus, therein, by the first line, the loftiness of generosity and the other perfections is illuminated; by the second, their lack of worldly motive; and by the third, their great purpose, because they accomplish the welfare of great beings.

Through the fourth [verse], their quality of inexhaustibility is indicated; thus, by these verses, this fourfold set of qualities should be understood: "The compassionate donor, through the application of superiority, overcomes the satisfaction derived from seeing [the recipient] and the satisfaction of fulfilling [their needs], as well as the lack of satisfaction felt toward the beggar, and even the hope [for a return]. (MSA 16.43)
For when a person who is a petitioner experiences joy upon seeing a donor, and then, having obtained what they desired, experiences the fulfillment of their wishes;
and when there is dissatisfaction from not seeing [the donor] or from the non-fulfillment [of their wishes];
and when there is the hope for seeing them and for the fulfillment of their wishes.

That [joy] arises more intensely in the Bodhisattva at all times from seeing a petitioner and from fulfilling their wish; whereas dissatisfaction arises from not seeing them or from not fulfilling their wish. Therefore, the compassionate giver overcomes that [dissatisfaction] entirely through the application of his superior state.
Since he always renounces his life, enjoyments, and wife for the sake of sentient beings out of compassion,
why would he not joyfully observe the restraint of abstaining from them?
Abstention from those [three] is "abstention from them," meaning abstention from the lives, enjoyments, and wives belonging to others.
By this, he demonstrates the quality of ethical discipline (*śīla*) as abstention from the three types of physical misconduct.
Disregarding [his own interests], with an even mind, fearless, and giving everything for the sake of compassion.
How could a noble one speak falsehood for the sake of harming others?
By this, he demonstrates the virtue of abstaining from false speech:
false speech might be uttered for one's own sake out of regard for one's body and life,
or for the sake of another out of affection for a beloved person.
Whether out of fear, such as fear of kings and the like,
or for the sake of some material gain, that is, for the purpose of profit;
whereas a bodhisattva is indifferent toward his own body and life.
He possesses an even mind toward all sentient beings through the state of regarding them as equal to himself;
he is fearless because he has transcended the five fears;
and he is a giver of everything because of his renunciation of all things for the sake of all sentient beings.
For what reason would he speak falsehood?

Desiring the welfare of others, compassionate, and extremely fearful of causing suffering to others, he is well-engaged in the discipline of sentient beings and remains far removed from the three faults of speech. (MSA 16.46)

Since the bodhisattva desires the welfare of all sentient beings equally, how could he engage in slander for the purpose of creating a rift between others? Furthermore, he is possessed of great compassion because of his intention to remove the suffering of others, and he is exceedingly afraid of causing suffering to others. (MSA_Bagchi 108)
How could he speak harshly for the sake of producing suffering in others?

Being correctly engaged in the discipline of sentient beings, how could he engage in frivolous chatter? Therefore, he is very far from the three faults of speech—slander, harshness, and frivolous chatter;
he is all-giving, compassionate, and highly skilled in the arising of phenomena through dependent origination.
How could he endure the affliction of the mind in every respect?
Covetousness, malice, or wrong view— respectively;
this should be understood as the quality of purity of ethical discipline for Bodhisattvas, due to its association with specific dharmas that are the antidotes to immorality.

When the compassionate one perceives joy in the benefactor and always perceives others' welfare—even in suffering—as being for the benefit of others, what is there that he must endure? Nothing at all. (MSA 16.48)

"For one must indeed practice forbearance toward an injurer; yet in that situation, the bodhisattva perceives the injurer as a friend because they serve as a cause for the accumulation of forbearance. Furthermore, suffering must be endured;
however, regarding that suffering which serves as the cause for the welfare of others, the bodhisattva always finds joy. Since this is so, what is there for him to endure, and why?"

For one who does not harbor the notion of an "injurer" nor the notion of "suffering," because they have abandoned the notion of "other" and always feel greater affection for others than for themselves,
the vigor exerted by one possessed of compassion in performing difficult deeds is indeed not difficult.
The bodhisattva is compassionate.

In that regard, concerning the compassion of the bodhisattva, the vigor exerted in performing difficult practices for the sake of others is both difficult and very difficult; how then is it not difficult?
Because the perception of "other" regarding others has been abandoned.
Because of his constant affection for others that exceeds even his own [affection for himself],
how could this be very difficult?
For such is that vigor which is free from the notion of "other" and possesses an affection exceeding even that for oneself.

For the meditation of the three [vehicles] is considered to be of little happiness, self-centered, sluggish, subject to decline, perishable, and accompanied by delusion; for Bodhisattvas, it is the opposite.
The meditation of worldly beings brings little happiness; that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is for their own self-interest.
It is sluggish for worldly beings because it is attached to the view of a real body (satkāya), and for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas because it is attached to nirvāṇa.

It is subject to decline for worldly beings, and it is exhaustible for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas because it is exhausted upon the attainment of nirvāṇa without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa).
It is accompanied by delusion for all [others], according to their respective afflicted or unafflicted delusions.

For Bodhisattvas, however, meditative absorption (dhyāna) is characterized by great bliss, brings happiness to both self and others, is non-attached, non-declining, inexhaustible, and free from delusion.
Just as darkness is dispelled by lamps in a covered place, so too is the threefold knowledge [dispelled].
But the incomparable knowledge of the compassionate ones is like the rays of the sun.
Just as knowledge gained by groping with the hands in the dark has a limited scope and is both indirect and indistinct, so it is for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Just as knowledge gained by lamps in a small room or an inner chamber is partial, direct, yet not entirely pure, so it is for the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
Just as knowledge [produced] by the rays of the sun is completely direct and perfectly pure, so it is for Bodhisattvas;
for this very reason, it is incomparable.
[This is due to] the basis, the object, the cause, and the dedication of the gift.
It is considered supreme by reason of its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support.
In this context, the basis is the bodhisattva.
Regarding the object, for the gift of material things (*āmiṣadāna*), the internal object is supreme;
for the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), it is the granting of safety to those who fear the miserable states and cyclic existence.
The gift of Dharma has the Mahāyāna as its basis,
compassion as its motive,
and the aspiration for the fruit of great enlightenment as its dedication.
The cause is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) from the previous practice of the perfection of generosity.

Knowledge is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), by means of which one gives a gift purified of the three spheres (*trimandalapariśuddha*), because of the absence of conceptualizing the giver, the gift, and the recipient.
The field is fivefold.
One who is in need, one who is suffering, one who has no refuge, one who practices misconduct, and one who possesses virtues—
these four are the supreme and highest fields;
in their absence, the fifth [is the field].
The basis is threefold, relying upon which one gives:
resolute belief, mental attention, and meditative concentration.
Resolute belief is as described in the analysis of cultivation regarding the mental attention of resolute belief.
Mental attention (*manaskāra*) is as described in that very same [text], where it is called "mental attention consisting of relishing, rejoicing, and approval.
Meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is as described in that very same [text], where its mastery (*vibhutva*) is explained through the Gaganagañja and other [samādhis].
Thus, the supreme conventional reality (*parasamaya*) regarding the basis (*āśraya*) and so forth is the supreme generosity (*dāna*).
This should be understood as the exposition:

that which gives, that which is given, that by which it is given, that to whom it is given, from whence it is given, by whose possession it is held, where it is given, and in how many ways—that is giving.
Morality is [defined] by way of its basis, its substance, its cause, and its dedication.
It is considered supreme by reason of its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support.
It is considered supreme by reason of its basis, its substance, its cause for forbearance, its dedication, its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support.
Vigor is considered supreme by virtue of its basis, its object, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 16.54)
Dhyāna is considered supreme by reason of its basis, its substance, its cause, its transformation, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 16.55)
Wisdom is considered supreme by virtue of its basis, its object, its cause, its transformation, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 16.56)
The supreme object of ethical discipline is the bodhisattva vow; the supreme objects of patience are those who take one's life, even if they are lowly or weak.
The cultivation of the perfection of vigor and the abandonment of its opposite;
the bodhisattva samādhis of meditative concentration;
and suchness for wisdom.

The Mahāyāna is the field for all [virtues] beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*); the remainder should be understood as previously explained. Giving that brings happiness to even a single sentient being is more meritorious than giving that causes harm over many eons.
This would be pleasing to the bodhisattvas, let alone its opposite.

Even if the gift of Bodhisattvas were to bring happiness to only a single sentient being while causing harm to themselves for many eons, it would still be dear to them because of their exceptional compassion; how much more so when it brings happiness to many beings and confers benefit upon themselves for many eons? For that very purpose for which embodied beings desire wealth, the wise relinquish it among those same beings.
Wealth is desired by people for the sake of the body, yet that very wealth is given away hundreds of times by the wise.
In this regard, the first half [of the verse] has been explained by the second half:

"When the mind does not suffer even as one is casting off the very body, what need is there to mention inferior wealth? That [state] of his is supramundane; therefore, whatever joy he derives from that, it is for him even more excellent than that. (MSA 16.59)

In this regard, it is shown that when his mind does not suffer even as he abandons his very body, that is "supramundane" (*lokottara*) for him. That joy which he attains through such suffering is "superior to that" (*taduttara*), meaning superior to that supramundane state.
Even though he is a seeker, he does not find satisfaction through the acceptance of desired objects obtained according to his wish.
Just as the wise one here attains satisfaction through the gift of all that exists, so too does he attain satisfaction through the satisfaction of those who seek his help.
"By obtaining what is desired and wished for" means by obtaining what is intended and sufficient;
"by the gift of all that exists" means even up to the gift of one's own life.
Even a beggar does not regard himself as possessing such wealth as one whose enjoyments are complete.
By giving away everything he possesses, the wise one, though possessing nothing, regards himself as truly wealthy.
Even after obtaining vast wealth, a seeker does not consider it a favor from the donor for the sake of that gain; rather,
having satisfied the seekers here with excellent gifts according to the prescribed rule, [he considers it a favor].
The wise one conceives the notion of great benefit toward them, just as [he does toward his parents].
This is due to a particular excellence of compassion.
The meaning of these two verses is already explained:
embodied beings, their own sorrow having vanished, are established in a state of well-being.

He who enjoys even vast wealth that belongs to another is none other than a Bodhisattva; he is like one who freely partakes from a tree of enjoyment on the road that is rich with the highest fruit. MSA 16.63.
He possesses the enjoyment of the delight of bestowing [gifts]; thus, he is one who enjoys the delight of bestowing. And it should be understood that he is none other than a bodhisattva.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.

Vigor is taught as that which is to be fully understood through its preeminence, its causes, its classification by action, its classification by type, its classification by basis, and its classification by way of being the antidote to the four obstructions. (MSA 16.64)
Diligence is to be fully understood through sixfold divisions:
by way of its preeminent distinctions and by way of its causal distinctions.
By way of the distinction of karma, the distinction of type, the distinction of basis, and the distinction of the antidotes to the four obstructions.
The exposition of this summary is provided by the subsequent verses:
"Vigor is supreme among the collection of pure qualities, for it is dependent upon it that their attainment occurs."
Through vigor, there is an immediately blissful dwelling, as well as supramundane and worldly accomplishment.
"Vigor is supreme among the collection of pure qualities"—thus the preeminence of vigor among all wholesome dharmas is indicated.
"Because, depending upon it, there is the attainment of those [qualities]"—thus the reason for its preeminence is indicated;
for the attainment of all wholesome dharmas is based upon vigor.

Through diligence, there is an immediately blissful dwelling, as well as supramundane and mundane accomplishment; thus is its function described. For by means of diligence, the supreme dwelling in happiness is attained in this very life, and all supramundane as well as mundane accomplishments are brought about. Through diligence, one obtains the desired enjoyments of existence, and through diligence, one attains powerful purity.
By means of vigor, they have transcended the view of a self-existent body and are liberated; by means of vigor, they have awakened to supreme enlightenment.
Thus, by way of synonyms (or through another synonym), the function of vigor has been indicated;
this is due to the distinction between mundane and supramundane accomplishments.
Among these, mundane accomplishment is "powerful" [in its own right], yet it is not ultimate because it is non-permanent.
Furthermore, vigor is considered to be that which involves decrease and increase, that which is sovereign over liberation, and another which consists of the favorable side and its opposite;
it is also described as that which has entered into reality, that which is transformative, and that which is of great purpose.
The Buddhas proclaim that vigor is of every kind: first, the vigor of armor; then, the vigor of application properly exerted; and the vigor of non-depression, imperturbability, and non-contentment.
Such is the classification of its types.
In that regard, the vigor of decrease and increase pertains to the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*): [two] for the abandonment of unwholesome states and two for the increase of wholesome states.
Vigor is the sovereign of liberation among the faculties (*indriya*),

because the faculties have the sense of being sovereign over liberation. Among the powers (*bala*), they possess both allies and adversaries, because the powers have the sense of being unsubduable by adversaries.
It is "entered into reality" because it establishes that [reality] within the factors of enlightenment on the path of seeing;
it is "transformative" because it is the cause of the final transformation of the basis within the factors of the path on the path of cultivation;
and it is "of great purpose" because the vigor whose nature is the perfections has as its objective the welfare of both oneself and others.
The vigor of armor is for the sake of donning the armor for application;
the vigor of application is likewise from such application;
the undaunted vigor is due to the absence of despondency even regarding a sublime goal to be attained.

Unshakable vigor (*akṣobhya-vīrya*) is so called because it is not disturbed by sufferings such as cold and heat. Vigor of non-contentment (*asaṃtuṣṭi-vīrya*) is so called because one is not satisfied with a meager attainment.
It is by means of these very [types of vigor], beginning with the vigor of armor (*saṃnāha-vīrya*), that [vigor is explained] in the Sūtra.

One who possesses strength, possesses vigor, is energetic, has firm prowess, and does not cast off the burden regarding wholesome qualities is described, respectively, as having inferior, middling, and superior vigor. Based on the support of persons engaged in the three vehicles, that vigor is considered to have small benefit or great benefit due to the association with a sluggish or exceedingly noble intention and intellect. (MSA 16.69)
Here, the classification of vigor is taught by way of the classification of its basis.
It should be understood that, based on the person engaged in the three vehicles, there is respectively inferior, middling, and superior vigor.
What is the reason?
This is due to the application of a sluggish or an exceedingly noble intention and intellect.
For the intention of those engaged in the two vehicles is sluggish, because their concern is solely for their own benefit;
whereas that of those engaged in the Mahāyāna is exceedingly noble, because their concern is for the benefit of others.

Therefore, in due order, that vigor is considered to be of small benefit or of great benefit, respectively, because it pertains to one's own welfare or because it pertains to the welfare of both oneself and others.
One who possesses vigor is not defeated by enjoyments,
nor is one who possesses vigor defeated by the afflictions.
The one possessed of vigor is never defeated by weariness,
nor is the one possessed of vigor ever defeated in his attainment.
Thus, this is the classification of the remedies for the four obstructions.
There are four kinds of obstructions to generosity and the other perfections by which one does not engage in them:
attachment to enjoyments, due to grasping after them;
Attachment to afflictions arises from the fixation on enjoying them;
weariness arises from becoming exhausted by the application and exertion in giving and so forth;
and attainment [of a limited state] arises from being satisfied with only a small amount of giving and so forth.
This fourfold vigor has been explained according to the distinction of its antidotes. Regarding the analysis of their mutual determination, there is this verse:
"Through mutual inclusion, through differentiation, through the dharma, and through the signs."
The definitive determination of the six perfections should be understood in every respect.
The determination [of their inclusion] is by way of mutual inclusion:
because through the gift of fearlessness (*abhayapradāna*), there is the inclusion of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*), since by those two one bestows fearlessness;
and because through the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), there is the inclusion of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), since by those two one bestows the Dharma.
Because energy belongs to both, it bestows both.
Through the ethical discipline that gathers wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*), there is a gathering of all [perfections] such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth.
In this way, the mutual inclusion of patience (*kṣānti*) and the others should be applied accordingly.
The determination according to classification:
giving is of six kinds, from the gift of giving to the gift of ethical discipline, up to the gift of wisdom,
because it establishes ethical discipline and the other perfections within the mental continuums of others.
The determination according to the Dharma is as follows:
those sūtras and so forth in which the meanings such as generosity and so forth are seen,
and those sūtras and so forth among the teachings in which generosity and so forth are seen.
Their mutual inclusion should be understood as follows:
determination is by way of the sign.
Generosity serves as the sign for ethical discipline and the other perfections.
Because one who is indifferent to enjoyments applies themselves to ethical discipline and the other perfections;
for ethical discipline is also the foundation for giving and the rest.

This is because the undertaking of the bhikṣu vows involves the relinquishing of all possessions, and for one established in ethical discipline, there is the application of patience and the other virtues.
The undertaking of the morality that gathers wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhakaśīla*) is the cause for all [perfections], such as generosity and the rest.
In this way, the mutual causal relationship between patience and the others should be applied accordingly. Regarding the analysis of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), there are seven verses.
There are four means of attraction.

Generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, and consistency of purpose: therein, generosity, pleasant address, purposeful conduct, and shared purpose are intended [to be practiced] through teaching them, causing others to undertake them, and following them oneself. (MSA 16.72)

Generosity is considered equal [to the perfection of generosity], just as pleasant speech is the teaching of those [perfections], and purposeful action is the instigation of others toward them; by the word "those," the perfections are included, meaning the teaching of the perfections and the instigation of others toward the perfections.
Consistency of purpose is one's own conformity to that very thing in which one instigates another.

But for what purpose are these four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu) maintained? For they are the means for others: that which bestows favor, that which causes one to grasp [the teaching], and that which sets [them] in motion.
Likewise, he should be known as one who conforms [to others] by means of the four bases of sympathy.
Generosity (*dāna*) is the means of favoring (*anugrāhaka*),

because it produces physical benefit through the giving of material things (*āmiṣadāna*). Pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*) is the means of causing comprehension (*grāhaka*), because it causes those who have not yet understood or who are doubtful to grasp the meaning.
Beneficial action is that which sets [others] in motion,
because it impels them toward what is wholesome; consistency of purpose is that which follows along [with others].
For when they recognize that the one who encourages them acts exactly as he speaks, others follow him in whatever wholesome state he has set them toward.
Through the first [verse], there is becoming a fit vessel; through the second, conviction;
through the third, practice; and through the fourth, purification. (MSA 16.74)
Through the gift of material things, one becomes a vessel for the Dharma by attaining the state of being compliant.
Through pleasant speech, one gains resolute faith in that Dharma by means of explaining its meaning and cutting through doubts.
Through purposeful conduct, one practices in accordance with the Dharma.
Through the quality of common purpose (*samānārthatā*), one purifies that practice by means of long-term application;
this is the function of the articles of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). The nature of the four articles of attraction is considered to be twofold in terms of their gathering [of beings].
[It is taught] by means of material gifts as well as by means of the Dharma, and by means of the Dharma through the basis [of the object] and so forth.
Furthermore, although the Blessed One has spoken of two other bases of attraction— attraction by material gifts and attraction by the Dharma—
it is these very four bases of attraction that are subsumed within those two.
The first [stage] is by means of gathering through material things;
the remaining ones are by means of gathering through the Dharma.
Furthermore, those are by means of three kinds of Dharma.
Through the dharma of the object, the dharma of practice, and the dharma of its purification, respectively,
the compendium is to be known as inferior, middling, and superior; generally barren and non-barren, and indeed non-barren in every respect, according to the distinction of their aspects.
This is the classification of the types of gathering.
Among these, the inferior, middling, and superior gathering of Bodhisattvas toward those engaged in the three vehicles should be understood as corresponding respectively:
for the most part, it is fruitless on the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
For those who have entered the [bodhisattva] stages, it is generally not fruitless;
it is entirely non-fruitless on the eighth stage and above, because the welfare of sentient beings is necessarily accomplished.
This method has been adopted by those engaged in attracting a following.
And for the accomplishment of all goals, it is praised as the means of happiness for everyone.
Whosoever are engaged in attracting a following, all of them rely on this very method, namely the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
For it is praised by the Buddhas as the most excellent and easy method for the accomplishment of all goals;
those who have been attracted, those who will be attracted, and those who are being attracted now, are all gathered by these means.
All of them are thus; therefore, that path exists for the ripening of sentient beings.
By this, he shows that in all three worlds, for the sake of ripening all sentient beings, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) constitute the single path;
for there is no other path.
Thus, with a mind constantly unattached to enjoyments, having reached the further shore of tranquility, restraint, and exertion, his self is firmly established.
Being free from conceptual construction regarding existence, its objects, and their signs, he becomes the gatherer of the multitude of sentient beings.

By this, he demonstrates the application of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for a bodhisattva established in the six perfections as previously described; for, by means of the perfections and the means of attraction, one accomplishes the welfare of oneself and others respectively. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Perfections, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The seventeenth chapter. In the analysis of the worship of the Buddha, there are seven verses.
Worship of the Buddhas, whether in their presence or in their absence, with robes and other offerings,
by one whose mind is deeply serene, serves to fulfill the two accumulations.
For one who possesses the vow that the birth of a Buddha may not be in vain,
the non-apprehension of the triad [of agent, object, and action] constitutes the perfected worship of the Buddha.
Another is for the sake of maturing immeasurable sentient beings; another is through material things and through the mind; and another is through inclination and through the storehouse.
And another [type of patience] arises from compassionate concern and forbearance in one's conduct;
furthermore, it arises from the application of the mind to the object, from awakening, from liberation, and from suchness.
Thus, by these four verses,
worship is demonstrated through its basis, its object, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its field, and its support. (MSA 17.5)
It should be understood as follows: therein, the basis consists of the Buddhas, whether manifest or unmanifest;
the object consists of robes and so forth;
and the sign consists of the mind accompanied by intense faith.
Dedication is for the sake of fulfilling the accumulations of merit and wisdom.
My previous vow was that the appearance of a Buddha might be for me a non-futile cause.
Wisdom is non-conceptual, because of the non-apprehension of the worshiper, the object of worship, and the act of worship.

The field consists of immeasurable sentient beings; it is so called because those [roots of merit] are directed toward their maturation and because they are planted within them. The support consists of the physical basis (upadhi) and the mind (citta).

Therein, based on material things (*upadhi*), there is worship by means of robes and so forth; based on the mind, there is [worship] by means of mental orientations consisting of relishing, sympathetic joy, and rejoicing.

Furthermore, it is by means of the aforementioned [factors] such as resolute belief (*adhimukti*) and so forth—namely, through resolute belief in the Mahāyāna Dharma and the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Indeed, "aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*) is what is meant here by the term "treasure" (*nidhāna*), due to the requirements of the metrical composition of the verse.
Through compassion for sentient beings;
through endurance of the suffering of difficult practices; through the practice of the perfections;
and through the proper mental attention to the Dharma.
For that is indeed non-erroneous because it accords with reality;
it is the full apprehension of the object on the path of seeing through right view.
For, by virtue of awakening to things as they truly are, it is the awakening to the object.
From liberation, because of the liberation from afflictions for the śrāvakas;
and from suchness, because of the attainment of great enlightenment—this is the classification of the types of worship.
Furthermore, it is distinguished by way of cause, by way of fruit, and by oneself as well as by others.
And it is also twofold: by way of gain and honor, and by way of practice.
Worship is considered to be limited or extensive, and it may be with or without pride; it is likewise regarded as being due to application, spiritual destiny, or aspiration. (MSA 17.7)
Thus, this is another classification of types based on the distinction between the path of objects (*arthādhvan*) and so forth.

In that regard, the past is the cause and the present is the fruit; the present is the cause and the future is the fruit. In this way, the past, future, and present are to be understood in terms of cause and fruit. That which belongs to oneself is internal (*ādhyātmikī*), while that which belongs to others is external (*bāhyā*).
In terms of gain and honor, it is coarse;
in terms of practice, it is subtle.
It is limited when inferior and great when sublime.
Furthermore, that which is accompanied by pride is inferior, while that which is free from pride is sublime because of the non-conceptualization of the three spheres.
That which is to be practiced at another time is distant;
that which is to be practiced at that very time is near.
Furthermore, that which is separated by a gap in the continuum is distant;
that which is immediately contiguous is near.
Moreover, whatever act of worship one resolves to perform in the future is distant; that which one has already resolved to perform is near.
Furthermore, what is to be understood as the supreme worship of the Buddhas? It is said:

Worship of the Buddhas is supreme by virtue of one’s own mind, through devotion to the Dharma, through intention, and through mastery; and by being embraced by non-conceptual means, and by entering into the state of having a single common purpose with all [Bodhisattvas]. (MSA 17.8)
Thus, by these five modes, worship of the Buddhas performed with one's own mind should be known as supreme;
namely, through faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma associated with worship,
and through intention, by means of the nine types of intention.
[These are] by means of the intentions of relishing, rejoicing, and delighting;
and by means of the wholesome intentions that are insatiable, vast, joyful, helpful, and untainted, which have been taught in relation to the cultivation of the perfections;
and by way of mastery through meditative absorptions such as the Gaganagañja (Sky-Treasury) and others.

[This is] due to the adoption of the means of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*) and due to the entry into the single activity shared with all great Bodhisattvas, because their activities are mixed and intermingled. There are seven verses in the analysis of the service to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

In this regard, by means of four and a half verses, service is demonstrated through its basis, its object, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support: "Service is shown by way of its basis, its object, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 17.9)

One should rely upon a friend who is self-controlled, tranquil, and thoroughly pacified; who excels in virtuous qualities, is diligent, and rich in scriptural knowledge; who has awakened to reality, is endowed with eloquence, is compassionate by nature, and is free from weariness.
A spiritual friend possessing such qualities is the basis for service:
one who is tamed through the practice of ethical discipline by means of restraint of the senses;
and one who is tranquil through the practice of meditative concentration by means of internal mental serenity.
It is "tranquil" because it pacifies the manifest afflictions through the application of wisdom;
it is "superior in qualities," being neither equal nor inferior.
One who is diligent and not indifferent toward the welfare of others;
one who is rich in scripture and not of little learning;
and one who has awakened to reality through the realization of reality.
It is endowed with speech, being possessed of the faculty of eloquence;
it is compassionate in nature because its mind is free from worldly desire;
and it is devoid of weariness because it teaches the Dharma continuously and with due respect.
"One should serve a spiritual friend with honor, gains, and personal attendance, as well as through correct practice.
This refers to the objects of service.
A wise person, possessing such an intention regarding the Dharma, should approach a spiritual friend at the proper time and with humility.
Thus, there are three kinds of signs:
the desire to understand and knowledge of the proper time.
And freedom from pride;
having no longing for honors or gains, he should dedicate them toward spiritual practice.
Thus, dedication is for the sake of practice through service, not for the sake of gain or honor.
And by practicing according to the instructions he has received, the wise one should thus please his mind.
Thus, practicing according to the instructions is the cause for service,
because by that means one pleases his mind.
Having attained skill in the three vehicles through wisdom, one should strive for the accomplishment of one's own vehicle.
Thus, through skill in the three vehicles, there is knowledge for the sake of maturing immeasurable sentient beings and for the accomplishment of a pure field. (MSA 17.13)
Thus, there are two kinds of fields for that service:
immeasurable sentient beings and the completely pure Buddha-field,
because [the Dharma] is established in them after they have heard it.
And established therein,
endowed with the quality of being an heir to the teachings rather than with material things, he should not depart from his friend;
such is the basis for service.
Relying on being an heir to the Dharma, one should attend upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
and not as an heir to material things (āmiṣa).
From this point onward, the differentiation of the modes of service should be understood through the following verse and a half.
A wise person should cultivate a friend both outwardly and inwardly by following the cause, the fruit, and the gateway to the Dharma.

The wise person should serve a spiritual friend through the gateway of the Dharma, both externally and internally; this is the distinction between the external and internal. "Externally" means following the stream of the gateway of the Dharma, while "internally" means through hearing the teachings and through mental application (*yoga*). This is the distinction between the gross and the subtle. [This is done] by means of the cause and the fruit, according to the distinctions of the past and so forth, as previously described, and by following the gateway of the Dharma with a mind that is equal and free from pride. Thus, the wise one should attend upon the friend. This concludes the section on the distinction between the internal and external. For "following the gateway of the Dharma" refers to the stream of the gateway of the Dharma; "externally" (*bahirdhā*) means "outside" (*bahitaḥ*). "Through hearing the teachings and through mental application" refers to the distinction between the gross and the subtle.
For hearing is coarse, while reflection and cultivation are subtle;

that very [subtlety] is the application (*yoga*) of the mind. There is a distinction between the inferior and the sublime based on whether one is devoted to a mind characterized by equality or a mind devoid of pride.
