Furthermore, the wise person should attend upon a spiritual friend by way of their [past] rebirths, their application, and their aspirations.
Thus, the distinction between "distant" and "near" should be applied as before.
Furthermore, the seventh verse asks: "What, then, is the supreme service? It is:
"The supreme service to a true friend arises from one's own mind through faith in the Dharma, through intention, and through masteries."
And by embracing the means of non-conceptualization, and by entering into the state where all [activities] have a single purpose.
Thus, as before;
there are twelve verses in the analysis of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
The sublime [states] are free from opposing factors, have reached non-conceptual knowledge,
function with respect to the three kinds of objects, and bring sentient beings to maturity in the steadfast one.
The sublime abodes are the four immeasurables:
loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Furthermore, these should be understood as having four characteristics in the bodhisattva.
By the abandonment of the discordant factors, by the possession of the excellence of the remedies, and by the excellence of its activity, because it functions with respect to three kinds of objects.
For they have beings as their object and phenomena as their object— and [some] have no object—
due to the distinction of their activity,
because they bring sentient beings to maturity.
Because they have sentient beings and phenomena as their objects:
furthermore, in which category of sentient beings or in which phenomenon do they operate?
And when they are without an object, upon what object do they depend?

For the wise, these [mental applications] operate toward those seeking happiness, those afflicted by suffering, those who are happy, and those who are distressed; as well as toward the Dharma taught for their sake and toward the suchness of that [Dharma].
Those having sentient beings as their object operate toward the entire range of sentient beings, from those seeking happiness up to those who are afflicted.
For instance, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has the aspect of wishing for sentient beings to be joined with happiness,
while compassion (*karuṇā*) has the aspect of wishing them to be separated from suffering.
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) has the aspect of being separated from suffering;
equanimity (*upekṣā*) has the aspect of bringing about the state of freedom from afflictions for those sentient beings with respect to their feelings;
and when having the Dharma as its object, it has as its object the Dharma taught by him.
In those [states] where your dwellings were taught, they are without objective support (*anālambana*) because they are within suchness (*tathatā*).
Indeed, because they are non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), they are "without objective support" in the sense that they are as if without an object; thus they are called *anālambana*. Furthermore:
Furthermore, because it has suchness as its object, due to the attainment of receptivity,
through purification, from two types of action, and also from the destruction of the afflictions, loving-kindness is without objective support.
Through these four reasons, it should be understood that loving-kindness is without an object:
because its object is suchness,
and because of the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena on the eighth stage.
It arises from the nourishment of the elements, from their purification,
and from two types of action;
that loving-kindness which is manifested through the outflow of bodily action [or vocal action].
And why? Because it is comprised by the exhaustion of the afflictions;
for it has been stated that the affliction is the object.
Because of the statement that "the objective support is cut off through the abandonment of the mental knots," they are both immovable and movable,
tasted by the wretched, and are not to be known [as such].
Furthermore, those sublime abodes (brāhmyā vihārāḥ) should be understood as being fourfold.
In that regard, the "wavering" [attainments] belong to the portion of decline because they are subject to falling away;
the "unwavering" belong to the portions of stability and distinction because they are not subject to falling away;
those that are "tasted" are afflicted, while those that are "untasted" are unafflicted.

"By the wretched" means by those who are greedy for pleasure and lack a magnanimous mind. This is the classification of the Brahmavihāras according to types such as those conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*). Furthermore, among these, "the Bodhisattvas are established in the immovable ones, which are free from attachment. (MSA 17.20)
Neither among those that are unstable nor among those that are relished;
those which are of an unconcentrated nature, whether weak, middling, or belonging to an inferior stage.
Those with inferior intentions are equal [to them], for they are inferior; otherwise, however, they are superior.
This is the distinction between the weak and the intense.
Among these, the six types of weak [faith] are by nature non-concentrated;
all [others], even when concentrated, are likewise [weak].
Those who are weak or middling;
those who belong to a lower stage when compared to the higher bodhisattva stages;
and those whose aspirations are inferior.
Although they are common to the śrāvakas and others, those who lack the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) are inferior; this means they are "weak.
Conversely, however, they should be understood as "superior" in the sense of being "intense," which is the opposite of what was just described.
When the wise one, having dwelt in the sublime abodes, is born among those subject to desire,
he thereby fulfills the accumulations and brings sentient beings to maturity.

And everywhere he is never separated from the sublime states (brāhmī vihārāḥ), yet he is free from their opposites; even when confronted by intense conditions for them, he does not undergo transformation, even if he were to become heedless.
There is a distinction between cause, fruit, and sign. In this regard, "having dwelt in the Brahma-abodes" is the cause;
"being born among beings who possess desire" is the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
He fulfills the accumulations, which is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*);
he brings sentient beings to maturity, which is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*);
and he is never separated from the sublime abodes (*brāhmyavihāra*) in any birth, which is the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
And being free from its opposite is the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
The sign [of this] is that one does not undergo transformation even by powerful conditions conducive to it;
"even when negligent" means even when the antidote is not present.
The distinction between virtues and faults is shown by the following four verses:
"For a bodhisattva who is possessed of malice, harmfulness, discontent, malice, and sensual desire, indeed encounters many kinds of misfortune. (Msa 17.24)
Such is the fault: because in the absence of the sublime abodes (brāhmyavihāra), one is joined with their opposites.

In this regard, ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and so forth are, respectively, the opposites of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others; ill-will and sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) are the opposites of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
How does one encounter manifold disadvantages? He says:

"By means of the afflictions, he destroys himself, harms sentient beings, and ruins his ethical discipline; he is accompanied by remorse, deprived of gain, and likewise lacks protection from the Teacher. (MSA 17.25)
One who possesses transgressions and does not acknowledge them is reborn in the states of non-leisure;
having lost both what was attained and what was not yet attained, he experiences great suffering in his mind.
Therein, by the first three phrases—“one intends for one’s own harm, for the harm of others, and for the harm of both”—he demonstrates this disadvantage (*ādīnava*).
By the six phrases beginning with “with remorse” (*savilekha*), he demonstrates that one generates fault pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadhārmika-avadya*).
And how does one generate it?
One's own self reproaches one;
others do so as well, as do the deities, the Teacher, and other wise ones.

His fellow practitioners censure him according to the Dharma; and an evil report, disrepute, and ill-fame concerning him spread in all directions and intermediate directions. By this, he shows [the consequences] in due order, from "being full of remorse" up to "being without fame. With the remaining three phrases, he shows respectively that one produces fault pertaining to the future life (*sāṃparāyika*), to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*), and to both the present and future lives.
This demonstrates the disadvantage that one experiences the mental suffering and dejection born thereof.
All these faults do not occur for one who is well-established in loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
Unafflicted, he does not abandon cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings. (MSA 17.27)
Thus, he demonstrates the threefold quality in the application of the divine abodes (*brāhmavihāra*):
the absence of the aforementioned faults, the non-abandonment of cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings despite being undefiled,
and [the fact that] such [qualities] do not exist even toward one's own virtuous only son as they exist toward all sentient beings.
This volition of loving-kindness and so forth toward sentient beings belongs to the sons of the Conquerors.
And by this, he demonstrates the intensity of the bodhisattva’s loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
Regarding the classification of compassion, there are two verses beginning with the distinction of its objects:
"Those who are aflame, those under the power of enemies, those overcome by suffering, and those shrouded in darkness..."
Those who have set out upon a difficult path and are bound by great fetters.
He feels compassion for sentient beings who are weak, who are greedy for great food mixed with poison, who have lost their way, and who have set out upon a wrong path.
In that regard, those who are inflamed by sensual desire are devoted to the pleasures of sense-desire;
those under the sway of the enemy have obstacles created by Māra and are not applied to what is wholesome; they are overwhelmed by suffering and afflicted by suffering in the hells and other realms.
Enveloped in darkness are those such as sheep-slaughterers who are exclusively devoted to misconduct;
because they are utterly deluded regarding the ripening of karma,
they have entered upon a difficult path and lack the nature for parinirvāṇa, since the track of saṃsāra is never severed for them.
The followers of other sects are bound by great fetters because they have set out for liberation while being tightly bound by the various bonds of wrong views.
Greedy for the great feast of poison, they are attached to the bliss of meditative attainments;
for them, that bliss of attainment is indeed defiled.
Just as delicious food is overcome by poison, because it causes one to fall away from that state;
so too are those with overweening pride lost to the path, because they have strayed from the path to liberation.

Those who have set out on a wrong path, those engaged in the inferior vehicle, those who are indeterminate, those who are weak, and those whose accumulations are incomplete— these ten kinds of beings are the objects of a bodhisattva’s compassion.
Regarding the demonstration of the five fruits, there is this verse on compassion:

"For one who relies upon the Dharma—which removes affliction, is the seed of supreme enlightenment, brings happiness, is the cause of protection and desired [results], and bestows its own nature—enlightenment is not far off for that son of the Victor. (MSA 17.31)
Thereafter, by virtue of its being the removal of affliction (*heṭha*), it demonstrates the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*) through the abandonment of violence, which is its opposite;
and by virtue of its being the seed of supreme enlightenment (*uttamabodhi*), it demonstrates the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) consists in bringing happiness to oneself and others respectively by way of being beneficial;
the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) consists in being the cause of what is desired;
and the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) consists in the nature of giving, because it bestows the fruit of distinguished compassion in the future.
Thus, by relying on these five kinds of compassion, it should be understood that Buddhahood is not far off.
There is a verse concerning the state of neither abiding in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa:
"Having realized that everything within saṃsāra consists entirely of suffering and is indeed devoid of self..."
The compassionate one of supreme intelligence neither falls into agitation nor is afflicted by faults.
Having thoroughly understood all of saṃsāra as it truly is, the bodhisattva does not experience agitation because of his compassion;
nor is he afflicted by faults because of his supreme intelligence.
Thus, he is established neither in nirvāṇa nor in saṃsāra, respectively.
Regarding the full comprehension of saṃsāra, there is this verse:

Observing the world as being of the nature of suffering, the compassionate one suffers and understands it as it truly is; yet, through the means for its abandonment, he does not succumb to weariness. (MSA 17.33)
"He feels pity" means he feels compassion.
And he knows that suffering as it truly is, according to reality, as well as the means for its complete avoidance—that by which his suffering is brought to cessation. He knows this.

By this, it is shown that even though he knows the suffering of saṃsāra as it truly is, as well as the means for its abandonment, the bodhisattva does not fall into despondency due to his particularity of compassion (*karuṇā*).
There are two verses regarding the classifications of compassion:
"Compassion arises by nature and through analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyā*), and previously through the application of the practice of its cultivation."
And because it has abandoned its opposing factors through the attainment of purity, this fourfold compassion belongs to those whose nature is compassionate.
This [distinction] should be understood respectively as being due to the excellence of the spiritual lineage (gotra), the examination of virtues and faults,
the cultivation in previous lives,
and the attainment of detachment (vairāgya).
When its opposite, harmfulness, has been abandoned, it is through the attainment of purity; that is, through the attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

That is not compassion which is not impartial or constant, nor which does not arise from resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) or from practice (*pratipatti*). For one who lacks dispassion or non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is not a compassionate Bodhisattva. (MSA 17.35)
In that regard, it is "equal" because one understands that whatever is felt among those who are happy and so forth is here [in this context] suffering;
because it is never exhausted in the nirvana without remainder;
and because of the "resolute intention," as those who have entered the stages attain the intention of the equality of self and others.
By way of practice, through the act of protecting others from suffering;
by way of detachment, through the abandonment of violence which is its opposite;
and by way of non-apprehension, through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
There are five verses on the reflection of the tree of compassion:

Compassion, patience, reflection, aspiration, birth, and the ripening of sentient beings—this is the great tree of compassion, beginning with the root and ending with the flowers, leaves, and fruit. (MSA 17.36)
Thus, this tree of compassion should be understood as consisting of roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Of this tree, compassion is the root and patience is the trunk.
Contemplation for the benefit of sentient beings is the branch;
aspiration for excellent births is the leaves;
and an excellent birth is the flower.
The ripening of sentient beings is the fruit. If compassion—the root—did not exist, there would be no endurance of difficult practices;
and a wise person who cannot endure suffering would never contemplate the welfare of sentient beings. (MSA 17.37)
One whose intellect is devoid of reflection would not make a vow for future births in the realms of purity;
and failing to pursue such auspicious births, one could never bring sentient beings to maturity.

Through these two verses, by means of the analogy of the production of a tree from its preceding and succeeding stages, he establishes that compassion and the other [virtues] constitute the root and so forth.

"Compassion is the watering; loving-kindness is the nourishment through joy in the suffering of those [beings]; vast growth of the trunk is to be known as arising from thorough mental attention. (MSA 17.39)
Through the relinquishing and taking up of leaves, through the non-interruption of the continuum of vows,
and through the accomplishment of the two kinds of conditions, from this [tree] there arises fruitful blossoming and fruit.

By these two verses, he demonstrates the similarity between the watering of a tree's roots and so forth, and the tree of compassion (*karuṇā*). For compassion is said to be the root of the tree; its "watering" is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because by means of that, it is nourished.
For one whose mind is imbued with loving-kindness (*maitracitta*), one suffers through the suffering of others.

Consequently, the suffering that arises for a bodhisattva engaged in the welfare of sentient beings from the emergence of compassion (*karuṇā*) results in the production of happiness; this is the meaning of "vast nourishment," namely, the nourishment of patience (*kṣānti*).
For that [patience] is said to be a "mass" (*skandha*).
And the trunk is vast;
through appropriate mental attention (*yonisomanaskāra*), there is manifold growth of branches in the Mahāyāna,
for reflection (*cintā*) is said to be the branch.
Because the continuum of aspiration is uninterrupted through the sequence of the cessation of the preceding and the arising of the succeeding,
the similarity of aspirations to the discarding and taking up of leaves should be understood.
Because internal conditions are established and one's own continuum reaches maturity, birth should be understood as fruitful, like a flower.
The ripening of sentient beings, which results from the accomplishment of external conditions and the ripening of the mental continuums of others, should be understood as being fruitful.
There is a verse regarding the benefits of compassion:

Who would not feel compassion for sentient beings, who possess the quality of great mercy, since even in suffering there arises for them an incomparable happiness born of that very compassion? (MSA 17.41)
Here, the quality of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is demonstrated by the second half-verse;
the remainder has already been explained.
Regarding compassion and detachment, there is this verse:
The minds of the compassionate, being permeated by pity, do not abide even in [personal] peace; how much less could they have attachment to worldly happiness or to their own lives? (MSA 17.42)
For all the world has affection for worldly happiness and its own life;
yet even among those who lack such affection—namely the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—their minds are established in Nirvāṇa, which is the cessation of all suffering.
However, because Bodhisattvas are permeated by compassion, their minds are not established even in Nirvāṇa.
How much less could there be affection between those two?
Regarding the excellence of compassion and affection, there are three verses: That affection which is both irreproachable and not worldly does not exist [among ordinary beings].
In the wise, compassionate affection is irreproachable and transcends the world.
For the affection consisting of craving toward one's mother, father, and so forth, is faulty;
that which consists of worldly compassion, even if faultless, is still worldly;
but for Bodhisattvas, it consists of [supramundane] compassion.
This affection is both irreproachable and transcends the worldly.
Furthermore, as to how it is irreproachable, he says:
[it is directed toward] the world which is dependent upon the great flood of suffering and ignorance and the great darkness.
How could that means which serves to uplift [beings] not be irreproachable?
The phrases "in the great flood of suffering" and "in the great darkness of ignorance" are to be applied [to the preceding].
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
To the question "In what way does he transcend the world?", he says:
That affection does not exist even among the Arhats in this world, nor among those awakened by individual enlightenment (pratyekabuddhas), let alone among others;
how then could it not be supramundane?
They have awakened to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
the rest has its meaning already explained.
There is a verse regarding the signs of both fear and delight.
When suffering is absent, that suffering which arises for Bodhisattvas through compassion initially terrifies them; yet once touched by it, they rejoice in it intensely.

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of suffering": the absence of suffering is the cause for the suffering that arises in Bodhisattvas through compassion toward sentient beings; this [suffering] initially causes terror on the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), because they have not yet touched suffering as it truly is by means of the equality of self and others. However, once touched on the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi*), the meaning is that they indeed rejoice in it.
There is a verse concerning the overcoming of happiness by the suffering born of compassion:

"What is more wonderful than this: that the suffering produced by compassion overcomes all worldly happiness—even that by which one who is already liberated and has accomplished his purpose is moved? (Msa 17.47)
There is nothing more wonderful than this: that for Bodhisattvas, suffering born of compassion becomes such a happiness that it surpasses all worldly happiness.
That happiness by which even the Arhats who have accomplished their goal are liberated, let alone others.
Regarding the benefit of giving performed out of compassion, there is this verse:
"The gift accompanied by compassion produces the happiness of giving for the wise."
The happiness found in the enjoyments of the three realms does not touch even a fraction of that [bliss].

And whatever pleasure belonging to the three realms is produced through enjoyments, that pleasure does not touch even a fraction of that [bodhisattva’s] pleasure; such is the meaning of the second half of the verse.
The remainder has already been explained.
There is a verse regarding the acceptance of suffering out of compassion:
Because of compassion, he does not abandon this saṃsāra consisting of suffering for the sake of sentient beings;
what suffering, then, would those possessed of mercy not undergo for the sake of the welfare of others?
For all suffering is included within the suffering of cyclic existence (saṃsāra);
by accepting that [suffering], all suffering becomes accepted.
Regarding the increase of its fruit, there is this verse:
For one who possesses compassion, compassion, generosity, and enjoyments always increase;
and from this, there arises happiness produced by affection and favor, as well as that which is brought about by power.
For Bodhisattvas, three things increase in all their births: compassion through its application;
that [compassion] through its cultivation;
and generosity through the power of compassion.
And enjoyments arise from giving; and from that triad, a threefold fruit of happiness results:
that born of affection arises from compassion.
That which is born from favoring sentient beings arises from giving;
that which is produced by the power of the act of favoring them arises from enjoyments.
There is a verse regarding the encouragement toward giving:
"I grow and I cause others to grow; I ripen them through giving and I bring them happiness;
I attract them and I lead them"—thus does compassion speak, as it were, to those who are despondent.
The phrase "those who have desisted from giving" is to be connected [to the following].
Compassion, as if through its own inherent increase, encourages Bodhisattvas who have desisted from giving by means of six qualities.
By means of enjoyments, through their increase;
by means of giving, through the ripening of sentient beings;
and because it produces happiness for the giver.
Because it draws forth other accumulations for the sake of great enlightenment, and because it leads one near to great enlightenment,
one finds happiness through the happiness of others.
There is a verse on this point:
"One who suffers when others suffer out of compassion—how could such a person be happy without bestowing happiness [on others]?
Therefore, the compassionate one makes himself happy by bestowing happiness upon others. (MSA 17.52)
Out of compassion, the Bodhisattva is pained by the sufferings of others; how could he be happy without bestowing happiness upon sentient beings?
Therefore, it should be understood that by bestowing happiness upon others, the Bodhisattva brings happiness to himself alone.
There are six verses regarding the instruction on giving out of compassion.
The compassionate one, always desiring no happiness for himself, instructs his own gift as it were:
"Make others happy with enjoyments, or else make me too happy, for our happiness is inseparable. (MSA 17.53)
For there is no happiness for the compassionate one without the happiness of others;
because his happiness is inseparable from theirs, the bodhisattva does not desire the happiness that is the fruit of his own giving without [the happiness of] others.
That fruitful gift was given by me to sentient beings with the happiness of their happiness;
if you have any obligation toward me, may its fruit accrue to them alone as much as they desire.
While giving a gift, both the gift and the fruit of that gift are given by me to sentient beings;
since their very happiness is my happiness, therefore,
let it bear fruit for them alone as long as it is to bear fruit— this is the imperative sense of the verb.

Out of compassion, the Bodhisattva instructs on giving: "For a donor who has no attachment to wealth, riches approach in even greater abundance. I do not consider that to be true happiness, because I am intent upon reaching the further shore through the practice of giving. (MSA 17.55)
For a donor who is detached from enjoyments, even greater and more excellent enjoyments come to pass;
this is simply the nature of things, because of the loftiness of his mind.
Indeed, that happiness which consists in the arrival of enjoyments is not considered by me to be true happiness;
for I am intent on giving, desiring the continuity of that practice rather than pleasure itself,
as you constantly observe me when I relinquish all possessions out of compassion.
Surely you must realize by this that he has no desire for the fruit of my [meritorious] action.

"I, who always relinquish the entirety of the fruit of giving out of compassion—surely from this very fact it should be understood that I have no personal desire for the fruit of my giving. Thus does the Bodhisattva instruct himself regarding giving:
"May I not become one who merely delights in giving; for if I were to obtain its fruit, I would not let it go.
For it is thus:"
One who delights in giving does not ever remain even for a moment without practicing generosity.
Thus the meaning of the verse is understood: "Since you do not bear fruit for one who has not acted [toward you], being indifferent to any return, you are not equal to me;
rather, you bear fruit for him who acts toward you."

Therefore, you should not regard me as your equal out of expectation for a return; for thus am I: "I have no expectation of a return, yet I shall grant you this fruit according to your desire. (MSA 17.58)
The meaning of this is already explained.
There are two verses concerning the gift of compassion.
The compassionate giving of the Sons of the Conquerors is irreproachable, pure, beneficial, protective, unsearchable, and unstained. (MSA 17.59)
In that regard, it is "blameless" because one gives without depriving another of their supreme [possessions];
it is a "pure basis" because one gives appropriate goods and substances,
by avoiding poison, weapons, intoxicants, and the like.
It is beneficial because it brings about welfare by gathering others through generosity and enjoining them to virtue;
it is accompanied by protection because one gives to another after ensuring that one's own retinue suffers no deprivation;
it is unsolicited because one gives of one’s own accord upon perceiving a need or distress even when not asked, and because one does not seek out a recipient of offerings.
It is "unstained" because it is free from desire for reward or karmic maturation.
There is another classification:
it is complete, vast, excellent, constant, joyful, non-materialistic, and pure.
The gift of compassion by the sons of the Conquerors is inclined toward enlightenment and inclined toward the wholesome.
In that regard, it is "complete" because of the giving of all internal and external things;
it is "vast" because of the giving of abundant things;
and it is "excellent" because of the giving of sublime things.
It is constant because of giving repeatedly;
it is joyful because of giving with gladness and without hesitation;
it is non-material because it is untainted.
It is pure like a pure state;
it is inclined toward awakening because of its dedication to great awakening;
and it is inclined toward the wholesome like that which brings about benefit.
Regarding the excellence of enjoyment, there is this verse:

A worldly enjoyer does not obtain such satisfaction from enjoyment as the compassionate one attains through renunciation, his mind nourished by the three kinds of happiness. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 17.61.
In this regard, there are three kinds of happiness: the joy of giving, the joy of benefiting others, and the joy of accumulating the provisions for enlightenment.
The rest is self-evident.
There is a verse concerning the compassion that brings about the perfections:
Compassion for the wretched, compassion for the fierce, compassion for the agitated, compassion for those who are heedless,
compassion for those dependent on sense objects, and compassion for those who are wrongly attached.
In that regard, the "miserly" are those who are stingy;
the "fierce" are those of immoral conduct who torment others;
and the "agitated" are those who are prone to anger.
The heedless are those who are indolent; those dependent on sense objects have minds distracted by sensual desires;
and those such as the non-Buddhist heretics are wrongly attached and possessed of poor wisdom.
The compassion directed toward those established in states that are the opposites of the perfections is "compassion for the wretched" (kṛpaṇādikaruṇā).
And because it serves to revile those opposites, it conduces to the accomplishment of the perfections;
therefore, it is called "the compassion that accomplishes the perfections."
There is a verse regarding the demonstration of the conditions for compassion:
The compassion of Bodhisattvas [arises] from pleasure, from suffering, and from that which follows them;
the compassion of Bodhisattvas [arises] from a cause, from a friend, and from its own nature. (MSA 17.63)
Therein, the first half [of the verse] demonstrates the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of compassion:
because one feels compassion by taking the three kinds of feeling as the object through the three types of suffering.
For neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is a consequence of pleasure and pain, since it brings them back again.
By the second half [of the verse], he demonstrates, in due order, the causal, dominant, and immediately preceding conditions of compassion through its causes, friends, and intrinsic nature.
Regarding the state of great compassion, there is this verse:
"The compassion of Bodhisattvas should be known as equal because of their intention."
Because of practice, because of detachment, because of non-apprehension, and because of purity.
In that regard, it is "equal" because, among those in the three states of feeling, one understands that whatever is felt here is suffering;
furthermore, it is equal by way of intention, because of the mind's compassionate concern,
and by way of practice, because of the protection afforded to them.
It is also [defined] by way of detachment, because of the abandonment of violence which is its opposite;
by way of non-apprehension, because of the non-apprehension of self, others, and compassion;
and by way of purity, because of the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena on the eighth stage.
The supreme cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] arises from one's own mind, from the Dharma, and from resolute conviction;
it also arises from intention, from mastery, from non-conceptuality, and from unity.
Thus, the meaning should be understood according to the previous explanation.

One who has produced great faith in the Blessed One, who performs extensive worship with material offerings and constant respectful service, who constantly attends upon spiritual friends of many virtues and benefits, and who has compassion for the world—such a person attains all success. (MSA 17.66)
By this, he briefly demonstrates the sequence and the quality of the aforementioned worship, service, and immeasurables.

One should be understood as "one who worships with great material gifts, constancy, and extreme reverence" because of performing worship through great material gifts (*mahopadhi*), constancy (*dhruva*), and extreme reverence (*satkriyā*).
Furthermore, reverence (*satkriyā*) should be understood as correct practice (*samyakpratipatti*).
In this way, one becomes a worshiper through material gain, honor, and practice;
such a friend possesses manifold qualities beyond those others.
He should be understood as beneficial by virtue of his compassion.
"He attains all success" means that he achieves the fulfillment of the welfare of both himself and others.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on Worship, Service, and the Immeasurables, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The eighteenth chapter: On the Analysis of Shame; sixteen verses.
Shame, when free from its opposites and accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge, has as its object that which is inferior yet irreproachable; it brings beings to maturity in the steadfast one.
By this, the fourfold characteristic of the bodhisattva’s sense of shame has been demonstrated through the perfection of its intrinsic nature, its companions, its object, and its activity.
Its object consists of inferior yet blameless things,
namely the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
And that [practice], being devoid of skillful means, is irreproachable according to the Mahāyāna;
yet for that reason, the bodhisattva feels shame.
How is it a "ripening" for sentient beings?
In that very sense of shame, because it causes others to be established [in virtue],
and because the six perfections increase through its presence while their opposites diminish for Bodhisattvas, shame is exceedingly perfected.
This is the shame of Bodhisattvas regarding increase and decrease;
for it generates extreme shame through the increase of the objects of the perfections and the decrease of their opposites.
Furthermore, shame arises from laziness in the practice of the six perfections.
And because the wise apply themselves to those qualities that are conducive to the destruction of the afflictions.
This is the shame of non-application, because it arises from the application of shame toward the non-application of the cultivation of the perfections,
and from the non-application toward those factors conducive to the afflictions, such as failing to guard the doors of the sense faculties.

Shame that is of an unconcentrated nature, weak or middling, belonging to a lower stage, characterized by inferior aspiration, or common with others, is indeed inferior; otherwise, it is superior. (MSA 18.3)
This is the weak and the intense degree of shame (*lajjā*).
The meaning of this verse should be understood in accordance with what was previously explained.
Hereafter, by means of four and three verses respectively, he demonstrates the distinction between the faults of the opposite of shame and the virtues of shame.
The wise one who lacks a sense of shame endures the afflictions through improper reflection;
harboring resentment, indifference, or pride, he harms both sentient beings and his own ethical discipline.
In this context, it is demonstrated that one intends for the harm of oneself, for the harm of others, and for the harm of both;
"unreasonably" means by way of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*).
How can one harm sentient beings through equanimity?
Due to negligence regarding the welfare of sentient beings,
he becomes remorseful because of his regret, and he suffers the loss of respect.
Because he is devoted to the True Dharma, he is disregarded by the assembly of humans. // Msa_18.5 //
He is censured by his fellow sons of the Conqueror and incurs ill-repute among the world;
by the phrase "in this present life," it is shown that he produces an offense pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadhārmika-avadya*).

Respectively, because of being censured by oneself, by others, by deities, and by teachers; because of being reproached according to the nature of reality (dharmatā) by wise fellow-celibates (sabrahmacārin);
and because of the spreading of one's evil reputation in all directions and intermediate points.
Otherwise, one is born again deprived of the [necessary] moment.

By this, it is demonstrated that he produces fault pertaining to the future life (*sāṃparāyika*), because of rebirth in the unfavorable states (*akṣaṇa*). By the statement, "He incurs the loss of both attained and unattained [qualities] through white dharmas," it is demonstrated that he produces fault pertaining to both the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*) and the future life.
Due to the loss of wholesome qualities already attained and the failure to attain those not yet attained, respectively,
he dwells in suffering; therefore, his mind also falls into a state of unease.
By this, it is demonstrated that one experiences the mental suffering and dejection born thereof.
All these faults exist in those who possess a sense of shame (*hrī*), but not in the sons of the Conqueror (*jinaputra*). From this point onward, the quality of shame (*lajjā*) is to be understood.
Since these faults do not exist,
the wise one is always reborn among gods and humans.
This is its fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, through a sense of shame (*lajjā*), that wise one quickly fulfills the accumulations for enlightenment;
this is its dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
And the Son of the Victor does not grow weary of maturing sentient beings.
This is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
He is born constantly both free from and not free from the adverse factors and their remedies;
these two are the fruits of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*).
That is to say, being free from opposing factors and not being separated from remedial factors;
thus does the Son of the Conqueror, possessing a sense of shame, obtain this benefit.
Thus it has been demonstrated that one attains the absence of the aforementioned faults and the possession of virtues:
"For the fool is defiled by faults even when well-concealed by fine garments due to a lack of shame;
whereas the Son of the Conqueror, though without garments, is clothed in shame and is thus freed from the stains of fault. (MSA 18.11)
By this, clothing is a qualification of shame (*hrī*);
for even one covered by other garments is stained by faults if devoid of shame,
whereas even one who is naked is stainless if possessed of shame.
Like space, the Son of the Victor endowed with moral shame (*hrī*) is unsullied by phenomena;
"by phenomena" refers here to the worldly phenomena (*lokadharmas*).
And adorned with modesty, he shines when in the company of the sons of the Conquerors.
By this verse, he shows that shame is equal to the ornament of space;
for toward those to be trained, the affection of Bodhisattvas is like that of a mother,
because they feel shame at neglecting sentient beings who ought to be protected.
And shame is also a protection for those wandering in saṃsāra against all faults.
Because it serves as the foundation for the elephant corps, the cavalry, and so forth;
by these analogies of clothing and the like, [the vihāra] represents the counteragent to the afflictions during one's stay, the counteragent to worldly dharmas during one's conduct,
and the suitability for dwelling together with fellow practitioners of the Dharma.
It shows that shame conforms to the non-maturation of sentient beings and conforms to an undefiled saṃsāra;
it consists in not acquiescing in all [unwholesome states] and in the practice of acquiescence toward all [wholesome ones].
Furthermore, engagement in all [virtuous] activities is the sign of one possessed of shame, as enjoined by shame itself.
By this, he demonstrates the fourfold mark produced by moral shame (*hrī*) in one who possesses it:
namely, non-endurance and non-engagement with all faults,
and endurance and engagement with all virtues.
The cultivation of moral shame (*hrī*) is preeminent by virtue of one's own mind, through the conviction in the Dharma,
through intention, through mastery, through non-conceptuality, and also through unity.
The explanation of this is as before.
Regarding the analysis of steadfastness (*dhṛti*), there are seven verses:
"The steadfastness of Bodhisattvas is [defined] by its characteristics and its classifications."
By virtue of its firmness, it excels all others distinct from it.
Vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as courage, steadfastness, and fortitude, are considered [the qualities] from which the bodhisattva proceeds fearlessly. (Msa 18.17)
By this, the characteristic of fortitude (*dhṛti*) has been explained along with its synonyms and its means of accomplishment;
*vīrya* and so forth are the characteristics, *sattva* and so forth are the synonyms,
and the remainder is the means of accomplishment.
From which three things is he fearless as he proceeds? It is said:
"Fear arises from dejection, from wavering, and from delusion regarding one's duties; therefore, one should recognize the designation 'fortitude' (dhṛti) in these three innate qualities. (MSA 18.18)
For in all undertakings, fear arises either from a depressed mind due to a lack of enthusiasm,
or from a restless mind due to mental instability,
or from delusion due to a lack of knowledge regarding the means.
And their respective antidotes are vigor and the others.

Therefore, the designation "steadfastness" (*dhṛti*) should be understood as applying to one's own three qualities—vigor and so forth—in the sense of being "inherent" (*nija*), meaning that which is to be performed without deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyāna*);
and likewise in regard to natural inclination and lack of dependence.
And toward the misconduct of sentient beings, and upon hearing of the profound and the sublime.

In the difficulty of disciplining those who are hard to discipline, in the inconceivability of the Victor’s body, in various difficult feats, and in the very non-abandonment of cyclic existence; (MSA_Bagchi 131) MSA 18.20.
And in that very state of being free from affliction, steadfastness arises for the wise one;
it is unequalled compared to others, since he is therefore considered the foremost among those possessed of steadfastness.

By these three verses, he demonstrates the divisions of steadfastness (*dhṛti*): respectively, according to lineage (*gotra*) and according to the production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*).
From the perspective of one's own welfare;
from the perspective of the welfare of sentient beings; from the perspective of the welfare of others; and from the perspective of ultimate reality.
By way of power,
by way of maturing sentient beings,
and by way of supreme enlightenment.
In this context, "independence" should be understood as being free from regard for one's body or life when engaged in one's own purpose; furthermore,
it consists in the practice of difficult austerities and in intentional rebirth in existence.
Furthermore, there is a distinction based on the absence of affliction:
"The hero does not tremble before a bad friend, suffering, or hearing the profound, just as Mount Sumeru is unmoved by locusts, the wind of its wings, or the oceans. (MSA 18.22)
By this, he demonstrates the firmness of the bodhisattva’s fortitude. The three similes are to be understood as corresponding respectively to the three types of immovability.
There are two verses in the section on the analysis of indefatigability.
The indefatigability of Bodhisattvas is peerless in three matters:
lack of satiety regarding what has been heard, great vigor, and [endurance] toward suffering; it is based upon a sense of shame and steadfastness.
Intense aspiration for great enlightenment and tirelessness are considered the qualities of the wise;
they are unaccomplished, accomplished, and well-accomplished across the stages.
By means of these two, indefatigability is explained in terms of its objective basis (*vastu*), its reliance (*niśraya*), its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and its classifications (*prabheda*).
Regarding the three bases:
[the first is] insatiability in hearing (*śruta*).
Relying upon a sense of shame and steadfastness, one undertakes vigor for a long period of time and endures the sufferings of saṃsāra.
For it is through those two that one feels shame at the arising of weariness and does not produce it;
thus, having intense aspiration for great enlightenment is its essential nature.
For when aspiration turns away, one becomes weary.
It is "unperfected" on the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*);
"perfected" on the seven stages;
and "thoroughly perfected" beyond that—this is the distinction.

Regarding the knowledge of the treatises, there are two verses: It is distinguished by its subject matter, its scope, its activity, its characteristics, its inexhaustibility, and the attainment of its fruit. (MSA 18.25)
For the wise, mastery of the treatises consists of the gates of meditative concentration and the dhāraṇīs;
these are acquired for the sake of maturing sentient beings and for upholding the true Dharma.
In that regard, the subject matter (*vastu*) of knowledge of the treatises (*śāstrajñatā*) consists of the five fields of learning (*vidyāsthāna*):

the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), and the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*).
Its purpose (*adhikāra*) is the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others.
In the first subject matter,
there is one's own practice and the explanation of that to others;
in the second, there is the thorough knowledge of its faults and the refutation of opposing disputants.
In the third, there is the correct explanation of terminology oneself and the communication of it to others;
in the fourth, the alleviation of the diseases of others;
and in the fifth, the sharing of that [knowledge] with others.
The definition of expertise in the treatises is that these very five subjects have been heard,
retained,
and mastered through speech.
They have been examined by the mind and thoroughly penetrated by vision,
because they were grasped in due order after being heard.
It is through study;
through reflecting on the meaning with a serene mind according to what is appropriate, by understanding its faults and virtues, and by determining what is well-expounded and what is poorly expounded.
Its inexhaustibility is due to its not being exhausted even in the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

The full attainment of the fruit is the knowledge of all aspects regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharmasarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, this knowledge of the teaching (*śāsrajñatā*) of the bodhisattvas is comprised of the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhimukha*) and the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*),
and it serves for the maturation of sentient beings.
Because one carries out those tasks by means of the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhimukha*),
and because one upholds them for the sake of mastering the true Dharma (*saddharma*) by means of the mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*).
There are four verses concerning the knowledge of the world (*lokajñatā*).
Indeed, the world-knowledge of the wise, which is peerless in terms of body, speech, and the knowledge of reality, excels that of all others.
How [does one act] with the body? It says:
"Always having a smiling face. How [does one act] with speech? It says:
The wise are those who speak first.
He asks: for what purpose is that? [He replies: so that sentient beings may become fit vessels.
In what sense is it for the sake of being a vessel?
For the practice of the true Dharma.
How is it by means of the knowledge of the truths? He says:
"Since the repeated arising of worlds is desired from the two truths, and their cessation is from those two, therefore one who knows that is called a knower of the world. (MSA 18.29)
The world’s arising— that is, saṃsāra— occurs again and again by means of two truths, considering both that which arises and that by which it arises.
Its cessation occurs by means of two truths, namely the truths of cessation and the path,
considering both that which ceases and that by which it ceases.
Therefore, one who knows that is called "one who knows the world," because they are endowed with the wisdom that perceives the arising and passing away of the world.
For the sake of their pacification and attainment, the wise person applies themselves to the truths.
For the wise one who has emerged from the stream of true knowledge is indeed called "one who knows the world."
By this, the function of knowledge of the world is indicated;
therein, "for pacification" refers to the truths of suffering and its origin, and "for attainment" refers to the truths of cessation and the path.
In the analysis of the reliances, there are three verses:
"The Dharma taught by the Sage, its intended meaning, that which is authoritative as the definitive meaning, and its attainment which is beyond verbal expression. (MSA 18.31)
This is the characteristic of the reliances (*pratisaraṇa*).
Among these, the authoritative meaning is that which has been established and analyzed by one who is an authority, whether by the Teacher himself or by one authorized by him.
Non-conceptual attainment is supramundane knowledge of realization.
Because it is inexpressible;
the rest has its meaning already explained.
[This applies] to one who rejects what has been stated, and to one who has falsely deliberated.
And here, the attainment of that which is accompanied by longing is taught as being precluded.
In the first reliance, the rejection of a person who repudiates the Dharma of the Sage is taught;
in the second, [the rejection] of the literal meaning of the phrasing rather than its intended meaning;
and in the third, [the rejection] of a meaning wrongly conceived and being led astray by error.
In the fourth [ground], there is indeed no loss for the wise, due to the knowledge that is accompanied by aspiration yet personally realized,
through resolute conviction and investigation, and from hearing correctly from others,
as well as from non-conceptual knowledge.
This is the benefit of the reliances:
by means of the first reliance, one does not fall away from conviction in the Dharma of the Sages;
by means of the second, through one's own investigation of the intended meaning.
By the third [verse], because of hearing the method of the non-erroneous meaning from others;
by the fourth, because of supramundane knowledge.
There are four verses in the analysis of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) of the bodhisattvas are peerless;
they are considered such by virtue of their knowledge regarding synonyms, characteristics, speech, and cognition.

The first [type of knowledge] pertains to synonyms: it is the knowledge of as many synonymous names as there are for each individual object. The second pertains to characteristics: it is the knowledge of the name belonging to a particular object. The third pertains to sentences: it is the knowledge of the various languages used in each respective region.
The fourth [analytical knowledge] is that which is self-manifesting within knowledge.
This is the defining characteristic of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*):
for one engaged in teaching, that which is taught and by means of what it is taught.
The teaching of both the Dharma and its meaning is carried out through speech and by means of knowledge alone.

The fourfold analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid) arises from the brief statement and detailed explanation of the Dharma, from the complete attainment of both [the meaning and the expression], and from the thorough understanding and removal of objections. (MSA 18.36)
This is the reason for the fourfold nature:
namely, that which is taught, that by whom it is taught, and the teaching itself for one engaged in it.
In that regard, there is a purpose for knowledge. But for whom is there teaching? For the sake of the Dharma and its meaning.

By what means? By the speech of the teaching and by knowledge. Among these, there is the teaching of both the phenomenon (*dharma*) and its meaning (*artha*), because of the brief statement and detailed explanation of the phenomenon.
Teaching by means of speech is because those two [the listener and the subject] are brought to realization in every way;
teaching by means of knowledge is because of the removal of objections.
Therefore, based on the knowledge of both that which is taught and that by which it is taught, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are established.
Having attained equality within oneself, that subsequent realization for the sake of destroying all doubts is called the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
By this, the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) and the function (*karman*) of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are shown.

Having personally realized the equality of all phenomena— that is, suchness (*tathatā*)— by means of supramundane knowledge, the subsequent thorough comprehension of synonyms and so forth by means of the knowledge obtained subsequently (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is the etymological definition of "analytical knowledge" (*pratisaṃvid*).
The activity [of this] is for the sake of destroying all doubts of others.
Regarding the analysis of the accumulations, there are four verses:
The accumulation of the Bodhisattvas, consisting of merit and gnosis, is unequaled.
One [type of bodhisattva] is for the sake of prosperity within saṃsāra; the other is for the sake of a cycle of existence that is free from affliction.
That which is the equipment and for what purpose it exists has been demonstrated.
The equipment is twofold;
therein, the equipment of merit leads to exaltation within cyclic existence.

The equipment of knowledge is for the sake of wandering through cyclic existence without affliction. Generosity and ethical discipline are the accumulation of merit; wisdom is the accumulation of knowledge.
The other three [perfections] belong to both, and all five are the accumulation of knowledge.
By this, he shows the inclusion of both accumulations by means of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
For it is through the power of patience (*kṣānti*), vigor (*vīrya*), and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that both are accomplished;
therefore, these three constitute the two accumulations.
Furthermore, because they are dedicated toward wisdom, all five perfections should be understood as the accumulation of gnosis (*jñāna-sambhāra*).
For that which is the repeated nourishment of virtue through continuous cultivation is the accumulation that accomplishes all goals for the wise. (MSA 18.40)
This is the etymological explanation and the function of the "provision" (*saṃbhāra*).
*Sam* means by way of continuity;
*bhā* means having attained cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
*Ra* means repeated nourishment;
*sarvārthasādhaka* (the accomplisher of all aims) is its function, because it accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others.
The accumulation for the wise is gathered for the sake of entry, for the signless, for effortlessness, for consecration, and for final perfection. (MSA 18.41)
This is the classification of the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*).
Among these, on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), the accumulation is for the sake of entering the [first] stage;
on the six stages, it is for the sake of the signless (*animitta*) comprised within the seventh stage.
In that [sixth stage], because of the non-occurrence of signs;
in the seventh stage, for the sake of effortlessness, which is comprised of the two stages other than that;
and for those two, the equipment for consecration, which is comprised of the tenth stage.
In that regard, there is the equipment for reaching the culmination comprised within the stage of a Buddha.
Regarding the analysis of the applications of mindfulness, there are three verses:
the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness occurs through fourteen aspects.
Because it is peerless among the wise, it excels all others.
By which fourteen [factors] is it distinguished? By way of reliance and by way of antidote, and likewise by way of entry, as well as by way of object, mental attention, and attainment. (MSA 18.43)
Through conformity and following, through thorough knowledge and arising, through measure and supremacy, and through cultivation and attainment, there is another [type of perfection].
Thus, the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness by bodhisattvas is distinguished by these fourteen aspects.

How [is it distinguished] by way of basis? By relying upon the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the Mahāyāna. How by way of antidote? Because it serves as the antidote even to the perceptions of impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self—which are themselves the antidotes to the four perversions—by means of entering into the selflessness of phenomena such as the body.
How is it by way of entry?

It is because one enters into the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path through the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) respectively, and because one causes others to enter them as well.
As it is said in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*:

How is it [practiced] by way of the object? By taking as objects the bodies and so forth of all sentient beings. How is it by way of mental attention? By the non-apprehension of the body and so forth.
How is it by way of attainment? Neither for the sake of dissociation from the body and so forth, nor for the sake of non-dissociation.

How is it "in accordance"? It is by way of being in accordance with the perfections (*pāramitā*), because it serves as the antidote to their opposites. How is it "by following"? It is by following worldly beings, as well as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, because one cultivates the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) associated with them for the sake of teaching them. How is it "through thorough knowledge"? It is through the thorough knowledge that the body is like an illusion, because it appears as a false form in exactly that manner.
Through the thorough knowledge that sensation is like a dream, because it is likewise a false experience;
through the thorough knowledge that the nature of the mind is luminous, like space;
and through the thorough knowledge that phenomena are adventitious, like the adventitious defilements of dust, smoke, clouds, and mist in space.

How is it [superior] by way of arising? Because, when intentionally taking birth in existence as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) or the like, there is no affliction despite the excellence of the body, sensations, and so forth.

How is it [superior] by way of measure? Because even a slight cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is superior to that of others, owing to the natural sharpness of their faculties.
How is it supreme? Because it is cultivated through effortless, integrated, and intermingled practice with those [perfections] that are fully perfected.
How is it through cultivation?
Because through such cultivation, it is inexhaustible even in the nirvana without remainder due to the ultimate nature of that cultivation.
How [is it understood] from the perspective of realization?
It is because of the realization [of the path] throughout the ten stages and in Buddhahood.
There are five verses in the analysis of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
The right exertions of the wise are unequaled by all embodied beings;
they are cultivated as the antidote to the defects of the [four] foundations of mindfulness.

The general definition of the cultivation of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) is that it serves as the antidote to the faults which are the opposites of whatever cultivations of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have been taught.
Furthermore, in terms of its specific divisions:
[it functions] regarding the enjoyment of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), the abandonment of the hindrances (*nivaraṇa*), and...
And regarding the relinquishing of mental attention, as well as its entry into the stages.
In the dwelling in the signless, in the attainment of the prophecy,
in the ripening of sentient beings, and in the empowerment of the wise.
For the sake of purifying the field and for the attainment of the ultimate goal,
the cultivation of the antidotes to the opposing factors is practiced by the bodhisattvas.
This is the classification of the cultivation of the right abandonments:
[it pertains] to the unafflicted enjoyment of the cycle of existence, to prosperity,
and to the relinquishing of the five hindrances.
In the relinquishing of the mental attention of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; in the entry into the [Bodhisattva] stages;
and in the dwelling in the signless on the seventh stage.
In the attainment of the prophecy, it is on the eighth stage;
in the ripening of sentient beings,
it is on the ninth stage.
And at the empowerment on the tenth stage;
for the sake of purifying the field, in all three [stages];
and upon reaching the culmination on the Buddha-stage.
Furthermore, the cultivation of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) should be understood as the antidote to those factors that are discordant with it;
this is its classification.
Based upon desire (*chanda*), there is the cultivation of yoga together with its signs (*sanimittikā*).
In all the right efforts, the antidote is defined.
By this, one generates desire,
exerts oneself, arouses energy,
and uplifts the mind.
"He applies himself rightly" (*samyak-pradadhāti*):
this is the explanation of the meaning of these terms.
For, relying upon desire (*chanda*), he exerts himself (*vyāyacchate*) by cultivating the yoga known as calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
And that cultivation is cultivated together with the signs of tranquility, exertion, and equanimity;
therefore, it is accompanied by signs.
Furthermore, how is it cultivated?
One exerts vigor as an antidote to the secondary afflictions of laxity and excitement, which are the opposites of serenity and exertion.
How does one exert it?
One uplifts the mind and applies it with effort.
In that context, "he exerts" means by means of wisdom; "he applies himself" means by means of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
And when equanimity has been attained, one applies effort.
This cultivation of yoga is called the antidote in all the right abandonments (samyakprahāṇa) according to the aforementioned classifications.
There are five verses on the analysis of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).
The four bases of psychic power are the supreme characteristics of the wise;
they arise for the accomplishment of all goals, both for oneself and for others. (MSA 18.50)
The accomplishment of all aims should be understood as both mundane and supramundane;
the rest has already been explained.
[This is known] through its basis, its differentiation, its means, and its actualization.
The wise intend for the establishment of the bases of psychic power to be understood in every respect.

This is the brief statement; the detailed explanation follows: "Relying upon the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), fourfold differentiation, as well as means and accomplishment, are prescribed in six ways. (MSA 18.52)
The basis of the perfection of meditation is its fourfold classification, according to the distinctions of concentration through aspiration, vigor, mind, and investigation.
The means are likewise fourfold. The actualization is sixfold.
What are the four kinds of skillful means? The first is that of exertion; the second is that which consists of assistance;
the third is that of binding; and the fourth is that of the antidote. (MSA 18.53)

Among the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), desire (*chanda*) and exertion (*vyāyāma*)—along with faith (*śraddhā*) which is the means for undertaking effort—are the [initial] application;
for one who has faith and seeks the goal, there is exertion.
Serenity (*praśrabdhi*) is the supportive factor.
Mindfulness and clear comprehension are the means of binding [the mind],
because by the first [mindfulness] the mind does not stray from the object,
and by the second [clear comprehension] one discerns such straying.
Volition and equanimity are the remedial means,
because they serve as the antidotes to the secondary afflictions of lethargy and excitement, as well as to the [root] afflictions.
What is the sixfold accomplishment?
The accomplishment consists of vision, instruction, the sport of remaining [in meditative states],
the power of aspiration, and the attainment of the Dharma.
In this context, "vision" refers to the fivefold eye: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the noble wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye.
"Instruction" refers to the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) in their respective order;
for by means of these, having approached [beings], and having understood their language, their thoughts, their coming, and their going, one instructs them for the sake of liberation.
The "play of abiding" (*sthitivikrīḍita*) is because Bodhisattvas possess a manifold play of meditative absorption (*samādhivikrīḍita*) through emanations and other such means.
"Vow" (*praṇidhi*) refers to that knowledge of vows by which Bodhisattvas, empowered by their vows, sport through the excellence of their aspirations—
such that it is not easy to calculate the extent of their bodies, their radiance, or their voices, as described at length in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
Mastery is as described in that same context where the ten masteries (*vaśitā*) are taught.
Attainment of the qualities (*dharmaprāpti*) is the attainment of the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).
Thus, this accomplishment of vision and the other [faculties] is sixfold.
In the analysis of the faculties, there is this verse:
Awakening, conduct, and learning are supreme here, as are tranquility and insight.
The basis of faith and the other [faculties] should be understood according to their role in accomplishing the goal.
The meaning is that awakening is the locus and objective support of the faculty of faith;
the conduct of a bodhisattva is that of the faculty of vigor;
and the hearing comprised within the Mahāyāna is that of the faculty of mindfulness.
The basis of the faculty of concentration is tranquility (*śamatha*),
and the basis of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā*) is insight (*vipaśyanā*).
It is precisely by virtue of their respective objects that these [faculties], beginning with faith, are called "faculties" (*indriya*) in the sense of predominance (*ādhipatya*).
Regarding the classification of the powers, there is this verse:
"Faith and the other [faculties], when they have entered the stages and their activities are no longer defiled, are designated as 'powers' because their opposing factors have become weak. (MSA 18.56)
The meaning of this verse is already explained.
Regarding the analysis of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), there are seven verses.
The formal establishment of the factors of enlightenment is prescribed for one who has entered the stages (bhūmi).
Furthermore, it is because of the realization of the equality of all phenomena and all sentient beings.
By this, that state in which the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are established through the realization of a particular [truth] has been taught.

This occurs in the state of having entered the stages (*bhūmi*), through the realization of the equality of all phenomena and all sentient beings, respectively, by means of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and the equality of self and others.
Hereafter, he demonstrates the analogy of the seven jewels, such as the wheel, for the factors of enlightenment.
Mindfulness operates everywhere for the sake of conquering unconquered objects of knowledge;
it is for the conquest of unconquered objects of knowledge,
just as the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch is for the conquest of unconquered territories.
And his investigation is for the sake of destroying all conceptual constructions and signs.
Just as the precious elephant is for the defeat of adversaries,
so too does his vigor proceed toward swift and complete awakening,
because it gives rise to the superknowledges quickly.
Just as the precious horse [is used] for traveling swiftly across the great earth bounded by the ocean,
so too is he surely filled with joy through the increase of the light of the Dharma.
For a bodhisattva who has initiated vigor, the lights of the Dharma increase;
from that, joy arises which always gladdens every activity,
just as a precious jewel gladdens a universal monarch by means of its special radiance.
Through liberation from all obscurations, one attains happiness by means of pliancy,
because of the eradication of all functional rigidity (dauṣṭhulya);
just as a universal monarch experiences happiness through the jewel of a woman.
And the fulfillment of intended aims arises from meditative concentration.
Just as [the Cakravartin king relies] on the householder-treasure,
he dwells everywhere at his pleasure through equanimity;
always supreme, he dwells with both the non-conceptual and the subsequently attained conceptual states.
Equanimity (upekṣā) is said to be non-conceptual knowledge; by means of it, the bodhisattva dwells everywhere according to his will,
because through the dwelling subsequently obtained from that [knowledge], he approaches some and departs from others.
Because he establishes his dwelling there through non-conceptual abiding by way of being effortless;
just as the counselor-jewel of a universal monarch brings forward the fourfold army that is to be led and withdraws that which is to be withdrawn.
Having gone there, he establishes his residence where the fourfold army proceeds without weariness. A Bodhisattva endowed with such qualities moves like a universal monarch (cakravartin),
constantly surrounded by the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) which are like the seven jewels.
Thus he concludes the comparison of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅgas) to the seven jewels:
"The factor of reliance, the factor of essential nature, and the third, the factor of departure;
the fourth is the factor of benefit, and the factor of non-affliction consists of three. (MSA 18.63)
By this, it has been explained how each factor is a limb:
mindfulness is the limb of support, because all [the other factors] proceed by depending upon it;
the investigation of dharmas is the limb of essential nature, because it is the very nature of enlightenment.
Vigor is the limb of departure, because by its sustaining power one does not stop short of reaching the ultimate goal. Joy is the limb of benefit, because it consists of mental happiness.
Serenity, concentration, and equanimity are the limbs of non-affliction.
By means of which, that which is relied upon, and that which is non-affliction—these three should be understood as the factors of non-affliction.
Regarding the analysis of the factors of the path, there are two verses:
"And following after awakening, [the path] arises thereafter."
The entry into the established state occurs according to the way awakening is established.
The purification of the three types of action, the cultivation of the remedies, and [the purification] of the obscuration to the knowable, of the path, and of the extraordinary qualities. (MSA 18.65)
Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is the continued engagement with the realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtāvabodha*) following the time of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) is the stabilization and discernment of that very realization.

Furthermore, since the Blessed One has established that stabilization in the discourses (*sūtra*) and other teachings, that [discourse] itself is the point of entry, because through it one realizes that meaning.
The purification of the three types of action consists of right speech, right action, and right livelihood,

because they subsume the actions of speech, body, and both together. The cultivation of the remedies— right effort and the others— should be understood respectively as the antidotes to the obscuration of the knowable and the obscuration of the path.

And through right effort, being untiring over a long period of time, one cultivates the antidote to the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which is the obscuration of the specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*). Through right mindfulness, because there is no sinking or agitation regarding the signs of calm abiding (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), one cultivates the antidote to the obscuration for the sake of bringing the path into manifestation.

Through right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), one cultivates the antidote to the obscurations for the sake of bringing forth the distinguished qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*); in this way, the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established.
Regarding the distinction between calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), there are three verses:
"From the mind’s abiding in the mind, and also from the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*),"
Relying upon right stability, there arise both calm abiding and insight.
Based on right concentration, because of the mind's abiding within the mind and the discernment of phenomena, calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are to be understood respectively;
however, they do not exist without right concentration— this is the defining characteristic of calm abiding and insight.
It is considered to be universal, partial, and the proximate cause for what is not partial.
That [pair]— calm abiding and insight— is universal because one cultivates them wherever one desires any particular quality,
as it is said in the Sūtra:

"If a monk should desire: 'O, may I be secluded from sensual desires,' and so forth in detail, up until: 'by that monk these two very dharmas must be cultivated, namely, serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā),' and so on;
[this] is serenity and insight in one part when he cultivates serenity."
Or [the practice of] insight (*vipaśyanā*).
When one cultivates both simultaneously,
both aspects are considered the proximate cause (*upaniṣad*) for the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of Bodhisattvas on the stage of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
In penetration, in departure, in the signless, and indeed in the unconditioned.
In both the purified and the completely pure states, calm abiding and insight—
this yoga, present on all stages, accomplishes everything for the steadfast one.
By the passage beginning with "This is the view of the Upaniṣads," the divisions and the function of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are indicated.
Yoga should be understood as the means (*upāya*).
In this context, "penetration" (*prativedha*) refers to the entry into the first bhūmi.
The departure extends up to the sixth stage,
because through those stages there is a departure characterized by effort involving signs;
the seventh stage is signless.
The other three stages are unconditioned because they proceed without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
For "volitional effort" is indeed the conditioned; since that is absent here, they are unconditioned.
And it is by relying upon those very three stages that one must purify the Buddha-field.
And Buddhahood is that which is to be attained; these two, respectively, are complete purity and purification. There are two verses concerning the analysis of skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
One attains skill in fulfilling the qualities of a Buddha, in bringing sentient beings to maturity,
in the swift attainment [of results], in the purity of action, and in the non-interruption of the path.
The skill in means of the bodhisattvas on all the stages is peerless;
relying upon this skill, they accomplish all goals.
By this, the classification and the function of skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) have been shown.
In that regard, non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is the means for the fulfillment of the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*).

The four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are for the maturation of sentient beings. For swift awakening, there is confession, rejoicing, entreaty, and dedication, expressed as: "I confess all evil... may my wisdom lead to perfect awakening.
For the purity of action, there are the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*).
Because they accomplish all purposeful activities, [this skill] exists in the non-interruption of the path and in non-abiding nirvana.
This fivefold skill in means across all the stages is the peerless expertise of Bodhisattvas, unequalled by others; such is its distinction.
Action is that which accomplishes all goals for both oneself and others.
Regarding the classification of the dhāraṇīs, there are three verses:
"The dhāraṇī [is attained] through maturation, through the practice of hearing, and through meditative concentration."
That [compassion] is small or great; furthermore, the great is of three kinds.
For the wise who have not yet entered or have already entered [the stages], it is small or middling;
for those on the impure stages, it is indeed great, while on the pure stages, it is vast.
