Relying upon that dhāraṇī, Bodhisattvas repeatedly proclaim the true Dharma and constantly uphold it.
Here too, the classification and the function of the dhāraṇī have been demonstrated.
In that regard, the dhāraṇī is of three kinds:
[the first] is through the maturation of previous karma;
Through the practice of hearing;
through great learning regarding the phenomena of the present life, characterized by a specific capacity for grasping and retaining;
and through reliance upon meditative concentration.

Furthermore, that [faith] should be understood as limited when it arises from the maturation [of karma] or from the practice of hearing [the teachings]. It is great when it arises through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Moreover, that great [faith] is also threefold.
For those who have not entered the stages, it is weak; for those who have entered the stages but whose stages are impure—that is, in the seven stages—it is middling;
but for those on the perfectly pure stages, it is superior. This is the classification of the dhāraṇī.
Its function is the illumination and the preservation of the true Dharma.

In the analysis of the vow (*praṇidhāna*), there are three verses: Volition conjoined with desire and impelled by knowledge—this is indeed the vow of the wise, which is peerless on all the stages (*bhūmi*). (MSA 18.74)
It should be understood as being both the cause and the immediate fruit;
it is for the sake of accomplishing one's welfare in the future, through the success that arises from mind alone.
Marvelous, great, and pure, on each successive stage up to enlightenment, it accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others for bodhisattvas.
Here, the vow is elucidated by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), its cause (*nidāna*), its stage (*bhūmi*), its classifications (*prabheda*), and its function (*karman*).
Its intrinsic nature is volition (*cetanā*) associated with aspiration (*chanda*);
its cause is knowledge (*jñāna*).
"In all stages" refers to the stage (*bhūmi*).
And that aspiration is the cause,
because its fruit arises immediately from the mind itself.

Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing intended aims in the future, the mind that yields immediate fruit should be understood as arising from the mind alone, through the fulfillment of intended aims exactly as desired—
that by which powerful bodhisattvas sport.
"It is not easy to calculate the number of his bodies," and so forth;

on the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), there is a manifold [aspiration] such as "may I become thus and thus. For one who has entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), there are the ten great vows (*daśa mahāpraṇidhānāni*).
It is pure because it becomes increasingly purified through the successive stages up until enlightenment; this is its classification according to its distinctions.
Its activity is the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others.
Regarding the analysis of the three concentrations, there are three verses.
One should know that selflessness is twofold, as is the basis for the grasping at a self;
their perpetual pacification is the objective domain of the three concentrations.
The range of the three concentrations should be known as being threefold:
the selflessness of persons and phenomena is the range of the concentration on emptiness;
the five aggregates of clinging, which are the basis for grasping at both of those as a self, are the range of the concentration on wishlessness.

The absolute pacification of that basis is the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*). That very concentration is to be known as threefold according to the state of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*);
and those concentrations which are the graspers of the threefold objective sphere (*gocara*) of the grasped.
Regarding those concentrations on emptiness and so forth, it should be understood that there are three concentrations in terms of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper;
furthermore, they are, respectively:
non-conceptual, turned away [from objects], and always associated with delight. (MSA 18.78)
The samādhi of emptiness is non-conceptual,
because it does not conceptualize a self in persons or phenomena.
The wishless [samādhi] is turned away from that basis which is the grasping at a self.
The signless [samādhi], associated with joy, is at all times directed toward the pacification of that basis;
for the sake of full comprehension, abandonment, and realization, the threefold purpose of the samādhis such as emptiness and the others has been proclaimed. (MSA 18.79)
Emptiness is for the sake of thoroughly understanding the selflessness of persons and phenomena;
the wishless is for the sake of abandoning the basis of that grasping at a self;
and the signless concentration is for the sake of directly realizing their pacification.
There are two verses concerning the classification of the summaries of the Dharma:
The four summaries of the Dharma have been taught to the bodhisattvas as the secret foundation of meditative concentration, out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings. (MSA 18.80)

In that regard, "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" and "all conditioned phenomena are suffering" are taught as the proximate cause for the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*); "all phenomena are selfless" is taught as the proximate cause for emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
and "nirvāṇa is peace" is taught as the proximate cause for the signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*).
What, then, is the meaning of "impermanent" up to the meaning of "peaceful"? He says:

For the wise, those four [meanings] are the meaning of non-existence, the meaning of non-conceptualization, the meaning of mere conceptual construction, and the meaning of the subsiding of conceptualization. (MSA 18.81)

For Bodhisattvas, the meaning of impermanence is the meaning of non-existence; that which does not exist eternally is what they regard as impermanent, namely, the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of unreal conceptualization is the meaning of suffering, which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of "mere conceptualization" is the meaning of selflessness.

By the word "only" (*eva*), there is a restriction: the imagined self does not exist, but mere conceptualization does exist. Thus, it is stated that the meaning of selflessness is the meaning of the non-existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of the cessation of conceptual construction is the meaning of peace; this refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*), which is nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the meaning of impermanence should be understood as the sense of momentary disintegration, pertaining to the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, there are ten verses in the analysis of momentariness for the purpose of establishing that.

Because of non-connection, because of arising from a cause, because of contradiction, because of not remaining by itself, because of non-existence, because of the exclusivity of the definition, because of persistence, and because of cessation. (MSA 18.82)
Because transformation is perceived, because it is both the cause and the fruit,
because of its being appropriated and its sovereignty, and because it follows after pure beings.
In this context, it should be understood that the proposition "everything conditioned is momentary" is stated later [in the text].
How, then, is that established?
Because the activity of conditioned phenomena is impossible without momentariness.
For activity (*pravṛtti*) consists in a continuous series (*prabandha*);
and that is not tenable without arising and ceasing at every moment.
Now, if it is maintained that activity occurs as a series by way of the cessation of the preceding and the arising of the succeeding after [the entity] has remained for some interval of time;
Immediately thereafter, there would be no further activity because of the absence of continuity (*prabandha*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which has arisen to exist at another time without continuity.
For what reason? Because its arising is from a cause.

For everything conditioned arises from a cause; this is the meaning of "it comes to be. If, having come into existence, it were to exist again at a subsequent time, it would necessarily have to possess a cause, because—just as at the very beginning—it would otherwise be non-existent in the absence of a cause.
Nor can that [subsequent state] arise from that very same cause, because its cause has already been consumed;
nor is any other cause perceived.
Therefore, it should be understood that at every moment, something else necessarily arises with a preceding cause.
Thus, for that which has arisen without a causal continuity, existence at a later time is not tenable.

Suppose, however, it were maintained that what has already arisen does not arise again—such that there would be no need for a cause—but rather that what has arisen ceases later after some interval of time, and not immediately upon arising:
by what, then, is it subsequently ceased?
If it is argued that [the effect exists] by the very cause of its arising, that is incorrect.
What is the reason?
Because arising and cessation are mutually contradictory.
For indeed, no common cause is found for two contradictory things,
such as shadow and sunlight, or cold and heat;
moreover, contradiction exists only with respect to cessation at a different time.
Because it contradicts [reasoning] and also because it contradicts scripture; for it was said by the Blessed One:
"O monk, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like an illusion; they are subject to ruin, temporary, and fleeting.
And through mental attention (*manaskāra*), for practitioners, as they attend to the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena, they perceive their cessation at every moment.
Otherwise, even they would not experience weariness, detachment, and liberation, just as others do not who perceive cessation at the time of death and so forth.
Furthermore, if a produced conditioned phenomenon were to persist for a period of time, it would have to persist either by its own power— being inherently capable of remaining—
or by means of some cause of duration (*sthitikāraṇa*).
First of all, its own abiding is untenable.
Why?
Because it does not abide by itself later on.
Or by what means would it be unable to remain at the end?
It is also not logical for it to have a cause of persistence, because such a cause does not exist;
indeed, nothing of that sort is perceived.
Furthermore, it might be argued that even in the absence of a cause for duration, a thing persists because of the absence of a cause for destruction;
however, once a cause for destruction is encountered, it subsequently perishes—just as blackness [perishes] upon contact with fire.
That is incorrect.
Because that does not exist;
for there is no cause of destruction whatsoever even subsequently.
It is well known—[though it is not actually well known]—that even by fire, blackness is destroyed.
However, its capacity for producing a dissimilar [result] is well-established;

for, through connection with that [fire], the continuity of blackness is perceived as becoming dissimilar, rather than ceasing entirely. Likewise, when water is being boiled, due to its connection with fire, it is perceived that because each subsequent production becomes increasingly diminished until extreme subtlety is reached, there is finally no further production.
However, its absence does not occur solely from contact with fire;
nor is it logical for anything that has arisen to persist,
because its defining characteristic is fixed.
For this characteristic of the conditioned has been declared by the Blessed One to be absolute, namely, the impermanence of the conditioned.

If, therefore, it were not to perish immediately upon arising, its impermanence would not exist for some period of time; thus, the characteristic of impermanence would necessarily be rendered non-absolute.

Now, it might be argued that if there were the arising of something entirely new at every moment, there would be no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) such as "this is that very same thing. To this we reply:
such recognition certainly occurs because of the persistence of similarity, like the case of a magician’s fruit;
the cognition of "that" arises from similarity, not from the actual existence of that [identical entity].
How is this understood?
From the perspective of cessation;
for there could be no cessation at the end of that which remains exactly as it was, since it would be indistinguishable from its initial moment.
Therefore, it is not determined that "this is that very same thing," because transformation is observed at the end.
For transformation indeed means becoming otherwise;
if it had not begun from the very start, then no transformation would be observed at the end of internal and external entities.
Therefore, it is established that change (anyathātva) has begun from the very outset; having increased gradually, it reaches its manifestation at the end, just as milk does in the state of curds.
However, as long as that change is not discerned due to its subtlety, because of the persistence of similarity, it is recognized as "this is that very same thing. Thus it is proven.
And thus, because there is change at every moment, momentariness is established. From what, moreover, is it established?
This means: by virtue of being its cause and its fruit;
that is to say, because it is a momentary cause and because it is a momentary fruit.
For it is well established that the mind is momentary, and other conditioned phenomena, such as the eye and visible forms, are its causes;
therefore, it is established that they too are momentary.
However, a momentary thing cannot arise from what is non-momentary, just as an impermanent thing cannot arise from what is permanent.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are indeed the fruit of the mind.
How is this understood?
Because they are appropriated, because of [the mind's] sovereignty, and because they follow the pure being.

For by the mind all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), such as the eye and so forth, together with their bases, are appropriated along with their coagulation, because they follow in accordance with its benefit.
Therefore, they are the fruit of the mind,
and the mind exercises sovereignty over the conditioned phenomena.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"By the mind this world is led, by the mind it is dragged along; it remains under the sway of the mind as it arises again and again.
Likewise, it has been stated that "name-and-form has consciousness as its condition."
Therefore, it is the fruit of the mind;
and because they follow the pure mind,
for the minds of yogins are pure and the formative forces (saṃskāras) conform to them.
As it has been said:
"A meditating monk, possessing supernatural powers and having attained mastery over the mind, if he were to resolve that this block of wood be gold, it would indeed become so for him.
Therefore, conditioned phenomena are the fruit of the mind.
And it is also due to conformity with sentient beings;
for thus, among sentient beings who commit evil, external things become inferior,
whereas among those who perform meritorious deeds, they become excellent.
Therefore, because they conform to that mind, it is established that conditioned phenomena have the mind as their fruit;
and from that, their momentariness follows.
For it is not logical that a non-momentary thing should be the fruit of a momentary thing, since [the fruit] must conform to its cause.
Thus, the momentariness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) has first been established without distinction by means of two verses.
Furthermore, five verses should be understood for the purpose of establishing it specifically for internal phenomena:
"By the first [moment], by the gradual increase, by accumulation, and by the state of having a basis..."
Likewise, through transformation and maturation, and by way of being inferior or superior.
Arising occurs through luminosity and non-luminosity, through movement to another location, through the state of being with seed or without seed, and through reflection.

Because there is no distinction in cause or measure regarding the fourteen types of arising, because accumulation and so forth are untenable, and because the state of being a basis is impossible; // Msa_18.86 //
Because there is no possibility of change for that which is stable, since it is indestructible from the beginning and undergoes no transformation;
likewise, this applies to both inferiority and superiority, as well as to luminosity and non-luminosity.
Because there is no going, because staying is impossible, because a final state is inconceivable,
and because the mind continues in succession, all conditioned phenomena are momentary.
The first [type] is even by degrees, up to the point that "all conditioned phenomena are momentary.
How is their momentariness established by these [arguments]?
For the arising of internal conditioned phenomena is of fourteen kinds.
The first is origination, which is the initial manifestation of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*). That which occurs by way of degrees is that which follows the first moment of birth.
That which occurs by way of accumulation is that which results from the accumulation [of growth] through food, sleep, celibacy, and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
In terms of its state as a basis: that which [occurs] through the bases such as the eye for the visual consciousness and so forth;
that which occurs through transformation by means of passion and so forth, due to the alteration of complexion and other qualities;
and that which occurs through maturation during the stages of embryo, infant, child, youth, middle age, and old age.
That which consists in inferiority and superiority for those being born respectively in the miserable destinies and the happy destinies;

and that which consists in luminosity for those born among the gods of the Heaven of Magical Creations, the Heaven of Others' Creations, and in the realms of form and formlessness, because these depend solely upon the mind.
That which pertains to those reborn elsewhere by virtue of being non-luminous;
that which consists in arising in another location upon the cessation of arising in one location through movement to another place;
and that which pertains to those with seeds, excluding the final aggregates of an Arhat.
That which occurs through the absence of seeds pertains to those very Arhats in their final [existence];

that which occurs through the nature of a reflection pertains to those who meditate on the eight liberations, consisting in the arising of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) as reflections by the power of meditative concentration (samādhi).
Regarding this fourteen-fold arising, the momentariness of internal conditioned phenomena is to be understood through such reasons as the distinction between cause and measure.
First, regarding initial arising, it is because of the distinction of its being a cause.

For if there were no distinction in its status as a cause, then no progressive distinction would be perceived in the subsequent activity of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), due to the lack of distinction in the cause.
And since there is a distinction, its difference from those that follow establishes its momentariness;
for there is a difference in measure (*māna*) in their production according to degrees. "Measure" (*māna*) here means "proof" (*pramāṇa*).
For indeed, without change at every moment, there could be no specific difference in magnitude; for if [growth] were produced through accumulation, such accumulation would be purposeless,
since accumulation is merely support.
Its [the body's] growth would be impossible without momentariness, because it would remain exactly as it was; furthermore, accumulation itself would be untenable,
for accumulation is not logically possible unless there is an arising that is increasingly more robust at every moment.
Because when [a thing] arises as the basis (āśrayabhāva), it is impossible for that which depends upon it (āśrita) to exist;
for it is not logical that while the basis remains, that which depends on it should not abide.
It would be like a person mounted on a vehicle remaining stationary while the vehicle itself moves; otherwise, the status of being a basis would be untenable.
Because it is impossible for that which remains as it is to undergo either transformation or maturation;
since there is no transformation for that which is without destruction from the beginning,
for indeed, no transformation by means of passion and the like is possible for that which remains exactly as it is.
Furthermore, ripening does not occur during other states, because if there were no destruction at the beginning, there would be no transformation at the end.
Likewise, momentariness should be understood to exist in the arising of the inferior and the superior, just as it exists in the arising of transformation and ripening.

For the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*) cannot find its operation while the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) remain exactly as they are; it is from this that birth occurs either in an evil destiny or in a happy destiny.
For it is logical that the attainment of activity occurs through a specific transformation of the continuum over time;
likewise, momentariness is logical even in the case of both luminous and non-luminous arising.
This is because, in the case of the luminous, it is impossible for something already so established to remain as it is, given that its activity is dependent upon the mind.
Furthermore, even in the case of what is non-luminous, since no transformation at the end is possible without destruction at the beginning;
and because there is no motion in the sense of moving to another location—
indeed, no action characterized by the transition to another location is logically tenable for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
For that [motion], whether already arisen or not yet arisen, would have to cause the conditioned entity to go to another location.

If it has already arisen, then at the time of going, nothing has gone; thus, for one who remains stationary, going is not logically possible. If, on the other hand, it has not yet arisen, then since going does not exist, it is not tenable to say "it has gone."
Furthermore, it is not logical that this activity (kriyā) should exercise its causal efficiency (kāritra) upon a latent impression (saṃskāra) located in that very same place,
because that which is stationary cannot reach another location.
Nor is it logical [for it to exercise its efficiency] upon one located in another place.
Because without action there is no reaching of another location,
and no action— whether situated in that location or elsewhere— is perceived apart from the conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, for conditioned factors, there is no "going" other than the arising of a continuum in another location.
And because of that absence, momentariness is established.
Motion, characterized by the continuous arising [of a thing] in successive locations, is to be understood through various causes;
it exists by the power of the mind, as in states such as walking and so forth.
There is [continuity] by the force of prior karma, as in the case of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
there is [continuity] by the force of propulsion, as in the case of a launched arrow;
and there is [continuity] by the force of connection, as in the case of those mounted on a vehicle or a boat crossing a river.
There is movement by the force of a push, as in the case of grass and other things impelled by the wind;

there is movement by the force of intrinsic nature, as in the horizontal movement of the wind, the upward flaming of fire, and the downward flowing of water; and there is movement by the power of influence, as by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs.
In the case of some iron [moving] by the power of a magnet,
and in the case of those possessing supernatural powers [moving] by the power of their *ṛddhi*,

momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) should be understood with respect to their arising in a state of being either with or without seeds, because of the impossibility of stability and because of the non-occurrence of a final [moment].
For it is not logical that something remaining as it is should again possess the nature of a seed at another time without having been a cause at every moment;
nor is it possible for it to be seedless in the final moment.
And this cannot be [maintained].
One must admit that there is the state of having seeds previously and the state of being seedless in the final moment;
for in the absence of that [previous state], the status of being "final" is impossible.
Indeed, the very nature of being final would not be possible.
In the arising of a reflection, momentariness is to be understood from its conformity with the mind,
because it arises at every moment by the power of the mind.
Thus, it has been definitively established that all internal conditioned phenomena are momentary.

Now, he establishes the momentariness of external things with three verses. The momentariness of the primary elements and of the sixfold objects is established because of their drying up and increasing, because of their inherent mobility, and because of their waxing and waning: *śoṣavṛddheḥ prakṛtyā ca calatvād vṛddhihānitaḥ //* (MSA 18.89)
Because it arises from that [earth], because of the fourfold transformation of the earth,
and because its color, odor, taste, and touch are identical, it is likewise [of the same nature].
Because its activity depends on fuel, because it is perceived with degrees of intensity,
because it conforms to the mind, and because of [the Buddha's] questioning, external objects as well are therefore momentary.
What, then, is that external [object]?
It consists of the four great elements and the sixfold object.

Color, odor, taste, touch, and sound, as well as the form belonging to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), are thus established as momentary with respect to the sixfold objects consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives. How is this established?
Regarding water, there is drying up and increasing;
in springs, lakes, ponds, and so forth, the gradual increase and drying up of water are observed.
Both of these would not occur without moment-to-moment transformation, because there is no other specific cause for the subsequent change.
Because wind is mobile by its very nature and because it undergoes increase and decrease, it cannot be stationary;

for that which is stationary cannot possess mobility due to its inherent nature—this has already been established [by the fact that there is no motion]. Furthermore, there can be no increase or decrease [in a stationary entity], precisely because it remains fixed in that state.
Because the earth arises from that and because of its fourfold transformation;
by the word "that," both water and air are included.
For at the time of evolution, the earth was produced from water together with air.
Therefore, because it is the fruit of that [action], it too should be understood as momentary.
Furthermore, four kinds of transformation of the earth are perceived:
that produced by karma, due to the specific karma of sentient beings; [and others].
That which is caused by external assault is produced by weapons and the like; that which is caused by elemental factors is produced by fire and the like;
that which is caused by time is produced through the transformation of a different period of time.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that [destruction] to occur without the arising of another [moment] at every instant, because there is no cause for destruction.
Since color, odor, taste, and touch have causes identical to those of earth and the other elements, their momentariness should be understood in the same way.
Moreover, the momentariness of fire is due to its existence being dependent upon fuel.
For when fire has arisen, the fuel that arose simultaneously with it does not remain in that same state;
nor is fire capable of persisting once its fuel is consumed,
lest there be a persistence of fire even at the end without fuel.
In accordance with the requirements of poetic composition (*ślokabandha*), the mention of color and the other [sensory qualities] comes first, followed by that of fire.

Furthermore, even regarding sound—which is perceived at a later time in the case of bells and the like—one should understand its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) because of the perception of degrees of intensity;
for if momentariness did not exist, there would be no perception of it becoming gradually weaker and weaker at every moment.
The momentariness of even that form which belongs to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is indeed established, because it follows the mind, as was stated previously.
Therefore, it is established that external [objects] are also momentary. Furthermore, it is asked: how is the momentariness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) established?
How so?
First of all, this proponent of non-momentariness should be asked:
"For what reason do you accept impermanence?"
If he should say that he does not accept the momentariness of conditioned phenomena because impermanence is not perceived at every moment, he should be asked this:

"Why do you not accept non-momentariness even in the case of things like lamps, whose momentary nature is well-established, simply because that [impermanence] is not perceived during their steady state?"
If he should say, "Because it is not perceived later as before," then he should be addressed with this:
"Why is the same not accepted for conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) as well?"

If he should say, "Because of the difference in characteristics between lamps and other conditioned phenomena," he should be addressed as follows: "For difference in characteristics is of two kinds: difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vailakṣaṇya*) and difference in mode of occurrence (*vṛtti-vailakṣaṇya*)."
If, first of all, it is intended that there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vailakṣaṇya*), then for that very reason their status as examples is appropriate;
for a thing cannot be an example of itself, just as a lamp is not an example of a lamp, nor a cow of a cow.

Alternatively, if it is a difference in mode of occurrence (*vṛtti-vailakṣaṇya*), then for that very reason they serve as examples, because lamps and so forth are well-known [to function in such ways].
Furthermore, because of the persistence of momentariness, he should be asked this:
"Do you maintain that while the vehicle remains stationary, the one mounted on the vehicle moves?
If he should say, "Certainly not," [then proceed].
He should be addressed as follows:

"It is not tenable that while the eye and other [faculties] remain, the consciousness supported by them continues in a stream. If he should say: "But is it not observed that while a lamp supported by a wick remains stationary, the flame continues in a stream?"
He should be addressed as follows:
"That has not been seen, because through its continuity, a transformation arises in the wick at every moment.
If he should say this: "If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are indeed momentary, why is their momentariness not established in the same way as that of a lamp and so forth?"
He should be addressed as follows: because it is a basis for error.
For their momentariness is not perceived due to the occurrence of a continuous series of similar moments;
consequently, despite there being distinct [moments] one after another, the error arises that "this is that very same thing."

Otherwise, there would be no misconception of the impermanent as permanent; in the absence of that, there would be no affliction (saṃkleśa), and how then could there be purification (vyavadāna)? It is precisely through such inquiry that the momentariness of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is established. There are twelve verses in the "Analysis of Selflessness" (Nairātmyavibhāga) for the purpose of establishing the selflessness of the person (pudgala-nairātmya).
The person (pudgala) should be said to exist as a designation, but not as a substantial entity;
because it is not perceived, because it is a misconception, because it is a defilement, and because its cause is defiled. (MSA 18.92)
Therefore, it cannot be described as being either identical to or different from [the aggregates], because of those two faults;
furthermore, because it would follow that the aggregates are the self, and it would follow that the self is a substantial entity.
If it were a substantial entity yet inexpressible, there would have to be a purpose for its being expressed;
to be inexpressible in terms of identity or difference without such a purpose is not logical.
Neither from the perspective of defining characteristics, nor from worldly observation, nor even from scripture,
is it tenable that fuel and fire are inexpressible [as identical or different], for they are perceived as a duality.
And since consciousness arises when there is a duality, that [duality] is not its condition;
therefore, from the point of view of being purposeless, it is not logical for there to be a seer, up to and including a liberator.
If [the self] were the master, it would not set forth that which is impermanent and undesirable;
its characteristic as the agent of action would be established, yet perfect enlightenment would be contradicted in three ways.
And that effort regarding seeing and so forth is not self-arisen even from the three [causes];
furthermore, seeing and so forth would be effortless if they were dependent on such effort.
Because there is no agent, because of impermanence, and because activity occurs simultaneously and eternally,
it is not logical for effort in seeing and so forth to be self-existent.
For that which remains as such, for that which has perished, and because of prior non-existence and impermanence,
as well as due to the absence of a third alternative, its status as a condition is not tenable.
All phenomena are selfless; in the ultimate sense, they are emptiness.
Furthermore, it is precisely because of this that the fault in apprehending a self has been taught.
Regarding both affliction and purification, as well as their distinct states and divisions,
it is indeed through the person (pudgala) that the distinctions of activity and continuity are demonstrated.
The view of a self is not to be produced, yet its practice is beginningless;
there would be effortless liberation for all, or else no liberation at all, if a person (pudgala) existed.
Should it be said that the person exists, or should it be said that it does not exist? He replied:
The person should be said to exist as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*), but not as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
And since it should be said to exist as a conceptual designation, it should be said not to exist as a substantial entity.
Thus, when one adopts this doctrine of multiple aspects (anekāṃśavāda), there is no room for the fault of either existence or non-existence.
But how is it to be understood that [the person] does not exist substantially?
Because of non-apprehension.
For it is not perceived as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) like form and so forth;
for "perception" indeed means comprehension by the intellect (*buddhyā*).
And yet, the proponents of the person (*pudgalavādinaḥ*) do not fail to comprehend the person through the intellect.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "In this very life, one perceives and designates a self. How, then, is it not perceived?
When it is perceived in this manner, it is not perceived as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
What is the reason?
Because it is due to perversion; for the Blessed One has stated that "self in what is not-self" is a perversion.
Therefore, this very grasping at a person is a perversion.
How is this understood?
From affliction.
For this affliction, characterized by the defilement of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), is precisely that which consists in "I" and "mine."
Furthermore, it is not possible for a non-perversion to be a defilement;
nor can it be understood how this [perversion] is a defilement except by virtue of its being a cause of defilement.
For it is from that [basis] that defiled states such as attachment arise, having it as their cause.

Furthermore, regarding that entity designated as "form" and so forth, which is called a "person" (pudgala), should that person be described as being identical to it or as being different from it? He replied:
Therefore, it cannot be described in terms of identity or difference.
What is the reason? Because of two faults.
Which two faults?
Furthermore, because it would follow that the aggregates are the self, and because it would follow that the person is a substantial entity;
for if there were identity, it would follow that the aggregates are the self and that the person possesses substantial existence.
If, on the other hand, the person were different [from the aggregates], it would possess substantial existence;
for in that case, since the person exists as a mere designation, its ineffability would be logical. Thus, the status of the indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*) is established.

Furthermore, those who, transgressing the Teacher’s instruction, maintain that a person exists as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ) should be addressed as follows: "If [the person] were substantially existent and yet inexpressible, you must state the purpose [for such a claim].
What is the reason?"
It is not logical to say that [the person] is inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different [from the aggregates], as that would be purposeless.
Now, they might wish to maintain the inexpressibility of the person on the basis of a mere analogy, such as:
"Fire is to be described as neither different nor non-different from its fuel."
They should be addressed as follows:

"The ineffability of fuel and fire is not tenable, either from the perspective of their characteristics, from worldly observation, or even from scripture; for they are perceived as two distinct things."
Fire, indeed, is the element of heat (*tejodhātu*), while fuel consists of the remaining elements;
since their characteristics are distinct, fire is therefore different from fuel.
Furthermore, in the world, fuel such as wood is seen even without fire, and fire is seen even without fuel; thus, their difference is established.

Furthermore, since the Blessed One nowhere in the treatises has stated that fire and fuel are inexpressible [as identical or different], this [position] is untenable. How, moreover, is it known that fire exists without fuel? It is known from perception; for instance, when dispersed by the wind, it continues to burn even at a great distance.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the fuel is there within the fire; for this very reason, the distinctness of fire and fuel is established.
Why?
Because the subject under discussion is "because they are perceived as two."
For two things are perceived there: the flame and the wind as fuel.
There indeed exists a person (pudgala) who is this seer, up to the knower, the agent, the enjoyer, the cognizer, and the liberator.
Yet, it is not tenable that he is a seer.
Nor, moreover, is there a liberator.

For he would have to be either the agent by virtue of being the causal condition for the consciousnesses designated as "seeing" and so forth, or [the agent] by virtue of being their master. Regarding these two possibilities:
Because consciousness arises in dependence upon a duality, that [duality] is not its condition.
Why?
Because it would be purposeless.
For no capacity whatsoever is observed in him with respect to that [universe]; or, if he were the master, he would not bring about what is impermanent and undesirable.
For if he were the master over the arising of consciousness, he would not bring about an undesirable consciousness, nor would he allow it to be impermanent;
since neither of these two cases is possible, [he cannot be the self].
It is not tenable that this [pudgala] is the seer, up to and including the liberator.
Furthermore, if the pudgala exists substantially, then its characteristic of action must be established.
If it exists as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*), its activity (*karman*) is also perceived,
just as the eyes and so forth have the characteristic of seeing and so on, and the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) and so forth.
But it is not so for the person (pudgala);
therefore, that [person] does not exist substantially. And if that were accepted as existing substantially, [it would contradict] the Buddha, the Blessed One’s...
Awakening is obstructed in three ways:
by the awakening to the profound,
and by the uncommon awakening.
And there is the supramundane perfect awakening.
For in the case of a person’s perfect awakening, nothing profound has been perfectly awakened,
nor is it something not shared with the non-Buddhist outsiders.
It is not in accordance with the world,
for this grasping is accessible to all the world and is clung to by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
And [the person] is one whose mind has been conditioned by long-term saṃsāra.
Furthermore, a person who is a seer, up to a cognizer, must be either with effort or without effort in regard to seeing and so forth.
Moreover, for one who possesses effort, that effort must be either self-existent or accidental.

Nor is there a self-arisen effort toward seeing and so forth based on that [perception], because of the three faults that will be explained. Therefore, for these very three reasons, [it is not established].
And the phrase "not being dependent on effort" continues [to apply here];
furthermore, it is established for that which exists without effort.
Seeing and so forth are effortless.
Thus, if there is no activity on the part of the person regarding seeing and so forth, how can he be a seer,
up to being a cognizer?
It has been stated that [this arises] from the three defects; from which three defects?
Because of being non-agents, because of impermanence, and because of acting simultaneously and eternally, it is not logical for effort in seeing and so forth to be self-existent.

If effort (*prayatna*) regarding seeing and so forth were accidental—that is, if seeing and so forth occurred by chance—then the person (*pudgala*) would not be their agent. In that case, how could he be a "seer" or, up to, a "knower"? Furthermore, if effort were accidental, it would be independent [of causes], and thus effort would never fail to exist;
nor, if effort were eternal, would there be the fault of seeing and so forth occurring simultaneously and eternally.
Therefore, it is not logical for effort to be self-arisen in regard to seeing and so forth;
likewise, because that which remains or that which has perished lacks prior existence and is impermanent,
and because there is no third alternative, its status as a causal condition is not tenable.
Now, if effort were to have the person as its condition,
then it would not be logical for that [effort], while remaining in such a state, to possess the status of a condition,
because of its prior non-existence.
For if that [person] were indeed a causal condition, it would never be the case that the person does not exist;
why then would there be no prior effort when [the person] has not yet arisen?
Furthermore, it is not tenable for that which has perished to be a causal condition, as it would entail the consequence of the person being impermanent.
Furthermore, there is no third alternative such that it would be neither abiding nor destroyed;
therefore, even an effort conditioned by that [person] is not tenable.
Thus, relying on reasoning, a person (*pudgala*) is not perceived as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
All phenomena are selfless; in the ultimate sense, they are emptiness. Furthermore, it is precisely because the fault in the apprehension of a self has been taught.
For in the *Dharmoddānas*, the Blessed One has taught that all phenomena are without self; yet in the *Paramārthaśūnyatā*, he has taught:

"Karma exists and its maturation exists, but an agent is not found who casts off these aggregates and reconnects with other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṃketa*)."
In the *Pañcaka-varga*, five disadvantages of the apprehension of a self (*ātma-upalambha*) are taught:

there arises the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of a living being (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*); one becomes indistinguishable from the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*); and one has entered upon a wrong path.
His mind does not enter into emptiness, does not become serene toward it, does not abide in it, and does not resolve upon it;
his noble qualities do not become purified.
Thus, even from the perspective of scripture, this is not tenable.

For the person (*pudgala*) has also been taught by the Blessed One in various places— as the one who fully understands, the bearer of the burden, and through the formal classification of persons such as the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*)— so why was it taught if it does not exist substantially? [It was taught] regarding affliction and purification, which are distinguished by their different states and divisions.
For the distinction between the continuity of modes of existence is indeed demonstrated by means of the person (pudgala).
For, regarding the distinctions of states in affliction and purification, as well as the distinctions of severance,
it would be impossible to teach the differentiation of their operation and the differentiation of the continuum without the designation of a person (*pudgala*).
In that regard, in the *Parijñā-sūtra*, the phenomena to be fully known are affliction, and full knowledge is purification.
In the Bhārahāra-sūtra,
the burden and the taking up of the burden are defilement;
the laying down of the burden is purification.

Without the designation of persons as "one who has fully understood" and "one who carries the burden," it would be impossible to teach the difference in their activity and the difference in their mental continuum.
Furthermore, the factors conducive to awakening exist in many states due to the distinctions between the paths of preparation, seeing, cultivation, and finality;

without the designation of persons such as "the follower by faith" and so forth, it would be impossible to teach the difference in their activity and the difference in their mental continuum regarding these factors.
The principle to be understood here is that the person (pudgala) was taught [by the Buddha] despite its non-existence as a substantial entity;
otherwise, the teaching of the person would be rendered purposeless.
For, first of all, it is not logical that this [teaching] was intended for the sake of producing the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), because:
The view of a self is not to be produced, because it has already arisen previously;
nor is it for the sake of practicing that [view], because of the view of a self.
Practice is beginningless from time without start.
And if liberation were taught as being through the view of a self,
then this would be the case.
Otherwise, liberation would be effortless for everyone;
for it would follow that those who have not seen the truths do not possess the view of self,
or else that liberation does not exist at all.
For no one, having previously grasped the self as non-self, would grasp it as a self at the time of the realization of the truths.
Just as one does not grasp suffering as suffering after having failed to grasp it as such before, so too, liberation would not exist as it did before.

Furthermore, if a self exists, there must necessarily be the notions of "I" and "mine," along with craving for a self and other afflictions caused by them; therefore, for this reason as well, liberation would not exist.
Or rather, one must not accept that a person (pudgala) exists;
for if such a thing existed, these faults would necessarily follow.
Thus, by these qualities, Bodhisattvas are eternally endowed.
They do not neglect their own welfare, and they accomplish the welfare of others.
The function of the qualities beginning with modesty and steadfastness has been indicated in brief.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment, in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra.
The nineteenth chapter: On the Analysis of Marvels, there are three verses.
The renunciation of one's own body and the concealment of one's excellence,
as well as patience toward the weak, belong to one who is indifferent toward both body and life.
The undertaking of vigor, the absence of relish even for the bliss in meditative absorptions,
and non-conceptuality regarding wisdom— this is the marvelous path of the wise.
Birth in the family of the Tathāgatas, the receiving of the prophecy,
the attainment of consecration, and the realization of enlightenment are considered the marvels.
Here, the marvel of practice is described by means of two verses concerning the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
For through generosity (*dāna*), the relinquishing of one’s own body is a marvel; and through the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*), there is the relinquishing of noble prosperity.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.

By the third verse, the marvel of the fruit is explained, beginning with the four fruits of a bodhisattva: on the first, eighth, and tenth [stages], there are three fruits of those in training (śaikṣa);
on the stage of a Buddha, the fourth is the fruit of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). Regarding the analysis of what is not a marvel, there is this verse:
Having cultivated detachment, compassion, and even the supreme meditative absorption,
as well as equanimity— it is not surprising that one is disciplined in these qualities.
Regarding the phrase "in those":
having attained detachment, application to generosity is not surprising;
likewise, having attained compassion, it is not surprising [to apply oneself] to ethical discipline and patience.
Having attained the supreme cultivation on the eighth stage, the application of vigor and the other perfections in a manner that is effortless and non-conceptual is not surprising.

Having attained the state of mind characterized by equality between self and others, the application toward all the perfections is not surprising, because there is no weariness in working for the sake of others as if it were for one's own sake. Regarding this state of equanimity, there are three verses:
Sentient beings do not possess such intense affection for themselves, their wives, children, friends,
or kinsmen as the wise possess for all sentient beings.

Impartiality toward those in need, the constant non-violation of ethical discipline, patience in all circumstances for the sake of sentient beings, and the undertaking of great vigor as well; MSA 19.6.
Dhyāna that is always wholesome and wisdom that is non-conceptual—
these should be understood as the equanimity of mind toward those very [qualities] of the bodhisattvas.
One verse concerns equanimity toward sentient beings;
two concern the perfections.
For the affection of sentient beings toward their own selves and so forth is neither accompanied by equanimity nor is it absolute;
for they sometimes even kill themselves.

But for Bodhisattvas, there is both equanimity and absoluteness regarding all sentient beings. Furthermore, among the perfections, equanimity of mind in giving consists in being without partiality toward those who seek help.
In ethical discipline, there is the constant non-violation of even the slightest precept;
in patience, there is non-differentiation regarding all places, times, and sentient beings;

and in vigor, there is the undertaking of vigor for the sake of sentient beings [and for the sake of all goals], through the equal application toward the welfare of self and others and for the sake of all that is wholesome.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
There are sixteen verses in the analysis of being a benefactor:
"Establishing [them] in the state of being a vessel, and planting them in the very precepts..."
Forbearance toward harm and the application of oneself to the welfare [of others].
Winning others over to this teaching, cutting through doubt,
and acting for the benefit of sentient beings— this is held to be the characteristic of the wise.
By these two verses, the manner in which Bodhisattvas provide assistance through the six perfections is elucidated.
For by means of generosity, they establish sentient beings as fit vessels for the performance of virtuous deeds;
and by means of meditative concentration, they win them over through the possession of extraordinary power.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
By the remaining verses, the quality of being beneficial is shown through their similarity to a mother and so forth:
"Those who always sustain sentient beings with an impartial intention..."
They cause [them] to be born in the noble stage and increase them through wholesome qualities.
They protect [beings] from misdeeds and cause them to master the sacred teachings; through these five activities, the sons of the Conquerors are like mothers to sentient beings. (Msa 19.11)
They are like mothers to sentient beings, acting as mothers for sentient beings;
for a mother indeed provides five kinds of assistance to her son:
she bears him in her womb.
It gives birth,
nourishes, sustains, and causes to grow;
it protects from states of woe.
And one teaches them speech;
by analogy with that, these five activities of a bodhisattva are to be understood.
The noble stages and the noble dharmas are to be understood [in the same way].
Because they always plant faith in all sentient beings,
and because they engage them in the training of higher ethics and so forth, as well as in liberation.
Through these five activities— soliciting the Buddhas and abandoning their obscurations— the sons of the Conquerors are like fathers to sentient beings.
For a father provides five kinds of assistance to his sons:
he plants their seed,
and he teaches them their craft.
He unites them with suitable wives, entrusts them to good friends,
and makes them free from debt so that they do not [incur further obligations].
A father's debt is made to be paid;
by analogy with that, these five activities of Bodhisattvas are to be understood.
For faith is the seed for sentient beings to obtain the noble body.
The trainees are his craft;
liberation is his wife; the experience of the joy and bliss of liberation is his [offspring];
and the Buddhas are his spiritual friends.
Obscuring is the state of debt:
for those who indeed conceal from sentient beings that which they ought not to teach,
yet criticize failure in training and praise excellence alone.
They bestow instruction and indeed make the Māras known;
through these five activities, the sons of the Conquerors are like kinsmen to sentient beings.
For relatives provide five kinds of assistance to their kin:
they conceal their secrets,
and they censure their misconduct.
They praise their good deeds, provide assistance in matters that ought to be done,
and restrain them from situations of calamity.
By way of analogy with that, these five activities of bodhisattvas are to be understood:
because they conceal the teaching of the profound Dharma from those who are unworthy; because they respectively censure and praise the failure and success in training;
because they provide instruction for the sake of realization; and because they perceive the works of Māra.
With their own intellects untiring regarding both affliction and purification,
they bestow all mundane prosperity as well as that which transcends the world.

Those who always seek the happiness and welfare [of others] and are undivided [from them] because they are untiring—such sons of the Victors are like friends to sentient beings by virtue of five activities. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 19.17.
For that indeed is a friend who is unerring regarding the welfare and happiness of a friend; who bestows both happiness and welfare; who remains inseparable;
and who always desires welfare and happiness.
Likewise, it should be understood that Bodhisattvas are like friends to sentient beings by means of five kinds of actions.
For worldly prosperity is happiness,
because one experiences happiness through it.
It is supramundane benefit because it is the antidote to the disease of the afflictions;
those who are always exerting effort for the sake of maturing sentient beings [attain this].
They speak correctly regarding the means of deliverance and are patient toward wrongdoings.
The sons of the Conquerors, who bestow the two kinds of perfection and are skilled in the means thereto, are like servants to sentient beings by virtue of five types of activity.
For a servant conducts himself properly through five kinds of actions:
he is endowed with diligence;
he is not deceptive regarding his duties.
He is patient toward verbal abuse, physical assault, and the like;
he is skillful through the performance of all tasks;
and he is discerning, being knowledgeable in means (*upāya*).

By way of analogy with that, these five activities of the bodhisattvas are to be understood; likewise, the two kinds of accomplishment—mundane and supramundane—are to be understood. And those who are considered to have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) [are also included].
They are instructors in all vehicles and directors of the perfected yogas.
With pleasant countenances, and indifferent toward both recompense and the ripening of results,
the sons of the Victors are like teachers of sentient beings through these five actions.
Through five kinds of action, the teacher becomes a benefactor to his disciples:
he is himself well-trained; [and so forth].
He teaches everything;
he teaches quickly;
he is pleasant-faced and of a gentle disposition.
And their minds are free from worldly desire;
by analogy with that, these five activities of bodhisattvas are to be understood. Those who are dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings fulfill the accumulations.
They swiftly liberate those who have gathered [the accumulations] and cause them to abandon their adversaries.
Through five types of actions, the sons of the Victors—resembling spiritual preceptors for sentient beings—unite them with the various worldly successes and with the supramundane. (Msa 19.23)
The preceptor is beneficial to his co-residents through five kinds of actions:
he causes them to go forth, he grants them full ordination,
and he instructs them in the avoidance of faults.
He gathers [beings] through material gifts and through the Dharma;
by analogy with that, these five activities of the bodhisattvas are to be understood.
There are two verses concerning the analysis of requital.
Through non-attachment to enjoyments, by not violating moral discipline, through devotion to gratitude, and by application to correct practice; MSA 19.24.
For embodied beings who abide precisely in the six perfections become,
in that way, those who repay the Bodhisattvas' kindness.
"So be it," [he said], for just as those Bodhisattvas are benefactors—
engaging in giving through non-attachment to enjoyments therein, and engaging in ethical discipline by not violating their vows— they shall likewise act.
Through the application of gratitude, there is [perfection] in patience;
for, out of gratitude toward the bodhisattva who has been a benefactor—since those [benefactors] are fond of patience—one practices.
Through the application of practice, there is [perfection] in vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, because of the means by which one practices and that in which one practices.
Regarding the analysis of aspiration, there is this verse:
They always desire increase and decrease, the maturation of sentient beings, progress to excellence on the stages, and unsurpassed enlightenment. (MSA 19.26)
Bodhisattvas always aspire to five things:
the increase of the perfections;
The abandonment of its opposites,
the maturation of sentient beings,
and the progression through the distinct stages.
And [the attainment of] unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
There is a verse regarding the classification of unfailing application:
"In the removal of fear, in the generation [of the thought of awakening], and also in the cutting off of doubt,"
And in the instruction on practice, the sons of the Conquerors are always unfailing.
The application of bodhisattvas toward the fourfold benefit of sentient beings should be understood as unfailing:
in the application of [removing] fear regarding the profound and vast Dharma,
and in the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

There are two verses concerning the cutting off of doubts for those who have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and regarding the instruction on the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*), as well as the classification of correct application.
Giving by one who is free from expectation and devoid of craving for rebirth;
ethical discipline and patience in all circumstances; and vigor for the arising of all that is wholesome.
Likewise, the meditative concentration and wisdom conjoined with skillful means, as well as the correct application toward the six perfections, constitute the practice of the wise. (MSA 19.29)
As it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa*:
"The ripening [of the fruit] is not to be expected from giving," and so forth.
There are two verses concerning the distinction between the factors conducive to decline and those conducive to excellence.
Attachment to enjoyments, susceptibility to flaws, pride, indulgence in pleasure,
relishing [meditative states], and conceptualization are the causes of decline for the wise.
For those bodhisattvas established in those very antidotes,
the factors conducive to distinction are to be known as being the opposite of these [hindrances].
The adversaries of the six perfections are conducive to decline; their opposites should be understood as conducive to distinction.
There are two verses concerning the distinction between counterfeit and genuine qualities.
One is the six-legged [insect];
hypocrisy consists in causing others to move away, displaying a pleasant countenance,
acting with greed, and likewise maintaining tranquility of speech and body.
Perfection in eloquent speech devoid of correct practice—
these are taught as leading to the non-reality of bodhisattvas; conversely, for those who apply themselves [to practice], they are taught as leading to that reality.
The six qualities of a bodhisattva, beginning with leading others [to maturity], should be understood as being the counterfeits of the six perfections.
The rest has been explained.
There is a verse regarding the classification of discipline:
"For those wise ones, through the application of generosity and the other perfections, discipline sentient beings by means of the sixfold opposition on all the stages. (MSA 19.34)
The adverse factors are of six kinds:
stinginess, immorality, anger, laziness, distraction, and faulty wisdom, corresponding respectively to the six perfections.
The rest has been explained.

In the section on prophecy (vyākaraṇa), there are three verses: The prophecy for the wise is twofold, according to the distinction of time and person; it is likewise proclaimed as being great in respect to enlightenment and in respect to the prophecy itself. (MSA 19.35)
Through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising [of phenomena], through the abandonment of pride and effortful striving,
and through attaining oneness with all the Buddhas and the Sons of the Conquerors.
Furthermore, that [propagation] is intended by way of the field, the name, the time, the name of the eon, and the persistence of the retinue of the True Dharma. (MSA 19.37)

In that regard, prophecy is distinguished by the difference between individuals, because there is prophecy concerning individuals who are established in the lineage, those who have generated the thought [of awakening], those who are present before one's eyes, and those who are not present before one's eyes.
It is distinguished by the difference in time, because there is prophecy for a limited period of time or for an unlimited period of time.
Furthermore, there is prophecy regarding awakening.

Or, regarding prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), it is when a Tathāgata of such-and-such a name will thus prophesy [one] at such-and-such a time. Furthermore, there is another "great prophecy" (*mahāvyākaraṇa*) which occurs on the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and through the abandonment of the conceit, "I shall become a Buddha."
Through the abandonment of the enjoyment of all signs,
and through attaining a state of oneness together with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is because no distinction is perceived within one's own mental continuum.
Furthermore, there is a prophecy by way of the field and so forth: "In such a buddha-field, one named thus will become a Buddha after such a length of time;
in a kalpa of such a name, his retinue will be of such a kind."
"For this long a period of time will the continuation of this True Dharma occur.
Regarding the analysis of the certainty of falling [into the stage of assurance], there is a six-line verse:
"The wise ones' certainty in the arising of prosperity and in the absence of weariness..."
And in the constancy of cultivation, in the non-falling away from meditative concentration,
in the accomplishment of what is to be done, in effortless spontaneity, and in the attainment of patience— in every respect.
With reference to the six perfections, this sixfold certainty is taught:
certainty regarding prosperity, because one constantly attains the prosperity of vast enjoyments;
and certainty regarding rebirth, because one constantly assumes rebirths according to one's wish.
The certainty of being untiring is due to not becoming weary from the sufferings of saṃsāra;
the certainty of constant cultivation is due to the perpetual continuity of cultivation.

There is a certainty of falling [into the state of non-retrogression] regarding the non-falling from meditative concentration and the accomplishment of the tasks to be done, because of the constant non-decline of meditative concentration and the fulfillment of the welfare of sentient beings.

There is also a certainty of falling [into that state] upon the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because of the constant dwelling in effortless, non-conceptual gnosis. Regarding the analysis of what must necessarily be done, there is a verse of six lines:
Worship, undertaking the training, compassion, cultivation of the wholesome,
vigilance in the forest, and likewise insatiability regarding the meaning of what has been heard—
these are the necessary duties for the wise on all stages.
With reference to the six perfections, this verse concerning the six kinds of necessary duties has its meaning already explained.
Regarding the analysis of what must be done continuously, there are two verses:
"Knowledge of the defects in sensual pleasures, and the examination of one's own transgressions..."
The endurance of suffering and the cultivation of the wholesome.
Non-attachment to pleasure and the non-conceptualization of signs—
this is indeed what must be practiced continuously by the wise throughout all the stages.
There are six constant practices for the sake of perfecting the six perfections.
The two verses [that follow] have their meaning already explained.
Regarding the classification of the principal matters, there is a verse of six lines.
The gift of Dharma, purity of ethical discipline, the very patience of non-arising,
the exertion of vigor in the Mahāyāna, the final state accompanied by compassion,
and wisdom— these are considered by the wise to be the primary [perfections] among the pāramitās.
Among the six perfections, these are the six primary ones.
Therein, purity of ethical discipline is the ethical discipline beloved by the noble ones;
the final one is the abiding accompanied by compassion, which is the fourth dhyāna conjoined with the immeasurable of compassion.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
There are four verses concerning the analysis of the establishment of designations (*prajñapti-vyavasthāna*).
The establishment of the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) is according to the distinctions in the forms of the Sūtras and so forth.
The wise should understand the establishment of the Dharma throughout all the stages.
Furthermore, the establishment of the truths is sevenfold based on suchness;
likewise, the establishment of reasoning and the vehicles is fourfold and threefold respectively.
Proper mental attention, right view accompanied by its fruit,
investigation by means of the valid cognitions, and the inconceivable object of knowledge— this is the fourfold reasoning.
The vehicle is held to be threefold by way of its intention, its teaching, its application, its equipment, and the distinction of its full attainment. (MSA 19.46)
The establishment of designations is fourfold,
distinguished by the designations of phenomena (*dharma*), truths (*satya*), reasoning (*yukti*), and vehicles (*yāna*). Among these,

the establishment of the five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*) should be understood as the establishment of phenomena, categorized by the various forms such as discourses (*sūtra*), verses (*geya*), and so forth.
For indeed, the other branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) are taught within the Mahāyāna for the sake of the bodhisattvas as being included therein.

However, the establishment of the truths proceeds by relying upon seven kinds of suchness (*tathatā*): the suchness of activity (*pravṛtti-tathatā*), the suchness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*), the suchness of representation (*vijñapti-tathatā*), the suchness of arrangement (*saṃniveśa-tathatā*), the suchness of wrong practice (*mithyā-pratipatti-tathatā*), and the suchness of right practice (*samyak-pratipatti-tathatā*).
The establishment of the designation of reasoning is fourfold: the reasoning of dependence, the reasoning of cause and effect, the reasoning of logical proof, and the reasoning of natural law.
The reasoning of logical proof,
and the reasoning of the nature of phenomena;
the formal establishment of the designations of the vehicles is threefold.
The Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna.
Among these, the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*) refers to appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*) in all three vehicles;

for, depending upon that and with that as the condition, supramundane right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) arises. The reasoning of causal efficiency (*kāryakāraṇa-yukti*) refers to right view together with its fruit.
The reasoning of establishment through proof is the investigation by means of valid cognitions such as direct perception;
the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*) is an inconceivable state,
for the nature of phenomena is established and is not to be further conceptualized.
From what kind of appropriate mental attention (*yonisomanaskāra*) does right view arise,

or from that [view] does the fruit, which is the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*), result? The establishment of the three vehicles (*yānatraya*) is to be understood through five aspects.
[The vehicles are distinguished] by intention, by teaching, by application, by equipment, and by attainment.

In this regard, the Śrāvakayāna consists of inferior intention, teaching, application, equipment, and attainment; the Pratyekabuddhayāna consists of middling [ones]; and the Mahāyāna consists of superior [ones].
For the teaching of the Dharma prevails according to the intention and according to the aspiration.
As is the teaching, so is the application;
as is the application, so is the equipment;
and as is the equipment, so is the realization of awakening.
Regarding the analysis of thorough investigation, there is this verse:

"The investigation of the adventitious nature of both name and object in relation to one another, and the investigation of the fact that the two kinds of designation herein consist of nothing but that [name and object]. (MSA 19.47)
There are four kinds of investigation regarding phenomena:
the investigation of names, the investigation of things,
and the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature.
And there is the investigation into the designation of specific qualities.
In this regard, the investigation into the adventitious nature of a name with respect to a thing should be understood as the "investigation of names.
The investigation into the adventitious nature of a thing with respect to a name should be understood as the "investigation of things."

In the connection between those two, the investigation into the fact that the designations of intrinsic nature and specific qualities are mere designations is to be understood as the "investigation into the designations of intrinsic nature and specific qualities.
There are ten verses in the section on the analysis of knowledge regarding the abandonment of things as they truly are:
"Because of the non-apprehension of everything, there is fourfold knowledge of reality."
For the wise, it arises on all the stages for the sake of accomplishing every goal.
The fourfold thorough knowledge of things as they truly are consists in the investigation of names and the investigation of entities regarding all phenomena.
It consists of the investigation into the designation of intrinsic nature and the investigation into the designation of specific qualities;
and this is to be understood as resulting from the non-apprehension of all these, beginning with names.
With the second half [of the verse], he demonstrates the greatness of thorough knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) regarding karmas:
"For the cause of bondage is indeed the sign (*nimitta*), which consists of the basis (*pratiṣṭhā*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and the seed (*bīja*);
for it is the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), together with their support and their seeds, that are bound therein. (MSA 19.49)
In this context, the basis-sign is the receptacle world;
the enjoyment-sign consists of the five objects, form and so forth;
and the seed-sign is their seed, which is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
In these three kinds of signs, the mind and mental factors, together with their bases, are bound;
and that which is their seed is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Furthermore, the bases should be understood as the eye and so forth.
The wise one, by thoroughly discerning every sign— both that which is placed before him and that which exists by itself— attains supreme enlightenment.

In this context, the "sign" (*nimitta*) established before one is that which has been made an object of focus through the application of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and is thus conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).
That which is "established by itself" is that which has become an object of focus by its very nature, being conceptually constructed without effort.
The "elimination" (*vibhāvanā*) of that sign is its disappearance, its state of no longer being an object of focus.
Non-conceptualization is the means for that [attainment] and the antidote to signs;
both of these occur sequentially:
first, that which was established [by effort], and subsequently, that which is established of its own accord.
In that regard, by eliminating the sign of a person (pudgala-nimitta) accompanied by the four perversions, the yogi attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
by eliminating the sign of all phenomena (sarvadharma-nimitta), he attains great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
By this, one proceeds toward liberation through the thorough knowledge of reality as it is—that is, through thorough knowledge according to the way things truly are.
That has been elucidated:

the wisdom that takes suchness as its object, which is free from the grasping of duality, and which directly perceives the body of badness (dauṣṭhulyakāya) at its exhaustion, is held by the wise. (MSA 19.51)
By this, it is elucidated how, through the thorough knowledge of the three natures as they are, one proceeds toward the exhaustion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
that is, by thoroughly knowing the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) through its having suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
The imagined nature is [defined] by way of being devoid of the grasping after duality;
the dependent nature is [defined] by way of the direct perception of the body of corruption;
it conduces to the destruction of that very body of corruption, which is the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna); for the sake of its destruction, and upon its destruction.
Knowledge that has suchness as its object, cultivated without diverse aspects,
is said to be direct perception regarding the reality of existence and non-existence, and to be sovereign over conceptual construction.
It is cultivated as being without diverse forms because one perceives no difference between the sign (*nimitta*) and suchness (*tathatā*).
By this, the distinction of the bodhisattva’s signlessness from that of the śrāvaka’s signlessness is elucidated;
for the latter perceive a difference between the sign and the signless.
Because they do not attend to any signs (*nimitta*) and attend to the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), [śrāvakas and others] enter the signless meditative attainment.
Bodhisattvas, however, seeing signs as non-distinct from suchness (*tathatā*), see the sign itself as signless; therefore, their knowledge is cultivated without diverse aspects.
It is said to be direct perception regarding the meaning of existence—that is, suchness—and mastery over conceptualization regarding the meaning of non-existence—that is, signs.
Because they have attained mastery over conceptual construction, all objects are successfully accomplished according to their conception.
For the foolish, reality is completely concealed and unreality appears everywhere; but for Bodhisattvas, having cast that [unreality] aside, reality itself appears everywhere.

By this it is demonstrated that just as for ordinary beings, by their own natural disposition, only what is unreal appears as the causal sign (*nimitta*) and not reality (*tattva*), which is suchness (*tathatā*); so too for Bodhisattvas, by their own natural disposition, only reality appears and not the unreal.
The non-appearance and appearance of the non-existent object and the existent object, respectively, are to be understood [in this way].
This liberation is the revolution of the basis, because of the attainment of mastery over one's desires.
The non-appearance of the unreal object, which is the causal sign, and the appearance of the real object, which is suchness, should be understood as the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
For by means of that, there is the non-appearance of the former and the appearance of the latter;
and that very [revolution] should be understood as liberation.
What is the reason?
