Because of acting according to one's will;
for at that time, one becomes independent and a master of one's own mind, by virtue of the fact that signs do not manifest by their very nature.
The great purpose of appearing as mutually similar in every respect creates obstacles; therefore, having fully understood this, one should abandon it.
This is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is regarding the means for purifying the field:
the objective world (*bhājanaloka*), though vast, diverse, and evolving, appears as being of a uniform nature, such that one thinks, "This is that very same [world].
Because it appears in this way, it becomes an obstacle to the purification of the Buddha-field.
Therefore, having fully understood this as an obstacle, one should indeed abandon it; thus it is proclaimed.
Regarding the classification of the immeasurables, there is this verse:
That which is to be matured, that which is to be purified, that which is to be attained, and that which is fit for maturing.
For the wise, the subject matter of the teaching on rightness is indeed immeasurable.
For there are five kinds of immeasurable objects for bodhisattvas:

the object to be matured, which is the realm of sentient beings without distinction; the object to be purified, which is the world-realm comprised of the container-world; and the object to be attained, which is the dharma-realm.

The realm of those to be trained is that which is fit for ripening; the realm of the means for training consists of the subject matter of correct teaching. There are two verses regarding the analysis of the fruits of teaching.
The arising of the bodhisattva-mind and the very patience regarding non-arising; the stainless eye and the inferior [eye], as well as the destruction of the outflows.
The long endurance of the true Dharma, the development of understanding, the cutting off of doubts, and the enjoyment [of the teaching]—
these should be known as the fruits of the teaching for the wise person who is devoted to it.
For a bodhisattva engaged in teaching, eight kinds of fruits of that teaching should be understood:
some among the listeners generate the thought of awakening (bodhicitta),
while others attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Some produce the dustless and stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena, which is comprised within the Lesser Vehicle;
some attain the destruction of the outflows;
and the True Dharma becomes long-enduring through its successive preservation.
For those who have not yet mastered the meaning, there comes mastery of the meaning;
for those who are doubtful, there comes the cutting away of doubt;
and for those who have reached certainty, there comes the enjoyment of the true Dharma—the blameless flavor of joy.

There are two verses concerning the analysis of the greatness of the Mahāyāna: "The greatness of the objective support, likewise that of the two practices, of knowledge, of the exertion of vigor, and of skill in means. (Msa 19.59)
The greatness of its attainment and the greatness of the Buddha's activity— indeed, because of its possession of these two forms of greatness, it is designated as the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna).
It is called the Mahāyāna because it is endowed with seven kinds of greatness:
(1) greatness of objective support (*ālambana-mahattva*), by virtue of being joined with the immeasurable and extensive teachings such as the sūtras;
and (2) greatness of practice (*pratipatti-mahattva*), by virtue of practicing for two purposes: one's own welfare and the welfare of others.

By the greatness of knowledge, because at the time of penetration there is knowledge of both—the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

By the greatness of the undertaking of vigor, because of the continuous and respectful application throughout three incalculable eons (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*). By the greatness of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), because of being undefiled while not abandoning *saṃsāra*.
[The greatness of the Buddha is established] by the greatness of his realization, because of his realization of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
and by the greatness of his buddha-activity, because he repeatedly manifests perfect enlightenment and great final nirvana.
There are two verses concerning the analysis of the inclusion within the Mahāyāna.
The lineage, zeal for the Dharma, the generation of the thought [of awakening], the practice of giving and so forth, and likewise the entry into the right method; MSA 19.61.
The ripening of sentient beings, the purification of the field,
non-abiding nirvana, and supreme enlightenment through vision.
By means of these ten kinds of topics, the entirety of the Mahāyāna is subsumed.
Among these, the ripening of sentient beings should be understood as occurring for one established in the stages (bhūmi) up to the seventh stage.
The purification of the buddha-field and non-abiding nirvāṇa occur on the three types of irreversible stages.
Supreme enlightenment is on the Buddha-stage;
it should be understood that therein the manifestation of perfect awakening and great final nirvana occurs.
The rest has its meaning already explained.
In the "Analysis of the Bodhisattva," there are ten verses:
one is characterized by resolute belief (*adhimokṣika*), and another is characterized by pure high resolve (*śuddhādhyāśayika*).
Whether in the sign, in the signless, or in the unconditioned,
these five types of bodhisattvas are to be understood as being present on all the stages.
In that regard, one who courses with signs does so from the second stage up to the sixth;
one who courses without signs does so on the seventh;
and one who courses without volitional effort does so beyond that.
The rest has been explained.

One who is unattached to sensual pleasures, whose threefold action is pure, who has overcome anger, who is devoted to virtuous qualities, who is immovable in the Dharma, whose vision of reality is profound, and who truly yearns for enlightenment—such a one is indeed a bodhisattva. (Msa 19.64)
By this, the characteristic of a bodhisattva has been elucidated through the practice of the six perfections and the aspiration for great enlightenment:
"Desiring to benefit others, having a view free from malice, and enduring injuries inflicted by others;
steadfast, vigilant, and learned, a bodhisattva is indeed devoted to the welfare of others. (Msa 19.65)
In that regard, he is steadfast because he has initiated vigor and does not despond due to sufferings;
he is heedful because he is unattached to the pleasures of meditative concentration.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.

A Bodhisattva is indeed one who perceives the danger in his own possessions, is unattached to enjoyments, has no concealed enmity, is skilled in signs, is free from wrong views, and is established within the inner self.
In that regard, one who is unattached to enjoyments renounces them and goes forth;
one who is skilled in signs through proficiency in the three signs such as calm abiding (*śamatha*);
and one who is inwardly established because of being unshakable from the Mahāyāna.
For the Mahāyāna is the inner domain of the bodhisattvas;
the rest has already been explained.
Endowed with compassion, established in the quality of moral shame, he endures suffering and is unattached to his own pleasures.
Preeminent in mindfulness, with a perfectly concentrated mind, the bodhisattva is indeed unshakable in his vehicle.
In that regard, one who is preeminent in mindfulness possesses meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because through the power of mindfulness the mind is concentrated.
One whose self is well-concentrated possesses non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The rest has been explained.

The Bodhisattva indeed endures suffering; he is the remover of suffering and not its creator, he is the one who dwells with suffering and is not afraid of it, he is liberated from suffering and does not conceptualize it as suffering. Msa 19.68.

In this context, "liberated from suffering" refers to one who possesses meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) due to detachment from the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), by way of liberation from the state of suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). "Assuming suffering" refers to the acceptance of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). The remainder has its meaning already explained.

Delighting in the Dharma and not delighting in what is contrary to the Dharma, naturally loathing what is contrary to the Dharma, and being devoted to the Dharma; having mastery over the Dharma, being free from darkness regarding the Dharma, and making the Dharma his primary concern—such indeed is a Bodhisattva. (MSA 19.69)
In this regard, one is "repelled by the Dharma" because of a repulsion toward non-forbearance;
one is "master of the Dharma" through meditative attainment.
One who is preeminent in the Dharma and for whom great enlightenment is the ultimate goal;
here, "dharma" is stated as "dharama" by way of following the meter.
The rest has its meaning already explained.

A Bodhisattva is indeed vigilant regarding enjoyments, vigilant regarding observances, vigilant regarding protection, vigilant regarding the wholesome, vigilant regarding happiness, vigilant regarding the Dharma, and vigilant regarding the vehicle. (Msa 19.70)
In this regard, he is heedful in guarding [the mind] because he protects the minds of both himself and others through patience;
he is heedful regarding the Dharma because he possesses the wisdom that discerns phenomena as they truly are.
The rest has already been explained.

The Bodhisattva is indeed one who feels shame regarding contempt, shame regarding slight faults, shame regarding impatience, shame regarding retrogression, shame regarding lack of extensive application, shame regarding inferior views, and shame regarding other vehicles.
In this context, "shame regarding contempt" refers to not treating those who come seeking help with contempt;

"shame regarding slight faults" refers to seeing danger even in the most minute transgressions; and "shame regarding slight views" refers to the penetration of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). The remainder is self-evident.
By all these verses, the characteristic of a bodhisattva has been elucidated through another sequence: by means of the practice of the six perfections and the aspiration for great enlightenment.

In this world and in the next, the bodhisattva abides in benefiting others through equanimity, the application of formative forces, the attainment of masteries, the teaching of tranquility, and the great fruit.
In this very life, he acts for the benefit of sentient beings through generosity;
in the next life, having attained a distinguished rebirth through ethical discipline;
and by means of the application of formative forces—that is, by means of the application of vigor.
"By means of the great fruit" refers to Buddhahood;
the rest has its meaning already explained.
By this, it is demonstrated how a bodhisattva proceeds in the service of benefiting sentient beings through the six perfections and the aspiration for great enlightenment.
In the analysis of the general names of Bodhisattvas, there are eight verses:
Bodhisattva, Mahāsattva, the Wise One (dhīmān), and the one of supreme splendor;
Son of the Victor (jinaputra), Support of the Victor (jinādhāra), the Conqueror (vijetā), and the Sprout of the Victor (jināṅkura).
He is valiant, most wonderful, a caravan leader of great renown;
he is compassionate, of great merit, a lord, and likewise righteous.

These sixteen are the general, etymological names of all Bodhisattvas: because of their awakening to reality (*sutattvabodha*), their awakening to the great purpose (*sumahārthabodha*), their awakening to all objects (*sarvārthabodha*), their constant awakening (*nityabodha*), and their awakening through skillful means (*upāyabodha*); for that reason, by way of such distinctions, one is called a Bodhisattva.
One is called a "bodhisattva" by virtue of fivefold distinctions of awakening:
through the awakening to the selflessness of persons and phenomena;
through the awakening to all aspects and all objects; and through inexhaustible realization even while manifesting parinirvāṇa.
Just as [it arises] through the awakening to the means of discipline for those to be trained,
through the awakening to the self, through the awakening to the subtle view, and through the awakening to manifold representations.
And because of his awakening to the fact that everything is an unreal conceptual construction, for that reason he is called a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, here he demonstrates a fourfold distinction in awakening: through the awakening regarding mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and through the realization that these are unreal imaginings (*abhūtaparikalpa*). In this context, "mind" refers to the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The mind (*manas*) has that as its object and is associated with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and so forth;
consciousness (*vijñāna*) consists of the six groups of consciousness.

[It is so called] because of awakening through non-awakening, awakening through subsequent awakening, awakening through the awakening to non-existence, and awakening through the subsequent awakening to origination.
And because of the awakening to non-awakening and the subsequent realization, for that reason he is called a *bodhisattva*.
Here, moreover, he demonstrates five kinds of distinctions in awakening:
through the awakening to ignorance and through the awakening to knowledge.
And because of the awakening to the three natures, beginning with the imagined (parikalpita):
therein, through the awakening to awakening by means of non-awakening, the awakening to the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is to be understood;
[this is so] because of the awakening to the non-existent, the awakening to the ultimate reality (paramārtha), the awakening to all objects, and the awakening to every object.
Because he awakens to that which is to be awakened to, the basis of awakening, and awakening itself, for that reason he is called a bodhisattva.
Here, he demonstrates fivefold distinction in awakening:
through the awakening to the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), and through the awakening to the perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Because of the awakening to the imagined characteristic;

because of the awakening to all objects of knowledge in all their aspects; and because of the awakening to the complete purification of the threefold mandala of the object of awakening, the subject of awakening, and the act of awakening.
Because of the awakening to perfection, the awakening to the stages, the awakening to the womb, and the awakening to the gradual manifestation [of the Buddha],
and because of the thorough abandonment of doubt through awakening— for these reasons, he is called a *bodhisattva*.
In this context, "awakening to perfection" is Buddhahood;
"awakening to the place" is that by which one dwells in the Tuṣita heaven;
and "awakening to the womb" is that by which one enters the mother's womb.

The realization of the manifestation of the sequence is that by which he displays the departure from the womb, the enjoyment of desires, the renunciation, the practice of austerities, and the perfect awakening.
The realization of the thorough destruction of doubt is that by which he turns the wheel of Dharma for sentient beings in order to sever all their doubts.
He is the one who has attained and the one who has not attained, the one established in wisdom, the awakener, the follower, and the teacher.
The wise one possesses a non-discursive intellect, has destroyed pride yet remains humble, and possesses both immature and mature understanding.
Here, the bodhisattva is elucidated by means of elevenfold awakening regarding the past and so forth.
Among these, he is respectively one who has attained, one who has not attained, and one whose intellect is established through awakenings of the past, future, and present;
and he is an awakener because of his own self-awakening.
"One who understands through another" indicates internal and external awakening by means of that [understanding].
"One who instructs" refers to the coarse and subtle [levels of] cognition.
"Proud" and "one whose pride is destroyed" refer to the inferior and the sublime [states].
"Unripened intellect" and "fully ripened intellect" demonstrate the distinction between distant and proximate awakening.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, on Qualities, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The twentieth and twenty-first chapters:
Regarding the analysis of the marks (*liṅga*), there are two verses.
Compassion, pleasant speech, steadfastness, open-handed generosity,
and the unraveling of profound intentional meanings— these are the marks of the wise.

The fivefold mark should be understood as consisting of: embracing [the Mahāyāna], attaining resolute conviction, being free from weariness, the twofold gathering [of disciples], and both intention and application. (MSA 20.2)

Therein, by the first verse he shows the five marks of a bodhisattva; by the second, their activity and their summary collection. Among these, compassion is for the sake of embracing sentient beings through the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); pleasant speech is for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain faith in the Buddha's teaching.

Fortitude is for the sake of being untiring through difficult practices and the like; open-handedness and the unraveling of profound intentional meanings are for the sake of gathering [beings] by means of two things—namely, material gifts and the Dharma—respectively.
Among these five marks, compassion should be understood as being rooted in one's underlying intention (*āśaya*).
The remaining [points] are understood through their application.
Regarding the distinction between the factions of householders and those who have gone forth, there are three verses:
"For Bodhisattvas, being constantly [reborn as] universal monarchs..."
For householders indeed perform the welfare of sentient beings throughout all their births.
The renunciation obtained through formal acceptance is supreme as it conforms to the true nature of phenomena;
and for the wise, there is also the illustrative renunciation throughout all the stages.
The side of the renunciant, however, is endowed with immeasurable qualities;
therefore, the ascetic is indeed superior to the householder bodhisattva.

By the first verse, it is illuminated how a bodhisattva, abiding in the state of a householder, acts for the benefit of sentient beings; by the second, how he does so in the state of one who has gone forth.
In that regard, three kinds of going forth are to be understood.
It is obtained through formal undertaking,
obtained through the nature of phenomena,
and it is demonstrative by means of emanations.

By the third [verse], the distinction of the side of those who have gone forth from the side of householders is elucidated. Regarding the analysis of the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), there is a verse of six lines: "The desire for a desirable fruit in the next world, and for virtuous conduct in this very life..."
And the desire for nirvāṇa in the wise is held to be the intention toward sentient beings;
it is considered impure, pure, and utterly pure throughout all the stages.

By this, five kinds of resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) have been briefly elucidated: the resolute intention for happiness; [the resolute intention for benefit, the resolute intention for non-abandonment, the resolute intention for the absence of pride, and the resolute intention for the absence of weariness].

The resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the desired fruit in the next world is [the intention] for benefit; the resolute intention for the engagement in the wholesome in this very life and the resolute intention for *nirvāṇa* are simply those two [types of] resolute intention, and no other should be understood [to exist].
The three types of resolute intention beginning with the impure belong to those who have not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*), while [the pure ones belong] to those who have entered the stages.
And they should be understood as pertaining respectively to those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-bhūmi*).
Regarding the analysis of "appropriation" (*parigraha*), there is this verse:
Appropriation [occurs] through aspiration, through equanimity of mind, and through sovereignty.
And because it attracts the wise throughout all the stages, [it is called the "Gathering"]. // Msa_20.7 //

The fourfold appropriation of sentient beings by bodhisattvas should be understood as follows: first, appropriation through aspiration, because by means of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), they appropriate all sentient beings; second, appropriation through equanimity, because at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they attain the equality of self and others;
and third, appropriation through sovereignty, which belongs to those over whom he has become the master.
And there is the drawing in and gathering of a retinue through the acquisition of a circle of disciples.
Regarding the classification of rebirth, there is this verse:
"By the sovereignty of karma, and another by that of the vow."
The arising of both meditative concentration and mastery is held by the wise to belong to those possessed of intelligence.

The rebirth of Bodhisattvas is fourfold: that which occurs by the sovereign power of karma, which is the taking of birth in a desired place by those established on the stage of practice through resolute belief (adhimukticaryābhūmi) through the force of their karma; and that which occurs by the power of their vow (praṇidhāna), which is the taking of birth in inferior states such as among animals for the sake of maturing all sentient beings by those who have entered the [bodhisattva] stages.

By the sovereign power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) after having turned back from the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). By the sovereign power of mastery (*vibhutva*), there is the manifestation of rebirths such as in the Tuṣita heaven through emanations (*nirmāṇa*).
Regarding the classification of the stages of dwelling (*vihāra-bhūmi*), there are thirty verses of inspired utterance (*udāna*).

The dwelling and the stage itself are defined by their characteristics, by the person, by the training, by the perfection of the aggregates, by their signs, by etymology, and by attainment. (MSA 20.9)
There are five verses beginning with the analysis of the characteristics:
"Emptiness, the supreme self, and the establishment [of the fruit] upon the destruction of karma."
Having dwelt in the blissful meditative absorptions (dhyāna), thereafter he takes birth in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
And then there is the dedication of the factors conducive to enlightenment toward cyclic existence,
and the ripening of sentient beings without mental affliction.
Furthermore, there is the intentional protection of affliction at the time of rebirth;
and the path that is exclusively signless, which adheres to the single way.
Even in the signless state, there is effortlessness, as well as the purification of the field;
thereafter, the perfection of the ripening of sentient beings arises.
The purity of the concentrations, the dhāraṇīs, and of awakening itself—
from this systematic arrangement, the characteristics of the stages (bhūmis) are to be understood.
There are eleven dwellings, which are the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).
Their characteristics are as follows:
in the first stage, the characteristic is the realization of supreme emptiness, due to the realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
In the second [ground], there is the establishment of the non-perishing of karmas, due to the knowledge of the variety of wholesome and unwholesome paths of action and their fruits.
In the third, having dwelt in the bodhisattva meditations accompanied by superior bliss, one is reborn in the desire realm without falling away from them.
In the fourth, even while dwelling extensively in the factors conducive to awakening, there is the dedication of those factors toward cyclic existence.

On the fifth [ground], by dwelling extensively in the four noble truths, one brings sentient beings to maturity through the composition of various treatises and arts, without any affliction of one's own mind. On the sixth, by dwelling extensively in dependent origination, one protects against affliction while intentionally taking birth in existence.
On the seventh, through its state of being mixed and intermingled with the eighth ground—the path of the single way—there is a path that is exclusively signless and closely connected to that stage.
On the eighth [ground], there is effortless spontaneity even within the signless state, because of dwelling in the signless without volitional effort, as well as the purification of the Buddha-field.
On the ninth, through mastery over the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there is the perfection of maturing sentient beings, due to the capacity to mature them in every possible way.
On the tenth, there is the complete purity of the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*).
On the eleventh stage, the Buddha-stage, the characteristic is the purity of awakening due to the abandonment of all cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the classification of persons established on these stages, there are two verses:
"One whose vision is pure, whose ethical discipline is perfectly pure, who is concentrated, and whose pride has been eliminated regarding phenomena..."
Regarding the distinctions of the continuity, affliction, and purification [of beings], he has attained awakening in a single moment through his power of emanation.
Equanimous, a purifier of the field, skilled in the ripening of sentient beings, and possessed of great supernormal powers;
with his body perfected and capable of manifesting it, such a Bodhisattva is indeed consecrated.
On the ten stages, ten types of bodhisattvas are established:
on the first stage, one is of pure vision, because of having attained the knowledge that serves as the antidote to the views of persons and phenomena;
on the second stage, one is of perfectly pure ethical discipline, because there is an absence even of the occurrence of subtle transgressions or lapses.
On the third stage, one becomes concentrated due to the attainment of the meditative absorption of non-falling-away (*acyuta-dhyāna-samādhi*).
On the fourth stage, one is free from pride regarding phenomena (*dharma-vibhūta-māna*), because pride concerning the diversity of phenomena such as the *sūtras* has been eliminated.

On the fifth stage, one is free from pride regarding the differentiation of mental continua (*saṃtāna-bheda-nirmāṇa*), because through the ten equalities of the purity of the mental disposition (*cittāśaya-viśuddhi-samatā*), one enters into the equality of all mental continua.

On the sixth [ground], there is mastery over the distinction between affliction and purification, because by dwelling frequently in dependent origination and suchness, one does not perceive the affliction or purification of suchness through the black and white sides,

based on its intrinsic purity. On the seventh [ground], one attains the awakening of a single moment of mind, because through the power of dwelling in the signless, one cultivates the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening at every moment.

On the eighth [stage], he is equanimous and a purifier of the field, because he dwells in the effortless and signless state and because his application is mixed and thoroughly integrated with those bodhisattvas who have entered the irreversible stage.
On the ninth, as before, he is skilled in maturing sentient beings.
On the tenth bodhisattva stage, the bodhisattva is established as one of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) due to the attainment of the great superknowledges (*mahābhijñā*).

He is established as one who possesses the complete *dharmakāya* and is capable of manifesting his physical basis through the radiation of immeasurable gateways of *samādhi* and *dhāraṇī*, because he manifests emanations such as dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven;
and he is consecrated in Buddhahood by all the Buddhas, because he receives consecration therein.
There are five verses concerning the establishment of the training (*śikṣā*).
Having realized the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) here, one trains further in higher ethics, in higher mind, and also in higher wisdom; for wisdom has two spheres of activity.
The reality of phenomena, as well as the mental activity consisting of ignorance and knowledge thereof, is the objective domain of wisdom; therefore, its establishment occurs on two levels.
Furthermore, there is another fourfold fruit of the trainings and of cultivation:
the first fruit is the dwelling in the signless with effort.
That very absence of volitional effort is intended as the second fruit;
as well as the purification of the field and the ripening and perfection of sentient beings.
And the accomplishment of the concentrations and the dhāraṇīs is the supreme fruit;
for these four kinds of fruits are based upon the four stages.
Having realized the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) on the first stage, one trains in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) on the second;
in higher mental cultivation (*adhicitta*) on the third;
and in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) on the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages.
For wisdom subsumed under the factors conducive to enlightenment exists on the fourth stage;
furthermore, that [wisdom] has a twofold objective range on two stages.
This "twofold" refers to the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) and the truths of suffering and so forth.
And the process consisting of the ignorance of that and the knowledge of that, and so forth, is dependent origination in its forward order (*anuloma*);
for the process beginning with the ignorance of that consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors.
And the activity consisting of that knowledge and so forth is [the stage of] vidyā and so forth.
Therefore, the establishment of the training in higher wisdom (adhiprajñā) occurs in both stages.
Beyond this, it should be understood that the fourfold fruit of training (śikṣāphala) rests upon the four stages respectively.
In that regard, the first fruit is the signless dwelling accompanied by effort;
the second fruit should be understood as that same signless dwelling being effortless, as well as the purification of the field.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
Regarding the establishment of the aggregates, there are two verses:
Having realized the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) here, there is the purification of the aggregate of ethical discipline;
thereafter follows the purification of the aggregates of concentration and wisdom. (MSA 20.22)
In the other [stages], there is the purification of the knowledge of liberation and the liberation itself from fourfold obstructions as well as from the obstruction of resistance.
"In the others" refers to the purification of both liberation and the knowledge of liberation from the seventh stage up to the Buddha stage.
Furthermore, that liberation should be understood as being [free] from the fourfold obscuration to the fruits.
And because of the obstruction of resistance on the Buddha-ground—
that by which the knowledge of others is obstructed regarding the knowable—
Buddhas, however, possess unobstructed knowledge everywhere due to their liberation from that.
The remainder has its meaning already explained.
With reference to the establishment of accomplishment, there are three verses:
"All the stages (bhūmis) should be understood as both unaccomplished and accomplished."
Though already accomplished, they are considered unaccomplished; yet again, they are considered accomplished.
Accomplishment is to be understood through mental attention according to the established order,
through the knowledge that it is a mere conceptualization, and through the non-conceptualization of that very [conceptualization].
Cultivation and its fulfillment are inconceivable across all stages,
because they are to be personally realized within oneself and because they transcend even the domain of the Buddhas.
Among these, the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) is unperfected;
the remaining stages are perfected. Thus are all these stages. Furthermore, even among those that are perfected, seven are unperfected.
The remaining [stages] are accomplished because they proceed without volitional effort (*nirabhisaṃskāra*).

Furthermore, regarding what was previously stated— that the stage of *pramuditā* and so forth is accomplished— therein, accomplishment is to be understood through the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the stages as they have been established,
by means of the knowledge that such an establishment of the stages is merely conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), and by way of non-conceptualization (*avikalpanā*) thereof.
When one knows that the establishment of those stages is mere conceptual construction,

and does not even conceptualize that "mere conceptual construction," then, through the attainment of non-conceptual knowledge regarding the grasped and the grasper, the perfection of the stages is said to have been achieved.
Furthermore, both the cultivation and the perfection of the stages across all levels are indeed inconceivable.
For it is thus: that [state] is to be personally realized by Bodhisattvas and is the domain of the Buddhas, not of others.
Regarding the analysis of the signs of one established on the stages (*bhūmi*), there are two verses:
"Adherence (*adhimukti*) accompanied by light is held to be the sign in all cases."
Absence of dejection, absence of despondency, and the state of not being dependent on others.
Pervasive penetration, equanimity toward all beings everywhere,
knowledge of means that is free from being led astray or partiality, and birth within the [Buddha] mandala.
The tenfold mark of a bodhisattva who has entered these stages should be understood to apply across all stages.
That there is illumination regarding the stage which has been entered and resolute conviction regarding that which has not yet been entered—this is one mark.
There is also the absence of dejection with respect to dharmas that are supremely vast and profound.
It consists of being undaunted in the practice of difficult austerities,
being independent of others regarding one's own stage,
the penetration of all stages through skill in their accomplishment, and the state of mind that regards all sentient beings as equal to oneself.
It is "inflexible" by virtue of the words "praise" and "blame.
It is "without attachment" toward prosperities such as being a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
It possesses "skill in means" because it is the knowledge of the means for attaining Buddhahood through that non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) [of those prosperities].
And being born at all times within the maṇḍalas of the Buddha’s assemblies— these are further marks of a bodhisattva.
There are two verses concerning the distinction of the marks of attaining the perfections on the stages (*bhūmi*).
He is not lacking in aspiration, nor is he greedy or small-hearted; he is not wrathful, nor is he indolent;
his disposition is not devoid of loving-kindness and compassion, nor is he of evil intellect, destroyed by conceptualization and discursive thought;
his mind is not distracted, nor is he overcome by pleasures, nor does he turn away from suffering.
He relies on a true friend, is devoted to sacred learning, and is intent on honoring the Teacher.

Having performed a vast accumulation of all merit and dedicated it toward perfect enlightenment as something not shared with others, he who knows the supreme means is always born in a favorable realm, performs only virtuous deeds, and sports with the qualities of the superknowledges.
Standing above all, that son of the Buddha is to be known as a treasury of virtues.
It demonstrates the sixteenfold mark of a bodhisattva who has attained the ten perfections.
The sixteenfold mark consists of:
being never devoid of the desire to practice the perfections; [and so forth].
Each [perfection] is characterized by being free from its respective opposite;
by being undistracted through mental attention toward other vehicles;
and by being unattached to the pleasures of prosperity.
Not turning back from practice despite the sufferings of misfortune and difficult conduct;
relying on spiritual friends;
and being devoted to learning.
Devotion to the worship of the Teacher;
right dedication through the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya-pāramitā*);
and rebirth in a favorable realm through the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), because of being born in a place not devoid of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Through the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*), you always perform wholesome deeds because of the non-intermixture of those factors that are its opposites;
and through the perfection of knowledge (*jñānapāramitā*), there is the playful mastery of the qualities of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
In this context, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote to ill-will (*vyāpāda*), characterized by the intention to bestow happiness.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the antidote to harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), characterized by the intention for the removal of suffering.
Conceptualization (*kalpa*) should be understood as the construction of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); discursive thought (*vikalpa*) is the construction of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).
Regarding the analysis of the benefits therein, there is this verse:
"The benefit for the wise on all stages and in every respect is considered to consist of two groups of five, pertaining to calm abiding and insight. (MSA 20.31)
In that very attainment of the perfections on all the stages, the fivefold benefit for Bodhisattvas of every kind should be understood as follows:
at every moment, they dissolve the basis of all functional rigidity (*dausthulya*);
and, through their delight in the garden of the Dharma, they attain the departure from the perception of diversity (*nānātva-saṃjñā*).
He perceives the manifestation of the Dharma as unlimited in form and immeasurable in every respect;
and non-conceptual signs conducive to purification manifest before him;
and for the sake of fulfilling and perfecting the Dharmakāya, he undertakes the gathering of causes that become ever more superior.
In this regard, the first and second [stages] should be understood as belonging to the side of calm abiding (śamatha);
the third and fourth belong to the side of insight (vipaśyanā);
and the remainder belongs to both sides.
There are nine verses in the analysis of the etymology of the stages (*bhūmi*). [The first verse:
For those who see that enlightenment is near and that the welfare of sentient beings is being accomplished...
Intense joy arises; therefore, it is called "joyousness" (muditā).
Nothing further needs to be explained here.
This stage is called "The Stainless" (vimalā) because it is free from the impurity of the exertion toward misconduct;
it is called "The Stainless" because it transcends both the impurity of misconduct and the impurity of mental attention directed toward other vehicles.

Therefore, since it is said, "In that case, when the realization is equal for all, we must apply ourselves precisely to the realization of purification in every aspect," and because it produces the great illumination of the Dharma, this stage is called Prabhākarī (The Illuminating).
For in that stage, by the power of meditative concentration, because of the seeking and retaining of immeasurable teachings, one produces a great illumination of the Dharma for others.
Since the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) are like flames that burn away [defilements],
this stage is called "The Radiant" (Arciṣmatī) due to its connection with them, because of the burning away of duality.
For that wisdom, which consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment, is predominantly present as the burner of duality;
moreover, "duality" here should be understood as the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration of the knowable.
It also effects the maturation of sentient beings and the protection of one's own mind.
The wise conquer suffering; therefore, it is called "difficult to conquer."
Therein, although he is devoted to the ripening of sentient beings, he is not afflicted by their misconduct; and because both of these are difficult to accomplish, they are "hard to conquer.
Because of the presence here of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, [the stage] is called Abhimukhī.
For the stage called "Facing" has been described as being based upon the perfection of wisdom.
For, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, because it does not abide in either nirvāṇa or saṃsāra, it is oriented toward both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Because it adheres to the path of the single vehicle (*ekāyanapatha*), this stage is considered "Far-Gone" (*dūraṅgamā*).
The path of the single vehicle was previously explained; because [this stage] adheres to that, it has gone far, having reached the culmination of its application (*prayoga*).
And it is called "Immovable" (acalā) because of the non-fluctuation of the two types of perception.
Because of remaining unshakable by two types of perceptions—
namely, the perception of signs (*nimitta-saṃjñā*) and the perception of the effort toward the signless (*animittābhoga-saṃjñā*)—
and because of the excellence of the intellect that possesses analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), this stage is considered "Excellent Intelligence" (*Sādhumatī*).
Because the wisdom of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is excellent, it is predominant;
the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*) is so called because it pervades the two, like a cloud covering the sky of the Dharma.

"Because of the pervasion of the two" means that, like a cloud pervading the expanse of the sky, it pervades the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*); thus, the Dharma heard and established within its basis is called the "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmamegha*).
Because one always dwells with delight in the various accomplishments of virtue.
In all respects, these are considered the stages of the dwellings of the bodhisattvas.

Because they always dwell with delight everywhere for the sake of accomplishing various forms of virtue, the stages (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattvas are called "dwellings" (*vihāra*). Furthermore, because they proceed ever higher through these immeasurable [stages], and because they serve the purpose of bringing about the immeasurable welfare of beings, they are indeed desired as "stages. (MSA 20.40)

Because they involve ascending higher and higher through immeasurable aeons for the sake of the welfare of beings who are immeasurable and free from fear, these very dwellings (vihāras) are further called "stages" (bhūmis).
The phrase "through immeasurable [aeons]" refers to the fact that each of the ten stages is itself immeasurable.
The phrase "because of the connection with ascending higher" means because of the connection with proceeding to the higher stages.
"For the sake of the immeasurable beings' freedom from fear" means for the sake of eliminating the fear of immeasurable beings.
There is a verse regarding the distinction of the attainment and dwelling [in the stages]:
"Because of the acquisition of the stages, because of resolute belief, and because of proceeding through the practices."
And it is fourfold through the penetration of the stages and their accomplishment.
The attainment of the stages is fourfold:
attainment through resolute conviction, which occurs on the stage of practice through conviction (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*) by virtue of the aforementioned resolute conviction;
and attainment through conduct, which occurs on that very same stage by engaging in the ten religious practices (*dharmacarita*).
The attainment of the penetration of ultimate reality occurs through the penetration of ultimate reality upon entering the stages (*bhūmi*).
The attainment of perfection occurs upon entering the stage of non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-bhūmi*).
Regarding the classification of conduct (*caryā*), there is a six-line verse.
For the sake of attracting those embodied beings who are devoted to the Mahāyāna and those who are in the Hīnayāna,
and for the sake of disciplining both,
the four practices of the wise have been taught according to the Sūtras. (Msa 20.42)
Therein, the practice of the perfections (pāramitā-caryā) was taught for the sake of those who have faith in the Mahāyāna;
the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-caryā) for those who have faith in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
and the practice of the superknowledges (abhijñā-caryā) for both those with faith in the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna, in order to attract them through spiritual power.
The practice of maturing sentient beings is for the sake of maturing these two [the bodhisattva and the sentient being] themselves; for here, "maturing" means disciplining.
There are many verses in the section on the classification of the Buddha's qualities.

In the analysis of the immeasurables, there is one verse beginning with that hymn of praise to the Buddha: O you who have compassion for sentient beings, whose intention is their union [with happiness] and separation [from suffering], whose intention is their non-separation [from happiness], and whose intention is their welfare and bliss—homage be to you! (MSA 20.43)
In this context, compassion toward sentient beings is demonstrated by the intention for their welfare and happiness;
furthermore, the intention for happiness is shown through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is the intention for their union with happiness.
And through compassion, there is the intention for them to be separated from suffering; through sympathetic joy, the intention for them not to be separated from happiness;
and through equanimity, the intention for their welfare.
Furthermore, that state of being free from affliction should be understood as having the characteristic of intentionality.

There are verses on the classification of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*): O Sage, liberated from all obscurations, you have overcome all worlds!
The knowable is pervaded by your knowledge; O you whose mind is liberated, homage be to you!
Here, he demonstrates the excellence of the Blessed One’s liberations (*vimokṣa*) by way of being liberated from all afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*).

He demonstrates the excellence of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) by way of his sovereignty over all worlds through the power of his own mind, such as the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of manifesting and transforming objects at will.
He demonstrates the excellence of the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) by way of the non-obstruction of knowledge regarding all that is knowable.

For this very reason, because he is liberated from the factors adverse to qualities such as the liberations, his mind is liberated (*muktacitta*). Regarding the analysis of *araṇā* (freedom from affliction), there is this verse: "O destroyer of all the afflictions of all sentient beings without exception!"
O destroyer of afflictions, who yet possesses compassion for those afflicted—homage be to you!

Here, the Blessed One demonstrates a specific excellence of *araṇā* (non-affliction) through his subduing of the afflictions of all sentient beings and by applying their antidotes even when afflictions have already arisen; he does so out of compassion for afflicted persons.

For other practitioners who dwell in *araṇā* merely remove the conditions for the arising of some affliction in sentient beings that takes them as its object; they do not, however, extract it from the continuum of the afflictions themselves.

There is a verse concerning the distinction of the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*): Homage be to you, who are effortless, unattached, unimpeded, and always in meditative equipoise; you who provide answers to all questions! (MSA 20.46)
Here, he demonstrates the excellence of the Blessed One’s knowledge resulting from his vow through five aspects:
by way of its manifestation without effort,
and by way of its manifestation without attachment.
Because there is no obstruction regarding all that is to be known,
because of being always in a state of meditative equipoise,
and because of cutting through all the doubts of sentient beings.
For others who have attained the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) manifest that knowledge by forming an aspiration through various efforts;
yet it is not unattached because it depends upon entering meditative absorption (samāpatti),
nor is it unimpeded because it is a knowledge restricted to a limited scope.
They are not always in meditative equipoise, nor do they sever all doubts.
There is a verse regarding the analysis of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*):
"In the basis and that which is based upon it, in the subject to be taught, in the speech, and in the knowledge that teaches."
O Excellent Guide, whose intellect is ever unimpeded, homage be to you!

In this regard, in brief, that which is taught and that by which it is taught—therein, because the Blessed One possesses an intellect that is eternally unimpeded, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are taught.
Among these, two things are taught: the basis and the Dharma.
And the meaning based upon that is taught by means of two: through speech and through knowledge.
By virtue of being a "good teacher," their function is thus demonstrated.

Regarding the classification of the superknowledges (abhijñā), there is this verse: "Having approached them, you know their speech, their conduct, their coming, and their going; you provide instruction to sentient beings regarding the departure from saṃsāra—homage be to you! (MSA 20.48)

Here, the Blessed One’s state of providing correct instruction is demonstrated by means of the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*): by approaching the presence of those to be trained through the supernormal knowledge of psychic power (*ṛddhyabhijñā*);

by knowing their speech through the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotrābhijñā*); and by knowing the course of their mental activity through the supernormal knowledge of the penetration of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*), as well as how they have come from the past, how they will go to the future, and how they emerge from saṃsāra.
Therein,
he gives instruction by means of the remaining three superknowledges (abhijñā) respectively.
Regarding the distinction between the primary marks (lakṣaṇa) and the secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana), there is this verse:
Upon seeing you, all embodied beings attain the state of true manliness;
O bestower of grace through the mere sight [of you], homage be to you!

Here, the function of the primary marks and secondary characteristics is shown to be the generation of serene faith in others through the mere sight [of them], by means of the conviction that the Blessed One is a Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Regarding the analysis of purity, there is this verse:
"In taking up, staying, and abandoning; in emanation and transformation..."
Homage be to you, who have attained mastery over meditative concentration and primordial wisdom!
Here, by means of the fourfold mastery of the Blessed One, the four purifications in all their aspects are fully elucidated:
the purification of the basis through mastery over the taking up, remaining in, and relinquishing of the personal existence;
and the purification of the objective field through mastery over emanation and transformation.
Purity of mind through mastery over meditative concentrations in all their forms;
purity of wisdom through mastery over primordial cognitions in all their forms.
There is a verse concerning the classification of the powers:
Homage to you, O Destroyer of Māra, who deceives sentient beings regarding the means, the refuge, purity, and the departure via the Mahāyāna.
In this context, the activity of the Blessed One’s ten powers is demonstrated as that which shatters Māra, who deceives sentient beings regarding four matters:
namely, by deceiving them concerning the means for proceeding to happy or miserable destinies;
and by deceiving them regarding refuge in gods and others when there is no true refuge.
Regarding the denial of purity through mere [mundane] purification involving outflows,
and the denial of the departure via the Mahāyāna:
by means of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthānajñānabala*), the Blessed One should be understood as the destroyer of Māra in the first sense.
By the power of knowledge regarding the ripening of karma, [he knows] in the second;
by the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, in the third;
and by the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties and so forth, in the fourth.
Because he avoids inferior faculties and the like, and because he applies [beings] to what is superior,
there is a verse regarding the analysis of the grounds of self-confidence:
"O Teacher of knowledge, abandonment, the path of departure, and the obstacles."
Homage be to you, who are invincible to the followers of other paths in the pursuit of your own and others' welfare.

In this context, the fourfold fearlessness of the Blessed One is manifested in sequence: for his own benefit, by virtue of being the one who effects knowledge and abandonment; and for the benefit of others, by virtue of being the teacher of the path of deliverance and its obstacles; and because he is invincible to other non-Buddhist teachers.
Regarding the analysis of the foundations of mindfulness as protection, there is this verse:
O you who speak with restraint in assemblies, free from the two-fold affliction, without need for protection, undeluded, and the leader of the assembly—homage be to you! (MSA 20.53)

By this, the Blessed One’s three forms of protection (*arakṣa*) and the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are elucidated, as well as their function: that of drawing forth an assembly.
For, by means of these, he is respectively one who speaks with restraint in assemblies due to being without need for protection;
and he is free from the two defilements because of the absence of attraction and aversion, and because his mindfulness is always present through non-forgetfulness.
Regarding the analysis of the eradication of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there is this verse:
"In movement and in rest, everywhere, there is no action of yours that is not that of an omniscient one;
at all times you are omniscient. Homage be to you, O Knower of Reality! (MSA 20.54)

By this, it is demonstrated that because there is no lack of omniscient activity at all times and in all places— whether in motion or at rest— the Blessed One has completely eradicated the latencies (*vāsanā*) of all afflictions (*kleśa*).

For one who is not omniscient, even if their afflictions have been exhausted, because they have not eradicated the latencies, they occasionally engage in non-omniscient behavior, such as encountering a bewildered elephant or a bewildered chariot, and so forth.
As it is stated in the Māṇḍavya-sūtra:
"And that [state] does not exist for the Blessed One because of his omniscience regarding the true nature of reality.
There is a verse in the *Asaṃmoṣatā-vibhāga* [on the analysis of non-forgetfulness]:
In all activities for the benefit of sentient beings, you do not let the proper time pass;
your deeds are always fruitful and never forgotten—homage be to you!

By this, it is shown that because the Blessed One never fails to act at the precise time when a particular purpose must be accomplished for a particular sentient being, his duty is always fruitful; thus, his nature of non-forgetfulness is demonstrated both by way of its intrinsic nature and its activity. There is a verse in the section on the analysis of great compassion:
Day and night, throughout all the worlds, you examine [them] six times;
endowed with great compassion and intent on the welfare [of others], homage be to you! (MSA 20.56)
Here, the Great Compassion of the Blessed One is elucidated both by way of its function and its essential nature.
For through Great Compassion, the Blessed One surveys the world six times during the day and night, [considering] such things as "who is declining? and "who is prospering?
And through its conjunction with that, the Blessed One always possesses the intention for the welfare of all sentient beings.

Regarding the analysis of the unique qualities (*āveṇikaguṇa*), there is this verse: In conduct, in realization, in knowledge, and in action, O Supreme One above all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, homage be to you! (MSA 20.57)
In this context, there are six unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma) comprised within conduct,
six comprised within realization,
and three comprised within gnosis.
And by means of the three [qualities] comprised within karma,
the Blessed One’s status as the supreme among all sentient beings is illuminated through his superiority even over those other excellent beings, namely the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
In that regard, there is no lapse on the part of the Tathāgata.
There is no outcry;
there is no loss of mindfulness;
there is no unconcentrated mind.
There is no perception of diversity;
there is no equanimity lacking discernment—these are the six unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) comprised within his conduct, which exist only for a Buddha and not for others.
There is no decline in zeal, nor is there any decline in energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, or liberation—these are the six comprised within his realization.
The Tathāgata possesses unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the past;
he possesses unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the future and the present—these three are comprised within knowledge.
All of the Tathāgata’s bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.
"All vocal action" and "all mental action"—these three are subsumed under karma.
There is a verse in the *Sarvākārajñatā-vibhāga*:
"Through the three bodies, he has attained great enlightenment in all its aspects."
Homage be to you, who cuts through the doubts of all sentient beings everywhere.

By means of these three bodies (*kāya*), because the Blessed One has attained awakening in all its aspects and possesses knowledge of all objects of knowledge in all their aspects, his "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is fully elucidated.
The three bodies are the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*), and the emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*).
Furthermore, the "knowledge of all objects of knowledge in all their aspects" is here indicated by the function of cutting through all the doubts of all sentient beings, such as gods and humans.
In the section on the fulfillment of the perfections, there is this verse:
O you who are unrestrained, faultless, stainless, and non-abiding;
O you who are unshakeable regarding all phenomena and free from conceptual proliferation—homage be to you! (Msa 20.59)
By this, the Blessed One’s fulfillment of the six perfections is manifested through his liberation from all that is contrary to the six perfections.
In that regard, "being without grasping" should be understood as being free from attachment to enjoyments.
Faultlessness is due to the stainlessness of the actions of body and so forth. Freedom from turbidity is due to not allowing the mind to become turbid by means of the worldly conditions or suffering.
Non-abiding is due to not remaining fixed upon the attainment of merely slight or minor obscurations.
Immobility is due to the absence of distraction;
freedom from conceptual proliferation is due to the non-occurrence of the proliferation of all discursive thoughts.
There are two verses concerning the distinction of the characteristics of a Buddha.
You have perfected the ultimate truth and emerged from all the stages;
you have attained the preeminence among all beings and are the liberator of all beings.
Endowed with inexhaustible and peerless qualities, you are seen in the worlds;
yet within the maṇḍalas, you are invisible in every way to gods and humans alike.
Here, the characteristic of a Buddha is elucidated by means of six aspects: essence, cause, fruit, activity, endowment, and manifestation.
Among these, purified suchness is the perfected ultimate reality;
and that is the essence of the Buddhas.
The cause is the state of having emerged from all the bodhisattva stages;
the fruit is the attainment of supremacy over all sentient beings;
the activity is the liberation of all sentient beings.
Yoga is the possession of inexhaustible and incomparable qualities.

It consists in being visible in various world-systems by means of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and also being visible within the circles of assemblies by means of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogikakāya*) in every respect.
And its state of being invisible by means of the *dharmakāya*— thus is the threefold classification of its activity.
This concludes the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Foundation of Conduct," from the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, spoken by the Great Bodhisattva Vyavadātasamaya.
And thus the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra is completed.
